Description: IFP Transcript 1 of RE. 19987. Palm-leaf; beginning leaf (25)19a. Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: October 23, 2009.
Country of publication: India Title: Aṃśumatkāśyapāgama (Aṃśumadāgama)
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, has four arms, and possesses a serene countenance. (1)
[He saw] Mahādeva, the bearer of the moon, the sole leader of all the worlds,
the supreme one accompanied by Pārvatī, peaceful, and situated in the midst of Mahendra.
Having prostrated at the feet of the God, who is served by gods, dānavas, siddhas, and others, and who is worshipped by the immortals, Kāśyapa, together with the assemblies [of sages], [did so]. (3)
O Pure One, you are the supreme reality, the tranquil cause of creation, for the sake of the prosperity of the worlds and the benefactor of yogins. || 4 ||

For the benefit of the gods, [he composed] this work arising from the knowledge of Śiva, which possesses great meaning in few words and has its scope defined by the knowledge of plowing and other [agricultural rites]. (5)
Indeed, you have previously taught the ancient *tantra* known as Aṃśumān,
as well as the *tantra* of you [the Lord] and of the deities who are the presiding authorities over the *yantras*.
O Lord, tell me briefly about the characteristics of short-lived people and other such individuals who are qualified [for this practice], ending with the description of their grace.
Excellent, excellent, O great Brahmin!
That which you have requested is difficult to obtain; I shall speak of it—listen with a one-pointed mind.
The six months beginning with the month of Puṣya, excluding the month of Māgha, are auspicious;
likewise, in the southern course [of the sun], the month of Āśvayuja, as well as Śrāvaṇī and Kṛttikā, are auspicious.
(2) When [the rites] beginning with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) have been honored, the remaining months are excluded;
[these are] Pauṣṇa, Āditya, Maghā, Svātī, Sāvitrī, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Maitraka. || 10 ||
Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, the Lord of Creatures (Rohiṇī), Tiṣya (Puṣya), Aśvayuk (Aśvinī), and the three Uttarās—these, when worshipped on the first, sixth, and seventh lunar days, [grant success]. || 11 ||
The third, the fifth, the second, the thirteenth,
and the tenth lunar days are auspicious, especially during the bright fortnight.
O best of the twice-born, the first day of the lunar fortnight, the full moon day, the second, and likewise the fifth, as well as the third, are declared to be middling in the dark fortnight.
The sixth and tenth lunar days of the dark fortnight, as well as the Kaniṣṭhā day, are censured;
whereas the days of Mercury, Moon, and Jupiter are most excellent and auspicious.
The ascensions of their degrees, as well as the horās and drekkāṇas, have been shown;
these should be understood as auspicious, except in the case of the moon's rising. 15.
Except for Cancer, Libra, Capricorn, Aries, and Sagittarius, the rising of the Aries zodiac sign is auspicious, bestowing the abundance of all prosperity. (16)
The Moon situated in its exaltation brings happiness, as does the Moon situated in a friend's sign;
however, the Moon situated in an enemy's sign or even in its fall causes the loss of wealth. (17)
If Mars, the Sun, the Moon, Rāhu, or Saturn are situated in the ascendant, there will be loss of longevity, wealth, and grain, and the destruction of the performer; of this there is no doubt. (18)
Malefic planets situated in the second house cause the destruction of wealth and grain;
likewise, when joined with the Moon, they bring about an increase of wealth and grain.
All [planets] situated in the house of brothers bestow all prosperity and abundance; those situated in the house of kinsmen are malefic and bring about all suffering and fear. (20)
If malefic planets are situated in the fifth house, there will be suffering from death;
if they are all situated in the sixth house, they bring about all kinds of misery and fear. (21)
O Jīvacandra, those stars situated in the position of the wife, as well as Bhārga,
always bestow longevity, wealth, grain, and all perfections.
When all [planets] have reached the *nidhana* [position], one should predict the death of the doer. A benefic planet situated in the ninth house brings all happiness and wealth. (23)

Malefic planets situated in the tenth house (karmasthāna) cause the destruction of all wealth and longevity; whereas benefic planets situated in the tenth house bestow all wealth and longevity. || 24 ||
Both inauspicious and auspicious [planets], when situated in the house of strength, are auspicious;
Mercury or Jupiter situated in the twelfth house brings about an increase in wealth. (25)

At the end of a lunar mansion, at the end of a month, at the end of a fortnight, when the asterism is pierced [by a planet], during the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Parigha yoga, the Śūla yoga, and indeed during the Kālakaṇṭhaka yoga; || 26 ||
Likewise, when there is a thorn [in the body], during an eclipse, on a cloudy day, at the fall of a meteor, when Venus is retrograde, and during the "poison" nāḍīs, [the time is unsuitable]. (27)
At the commencement of the six-aśīti period, and likewise during the month of Śūnya,
one should avoid all activities from plowing the land up to the consecration ceremony.
The lifespan of mortals is diminished like the moon during the dark fortnight;
therefore, one should diligently and swiftly gather merit through dharma. || 29 ||
One should collect days that have few defects and an abundance of virtues, as well as those characterized by growth;
however, one must avoid days, ascendants, and [other factors] that are filled with many millions of defects. (30)
O best of the twice-born, by means of the vision of the individual soul (jīva-dṛṣṭi), one goes to that which is most free from defects;
for the destruction of many millions of defects occurs through the single soul alone.
Just as everything perishes by the light of a single lamp when enveloped in darkness at night, even so, all the arising of defects is destroyed by the vision of the living soul (jīva-dṛṣṭi). || 32 ||
Having examined it thus in many ways, one should perform the plowing and other rites;
one should build the dwelling on this very spot, so plow that location.
A temple of Śiva should be constructed in the eight directions within villages and other settlements;
however, one should build the temple facing away [from the village] on a site belonging to the Piśācas.
The moats, beginning with three *daṇḍas* and extending up to thirty, should likewise be constructed; in that very direction desired, the temple of Śiva should be built.
Either within the moat, or on a site belonging to the Piśācas,
or even on a human site, a temple of Śiva should be constructed.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as those born in the natural order (anuloma),
were indeed creators of equal emanations for the welfare of all living beings.
Having struck that [ground] to a depth of one cubit (hasta) in the center of that site,
once it has been filled with that earth, the wise man [should know that] if it is higher, the ground is excellent.
Equanimity is called the middle; when it is deficient, it is remembered as the lowest. When it is fully grasped, it is supreme; when only partially grasped, it is the lowest earth.
White, red, yellow, and black are the four types of earth, corresponding respectively to the Brahmins and the other castes; each is auspicious according to its respective caste. (40)
For others, other [lands] are recommended; for those who have both self and others, [lands] excluding the supreme [heaven];
therefore, make it a dwelling place for mortals, taking whichever land is appropriate for each. (41)
All this is highly praised by the earth, especially by the gods;
one should offer an oblation of curd-rice to the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
One should expel these by means of the weapon-mantra (astra), and thereafter perform the rite of attraction (karṣaṇa).
White, red, tawny, and black are the colors corresponding to their respective castes in order.
In their youth, they were previously endowed with strength, though deprived of their tusks;
they possessed horns and hooves of gold and were untouched by any other color.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the Vṛṣagāyatrī, the wise man should first perform the formal offering; then the two bulls should stand facing the east.
The yoke and plough should be made of strong wood according to the prescribed characteristics;
the length of the plough should be three cubits, and its circumference should be seven finger-breadths.
The entire base should be circular, with corners measuring one-fourth of the side;
the height of the girdle (mekhalā) should be three tālas, and its thickness should be three mātras. || 47 ||
The base should be six mātrās in width and four aṅgulas in thickness;
from the base to the tip it gradually tapers, while the middle portion is slightly diminished.
At the base of the girdle (mekhalā), however, there is a projection (viryaveśa) of nine finger-breadths;
at the edge of that projection, the width is two finger-breadths and the thickness is half of that [half], i.e., one-quarter.
O Kāśyapa, the length of the nose is twenty-four finger-breadths;
the height of the nose above the bridge is declared to be five finger-breadths.
One should make the nose and belly face outward, with that [portion] extending the measure of a *manu*;
the remainder is known as the *citra*, at the junctions of the *sīra* and the *mekhala*.
The width of the nose is six mātrās, and its thickness should be four aṅgulas;
the tip, shaped like a needle, should become slender toward the end.
It is said that [the tongue] should be about three finger-breadths long, reaching as far as the tip of the nose;
the wise man should then apply an iron plough-tongue to the tip of the nose.
I shall not [use] a yoke that is as long as the distance between the two plow-poles, nor one with a hole for the yoke-pin;
it should have a circumference equal to the little finger and a length of two armspans, like a cow-hide.
Having recited the heart-mantra and formed two bulls resting on a yoke,
one should form a plough between the two yokes, leaning slightly toward the right.
The wise Brahmin should clear away the grass and other debris, and then sow sesame, mustard, and mung beans with the Netramantra. || 56 ||
One should honor the preceptor and give him a pair of bulls;
among those who perform the rite for three nights, the best are those who know the Vedas, while the middling are those who do not.
The night of the spirits (bhūtarātra) is the lowest; one should avoid it entirely.
One should protect the cattle from [the time] when the flowers appear until they bear fruit, and then offer them to the herds of cows.
One should cause the cows to stay in that very place for one night or two nights,
with cow-urine placed in their mouths and with praises consisting of cow-dung.
Afterwards, one should honor the architect (sthapati) with garments and other offerings according to one's means.
Then, the preceptor [should select] a commendable site on the earth, level in its center. (60)
Having smeared the ground with cow-dung, perform the demarcation of the directions;
the peg (śaṅku) is said to be one-sixteenth of an angula in length, and its circumference is equal to that.
The width at the top is one-eighth less than the width at the base;
the base and the top are shaped like a bud, with the base and top becoming gradually thinner.
One should fashion a well-rounded, straight piece of heartwood that has been dried;
then, using a peg twice its length as a measure, one should draw a circle in the middle of it.
In the center of that, one should place a gnomon (śaṅku) such that it stands equally in the four directions;
this is done by means of the shadow at the two times of forenoon and afternoon, [marking] the two ends of that circle.
Having observed the tip of the shadow at midday, and likewise in the afternoon,
the line passing through those two points is intended for the directions East and West.
Having rotated the three intermediate points like a fish facing away from others,
one should extend the thread through their center, running from south to north.
But for those mortals who occupy the middle portion, the mandala should extend by one shadow-finger; when divided, the smallest [mandala] is by means of a cubit (kubja-tāla).
When the sun has entered twenty-seven degrees and seven minutes of the northern [solstice], it is said to be "straight" (ārjava); and for Virgo, it is exactly the same.
In Pisces, one should increase [the duration] by only the middle portion, starting from the twenty-eighth degree and so forth; in Gemini, it extends up to the end of the twenty-seventh degree.

(8) Therefore, the half-mora would be diminished for each successive part, especially in the case of *kanyā* (the sixth tone), due to the increase of the half-mora from the twenty-eighth part. || 70 ||
In the sign of Sagittarius (Cāpa), up to twenty-eight degrees, it is likewise short;
thus indeed is the increase and decrease of shadow proclaimed from the center of the gnomon.
One should walk toward the measurement of the shadow and extend the Brahma-thread through its center;
one should avoid the measurement of the shadow during the intervals between the forenoon and the afternoon.
One should lay out the thread starting from the east and extending all around according to the desired measurement;
thereafter, having dug to the depth of the temple's foundation, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
The Guru, having worshipped the deities of the site (vāstu) by name within eighty-one squares corresponding to the extent of the palace, [should proceed]. || 74 ||
One should offer a bali-oblation of cooked rice mixed with curd, clarified butter, and jaggery;
one should perform the bali-rite beginning with the syllable Om, inserting the name in the middle, and ending with Svāhā.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma either in the center or in the north—
wherever the Vāstuhoma is not performed, the site (vāstu) perishes.
Having performed the rite of circumambulation with fire, one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The master builder (sthapati) should be fit for the ritual act, and the installer (sthāpaka) should be fit for the mantra.
Thus the ploughing has been described; now hear concerning the architecture of temples.
Thus ends the first chapter on the procedure for ploughing in the *Aṃśumatkāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the Vāstu for a temple;
when the expanse of the temple has been divided into nine parts: || 1 ||
There should be ten threads with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise ten with their tips pointing northward;
thus, in each of the nine sections, Brahmā resides in the center, occupying the central ninth part.
Marīci is in the eastern quarter, Vivasvat likewise in the south;
Mitra is in the western quarter, and Pṛthivīdhara in the north. || 3 ||
Having gazed upon Brahmā and remained there like bees,
Āpa and Apavatsa likewise took their stand in the northeastern direction.
Savitra and Sāvitra are indeed stationed in the southern direction;
Indra and Indrajaya are stationed in the southwestern direction.
Rudra and Rudrajaya are situated in the northwestern direction;
these two are the enjoyers of bipeds, each possessing half and a half-and-a-half [respectively].
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendraka, Āditya, Satyaka, Bhraṃśa, and Antarikṣaka; || 7 ||
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, the Rākṣasa, Yama, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are likewise in the south. (8)
Nirṛti, Dauvārikā, Sugrīva, Puṣpadantaka,
Varuṇa, Śoṣa, Roga, and Pāpayakṣmā are located in the west.
Vāyu, Nāga, as well as Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma,
and Ṛgāditidyuti likewise share one part each on the exterior.
Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī are situated in the outer corners beginning with the northeast (īśāna), occupying squares that are devoid of [other] grids.
In the four directions starting from the east, Skanda, Vaicāryama,
Vijṛmbha, and Balipiñcha are likewise [to be placed], excluding their [specific] positions as before.
These forty-nine deities have been proclaimed;
all of them are indeed bound by means of twenty threads, forming the body of Vāstu.
Having laid them face down, they are extracted and placed beneath the pedestal.
O Lord! How is the Vāstu-mūrti [to be treated]? Having bound it, how should one cause it to lie? (14)
Whenever a great war between the gods and the asuras took place,
Śukra would then perform austerities for the benefit of the asuras.
Then, born from that asceticism, a being of great strength and elemental form appeared;
and though unawakened, he engaged in battle with the gods.
That god cannot be harmed by any of the weapons of all the gods;
and all the gods [saw] that being lying with its face downward.
Having bound that Bhūta with twenty threads and having pressed it down, he remains there;
he attains the state of Vāstupuruṣa, and he is called the Vāstumūrti.
Indeed, if it were thus turned face-downward in that form, it would bring suffering to all;
therefore, whatever the layout of the site may be, all of that is embodied in the Vāstu-mūrti.
For the sake of removing that [obstruction], for the warding off of all suffering,
and for the purpose of accomplishing all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), perform the *vāstu-homa* and the ritual offering (*bali*).

The twice-born should perform the *homa* and *bali* offerings for the satisfaction of the deities beginning with Brahmā; when their satisfaction has been achieved, the site and its inhabitants are no longer afflicted. (21)
Therefore, with every effort, one should offer an oblation (bali) to Brahmā and the other deities;
and the Vāstuhoma sacrifice for Brahmā and the others should be performed according to their respective names.
The head is indeed in the northeast, while the feet are in the domain of Nirṛti;
the elbows lie in the southeast, and the knees rest toward the direction of Vāyu.

The deities residing in the body and the house are as follows: Svīśāna is situated at the junction of the head; Parjanya is in the location of the eyes; and Jayanta, Trika, and Bhṛgu [are located] there.
Above the throat and other parts is Āpaḥ, and likewise Āpavatsa; at the navel-sūtra is Parabrahman, and in the seed-syllable is Indra.
Indrajaya is in the linga, and likewise Nirṛti is in the two feet;
Samarī and Pṛthivī are situated in the position of the breast-string (stanasūtra).
One should visualize Savitṛ situated within the cavity on the side of Vivasvat’s belly and likewise upon the surface of his upraised palm.
One should install Sāvitra in the middle of the thighs and forearms;
and on the left side, as before, Rudra and Rudrajaya.

O Brahmin, one should cause the forms of the deities beginning with Mahendra and ending with those of the intermediate space (antarikṣa), situated in all their limbs, to be placed upon his knees and forearms;
and from the name onwards up to the *ṛc* verses, one should place them on the right side of his shanks.
Dauvāri, Pāpa, and Yakṣman are located on the right side of the shank. || 30 ||
One should place the form of Vāyu above the left elbow and knee; and [the deities] beginning with Nāga and ending with Ṛk are situated on the left arm. (31)
Carakī and the others are situated at the tips of the corner-lines in the four corners;
O best of the twice-born, these deities of the Vāstu-form face downwards.
The twice-born should offer the bali-oblation as before and consecrate the site (vāstu);
for the temple-site likewise, he should perform the vāstu-homa thereafter.
Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the characteristics of the site for palaces, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] by Kāśyapa.
Now I shall explain in detail the supreme ritual procedure for the Vāstu-homa,
[to be performed] at the time of laying the first bricks of a palace, as well as during the installation of a Liṅga.
In the installation of the complete [liṅga], as well as in the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa), in the consecration of a child-liṅga (bālaliṅga), and in the pavilion for the dance arena; || 2 ||
One should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice either in the assembly hall or in the sacrificial shed;
one's own preceptor, endowed with the characteristics of an Ācārya, should perform the homa.
In an auspicious, gentle, or Brahma-pada,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with sand, measuring exactly one cubit in width.
Make the excavation two finger-breadths deep and square and level;
O best of the twice-born, one should place the water-pot in the eastern direction in the midst of rice grains.
Having filled [the vessel] with scented water, one should place gold therein;
one should also cause palāśa leaves and dūrvā grass to be placed in that water.
Having worshipped the water-deity within that water with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
one should perform all the rites beginning with the establishment of the fire as prescribed for the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya).
One should invoke the deities of the site (vāstudeva) starting from the east and ending in the center of the fire;
one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and incense, each by their respective names.
One should perform the oblation beginning with the syllable *praṇava*, ending with *svāhā*,
and using fuel-sticks of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree for each individual offering.
One should perform oblations with cow's ghee one hundred times, then half of that [fifty times], and then half of that again [twenty-five times];
likewise, one hundred oblations each should be made with milk-rice (pāyasa) and sacrificial porridge (caru).
One should cause the Jaya and other oblations to be offered, as well as the Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings;
one should perform the Indra-oblation, the Kūṣmāṇḍa oblation, and the expiatory oblation.
One should perform the oblation with clarified butter using the mantra "havyavāha," the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," and the mantra "yad asya."

Then, having performed the sprinkling with the mantra "prāsāvīḥ," one should offer the oblations in sequence to the strewn grass (paristara) and the enclosing sticks (paridhi) as prescribed for the clarified butter.
One should grant a boon to Brahmā, or [offer it] into the fire or within the solar orb;
having sprinkled oneself with consecrated water using the Pavamāna verses.
Having thus completed the fire sacrifice, the wise one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness; then, with dried *darbha* grass and *palāśa* leaves, he should perform the binding.
Having ignited that [fire] in the fire-pit, perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) around the temple, the pavilion, the enclosure wall, and the location of the gate-tower.
Having extinguished that external fire, the wise and learned man should sprinkle everywhere with the water that has been set aside, reciting the mantra: "śucī vo havyam. (17)
O Vāstudeva, perform the circumambulation with fire; this is declared to be the Vāstuhoma. Now hear the procedure for the sacrificial bricks (iṣṭakā). || 18 ||
Thus ends the third chapter [of the *Aṃśumat*], concerning the ritual procedure for the fire-oblation of the site (*vāstuhomavidhi*) within the *Kāśyapa* [tradition].
Now I shall speak specifically of the first brick; listen!
[It is used] in a temple, a pavilion, a hall, and likewise in a city gate.
One should place the first brick upon the site for the retinue;
the characteristics of the ground are of two kinds: smooth and likewise rough.
That earth which is smooth, rich in gravel, difficult to dig, oily, and covered with fine sand is well known [as the best]. (3)
When water is seen at a depth of only one *puruṣa-āñjali*,
that earth is known to be very smooth and should be excavated without difficulty.
O Brahmins, one should dig a pit measuring one cubit deep and two cubits wider than the width of the palace, on ground that is very smooth.
To the extent that water is seen [in the well], to that extent one should dig a moist pit;
having filled the pit with coarse sand, it should be provided with water. (6)
After filling the dry land with water, make it level;
then, using pestles, hands, feet, and large stones, make it smooth.
In this manner, having made the foundation and the measurement, the preceptor should fashion the pit of the desired size; there, he should cast down the mental lines and the [physical] threads.
The first is the thread for the ground (mānasūtra), the second is the layout (vinyāsa),
the third is the boundary of the main pedestal (adhiṣṭha-sīmā), and the fourth is the boundary of the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha-sīmā).
The fifth is the *Homasūtra*, and the sixth is the *Prakṛtisūtraka*;
having thus laid down the six threads in this sequence, O best of the twice-born.
To the north of that, having constructed a water-shed measuring nine cubits, provided with sixteen pillars and adorned with canopies and banners; || 11 ||
It was adorned with arches, garlands of darbha grass, and strings of pearls;
its width was one-third of the pavilion's total extent.
One should construct fire-pits around it on the four cardinal directions, each one cubit in height and resembling the surface of a mirror.
For Indra and the other [directional guardians], the altars are respectively quadrangular, bow-shaped, circular, and lotus-shaped;
they should be one cubit in width and have a height with three tiers.
Having smeared the ground with cow-dung, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having adorned it with flour-powders, one should then indeed provide a meal for the Brahmins.
Having cleared away the remnants and performed the Vāstuhoma thereafter,
one should perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) and then sprinkle [the site] with water from kuśa grass.
On the altar-platform, however, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight droṇas of śāli rice,
half as much (four droṇas) of rice grains, and half as much again (two droṇas) of sesame seeds.
The wise man should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and cover it with Darbha grass and flowers;
however, on a stone temple he should use stones, and on a wooden temple, wood.
The first brick must be made correctly; one should not act contrarily.
One should have the first brick fashioned from stones that possess masculine gender characteristics.
The door should be secured, especially with stone slabs for women;
and with a stone from a eunuch, O best of the twice-born, one should place the brick upon the top.
One should construct a firm wall using only non-hermaphrodite stones, or the walls, pillars, and so forth may be made with whatever stones are available. (21)
Beginning from eight finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step,
up to thirty-eight finger-breadths, the length shall be one *kalā*.

The width should be half the length, and the thickness should be half the width; it should be constructed using the standard measurement unit (mānāṅgula), and one should not employ any other measurement. || 23 ||
Starting from nine finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths each time,
up to thirty-nine, according to the measurement of the *bhedabhoja* finger-breadth.

The extent and thickness [of the earth] are subsequently described, as well as the number of its levels; the sequence of the stages (bhūmis), beginning from one and ending at sixteen, is now declared. (25)
One should examine the top bricks by means of lines beginning with the male [sign]. An odd number of straight lines is proclaimed as being of masculine gender. (26)
A line with two [conjoined] marks and a discus is proclaimed to be feminine;
a line with two [conjoined] marks or a pair, or a pericarp, is neuter. (27)
One should carefully avoid those [manuscripts] that have lines, dots, or stains, or are infested with moths; however, one should accept a manuscript that is free from such defects.
That which has its base slightly elevated and its tip bent downward is called *ūrdhvabhāgamukha*; the other is known as *bhūpatāṃśaka*. (29)
The stone situated on the ground is said to be the front (agra), while the other is the upper part (ūrdhva).
That which faces the northeast is indeed proclaimed to be the head (śīrṣa).
The root is known to be other than that; the ritual measure is like that of the iṣṭakā.
Having bathed it with cow-products and scented water, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) during the first part of the night.
Born into a family of Śiva-brahmins, endowed with Śiva-initiation,
possessed of all auspicious marks, devoted to Vedic conduct, and pure.
One should perform the bath by carrying water and the bath with ashes;
then, wearing new garments and a turban, along with an upper cloth and ointment.
Having adorned [the deity] with perfumes and garlands, having consecrated his body (sakalīkṛtavigraha),
and having decorated him with the five-fold ornaments, one should wash the first bricks.
Having tied a protective cord (pratisara) made of gold or cotton thread with the heart mantra,
one should place it upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) outside the pericarp in the four cardinal directions.
The letter *la* is in the eastern quarter, the letter *va* in the southern region, the letter *ra* in the western direction, and the letter *ya* in the northern region. (36)

Having drawn them with rice-flour and wrapping each one individually in cloth, [place] the first with its tip pointing east and the second toward the south; the remaining two should have their tips pointing north.
Having worshipped them thoroughly, one should place nine jars— consisting of the elements beginning with earth, numbering nine, provided with threads, and wrapped in cloth— in their proper sequence.
One should place [the jars], complete with their threads and lids, filled with various fragrant waters and joined with golden lotuses, in order starting from the center.
In the center of the jar, however, one should place Sādākhya, and around it the world-protectors;
having meditated upon them, one should assign their respective mantras to the jar and worship them with perfumes and other offerings.
The wise one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented; thereafter, he should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
He should perform everything beginning with the establishment of the fire (agnyādhāna), as prescribed for the ritual of the sacred fire (agnikārya). || 41 ||

One should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* to Indra and the other deities respectively; one should then offer clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root-mantra of Sadyojāta.

One should likewise offer oblations of rice with the *aghora* mantra, sesame seeds with the *netra* mantra, and mustard seeds with the *kavaca* mantra; for each, there shall be one hundred and eight offerings.
One should perform the offering of oblations (āhuti) with specific mantras for each substance;
thus, the best of preceptors should keep vigil at night and [perform the rites] at dawn.
One should perform the rites such as immersion in water just as before;
however, one should especially worship the bricks, the pitcher, and the fire.

One should offer the oblations of Jaya and the others, as well as the Abhyātāna and Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings; then, with the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne," one should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 46 ||
Having honored the master builder with garments, gold,
and rings, and when the auspicious moment had arrived, the preceptor then led him to the doorway.
To the south of the door, at the base of the pillar within the space between the walls,
the best of preceptors should install either a brick or a stone.
One should perform circumambulation to the right when exiting the palaces and pavilions,
and circumambulation to the right when entering the halls and gate-towers.
Within the enclosure wall, however, one should place the *gopuras*;
the tip [of each] toward the northeast, and the base toward the southwest.
Having recited the five Brahmans, one should place [the mantras] in the fire or in the region of the wind, joined with the root and the tip, in the sequence starting from the east.
In the center of that, one should place jewels together with a golden lotus;
having smeared it with the five earths, one should fill it with water from the pitcher.
A clockwise rotation is auspicious, while a counter-clockwise rotation is inauspicious;
if it rotates counter-clockwise, one should properly perform a pacifying fire-offering (śāntihoma).
One should cause all the implements of the sacrifice to be presented to the preceptor. || 53-1/2 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, concerning the first brick, in the section on Aṃśumat by Kāśyapa.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme procedure for the secondary seats (upapīṭha),
which should be equal in height to the Svādhiṣṭhāna, or three-quarters, or even half [of it].
It may be one-fifth, or one-fourth, or with a quarter added, or even half;
or specifically, it may be one-and-a-quarter times, or twice the size.
Thus, O twice-born one, the arising of the eight Upapīṭhas has been declared;
the Adhiṣṭhānas are tenfold, consisting of groups of one, two, three, and four.
Alternatively, the *pādukā* of the *adhiṣṭhāna* may extend out by one-fifth;
the *nīrva* of the *upapīṭha* is likewise proclaimed to be fivefold.
One should fashion that *nīvra* on the pedestal as a foot-projection;
alternatively, it may be similar to the front foot, or likewise double and then double again.
The projection of the *upapīṭha* should be equal to the *jagatī*, or similar to it, or like a *upānaha*;
thus, there may be five varieties of the *upapīṭha* projection.
The projection of the staff for the *sabhā* and other [structures] is said to be that of the *upapīṭha*;
however, the projection of the staff for the *sabhā* and others is said to be external to that. || 7 ||
Now, beginning with one staff and ending with nine staves, the footwear is of nine kinds; the intense [type] consists of three groups of three, starting from the lowest.
In that same *ucca*, at the twelfth part, the *upānocca* is made with two parts;
the lotus is to be made with one part, and the *kampa* is said to be half a part. || 9 ||
The neck should be five parts high, and the lotus-base (pedestal) as before;
one should make the horse's head one and a half parts, and the fillet (kampam) should be made with half a part.
Thus, the eight-limbed [mandala] has been described; that which is six-limbed is the same, but without the lotus.
However, the lotus should be joined with the trembling [measurement], along with the auspicious pedestal (bhadra-upapīṭhaka). (11)
Alternatively, even without the *ūrdhvakaṃpa*, there is the five-fold *upapīṭhaka*;
the height of this *upapīṭha* is divided into twenty-seven parts.
The height of the pedestal (pādukā) shall be two parts, and the lotus (paṅkaja) should be equal to that;
the fillet (kampa) is said to be one part, and the emergence of the neck (galodaya) twelve parts.
The upper part is one part, and the lotus above it is equal to that;
the height of the *kapota* (dove-cornice) is three parts, and the *mañcamālin* is desired [to be] one part.
One should make it one-third less by means of a single part, and the *vājana* [the neck] one-half less by means of a single part; by name, that is called the *pratibhadraka*.
The height of the pedestal (pāduka) should be two parts, and the emergence of the lotus (paṃkajodaya) should be two parts;
the fillet (kampa) should be made with one part, and it should be separated by a single interval. || 16 ||
The height of the neck (pratituṅga) should be two parts, while the horse's head (vājina) is one part;
the measurement of the throat (gala) is one-eighth [of the total], and one should fashion the fillet (kampa) with one part.
One should construct the lotus-base with one part; the height of the pigeon-niche (kapota) should be three parts;
and the measurement of the liṅga should be fashioned with one part, while the inner space (mantara) should be made with a portion of that.
The *pratituṅga* is two parts, and the *vājana* is one part;
in twenty-seven parts, that is known by the name *pratisundara*.
The height of the *upapīṭha* (subsidiary pedestal) should be divided into twenty-one parts;
the *upāna* (plinth) shall consist of two parts, and the emergence of the lotus (*ambujodaya*) shall be equal to that.
The *kaṃpa* should be made with one half [of the width], and one should cause the lotus to be made with the other half.
The great band (*mahāpaṭṭī*) should be two parts, and one should cause the lotus to be made with half [of that]. || 2 ||
The *kampa* should be made with half [of that measure], and the height of the *karṇa* with one-eighth;
with one part for the *padmakampa* and half a part for the *kapotaka*.
With three parts, half of that, and half a name-unit, it is called the Saubhadra;
with two parts for the upānaha, half-units for the [other] parts, and one lotus-unit for the neck (kandhara).
The lotus should be made with two parts; the fillet (paṭṭikā) should be equal to that.
One should fashion the lotus-base (padmaka) with one and a half parts and the fillet (kampa) with half a part.
One should make the height of the neck seven parts, and the *kampa* half of that;
the lotus [pedestal] with one and a half parts, and the great fillet (*mahāpaṭṭī*) with two parts.
One should fashion the lotus with one-eighth of that portion, and the *kampa* (fillet) with half [of the remaining].
When the height of the five subsidiary pedestals (*upapīṭha*) has been divided into equal parts, [the fillet] should be two such parts.
O best of the twice-born! Thus has been described the secondary sacred seat (upapīṭha) known as Kalyāṇakārikā, which is worshipped under that name in all abodes and is said to possess six limbs.
And it was adorned with ornaments extending from its limbs, arranged according to the rules of architectural design,
and decorated with spirits, serpents, elephants, lions, crocodiles, and various kinds of birds.
O Brahmin, one should adorn the neck of the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha) with all the characteristic marks;
it should have the luster of a fresh crocodile and its entire head mounted upon a flame.
One should perform the consecration of Avala, Balavardha, and Adhiṣṭhānottama;
this is declared to be the Upapīṭha. Now listen to the procedure for the Adhiṣṭhāna. (p. 23) || 30 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the section on the Upapīṭha-vidhāna, in the Āṃśumatī-kāśyapa [Tantra].
Now I shall describe the procedure for the foundation; listen, O observer of good vows!
The surface of the earth is the foundation, and the earth is its support.
*Bhuvana*, *pṛthivī*, and *bhūmi* are synonyms, as indicated by their usage and other linguistic evidence.
Furthermore, *kūṭa* and so forth refer to the pinnacle of a palace, while *nīvraka* refers to the foundation and the roof-base. (2)
Therefore, that should be the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha), with the sacrificial offerings emerging from the threshold (nīvra);
from there, one should cause the natural threshold and the laying of the thread to be made.
One should determine the measurement exactly where the laying of the first brick occurs;
from that point, one should thus fashion the solid wall up to the end of the *prakṛti*.
Above the height of the *prakṛti*, the *svabhāva* should be one *prakṛti* plus one *hasta*,
or two *prakṛtis* plus one *hasta*, or three *prakṛtis* plus one *hasta* in solid form.
With a height of six finger-breadths, and increasing by six finger-breadths each time, there are the superior, the middling, and likewise the inferior [measures]. || 6 ||
The area up to the *prakṛti* is known as the interior circle (*antarmaṇḍalaka*).
Having done this, the preceptor should resolve upon performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) above the *prakṛti*.
The width of the base of the wall should be double or even triple [the thickness];
this is known as the *homanīvr̥* (sacrificial neck), and its half should be provided with a thick layer.
Its *nīvrā* (plinth) may consist of one, two, or even three *daṇḍas*, following the proportions of the *homāprakṛti*;
it may extend outward from the base of the wall, or it may reach up to the neck of the *upapīṭha*.
O best of the twice-born, it is declared that there are two kinds [of fire-pits] equal to the measure of the *homa-nīvrā*;
one should fashion the lotus above the *homa* according to half the measurement of the height of the *homa*.
The base (veśa) should be equal to the height of the lotus-base (abja), or it may be comparable to something higher than the lotus-base;
above that is the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna), which may be provided with a plinth (upapīṭha).
Other than the *homa*, one should arrange the pedestal (*upapāna*) above the *prakṛti*;
above that, either the ground-level (*dharātala*) or the secondary pedestal (*sopapīṭha*).
One should arrange the sacrificial fire (homa) either above or without a supporting vessel;
however, the best of artisans should arrange it according to the sūtra of equal proportions.
One should place the *homāpadas*, lotuses, drinking vessels, and so forth within the palace;
and the height of the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) should be measured according to the proportion of the height of the accessible [structure]. 14.
The width of the front foot (agrapāda) should be equal to half the height of the pedestal, or else one-sixth, one-sixth, or one-eighth [of that height]; this is designated as the staff (daṇḍa).
Starting from a single staff and increasing by half a staff at each step,
there are five in number, ending with the staff of fire (agnidaṇḍa).
Outside the base, that which extends beyond is divided into three parts;
one part is the width of the upāna (the lower molding), and the remainder is the width of the jagatī (the plinth).
The *kumuda* band is one part of the *veda*; its *nivra* is equal to that of the world.
Above the *kumuda* is the *paṭṭaveśa*, which is equal to the *kaṇṭhaveśana*.
The height of the fillet for all lotus-shaped [mandapas] should be equal to the height of the base-moulding (nīvrata);
that entire upper fillet, or the neck-enclosure, should be equal to it.
The *nīvraka* of all the *kampās* is one-fourth [of their height],
or it may extend outwards from the great pillar (*mahāvāja*) to a measure equal to half its height.
Or else, one should lead [the breath] through three quarters or until its exit, according to the strength of one's power;
[this applies] to the five groups beginning with birth, ending at each respective limb.
One should cut that lower surface to the extent of half a door-measure or half a ground-measure;
[therein one fashions] the upāna, the jagatī, the kumuda, and the kaṇṭhapaṭṭikā.
The wise one should know that what is renowned as the "group of five" consists of the foot-binding, the base, the door, the water-channel, and the dry land, along with the supporting structures. (23)
However, one should perform the cutting of the limbs from above;
one must not cause the cutting of minor limbs, for that is always a source of calamities.

Therefore, with every effort, one should know that the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) is twofold—consisting of the obstruction and the binding of the feet—even without the cutting off of each individual limb. (25)
O best of the twice-born! It is proclaimed through its various single and multiple divisions;
among all the meters, the Kumuda is said to be the standard measure (vṛtta). || 26 ||
(26) However, for the soles of the feet, there should be an eight-petaled *kumuda* lotus.
If these two are combined in a single [mandala], it brings about the destruction of the practitioner. (27)

The construction of palaces, fortifications, and various types of mixed structures, such as watchtowers and storehouses, should be carried out in accordance with their respective classifications; this brings about auspiciousness.
Likewise, if there is a connection of the feet or an excellent commingling within it, yet it is inauspicious or contrary, it will bring ill fortune to the kingdom and the king. (29)
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid mixing [the materials] within the group;
and the height of the foundation should be nineteen parts.
The *upāna* (plinth) shall be one part, and the *jagatī* (moulding) seven parts;
the height of the *kumuda* (water-lily moulding) shall be thirty-six parts, and the *āliṃla* (fillet) one part.
The triple-band (tripaṭṭa) shall be one part, and the projection (pratyutsedha) two parts;
the fillet (vājana) shall be one part—this constitutes the binding (pratibandha). || 32 ||
The remainder, excluding the pedestal (upāna), is as before; the reality is manifold. The height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is divided into twenty-five parts. || 33 ||
The height of the pedestal (pādukā) is one part of Śiva; the jagatī is eight parts;
the height of the kumuda is one part of the base (dhātu); and the kampamānaka is one part of the void (vyoma).
The height of the neck (galotsedha) should be one part of fire (three parts), and the upward projection (kampa) should be one part of the moon (two parts).
The great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) should be three parts, and above that, the projection should be one part.
That which is known as *pādabandha* is likewise devoid of sandals;
and this *pādabandha* is proclaimed to have various subdivisions. (36)
Having made the height of the base (tala) seven and a half parts, the pedestal (pādukā) should be made with one part;
the lotus (ambuja) should be one and a half parts, and the fillet (kampa) is said to be half a part.
The height of the world (the base) is seven parts; the emergence of the lotus (the capital) is six parts;
the neck (āliṅga) is one part, and the triple band (tripaṭṭa) is also one part.
The *pratituṅga* should be two parts, and the *vājana* one part;
this is known by the name *pratikrama*, while the *pratibandha* is distinguished [as follows]. || 39 ||
One should fashion the *upāna* (base molding) from that same portion using one part;
the height of the *āliṅga* (plinth) is two parts, and the remainder is exactly as before.
One should avoid placing a lotus or a bell directly upon the plinth;
that which is elevated above it is known as *pratikrama*, suitable for all types of temples. || 41 ||
One should divide the height into twenty-six parts;
the plinth (upāna) should be made with one part, the pedestal (dala) with two parts, and the fillet (kampa) should be fashioned with one part.
Six parts should be the height of the jagatī, one part the *dalamānaka*,
the neck (*kaṇṭha*) should be made with one [part], and the height of that neck with two parts.
One part shall be the trembling peak (kampatuṅga), and the emergence of the petal (dalodaya) shall be equal to that;
the great band (mahāpaṭṭī) shall be two parts, and the petal shall be measured at one part.
One should perform the *kampita* [meter], which is eight-sided and endowed with *kumuda*;
it is known as having lotus filaments, yet it is distinguished by its foot-structure. (45)
When the height of the base (tala) is divided into nineteen parts, the plinth (upāna) is one part, and the height of the lotus (padma) is two parts. (46)
The height of the *kampa* is half a part; the height of the *jagatī* is four parts;
the lotus is half a part; and the neck (*gala*) is measured at half a part. || 47 ||
The lotus should be half a part in height, the fillet (paṭṭamānaka) three parts, and the lotus again half a part; that which is equal to this is called the *kampa*. || 48 ||
The height of the neck (kaṇṭha) should be made one and a half parts, and the fillet (kampa) half of that;
the lotus (padma) should be made with half a part, and the band (paṭṭikā) with one and a half parts.
One should fashion the lotus with one half of its portion and the tremor (kampa) with the other half;
this is declared as the "Abundant Flower" (puṣpapuṣkala), distinguished by its foot-binding (pādabandha). || 50 ||
One should divide the height into thirty-two parts:
the upopāna should be two parts, the upāna one part, and the height of the lotus seven parts.
One part should be made for the neck, and one part should be used to fashion the lotus;
the height of the kumuda is four parts, and the throat is said to be one part.
One [unit] should be made as the tremor (kampa), and the portion of the quality (guṇāṃśa) as the neck (gala).
With one [unit] the tremor, and with another, one should fashion the lotus above.
The *kapota* (dove-cornice) should be as high as two parts, the *āliṅga* (embracing band) one part,
the intervening space (*antarita*) one part, and the *pratituṅga* (counter-projection) two parts.
One should fashion the *vājana* (the weight) by means of a single part according to the sequence;
however, in the case of an obstruction, there would be a division taken from that which is separated by the *śrībandha*.
The height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is divided into twenty-eight parts;
the plinth (upāna) is one part, and the height of the wall (jagatī) is six parts. (56)

One should cause the *kumuda* to be made with five parts and the *kampaka* with one; the portion for the neck (*gala*) should be three measures, and one should cause the *kampaka* to be made with one [part]. || 57 ||
The lotus (padma) should be made with one part, its height being three parts;
the neck (āliṅga) should be fashioned with one part, and it should be separated by an interval.
The *pratituṅga* (the height of the base) is two parts, and likewise the *vājana* (the fillet) is one part;
this is declared to be the *mañcabandha* (bed-style) for the class of *pratibandha*.
That same [meter] is called *Śrīkāntaka* when it is without the *aliṅgikā* [opening], with twenty-two syllables in each successive line; however, it is distinguished by its specific foot-structure.
When the height is thirty-six parts, one part shall be the pedestal (pādukā),
two parts the measurement of the neck (gala), and the height of the fillet (kampa) shall be one part.
The height of the *jagatī* should be six parts, the emergence of the *ghaṭa* four parts;
the *kampa* should be made with one part, and the height of the neck (*kaṇṭha*) with two parts.
Then, one part is for the upward vibration (*ūrdhvakampa*), and the non-protruding portion is with two parts;
the weight (*vājana*) is [as specified], and two parts are said to be the neck (*kaṇṭha*).
The *vājana* should be made with one part, the *kamalodaya* with one and a half parts, and the *kampam* with half a part; this is the supreme *śroṇībandha*.
In the case of the foot-binding (pādabandha), there should be a division adorned with saṃhatya and vyāla;
having made the height of the base (tala) three and six parts, the pedestal (pāduka) shall be one and a half parts.
It is said that the tremor (kampa) is half a part, and the birth of the lotus (paṅkajodaya) consists of a full part.
The neck (gala) should be made with one part, and one should cause the lotus (padma) to be made with one part. || 66 ||
The height of the *kumuda* (pedestal) should be three parts; the petal (*dala*) should be one part in measurement;
the *āliṅga* (enclosure) should be one part, and the *antarīta* (inner space) should be equal to that.
With two parts raised above the *prati* and one part for the *vājana*, this is known by the name *abjabandha*; its variation occurs when it is inverted.
The base (tala) consists of twenty-two parts; the height of the pedestal (pāduka) is two parts.
One should fashion the lotus (abja) with one part and the fillet (kampa) with one part.
The portion of the jagatī should be a kumuda made with four parts;
the lotus (padma) should be made with one part, and the kampaka should be fashioned with one part.

One should fashion the neck-protrusion (*kaṇṭhatuṅga*) with two parts and the vibration (*kampa*) with one part; the measurement of the petal (*dala*) is one part of Śiva, while the great fillet (*mahāpaṭṭī*) consists of two parts.
A single *kampa* (vibratory movement) is to be performed; this is known as the "continuous wall" (*vaprabandha*), which is honored in all abodes of the *pādabandha* class. (72)
In the measurement of that great fillet (mahāpaṭṭikā), there is a pigeon (kapota) and a pigeon-band (kapotabandhaka);
above the tremor over the pigeon, there is a triple-fillet (tripaṭṭa) made with one part.
The *vājana* should be made with two parts of the height, and the *pratisundara* with one part; this arrangement is prescribed when the total height is divided into twenty-six parts.
The height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) should be divided into twenty-three parts;
with one part there is the upāna, with one part the lotus (padma), and with one part the kampa.
One should know that the neck (kaṇṭha) consists of two parts, the *kampa* of one part, and the lotus (padmaka) of one part;
the fillet (paṭṭikā) should be made of two parts, and the *kampa* should be fashioned with one part. || 76 ||
One should fashion the lotus with one part and the neck with one part;
one should make the water-lily with one part and the emergence of the lily with three parts.
The lotus should be made with one part, the embrace (āliṅga) with one part,
the triple band (tripaṭṭa) with the portion of Śiva, and the pedestal (pratimānaka) with two parts.
One should arrange the *vājana* in one part according to the sequence;
however, in the case of an obstruction, there should be a division, and that is declared to be *Śrīkaṇṭha*.
The *upāna* (base molding) is one part; the lotus (*padma*) is one part; the *kampa* (fillet) is two parts;
the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is one part; the *kampa* is two parts; and the band (*paṭṭikā*) is two parts.
One should fashion the *kampa* with one part and the *padma* with one part;
the *kumuda* with three parts, and the *padma* according to the measure of one part.
One should fashion the *āliṅga* with one part separated by a lunar portion (*śaśibhāga*),
the *prati* with two parts, and the *vājana* with one part.
When the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is divided into twenty-two parts, this constitutes the karīrabandha; however, it is modified in the case of the pratibandha.
The *pādukā* (pedestal) should be made with one part, and the height of the lotus (*abja*) with two parts;
the *kampam* (fillet) should be made with one part, and the measurement of the neck (*kaṇṭha*) with two parts.
One *kampa* is made with two parts, and the *paṭṭikā* (fillet) with one part;
the *kampa* is two parts, while the *gala* (neck) is measured at one part. || 85 ||
The lotus is one part, the measurement of the pitcher (kumbha) is three parts, the measurement of the neck (gala) is one part, and the liṅga is said to be two parts. (86)
The triple-band (tripaṭṭa) is made with one part, the pedestal (pratimāna) with two parts, and the base (vājana) with one part;
[this applies] when the portion is doubled.
And this should be the obstruction, the division, and the binding of the jar; and the height of the base, divided by twenty-four. (88)
The portion for the pedestal (pādukā) should be one part, and the arising lotus (paṅkajodaya) should be equal to that;
the hoof (khura) should be made with one part, and the height of the base (jagatī) should be six parts.
One part for the lotus, one part for the neck, and one part for the lotus;
four parts for the height [of the body], and one part for the pitcher (kalaśa).
The *āliṅga* should be one part, separated by one part;
the height of the *pratitūṅga* should be two parts, and the *vājana* one part. (91)
The *pratibandha* (the connecting band) should be the *bheda* (the division); it is called the auspicious (*śrīkara*) name.
At two parts of the sun (*bhānu*), the *talocca* (the height of the base) should be two parts, and the *pāduka* (the pedestal) should likewise be two parts. || 92 ||
The base (upapīṭha) should be one part of Śiva; the measurement of the neck (gala) should be six parts;
the throat (kaṇṭha) should be made with one part, and one should fashion the lotus (abja) with one part.
One part of the string is for the forming of the pot;
one [part] is for the rounded neck; one [part] is for the vibration; and one [part] is for the vibrating throat.

The space for the *vyoma* should be one part, the *kampa* one part, and the *paṭṭikā* should be two parts; the measurement of the *gala* should be one part, and one should fashion the *kampa* with one part. || 95 ||
(On page 33: But in the verse-structure named Sundarāmbuja, it is divided into four, seven, and two parts; that respective measure is distributed accordingly.
The sandal (pādukā) is known to have two parts; the width of the petals is four parts, the neck (gala) should be made with one part, and the lotus (ambuja) with two parts.
Two parts of the measurement of the fillet-band (paṭṭikā) are said to be the base (pāduka);
O best of the twice-born, the jagatī is four parts, and the lotus (padma) is one part.

A lotus should be made with one part of the neck's measure, while a crescent moon is prescribed with one-sixteenth part; a lily should be as high as three parts, and one should fashion a lotus with one part.
The triple-band (tripaṭṭa) should be made with one part, and the single-band (ekabhāga) with one part;
the pedestal (pratimāna) should be two parts, while the base (vājana) is one part of Śiva.
In this way, it shall be "Lotus-Lovely" (Nalinakānta), which brings delight to all the gods;
when the height of the base is divided into twenty-three parts— || 101 ||
The height of the *pāduka* (pedestal) shall be one and a half parts; the *upapāna* (lower lip) shall be one part of Śiva (one part);
the lower lotus shall be two parts; and the neck is said to be one part.
Above that is a lotus one part high; the height of the *kumuda* is three parts. Above that is a lotus one part high, and one part is for the *kampamānaka*.
The neck should be made with two parts, and the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā) one part;
the height of the lotus (padmatuṅga) should be one part, and the rise of the cornice (vājanodaya) one and a half parts.
The *padmatuṅga* should be one part, the *āliṅga* one part, the *tripaṭṭa* likewise one part, and the *pratimāna* two parts. (105)
One should perform the measurement with a single [unit]; this is declared to be glorious beauty.
There shall be a distinction regarding the obstruction, and this is likewise in front. (106)
When the height of the base is divided into twenty-four parts,
the plinth (upāna) shall be one part, and the emergence of the petals (dalodaya) shall be two parts.
Above that, one should fashion the *kaṃpa* as one part, the height of the *jagatī* as five parts,
the height of the *kumuda* as four parts, and the lotus (*padma*) as one part.
The neck is said to be one part; the upper lotus is a portion of Śiva.
The height of the fillet (vājana) is two parts, and the lotus portion is one part. 109.
The *āliṅga* should consist of one part; the *tripaṭṭa* should be equal to that.
The *pratimāna* should be two parts, and the *vājana* should be one part. (110)
When the obstruction has been broken, one should divide this [structure] named Skandakānta,
which rises high above the ground, into twenty-three parts.
One part is for the pedestal (upāna), six parts for the lotus-base (ambujodaya),
one part for the measurement of the neck (kaṇṭha), and the upper lotus is one part of Śiva.
The portion for the *yumaṃśa* and the height of the *kuṃbhaka* should be one part; the measurement for the lotus (*padma*) should be one part;
the *kampa* should be made with one part, and the emergence of the neck (*kaṇṭharodaya*) should be two parts. (113)
One part is trembling, and the upper lotus is equal to that;
the *kapota* is three parts high, and the *āliṅga* is one part.
This [meter] may be called *ambujakānta*, but when its feet are varied, it is called *dharātala*; thus it is described through many different varieties. (115)
In the same way, even if it is one long syllable too many or too few, it does not incur a fault;
nor does it matter if it is half, a quarter, or three-quarters [of the measure], provided it is endowed with strength and grace. (116)
The broad triple-band (tripaṭṭa) is prescribed as being of two kinds;
the triple-band is at the base of the foot, having a width equal to one-quarter of the measurement of the root-foot.
The width of the three bands at the end of the foot should be three-quarters and half [of the foot's width];
the projection outside the foot and the *nīvra* (fillet) should be equal. || 118 ||
One should arrange pairs or even groups of four within the intervals between the feet;
it is adorned with lions, elephants, crocodiles, serpents, spirits, and swans. (119)
One should fashion a golden image everywhere above the triple-band (tripaṭṭa), representing the emergence from the foot-base [of the pillar] by means of fresh sea-monsters and serpents.
One should fashion a circular *kumuda* (lotus) provided with upward- and downward-facing lotuses;
all other flowers should have their stalks bound together.
One should fashion the shape as circular and octagonal in due order.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the characteristics of the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*), in the *Aṃśumat* of Kāśyapa.
Now I shall describe in detail the characteristics of the *nirmālya* (remnant offerings) and the door;
[the former] at the end of the *pratibandha* and the *prati*, and the latter near the *paṭṭikā*.
At the end of the throat, or at the end of the *kumuda*, or at the edge, or at the tip of the *pādukā*, one should fashion a tube;
below and above that, one should properly join the tube.
Starting from twelve finger-breadths and increasing by three finger-breadths at each step,
one should fashion that [staff] in five varieties up to twenty-four finger-breadths.
For this [mandala] is situated outside the wall; half of it is the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
Alternatively, having entered [the space], it may be made equal to the interior of the wall.
Starting from eight finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths each time,
the width is fivefold in sequence, ending at one-sixteenth of a finger-breadth (kalāṅgula).
The width at its base should be five parts, the width at the top three parts;
its breadth should be equal to that [width], or three-quarters, or half of it; and its thickness should be one-third of that.
Its height should be one-third of its width, and it should be similarly sloped; however, in the middle of the stalk, it must be made free from depressions and elevations.
Slightly bent from its base to its tip, the base of the lion is bound;
it is held like an elephant's trunk, beautiful as it extends forward. (8)
Or, having assumed the form of a serpent, an elephant, or a lion, one should remain seated upon a stalk;
in this manner, the stalk [posture] should be performed in the gentle, eastern, and middle directions.
Having specially established [the image] according to this rite, the wise one, having bathed it with perfumed water, products of the cow, and then with [ordinary] water; 10.
The bath-giver, with a well-pleased mind, should perform the *śānti* oblation while reciting the *vāruṇa-sūkta*, at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction.
The wise architect, accompanied by the installers, should not, however, establish [the image] adorned with all ornaments and provided with all musical instruments. (12)
One should bind it very firmly with lime and molasses;
the stalk of the male stone (puṃśilā) should be well-fashioned, reaching up to the lord of the feet.
Thus is described the characteristic of the pillar, beginning with the installation of the shaft. This concludes the seventh chapter, the *Nālasthāpanavidhi*, from the *Aṃśumat* of the *Kāśyapa*.
Now, O observer of noble vows, I shall describe in detail the length, width, form, and ornaments of the *caraṇā* [temple]; listen briefly.
Stamba, talipa, caraṇa, and jaṅgha, as well as sthāṇu, sthūṇa, and pāda—these are synonyms. (2)
The length of the base (pāda) is prescribed according to a measurement of one part of the height of the authoritative [structure];
or else, the height of the base (aṅghri) is twice that of the height of the plinth (adhiṣṭhāna).
Therefore, the height of the base (pāda) should be as high as the ground level, or increased by six or eight parts;
or else, the height of the base should be one part out of nine or eight parts of the series of base-heights.
This [measurement] may indeed extend to the wooden pillars, or it is said to extend to the wall-pillars;
or it may be half of that, or less by a third, or even less by a fourth part.
In all dwellings, the space between the wall and the pillar should be as wide as the wall itself.
The area from the northern boundary of the *prati* to the pillar is called the *ṣālastambha*.
The portion from the upper edge of the pedestal (upāna) to where the pillar is fixed is called the *nikhāta-stambha*.
This height (*tuṅga*) should be divided into seven, eight, or nine parts.
Having divided [the total] into eleven parts, one part is the extent of the foot;
that is declared to be the root-tāra, and one should likewise apply that tāra.
But the remainder, diminished by one part, should be wide at the top;
one should perform this procedure for each level from the first up to the sixteenth.
From the base to the top, it is octagonal and joined with a pitcher, a pedestal, and so forth;
this is known as Brahmakānta, while the eight-sided one is Viṣṇukāntaka.
The *indrakānta* [pedestal] should have six corners, and the *candrakānta* should have sixteen corners;
at its base, one should fashion a four-cornered [base] according to the measurement of the neck.
The top of the pillar should be square according to a single measurement;
the middle portion between those two should be octagonal or even sixteen-sided.
O Brahmin, it may also be circular in shape, adorned with jars and other ornaments;
this is known as Rudrakānta, being round from its base to its tip.
That which is devoid of the *kuṃbha*, *maṇḍī*, and other [ornaments], and which pervades [the entire form], is called the *rudrakāntaka*;
it is said to have eight corners at the base and apex, while in the middle it has eight corners.
The lower portion should be square, the middle portion octagonal, and above that it should be circular; thus it shall consist of three parts, resembling a mountain peak.
This is known as the Śivacchanda, praised in the abode of Śiva.
At its base, the emergence of the lotus seat should be one and a half daṇḍas or two daṇḍas. (16)
One should have its width made double that [of the base] and shaped like a lotus;
one should perform the installation of the feet upon the pericarp of that lotus.
It is endowed with a form according to one's desire, joined with a water-pot, a pedestal, and so forth,
adorned with a circle of lotuses, creepers, and the like, and possessing lotus-like feet.

At the base of the feet, however, one should fashion a lotus; at the base of the calves, a serpent, which is called the "serpent-foot"; and at the base of the thighs, an elephant, measured according to that same proportion, which is declared the "elephant-foot. (19)

At its base, it is joined with lions and other figures, endowed with whatever form is desired, and adorned with pitchers and so forth; it is celebrated by various names according to those specific features.
That which is circular in shape and long in extent, provided with *śuṇḍupāda* legs,
and joined with *kumbha*, *maṇḍī*, and other features, is declared to be a *śuṇḍupāda*.
Having adorned the pedestal-base (piṇḍipāda) with strings of pearls,
one should fashion a square at the top of the pillar according to the measurement of the width and the diagonal.
With a staff half the length of that [staff], one should fashion an eight-sided lotus; below that, according to the measurement of the staff, one should arrange an eight-sided base.
Below that, as before, is a lotus; below that, according to the measurement of the stalk, is a square base, and below that again, as before.
At the base, however, the remainder is said to be either four-cornered (quadrangular) or variegated;
in its center is a cloth-strip (paṭṭa) that is eight-cornered, which is declared to be Śrīkaṇṭha.
If the middle band is triangular, it is called the Śrīvaktra pillar;
from its base to its top it should be octagonal, provided with three bands and a *kṣepaṇa*.
The projecting pillar (kṣepaṇastaṃbha) is described as being adorned with bands, leaves, and so forth;
it should be one-third or one-fourth of the height of the pillar.
One should fashion Śivā in the middle of the pillar, specifically at the top and the bottom;
however, at the base of the pillar, one should arrange lotuses and other ornaments according to the measurement of the pillar.
The characteristics of the pillar have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the time for awakening.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of the Pillar, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kāśyapa.
Now I shall describe specifically the supreme characteristics of the time for awakening:
that which has a width equal to the root-base is excellent; that which is equal to the middle [base] is middling. (1)
The minor shrines (kanyasabodhikās) are equal in width to the breadth of the front foot;
their height is equal to their width, and they are endowed with a length of five daṇḍas.
The supreme [image] is said to have a height of two and three parts of the *tāra*;
that which is endowed with a length of four *daṇḍas* is proclaimed as the middling one. (3)
Its height is half its width, and it is provided with three staffs;
this is known as the *kanyasā* (smallest) *bodhikā*, while the *aṅghriyā* is provided with *bodhikās*.
On the upper third of the *bodhikocca*, there is an upper fillet (*ūrdhvapaṭṭikā*) occupying one part;
in the middle part, it may be adorned with waves, creepers, and so forth.
Below that, however, one should have the waist-band (kukṣibandha) made with one part;
the staff (daṇḍa) should be three-quarters or half [of the height], and the measurement of the shadow at both ends [should be] as prescribed.
One should fashion the form of a shadow beneath the upper fillet;
now I shall describe the ornamentation below by means of the proportions of the bodhikā.
One-third of the middle band, or even half of its width,
on both sides is said to be the space for the wave-design.
The middle band, adorned with leaves, should be accompanied by small projections;
on both sides there should be wave-patterns, which are equal and mutually diminishing.
The Bodhikā is either half or three-quarters of a vistara, with its front unobstructed; its width is equal to that [of the vihāra], as devised by the Saṃbhojakas. (10)
Having divided that height into six parts, one part above should be made for the fillet (paṭṭikā);
then, with one part, the upper lotus, and with half [a part], one should fashion the corner (karṇa).
The lower lotus is two parts; below that, the fillet (paṭṭya) is said to be one part.
One should fashion the lower lotus as half a part, following this sequence.
Make it shaped like a lotus bud, extending from the tip; or it may be joined with a protruding tip, or even shaped like an umbrella. (13)
On the two sides, the tips of the bound fists are fashioned in the form of serpents and the like; it is further adorned with spirits, sea-monsters, serpents, and dramatic scenes and so forth. (14)
p. 42) Or else, there may be a jeweled binding (*ratnabandha*) or a variegated one (*citra*) struck at the tip of the mouth;
there should be a wave (*taraṅga*) between the two tips of the *bodhi*, with a measure of a staff (*daṇḍa*) in its middle. || 15 ||
O you of excellent vows, a cloth banner shaped like a yoke should be made with a height equal to that of the *tāra*;
having adorned it with various colorful patterns, it becomes a "wondrously enlightened" (*citrabodhikā*) enlightenment-banner.
A bodhi tree adorned with leaves is celebrated as a *patrabodhikā*;
one should fashion waves resembling the ripples of the great ocean.
The projection of a wall or pillar should be one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters [of its width];
it may be square, octagonal, or circular, or it may be common to all these shapes in sequence.
The *bodhikāya* is at the bottom, while the *vīrakāṇḍa* has eight corners;
its height is said to be equal to three-quarters of the length of the front foot.
For all the bases (pādas), the hero-section (vīrakāṇḍa) consists of four corners;
listen now to the characteristics of the plank (phalaka) situated below the hero-section. || 20 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of the Time of Awakening, in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapaparivarta*.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the wooden planks (phalaka):
the width of the plank should be three daṇḍas, equal to one and a half times the smallest measurement.
The upper plank (uttamā phalakā) should be fourteen daṇḍas wide;
alternatively, the width of the plank may be equal to a kumbhakarṇa. || 2 ||
The height of all the lintels (phalaka) should be three-quarters of the pillar (daṇḍaka).
Dividing that height into three parts, the upper portion is called the joint (utsandhi). || 3 ||
Below that, one part is for the cane; below that, one part is for the lotus, which has the form of a serpent's face and resembles the shape of a foot from the ankle down.
All the fruit-panels (phalaka) should be made with four corners and a luster like the twilight;
below that, one should fashion a jar (ghaṭa).
The height of the pitcher (ghaṭa) is of four kinds: two daṇḍas, or one and a half daṇḍas, or one and a quarter daṇḍas, or three-quarters of a daṇḍa. || 6 ||
"Priyadarśanasaumya," "Candrakānta," and "Śrīkara"—these are the names of the jars as they are proclaimed in their respective order. (7)
One should fashion the height of the jar with nine parts;
the height of the neck should be one part, and the height of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be four parts according to measurement.
One should fashion a lotus with one part from the height of the mouth, and with half of that [part] a circle;
the wise man should conceive [the remaining parts] as being reduced by half.
One should cause it to go from above downwards in this sequence; thus has the *ucca* [type] been fully described. Now hear about the *niṣkaṃbha*.
The width of its base is equal to the height, and its ear-like protrusion is as wide as that;
the mouth is especially wide, being equal in width to the kumbha itself.
The width of the base (dhṛk) and the neck (kaṇṭha) is said to be equal to the breadth of the pillar; below that is the bulbous base (laśuna), measuring one part in height and circumference.
One should fashion the lotus with a measurement that is half of that, and half of that again;
the location for the face is said to be at half a cubit from the base of the lotus. (13)
Its lower part was adorned with pearl strings according to its proportions;
likewise, there were garlic, lotus petals, and pearl strings.
The one most skilled in ritual procedures should fashion the width [of the pedestal] equal to the width of the pillar;
or else, I shall now describe the elevation for the Bodhika and other types.
Having made one part out of the total three parts the height of the base (caraṇotsedha), one should go down two parts;
then, having taken the upper portion, it shall consist of twenty-two parts.
The height of the *bodhika* and the *vīrakāṇḍa* shall each be one-sixteenth part;
the height of the *phalaka* shall be one-fifth part, and the *ghṛtamāna* shall consist of one-sixteenth part. || 17 ||
One should fashion the height of the pot as four parts, the measurement of the neck as one part of Śiva (eleven parts), the elevation of its mouth as one part,
and the lotus as one part.
The wealth should be made with half [of that amount]; diamonds are said to be equal to that.
Garlic, lotus-vines, pearl necklaces, and so forth are as before. (19)
Thus should be the ornamentation of the pillar, and likewise the characteristics of the pedestal.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the Ornamentation of Pillars, in the *Aṃśumat* of Kāśyapa.
(p. 45) Now I shall explain specifically the supreme characteristics of the altar (vedikā). One should fashion it upon the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna), at the base of the pillar. || 1 ||
O twice-born one, a sacrificial altar (vedikā) should be constructed above the grass-bundle (prastara);
the smallest and lowest altar measures one and a half daṇḍas.
The middle [height] should be two daṇḍas, while the most excellent height is three daṇḍas;
or else, the elevation of the pedestal (vedikā) is stated according to another method.
When the rise of the feet is divided by six, seven, or eight,
one part represents the measurement of the altar (vedikā), which is respectively the best, intermediate, and lowest.
Thus, at the base of the *caraṇa* (pedestal), there should be the emergence of the altar (*vedikā*);
above that, the height of the pillar (*bhūmyaṅghri*) should be divided into seven parts.
One part is desired for the height of the pedestal (vedikā) of the neck-pavilions;
the height of the neck (gala), when divided, is three, four, or five parts.
At the base of the neck (galamūla), the height of the pedestal (vedī) should be one part; the best is the middle [measure], while the lowest is one part less.
Alternatively, at the base of the neck, the pedestal may be measured as one part of the total height.
The height of the altar (vedikā) should be six parts; the measurement of the neck (gala) should be three parts.
Above the neck, one part should be for the fillet (kaṃpa), and with one [part] one should fashion the lotus (abja).
O best of the twice-born, the upward tremor should be performed with one [unit];
at the seventh and eighth parts, the height of the altar (vedi) is fourfold, and the neck (gala) follows in sequence.
One should fashion the *kampapadma* and the *kampa* exactly as before;
at its base, one should fashion the *kampa* with a measure equal to that of the ear.
The remainder is declared to be the *karṇodaya* (the rise of the corner), or it may be free from that *kaṃpa*.
The lotus (*padma*) should be one and a half parts in height, or even two parts. (11)
The altar (vedikā) is considered to have variegated limbs with the luster of lotuses and śaivala leaves;
indeed, for all altars, the neck and the feet are adorned.

The width of the wall and the pillar should be equal to that of the roof and the base of the altar; now listen, O observer of noble vows, to the method of entering the altar situated above the stone slab.
The pedestal-base (aṅghrive-dyā) and the entrance to the base (aṅghriveśana) shall each be one-third of the inner wall of the sanctum;
or alternatively, the entrance may be one-fourth [of that]. || 14 ||
The outer base of the altar should be outside the wall and pillar, as well as the outer entrance;
or else, listen to another way regarding the extent of the altar.
The wall, however, being measured from the outside, should be divided into six, seven, eight, nine, or ten parts on both sides as well. || 16 ||
The remaining width of the pedestal (vedikā), excluding one part, is its extent;
in the Nāgara style, it takes the form of a four-cornered pedestal atop the plinth (prastara). 17.
In a Drāviḍa or Vesara temple, the altar (vedikā) takes the form of an octagon;
or else, in a Vesara temple, the altar may even be circular.
