The corners of the neck and the corners of the pedestal are likewise manifold;
the characteristics of the pedestal have been declared—now hear the characteristics of the lattice-work (jāla). || 19 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the characteristics of the altar, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kaśyapa. 11.
Now I shall explain specifically the characteristics of the *jālaka*; listen.
The locations of the *jālaka* are said to be in the group of feet and likewise in the throat. (1)
A wise man should construct a window in palaces, large halls, and in the middle of the interior spaces, according to this rule.
O best of the twice-born, one should place the lattice-work above the pedestal;
however, cutting away even half of the lattice-work of the pedestal leads to total destruction.
Therefore, one should not cut away even half of the lattice-work from the altar with effort;
the width of the lowest [altar] should be two daṇḍas, and that of the middle one should be three daṇḍas.
That which is fourteen daṇḍas in width is proclaimed as the best;
its height is equal to its width, increasing by one daṇḍa [at each successive level].
It should be twice as high as its width; within these various heights and widths, one should adopt whichever is desired.
The thickness of the pillar should be half the width of its base;
the thickness of the capital (kapota) should be one-fourth of its width; and the thickness of the entablature (ghana) should be half its width, or alternatively, three-fourths of it.
In the center, one should avoid the pillar and the lintel, and instead construct a lattice-work;
that which is joined with paired feet is called a *yugmaka* (*pena*).
The sixfold [types of] *jālaka* are: *gonetra*, *hastinetra*, *nandyāvarta*, *ṛjukriyā*, *puṣpaghaṇḍa*, and *rasakaṇṭha*. || 9 ||
A long quadrangular opening in the throat is designated as "ox-eye" (gonetra);
a quadrangular opening in the throat is declared to be "elephant-eye" (hastinetra). (10)
When the five-threaded cord, having been made by way of circumambulation,
forms a gap resembling a flower, it is declared to be a *nandyāvarta*.
Straightness, the *saṃbhaka*, the two [types of] *jālaka*, that which is straight in action, the *puṣpakhaṇḍa*, the *karṇa*, and a form like the *nandyāvarta*. || 12 ||
The pillar-joinery and the door-panel situated outside the middle of the wall may consist of either a pair or a single panel,
capable of being closed or opened by means of a bolt.
One should construct the lattice-work for the assembly halls and other structures using the middle measurement;
the lattice-work may be made of iron, wood, lotus-stones, or bricks.
One should apply that substance, which is of three kinds, to that very place;
thus indeed is the lattice described, followed by the characteristics of the archway (toraṇa).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Net," in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*. 12.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the archways (toraṇas). When the height of the pillar is divided into ten parts, the height of the base (caraṇa) shall consist of seven parts.
The remainder is declared to be the portion for the qualities (guṇas), measured according to the [total] height;
in the ninth part, the height of the foot is one-quarter, while the length of the foot is six parts.

The remainder is known as the height of the *jhaṣa* (the fish-base); the height of the pedestal (*vāṅghri*) is one-eighth [of the total], the height of the foot (*caraṇa*) is one-fifth, and the height of the *jhaṣa* itself is one-third. (3)

The width [of the arch] at the base of the toraṇa is fourfold: it may be half the height, or equal to the height, or five times the height, or six times the height. Thus, the breadth is of four kinds.
A toraṇa should be constructed by this same procedure either in the middle of palaces, pavilions, and the like, or on the exterior of the walls.
First is the arch known as *patra*, the second is the *makara* arch, and the third is named *citra*;
such is the threefold form of the arch.
That which has the form of a half-moon and is adorned with leaves and other ornaments is called a *patratoraṇa*; after that, the *makara* is described.
It is endowed with five faces, with makara-muzzles on its sides,
joined in the center by a stream of feces, and adorned with various kinds of creepers.
Adorned with various ornaments and provided with arches shaped like sea-monsters (makaras),
that very [structure] was situated between the two sides of his city.
The face should be fashioned with a beak-like snout and mouths of spirits and vidyādharas;
the protective wall [of the temple] should be adorned with lions, elephants, serpents, swans, and the like, and with garlands of pearls.
Adorned with various other wonderful designs and jeweled bands, this shall be the "Variegated Arch" (citratoraṇa); thus the triad of arches is described.
The wise should apply the arches (toraṇas) below the upper part;
the height of the base (pāda) shall be two parts out of five, six, or seven divisions, while the tip of the arch (toraṇāgra) shall be one part. (12)
The remainder is known as the *pādodaya* [type]; thus this may be variegated (*citra*), or it may consist of eight squares, or it may be circular with arch-shaped pillars.
It may be provided with a water-pot, a decorative border, and so forth, either devoid of a *bodhikā* or accompanied by a *bodhikā*,
and likewise endowed with a *vīrakāṇḍa*.
O best of the twice-born, it is said that the width of the base of the arch (toraṇa) should be half the width of the wall or pillar, or three-quarters, or equal to it. || 15 ||
Having consecrated the northern vessel, the vessel with the lotus, and the vessel for the *kudrava* grain in their proper order according to this rite, the wise man [should proceed]. (16)
The archway (toraṇa) should have wide pillars, or it may have three feet with the northern side rising;
the height of the fillet (ājana) should be half of that, and the height of the petal (dala) should be half of that [fillet].
The *dalordhvākṣepaṇa* is well known; half of that is the *kṣudravājana*.
The *uttara* should be above the *bodhika*, or it may be on the *vīrakāṇḍa*. (18)
At the end of the junction (utsandhya), one should fashion a makara-pedestal with its front sloping downward;
it should be as wide as the top of the archway and half the height of the wall and pillars.
The top of the architrave (toraṇāgraka) should be at the width between two walls or pillars,
or at the end of the leg-like staffs (aṅghrivetra), or even more than a daṇḍa beyond that.
Thus, the fourfold type known as the broad arch-top has been described;
the wall-arch and the door-arch are now declared.
The width [of the arch] should be equal to the height of the door; the space between the feet of the architrave should be even;
and there should be a lintel, a base, a lotus-pedestal, and the eight auspicious symbols.
Construct a lintel (phalaka) adorned with five faces according to the previously mentioned rule;
it may be of the leaf-pattern (patrākhyam), the crocodile-pattern (makarākhyam), or even a variegated archway (citratoraṇam). || 23 ||
In the middle and above, it is joined with a trident and provided on both sides with a mirror,
a full water-pot, a bull, and a pair of chowries.
The Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, the conch, the lamp, and the eight auspicious objects of the gods;
one should place the Śrīvatsa in the center, while the remaining ones are on its two sides.
The door-architrave (toraṇa) should be constructed from iron, wood, or stone;
indeed, such a door-architrave is also called a pillar-architrave (staṃbhatoraṇa). || 26 ||
Divide the height of the pedestal into three parts; two parts shall be the elevation of the base (caraṇa), and one part, joined with all its limbs, should be made devoid of the *bodhikā*.
The upper vessel is shaped like a lotus-bowl and is concave;
above that, there is a section shaped like a fish, adorned with various wonderful patterns.
The archway known as Makara, however, has two necks at the base of the stalk;
joined with the self of the sky, fire, and wind, this shall be the pillar-archway.
In all temples, it should be made either between the feet, or on the necklace, in the middle of the ear-pavilion, or within the central space of the hall.
The pillar and the architrave have been described; now hear the rule for the water-pot and the creeper.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter on the characteristics of the architrave in the *Aṃśumat* of the *Kāśyapa*. 13.
Now I shall explain in detail the ritual for the "Pot-Creeper" (kumbhalatā); listen.
One should arrange a lotus seat upon the altar at the base of the pillar.

The height should be equal to the width of the base; the lotus [pedestal] should extend seven parts, and its height should be one-eighth of the height of the plinth (vasudhā). This is declared to be the measurement for the *kampa*. || 2 ||
The lower lotus is three parts, while the neck is said to be one part;
the upper lotus is two parts, and one should fashion the *kampa* with one part.
Above that, the height of the pitcher (kumbha) should be equal to the height of the lotus;
I declare that the diameter of the pitcher should be twice its height.
The pitcher (kuṃbha) has a pillar-like projection (staṃbhaniryūha) joined with a circular creeper-pattern (vallīmaṇḍala),
equipped with the pitcher-base and other ornaments, and devoid of the hero-stalk (vīrakāṇḍa).
One should fashion a lotus upon the *phalaka* according to the measurement of the *kumbha*;
for each *kumbha*, this creeper is prescribed, though it is described differently by the wise in other cases.
That very [pillar], when provided with a *vīrakāṇḍa* above the *utsandhi*,
but devoid of a *bodhikā*, is known as the *staṃbhakuṃbhalatā*.
O twice-born one, a creeper-arch (toraṇalatā) should be fashioned at the top like a pillar-arch;
thus, according to the threefold rule, the pitcher-creeper (kuṃbhalatā) is described.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Kumbha-creeper," in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*. 14.
Now I shall explain specifically the characteristics of the *vṛtta-sphuṭita* [type of drum], beginning at six finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step. (1)
The width [of the base] extends up to six types, measured in units of finger-breadths (kalāṅgula);
its height, however, is half the width, or two-thirds, or one-third of it. || 2 ||
The archway (toraṇa) should be circular in shape and as long as the base;
above that, it should be provided with a neck (sakandhara) or else be adorned with a gargoyle (śukanāsa).
Alternatively, one may fashion the *karṇa* (corner) in the shape of a peak or a circular form;
it should be two parts in length at the base, within the four-part height of the pillar.

The height of the *prastara* (pedestal) shall be one part, and the height of the *śukanāsa* (frontal projection) shall be one part; that indeed is the measurement of the *kūṭa* (pinnacle), according to the conclusion stated for each respective case.
Alternatively, construct an inner platform according to the prescribed method;
it should indeed be circular, hollowed out, and adorned with a circle of creepers.

O twice-born one, one should likewise fashion the archway known as the pillar (staṃbha), as well as the jar and the creeper (kumbha-latā); and one should arrange the circular (vṛtta) and the cracked (sphuṭita) forms within the intervals of the pearl necklaces (hārāntara).
Or it should be performed on a pillar, especially for palaces and the like.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Cracked Circular [Structures]," in the *Aṃśumat* of Kāśyapa.
Now I shall specifically describe the characteristics of the arrangement of the door:
having divided the height of the base (pāda) into ten parts, the pure door (śuddhadvāra) consists of nine parts.
The base (caraṇa) is to be divided into nine parts, and the measurement of the door is eight parts; alternatively, the height of the pedestal (āghrika) is divided into eight parts.
The measurement of the door shall be seven parts; the remainder, when divided by six, shall constitute the height of the serpent-base (bhuvaṅga) above, consisting of three and a half parts.
Below the pinnacle (pataṅga), however, it is said to be two and a half parts;
the height of the pure doorway (śuddhadvāra) is half [of that], and the width of the pure doorway is [the same].
The width [of the pedestal] should be one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine finger-breadths;
it may be more or less than half the height, up to nineteen [finger-breadths].
Thus, the division is declared to be threefold, and the height of the door should likewise be threefold;
for all types of mansions, the door should be placed in the middle.
The width of the door-assembly (dvārayoga) should be one and a quarter, or one and a half, times the thickness of the base; half of that is said to be its depth.
Or else, the height [of the pedestal] should be one-eighth, half, or three-quarters of its width;
however, for the yoga-tuṅga, it should be one part out of four parts of the combined measurement.

The portion of the qualities (guṇāṃśa) is known as moving upwards; the outer lotus is joined with the throw (kṣepaṇa). The outer lotus, endowed with the throw, is conjoined with the star situated on the earth.
The *pataṅgatāra* is equal to the *yoga* but devoid of the *abja*;
the *bhuvaṅga* and the *pataṅga* are situated in the middle and endowed with a circle (*valaya*).
Alternatively, two copper rings or two rings made of wood, bound with pins, should be inserted into the junction of the tip [of the tongue], which occupies one-third of its width. (11)
And [the two syllables] śailaja and bhuvaṅga, joined with the peak of the foremost yoga;
and [the two syllables] bhuvaṅga and pataṅga, joined with the entry into the tips of the apertures.
Having thus made it firm,
one should thereafter perform the installation of the yoga on an auspicious lunar mansion, on a favorable day, and at a propitious hour for the fire-oblation (homa).
O Brahmin, one should establish the yoga preceded by a peace-offering (śānti-homa);
when the width of the wall is divided into five parts, the [central] portion ending with the fifth part is formed by two [parts].
The middle extent of the yoga is the boundary of seven parts within;
outside that and also within, the expansion of the yoga rests upon the [preceding] measure.
Having established and made firm the yoga joined with all ornaments,
they subsequently resorted to the yoga at the two side-panels of the door.
O Brahmin, having made the door-panel firm, one should remain inside for one fortnight, or two or three fortnights, or even until the end of the autumn season.
These two [pillars] stand between the three central pillars, rising upwards and downwards;
they are bound to the outer and inner pillars by means of smooth, solid wooden beams.
Or [the number of sticks] may be three, five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen, or seventeen; or there may be a single stick on one side, with the total number being as specified.
In the same way, it should be made firm on both sides with iron bolts;
on the left side, however, one should attach a strong leather strap to the door-panel.
The width of the door-slab (dvārapaṭṭikā) should be three, four, or five units;
one-third of that measurement is declared to be its nīvrā (projection).

That [measurement] is known as the *nīvrā*, which is double the *nīvra*; it is indeed located on the two door-panels (*kavāṭa*), at the front of the panels, in the middle, and on the sides of the left wooden strips.
The iron [stake] should be provided with a ring; the Vetāla [stake] is bound with a wooden pin.
Furthermore, the outer and inner staffs may be made of either iron or wood. (23)
Their width shall be three finger-breadths, with half that thickness for the bolt, joined with solid metal;
having fashioned two door-panels, they should be made firm with wood and iron.
One should employ an unobserved machine for locking and unlocking that is equipped with bolts and other such parts, capable of locking and unlocking those of others.
One should perform this likewise in a palace, a pavilion, and a gate-tower; thus the door has been fully described. Now hear about the "trembling door. || 26 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter on the characteristics of the major marks in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*. 16.
Now I shall specifically describe the supreme procedure for the doorways of the kūpa (well) in the four cardinal and intermediate directions of temples, pavilions, and other structures.
O best of the twice-born! Between those two, or indeed wherever Homa and Abhīṣṭa may be, one should properly construct the Kaṃpa-door right there.
That which is constructed with cloth-patterns, having a wide extent arranged in rows,
should extend from the vessel to the northern boundary, with the emergence of the door of the archway.
Having made the bhūmaṅga and pataṅga yogas extended and firm as before,
and having bound them very tightly, one should join the intervals of the feet.
Having made the distance between the feet long through the practice of yoga,
one should then place the two hands at the base and the tips [of the feet] and form the *tārāṅghri* posture.
One should join it firmly at the joints, the wings, and the hollows,
using four, five, six, eight, ten, or even twelve [pieces].
Or one may imagine sixteen such [lotuses] within the feet, arranged one after another,
capable of supporting the coming and going [of the breath], provided there is no excessive interval between them.
One should join the inner door-posts (antarāṃghris) and fix them like a door-joint;
one should then join the two door-panels (kavāṭas), either individually or with the void (vyoma).
One should fashion the door-panel as two voids and the mouth as the three voids and the *grava* (or *grasa*),
making the door very firm so that it cannot be moved even by an elephant.
The door with the pivot has been fully described; now hear about the lintel.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Pivoted Door," in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] by Kāśyapa. 17.

Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the *prastara* (the uppermost tier): its height should be half that of the pillar, or equal to the measurement of the *mañca*, or indeed one part of the total height.
That [height] being divided into twenty-one parts, the *tara* (the interval) consists of three parts;
the *vājana* (the weight-projection) is one part, and the *bhūtamālā* (the garland of elements) extends over three parts.
Above the *bhūtamāla*, however, there is a *vājana* of one part;
the height of the *kapota* is seven parts, and the *āliṅga* is of one part. (3)

One should make the recessed portion (antarita) one part, the height of the counter-projection (pratyutsedha) three parts, and the base-molding (vājana) one part; or else, it may be made according to another method.
One should make the *tuṅga* nineteen parts increased by three; the *vājana* should be made with one part, and it should be adorned with three fire-parts (three parts). || 5 ||
The *vājana* should be made with one part, the height of the *kapota* with six parts, and the *āliṅga* with one part; it should be so constructed that there is an intervening space.
The projection (pratyutsedha) shall be two parts, while the fillet (vājana) shall be one part;
thus the height is described, and now the neck-ornament (aṅganīvrata) is discussed.
From the pillar, however, the *bodhikā* beam rises; likewise, the *bodhikā* is higher than that.
The projection of the *vājana* (frieze) extends outward, and the *vājana* is elevated above the *uttarā* (upper beam).
The *vājana* (cornice) and the *nīvraka* (frieze) should resemble a high *valabhī* (pavilion roof);
they may be three-quarters of that height or half, while the *vājana-nīvraka* is as described previously.
The sacrificial fee (*vājana*) for the dove consists of the *nīvra* at the conclusion of the oblation;
or it may extend to the edge of the *upānasī*, or to the end of the *jagatī*, or even beyond that. (10)
The *vājana* [should be] half a *daṇḍa*, or two *daṇḍas*, or two and a half *daṇḍas*;
the *kapota* [should be] equal to the height of the *nivra* plus the *cālaṅghana*. || 11 ||
The *kapota* (dove-shaped molding), whether accompanied by a *gopāna* (ridge-pole) or devoid of a *gopāna*, is said to be equal to the outer base; it is called the *āliṅga*. || 12 ||

The *āliṅga* should have its width concealed; the *nīvraka* should be equal to the height [of the base]; the *vājana* is said to be equal to the height of the *vājana* itself; and such is the projection of the *vājana*. (13)
The staff should be three-quarters or half [the length of the body], and its upper part should be covered.
The covering should be in accordance with the upper garment, and it should be tucked into the waistband.
One should decorate the uppermost part with haṃsas (swans) and other figures serving as *valabhīs* (pinnacles),
and on the *kapota* (cornice) one should fashion *karṇapālikās* (ear-ornaments) using various leaf and creeper designs.
O best of the twice-born! Thus is described the group of stone ornaments, beginning with the *kakarī* (arch) and the *pratisiṃha*, and so forth. 16.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sacrificial Grass," in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*. 18.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the neck-ornament;
the measurement of the neck is declared to be elevated at the top and high. (1)
O best of the twice-born! The measurement of the neck may be one part of the total height of the sanctum;
its height, or the elevation of the pedestal (vedikā), may be three, four, or five parts.
The remainder is known as the emergence of the neck (galodaya), or the entire [height] may be the emergence of the neck;
the width of the pedestal (vedikā) should be four, five, or six parts.
The width of the bolt (argala) is three, four, or five [units], and their number follows that sequence respectively;
the entry [of the bolt] into the foot is two [units], and its entry into the pedestal (vedi) is four [units]. This is the entry of the bolt into the pedestal.
The entry into the throat of the foot of the Vedyapada may be three-quarters of it or half of that;
thus one should determine it according to the will of the practitioner amidst its many varieties.

In the Nāgara style, the neck should be quadrangular; in the Drāviḍa style, it should be octagonal; and in the Vesara temple, the neck should be circular; one should thus fashion it in accordance with the remaining [architectural] rules.
In the [eastern] direction, it should be joined with the Bhadra [moulding], with the neck following the profile of the nose;
the height of the neck should be two parts of the sun (twelve parts), while the rise of the neck itself is one part.
The height of the upper molding (uttarocca) should be one part, while the vājana should be one part;
the measurement of the valabhī should be three parts, and the height of the vājana should be one part.
In the upper half, the neck (nīvra) and the mouldings such as the fillet (vājana) are as described previously;
alternatively, the emergence of the neck is said to be one part (bhāga).
The height of the *uttarocca* (upper part) should be one part of the [total] dimensions, or one part of Śiva;
above that, the height of the *muṣṭibandha* (fist-binding) is declared to be one and a half parts.
The *mṛṇālī* should be one part high, while the *guṇāṃśa* (string-section) should be one part; the *paṭṭikā* (band) should be one part.
The height of the *daṇḍikā* (staff) should be one and a half parts, and the *varṇapaṭṭikā* (color-band) should be one part. (11)
One should cause the *gopānas* (rafters) to rise upward, or indeed perform the mounting of the *lupā*;
the *vājana* and other elements should extend outward, each being equal in height to the one preceding it.
Thus have the height of the neck, its width, and its ornamentation been described.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Neck Ornaments," in the *Aṃśumat* by Kāśyapa.
Now I shall specifically describe the characteristics of the spire (śikhara):
the height of the spire should be equal to the height from the ground level to the top of the base.
The height of the pinnacle (śikhara) should be one part out of the total height of the structure,
or the pigeon-niche (kapotaka) of the pinnacle should be equal in width to the base-moulding (vedī).
The roof-ridge (nīvr̥), the eaves (valabhī), or the beam (daṇḍa) should be one and a half [units];
or the nīvr̥ and the supporting beam (ālambana) may be two daṇḍas or two and a half daṇḍas, being equal [in measure].
The *kapota* (dove-cornice) should be as high as the *nīvraka* and shaped like a *valabhī-vājana*;
the *tāra* (beam) should be at the top of the *kapota*, and the *valabhī-vājana* should be level with it.
On the summit, the middle width should be similar to that at the end of the *kapota* (dove-cot);
thus, the *vātāra* is of four kinds, namely three-quarters, one-half, and one-quarter [of the base]. || 5 ||
In that regard, the *tāra* (spire) shall have five parts, while the *balika* (neck) and *vistara* (base) shall each have three parts.
At the summit (*śikhara*), the location for the *balikā* occurs at the fifth part, while the emergence of the head (*śirodaya*) occurs at the ninth part.
At the conclusion of each Vedic section, however, there is a circular shape for the *balika*;
its thickness shall be one-fourth of that diameter.
One should arrange them symmetrically on all sides, either in pairs or in even numbers;
and below and above the *balikās*, one should place a bamboo pole measuring half that size.
In the portion consisting of the back, the width, and the earth-element (kavyāsabhūtāṃśa), the extent of the lotus is one-fourth (yugāṃśa);
the height of the lotus is declared to be up to the measurement of the pinnacle (śikhara).
The width of the lotus is one-third [of the total height]; the dome (stūpī) is as wide as the pitcher (kumbha);
the width of the pitcher is one-third [of its own height]; and below the pitcher is the neck-band (balagnaka).
One-third of the circumference of the waist is the neck above the pitcher (kumbha);
the neck is three times that, and its bud (kuḍmala) is one-third of the circumference of the base (pālita).
Make the neck broad at its base and large at the top;
from the middle of the head down to the waist, make it gradually slender.
From the middle, make it gradually thinner until it reaches the width of a thumb;
from there, make it wider again in the sequence of the pigeon's neck.
Half of the height of the pinnacle (śikhara) shall be the elevation of the stūpikā above the lotus;
one should divide that height into twenty-two parts using a unit equal to half the measurement of the lotus.

The lower *kaṃpa* is said to be half a unit (*ardhāṃśa*), and the neck (*gala*) is likewise measured at half a unit; the upper *kaṃpa* is equal to that, and one should fashion the lotus (*padma*) with one unit (*aṃśa*).
The *bhūtabhāga* should be the height of the pot; the *kaṃpa* should be made with a measure of half a part.
The lotus should be made with one part, and the *kaṃpa* with a measure of half a part. (16)
The neck of the *pālikā* should be five parts; the *kampa* is said to be half a part.
A lotus should be made with half [of that], while the height of the *pālikā* is one [unit].
Half [of the height] is for the lotus, half for the *kaṃpa*, and the remainder is for the bud;
the *kumbha* should be shaped like a pinnacle, and the *pālikā* likewise has the form of a bud.
In the Nāgara style, the pinnacle (śiraḥ) is square in appearance; in the Drāviḍa style, it is octagonal;
and the Vesaraharmya is circular, with each succeeding style following its respective form in sequence.
One should beautifully adorn the pinnacle with various kinds of creepers and climbing plants.
The characteristics of the pinnacle have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the nose.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Peak," in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of the *Kāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe specifically the supreme characteristics of the nose:
the forehead and the nose are said to be like the peak and the pinnacle [of a temple]. (1)
The width of the pinnacle (śikhara), when divided by three, four, or five,
results respectively in the large, medium, and small portions for the excellent, middling, and inferior [types].
That which is known as Mahānāsī is proclaimed to be of three kinds:
equal [in height], three-quarters, or half [the height] of the pinnacle; it is the nose-like projection from the top.
That [measurement] should be reduced by three or four parts;
the remainder is designated as the height of the neck above [the base], or alternatively, it may be the height at its center.
Above that, however, the Śaktidhvaja (the spear-banner) should be half the height of the nose, or one-third, or even one-ninth of its height. || 5 ||
The height of the flagstaff should be equal to that [height], divided into nine parts;
two parts constitute the face of the *kiṃpuruṣa* (the figure at the top), and the remaining portion is the measurement for the neck.
The staff should have its tip curved; the face of the *kiṃpuruṣa* should be double [the size of the base].
Above the spear and the banner, there should be a leaf or else a trident.
The height of the *kiṃpuruṣa* face should be equal to the rise of the *śūla*;
if the leaf is made according to that measurement, it will possess beauty.
The width of the face-band (mukhapaṭṭī) should be half of the middle staff, or even less;
one should decorate the face-band with vine-patterns, circles, and various other designs.
The *mukhapaṭṭī* is specifically described as being deeply immersed;
it resembles a cloth spread over one who is lying down or sitting, and is adorned with lotus stalks and the like.

It may have the appearance of a palace or a mansion, with a floor free of defects, containing wild beasts and water for recreation; or it may be adorned with garlands, gabled chambers, storehouses, and the like, resembling a celestial chariot.
Alternatively, the top of the archway may be called *citrapatra* (variegated-leaf) and shaped like a *makara*;
it should be adorned with auspicious designs, possess great nostrils, and be beautiful in its feet and all its limbs.
(65) Having specifically fashioned the upper part of the lotus-face, the nose and so forth, and the hands and other parts according to their measurements. || 13 ||
Above, it should be as wide as the nose-pillar, or three-quarters of its width, or even half;
it should rise up as far as the upper limit of the neck.
Its shape may be square, circular, or shaped like a yoke;
it should be two or three daṇḍas in width from the nose.

The remaining portion should be narrow at the base and broad at the top; there should be no outer boundary line at its summit. Between the two feet of the nose, perform the installation of the deities representing the cardinal directions.
This has been declared regarding the Mahānāsī; now hear the procedure for the Kṣudranāsī.
It should be one and a half daṇḍas, two daṇḍas, or [three] daṇḍas in width.
The *tattāra* (the width of the neck) should be three-fourths less than the remaining height;
one should then determine the height of the nose and the level of the *kakṣa* (armpit) based on the support of the *kapota* (dove-cot).
One should extend the limit of the *prativājana* up to the raised banner;
having divided that height into three parts, one part is the measurement for the neck (*kaṇṭha*).
The remainder should be brought to the height of the *kiṃpuruṣa*-face by means of logical proportion.
The nose should extend to half the depth of the *sītā*, and half of that depth should be the *mukhapaṭṭikā*.
Vyāsa should be adorned with creepers and the like, endowed with various ornaments;
one should fashion the shape of a svastika for each of the pigeon-foot [footprints].
In the middle of the gabled halls (kūṭaśālā), one should especially fashion small nose-projections (nāsikā) within the lattice-work (pañjara),
and on the spire (śikhara), large nose-projections (bhadranāsikā).
The nose called Lalāṭā should be made at the two tips of the śālā;
one should fashion the nose called Mahānāsā in the place of the pañjara.
The characteristics of the nose and likewise the measurement of the temple have been declared.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of the Nose, in the *Aṃśumat* of the *Kāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe in detail the characteristics of the measurements of the temple (prāsāda);
[it is called] prāsāda, sadana, sadma, harmya, dhāma, and niketana.
A temple, a palace, an extensive mansion, a divine celestial chariot, a dwelling, a refuge, and indeed a beautiful support. || 2 ||
The terms *āśāma*, *avrata*, and *dhiṣṇya* are synonyms for this [atom].
Because there is nothing subtler than it, it is called the "paramāṇu" (the ultimate atom). || 3 ||
Eight *aṇu*s make one *rathāreṇu*; eight *rathāreṇu*s make one *picu*;
and eight *picu*s are known by the name *keśāgra*. (4)
For children, that [measurement] would be excessive; therefore, the tip [of the hair] is prior to its shaving.
It is taught that one should mark eight such tips of hair as the "likhya" (the measurable unit).
Eight *līkhyās* make one *yūka*; eight *yūkas* become one *yava*.
A measure (*māna*) eight times that of a *yava* is declared to be an *aṅgula*. (6)
A descent of seven finger-breadths is called the middle finger-measure;
a descent of six finger-breadths is traditionally known as the inferior finger-measure.
A length of four śāli-finger-breadths is designated as "superior" (uttama);
a length of three and a half śāli-finger-breadths is designated as "middling" (madhyama). || 8 ||
The inferior [measure] is declared to be three times that length of the śāli;
likewise, there are the white śāli, the great śāli, and the red śāli.
The *saugandhī*, *hemaśālī*, and other rice varieties are known to be fivefold;
among these, one should select the long red rice (*raktaśālī*), measuring half a finger-breadth in length.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the sixfold *mānāṅgula* has been declared;
the space occupied by the moon and the sky is called the one-finger measure (*ekāṅgula*).
The eyelashes are Aśvinī; the second finger is known as Bharaṇī; the time is Kṛttikā; the rudrākṣa is Rohiṇī; the trident is Mṛgaśiras; the stylus is Ārdrā; and the string is Punarvasu. || 12 ||
Those known as the third finger [the ring finger] increase by four, four, two, and one; those known as the fourth finger [the little finger] increase by five, five, five, and four. (13)
The designations for five fingers are indeed *ṛtu*, *ṣaṭka*, and *auśika*;
those for six fingers are *rasa*, *gāyatrī*, and *kṛttikā*.
The Pātāla and Ṛṣidhātu are designated as seven finger-breadths each;
likewise, the Mātṛloka and Svara are also designated as seven finger-breadths.
The elephant, the mountain, the serpent, and likewise the Vasus as embodied forms—these are the designations for the eight fingers, as well as the spear, the door, and the planets. (16)
The *sūtranandana*, the *nāṭya*, and the *bīja* measures are nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each;
the *nāḍikā*, *aṣṭhāyudha*, and *dharma* are designated as ten finger-breadths.
Īśāna, Īśvara, and Rudra are known as eleven finger-breadths (ekādaśāṅgula);
Abda, Bhāra, and Bhānu are designated as twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśāṅgula).
Those called the thirteen-finger [measurements] consist of the portions of Candra, Āditya, and Śiva;
likewise, those called the fourteen-finger [measurements] consist of two Ṛṣis and a Manu.
The fortnight (pakṣa) and the lunar day (tithi) are each recorded as fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
the pair consisting of the digit (kalā) and the form (mūrti) is designated as sixteen finger-breadths.
Twenty, thirty, and likewise forty;
fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, and one hundred. (21)
Pratyaya, Triṣṭubh, Ṣaṣṭi, Jagatī, Sugati, Śakvarī, Saśakvarī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Dhṛti; || 22 ||
And Sudhṛti; these names, beginning with ten and ending with a hundred, are to be sung:
one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, and likewise ten thousand. (23)
Niyuta, prayuta, koṭī, arbuda, bṛnda, kharvinī, kharva, śaṅkha, padma, samudra, madhyama, and tara. (24)
The first, the next, and the highest [measures] are proclaimed by increasing tenfold;
or else, through other superior, middling, and inferior [proportions], the *tāla* shall be twelve finger-breadths (*bhānu-aṅgula*). (25)
O twice-born one, two *bhānu*s (twelve fingers) constitute an *aṅgula*; four *aṅgulas* are called a *kiṣku*, and four *kiṣkus* are called a *hasta*.
Thus, the *hasta* is prescribed to be fashioned according to the best, middling, or lowest measurements.
The staff (daṇḍa) should consist of four [units]; by that one should measure the site.
The wise man should know the Prājāpatya hand to be twenty-five mātras.
The Dhanurmuṣṭi is twenty-six [aṅgulas], the Dhara is twenty-seven,
the Prācya is twenty-eight aṅgulas, and the Vaideha is twenty-nine.
The width is thirty finger-breadths and the length is thirty-one;
thus, O best of the twice-born, there are eight types of cubits, each distinct. (29)
Thus, according to the division of inferior, middling, and superior, one should begin the houses of the twice-born with two [types] each, using the *dhanurgraha* and *prakīrṇaka* [plans]. (30)
With the *vaipulya* and *dhaurmuṣṭi* meters, compose the *gṛha* for the Kṣatriyas;
likewise, the *prājāpatya* is for the Karas, and the *vaideha* is suitable for the Vaiśyas. (31)

A staff measuring one *kiṣku* (forearm) in length is suitable for the Śūdra caste; for those of higher castes, the staff should be one *hasta* long, while for those of lower castes, it should be less than that. Thus one should assign them accordingly.
A hand of low birth brings misfortune, while a superior hand brings auspiciousness;
a hand that is elevated is honored in every home. (33)
Furthermore, one should honor other deities in their appropriate abodes;
or else, [the measurement] of one cubit and a half (kikṣuhasta) may be suitable for all castes.
One should measure vehicles and beds with the *kikṣu* hand, but parks, gardens, and dwellings with the *prājāpatya* hand. (35)
One should measure villages and the like by the span of a bow-grip;
likewise, one should measure ponds and such, as well as rivers and roads, by the length of a drawn bow.
O best of the twice-born, for all types of sites,
one should begin with three or four cubits and increase by two cubits at a time.
The end of the nine rows shall indeed be a single level of illumination;
thus the eightfold measurement consists of pairs and non-pairs, four by four.
Starting from five or six cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time, up to eleven cubits—
the Ābhāsa [temple] is thus eightfold, with two types for each.
Beginning from seven or eight cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time, up to fifteen cubits,
there are ten types of *ābhāsa* temples with three stories.
Beginning with the ritual of the planets, there are seven or eight additional rows;
or else, they may be four or five stories high, and those [pillars] are ten in number, both even and odd.
O best of the twice-born! having divided the width into seven, six, and five parts, one should decrease it by portions of six, five, and four respectively from the width.
O twice-born one, in the case of a temple with an image, the height should be declared as fivefold: twice the width, plus one-eighth more. (43)

Pacifying (śāntika), enriching (pauṣṭika), victorious (jayada), and likewise marvelous (adbhuta), as well as that which fulfills all desires (sārvakāmika)—these shall be the names in their respective order. (44)
If the hand is increased by one, or otherwise, one should perform the full [measurement];
this is declared to be the Ābhāsa type of mansion. Now listen to the description of the Vikalpa. || 45 ||
Starting from nine rows and ending at fifty-six hands,
there are twenty-four [varieties] by increasing the number of hands two at a time.
Starting from the five levels up to the surface of the sun, there are three divisions of the ground in sequence: inferior, middling, and superior. || 47 ||
Starting from a row of seven or eight and increasing by three cubits at each step,
the height— calculated as before— reaches eighty, with increments of six, seven, or eight.
Thus the classification has been explained; now hear concerning the path of desire (chanda-mārga), which begins at thirteen cubits and increases by two cubits at each stage. (49)
Its width is sixty-five or sixty-six cubits, and its length is twenty-seven cubits,
beginning from the ground of the Vedas and ending at the ground of the Sun (Bhānu).
The measurements for the base, middle, and superior [altars] should be determined according to the palm-span (tala);
they range from seven, eight, and ten cubits (hasta), increasing by three cubits each time.
From ninety-five up to one hundred and five, according to the same numerical sequence as before,
there are the three grades of height— low, medium, and superior— measured from the base.
Thus has *Chanda* been fully described; now hear concerning the *Jātiharmya*.
It begins with seven, eight, or ten cubits, increasing by two cubits each time. (53)
p. 72) Starting from twenty-seven [units] up to seventy cubits, beginning from the fourth level (bhūmi) as far as the solar level (arkatala). 54.
The width has been declared; now hear, O observer of good vows, about the height:
starting from twenty-one cubits, it increases by three cubits at each step.
Up to a height of one hundred cubits, according to the previously mentioned numbers, the heights are declared in order as inferior, middling, and superior. (56)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the pride of birth has been explained as twenty-sevenfold, along with the conceptualization of the desire for birth, by means of its manifestation.
The large, the intermediate-small, and the small are mentioned in sequence by name;
when the measurement of the *yuga* corners has been stated, one should then lay down the measuring cord (*mānasūtra*).
In the case of mansions shaped like a half-moon, the filling of the moats occurs at the four corners;
wherever it is excluded, that is prescribed as the *mānasūtra*.
The width of the palaces, however, should be measured either from the outside of the wall-base,
or up to the end of the inner side of that base, or indeed to the middle of that base.

The height [of the structure] extends from its base, including the plinth and so forth, up to the pinnacle or the top of the head; for assembly halls, pavilions, and halls, it extends from the middle of the wall to its termination.
The pillar may be centered within the wall, or on the outside of it, or in the middle, or even inside;
the two pillars may be situated on the outside of the wall, or on the outside, or even inside.
O best of the twice-born! Then, the measuring line for the mind (mānasūtra) should extend from the middle of the feet to the end;
on the width of the wall, it should go out by twelve parts, and then by one part. (63)

O best of the twice-born! Having set aside the inner portion consisting of one yuga (four parts), the remainder is declared to be the middle wall, which has the width of one *aṅghri* (one-sixteenth part) at the location of the *aṅghri*.
Alternatively, it is stated that the foot [of the pillar] should extend beyond the wall;
or else, for the halls, it may be placed within the wall, outside the wall, or even inside.
The line between the middle of the feet of vehicles and beds is called the *mānasūtra*;
this *mānasūtra* is declared for all dwellings and the like.
Outside the Mānasūtra, however, there is the enclosure consisting of the gables, halls, and so forth;
the width of the gable is said to be equal to the [main] hall, or three-quarters, or even half.
The projection [of the spire] beyond the mental line (mānasūtra) shall be one-quarter, or one-and-a-quarter, of the height;
alternatively, the projection of the kūṭa and other elements may be according to the measure of the shaft (daṇḍa). 68.
The [projection] outside the mental cord (mānasūtra) may be one daṇḍa, or one and a half daṇḍas, or two daṇḍas, or one and a half times two daṇḍas, or three daṇḍas. || 69 ||
The abode of pride is always the seat of calamities within;
therefore, with every effort, one should remain outside the thread of pride.
This is the thread for the layout, or it may be an equal thread, or indeed even; the thread that has gone outside the sacrificial fire-altar is declared to be the final limit.
The sūtra for the placement of men and its conclusion are declared to be threefold; O Brahmins, listen briefly to the characteristics of the āyādi.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, concerning the characteristics of the Mānādi-sūtra, in the Āṃśumatī-kāśyapa [Tantra]. 22.
Now I shall explain specifically the supreme characteristics of longevity and so forth: one should divide the number of cubits of the mansion's width by eight, using the system of guna and vṛddhi.
The remainder shall be the flag and so forth, and the wise man should take one cubit as the height;
he should increase it by eight in the case of an increase, and by one asterism in the case of a decrease, starting from the day and the lunar mansion.
The wise man should calculate the increase of nine around the cubit and cause it to be protected by the netherworlds (pātālas);
the remainder shall be the day of the week starting from Sunday, and the multiplier for the width and length is by the qualities (guṇas).
In the case of a decrease, one should increase by thirty; the remainder is the rising of the first lunar day (pratipad).
Thus the lunar days are fully described, increasing by eight and five [respectively] during the periods of exaltation and the hand.
O twice-born one, the remainder should be removed by the divisor; this is called *āya*.
One should first multiply the *tuṅga* by nine and increase it by the increments, then divide by the *nāḍīs*.
The remainder is known as expenditure (vyaya); when income exceeds expenditure, it is loss (kṣaya).
Ketu, the lion, the bull, and the elephant are remembered as auspicious origins.
Venus, the Sun, Mercury, and Jupiter are remembered as the auspicious days;
likewise, the birth asterism of the patron and a day free from conflict [are required]. || 7 ||
The site should be favorable for one's birth and also favorable for the king;
having thus examined it in many ways, one should collect the solar measure (aṃśumāna).
Alternatively, when the width multiplied by eight is divided by twelve, the remainder is called the length (āyāma) by the wise. (9)
When [the lunar day] increases by nine, it is decreased by ten; the remainder is declared to be Vyaya. (p.
75) When the asterism is multiplied by eight and divided [by seven], the remainder is [the Nakṣatra] beginning with Aśvinī. || 10 ||
When eight [units] are subtracted from the circumference multiplied by seven, the remainder indicates the *dhvaja* (banner) and other *yoni*s;
when nine [units] are added to the circumference, one should subtract seven [units] to obtain the number of cubits.
The remainder shall be the day of the week, such as Sunday and so forth; when there is a decrease by thirty, the lunar date (tithi) is obtained through an increase of nine.
Having observed the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness as previously described, one should indeed collect the measure of the auspicious.
The pair of birth asterisms, the sixth, eighth, and ninth, when occupied by benefics, are declared to grant the attainment of desired goals; the remaining asterisms, however, are to be avoided.
O Brahmin, the wise man should count from the birth asterism of the king-founder until the final asterism of the house; let the auspicious measure be taken.

One should avoid the eighth house from the ascendant, destruction, and malefic planetary combinations. Thus has the method beginning with *āya* (income/profit) and ending with *reva* been declared; now listen to the procedure beginning with *nāgara*.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Āya and Other Factors," in the *Āditya-kāśyapa*.
The characteristics of the celestial chariots (vimānas) of the Nāgas and others shall now be described;
the region situated between the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain (Himavat) and [the other mountain] has been declared.
That region also, divided into three parts according to the qualities arising from each respective place,
is like the body of embodied beings, O Lord, consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm.
In the same way, everything to be known as the staff is composed of the three qualities;
they are traditionally taught to be of three kinds: sattvic, tāmasa, and rājasa.
Between Himādri and Siddha lie the Sāttvika regions;
from Siddha down to Kṛṣṇavarṇa, the earth is known as Tāmasa.
The ground from the black-colored [soil] up to the end of the kanyā [type] is rājasa;
the nāgara region is sāttvika, while the vesara is likewise tāmasa.
The Drāviḍa region is proclaimed as rājasa;
the Nāgara mansion is sāttvika; and the Vesara temple is tāmasa.
The Drāviḍa temple is of the nature of passion (rājasa); they are, respectively, male, neuter, and female.
Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and Dhātṛ are, respectively, the presiding deities of these temples.
One should know the Nāgara as a Brāhmaṇa, while the Vesara is said to be a Vaiśya;
the Drāviḍa, however, is to be known as a King (Kṣatriya). Listen now to their physical forms, O observer of noble vows! || 8 ||
The kūṭa and koṣṭha are situated along the line of emergence;
they possess elevations and depressions respectively, according to their sequence.
O twice-born one, it had pillars of both single and multiple slabs, was adorned with leaf-patterned arches, contained small inner chambers, and possessed large openings.
The pinnacle (kūṭa) should be provided with a railing and a lattice, with a four-cornered top; it may have one or many stories, and may or may not be provided with a portico (ālinda).
The neck [of the temple] should have the head of a deity or be shaped like a spear;
such is known as the Nāgara style of building, and it is prescribed for that region. (12)
As before, the *kūṭa* and so forth emerge from the *koṣṭha*, or rather, they extend from the *kūṭa*;
the *kūṭa* is outside the measurement-line (*mānasūtra*), while the *nīvra* is the *kūṭa* itself, which is the *koṣṭhaka*.
O best of the twice-born! The central chamber may be either *sabhadra* or *vibhadra*, or it may be like a cage (*pañjara*) according to the *mānasūtra*, resembling that which issues from the *kūṭa*.
The hall is elevated and depressed, with well-proportioned chambers in due order;
the platform is raised with intervals, and it is subsequently devoid of bedding.
On each floor, it is sequentially quadrangular, octagonal, and circular in appearance;
it is adorned with various *masūraka* ornaments, pillars, altars, lattices, and arches.
It is called *vṛtta* when it has protruding elephant-trunk-like [projections] on the dome, such as pot-shaped ornaments (*kumbha*) and so forth;
or it may be provided with small cells (*kṣudrakoṣṭha*) in the intervals between the necklaces and above.
In that very place, there may be a hand-poster (hastikuṭṭana) or a "good-nosed" [pillar], or even a small one;
it may have a base or be without a base, and it may consist of one or many stories. || 18 ||
The Drāviḍa Vimāna may have a circular head, or a circular neck, or an octagonal head, or a quadrangular head; such is the metrical form of the Drāviḍa temple. || 19 ||
One should fashion that very base for the feet in a single form;
however, within the space between the necklaces, circular, smooth, and other such features should be fashioned with particular care.
The two kūṭakoṣṭhas (gabled chambers) should be equal and provided with an intervening floor;
or the two may be deficient in having an intermediate mañca (platform), while the nīvra (pedestal/base) remains aligned on the same axis.
Within the intervals of the necklaces (hāra), one should fashion a *bhadrapañjara* or a central *kapotapañjara*, provided with intermediate moldings (*prastara*).
The top of all the ear-projections (karṇakūṭas) shall be a quadrangle;
the head [of the structure] is an octagon provided with a pedestal, while the mandala is the head and the neck.
One should fashion the head as having eight corners or the neck as having four corners;
this is known as the Drāviḍa style, as well as the Hemādikuḍmala.
Whether it has eight sides or six sides, that is called Drāviḍa;
thus, according to the rule, the Drāviḍa-ālaya is well described as being of three kinds.
In the *vesara* style, the *kūṭa*, *koṣṭha*, and so forth should have a uniform alignment of lines;
one should fashion the *karṇakūṭa* as circular in shape and provided with a pinnacle (*śira*).
The structure should be circular in the shape of a sanctum, or appearing circular on the exterior;
it should be provided with a circular neck and head, or with a pinnacle as desired.
Whether it be a *sālinda* (with a portico), a *sabhadra* (with auspicious projections), or one with a single or multiple stories; whether it be square, oblong, circular, or oval. || 28 ||
The palace may be either rectangular or circular, provided with gables, chambers, and so forth;
the gables and chambers should be arranged in sequence, being respectively elevated and depressed.
A *vesara* mansion is known as being either symmetrical, consisting of two wings (*kuṭa-koṣṭha*), or having many floors yet forming a single unit; or it may be of another type altogether.
From the base (janma) up to the dome (stūpī), the Nāgara style shall have eight corners;
the Drāviḍa temple shall have an eight-cornered head-piece (śīrṣaka) and neck (kaṇṭha). || 31 ||
A mansion (harmya) is said to be vesara, provided it has a rounded neck and a pinnacle; these [features] are prescribed for mansions that are devoid of gables (kūṭa) and inner chambers (koṣṭha).
In the Vesara style of temple, construct a base joined with various superstructures, divided at every foot, and with circular feet everywhere.
The liṅga, the pedestal, and the temple, beginning with a single story—there shall be the abundance of all prosperity for the king and for those born of the site. (34)
If it is contrary [to this], there will be misfortune, bringing fear to the king and the kingdom;
therefore, with every effort, one should practice as if belonging to a single caste.
In the Nāgara style, everything is peaceful; in the Vesara style, there are the forms of vehicles; and in the Drāviḍa temple, there shall be the Bhogavīra and the dancing [deities].
Otherwise, there would be misfortune for the builder and for the embodied beings who receive alms;
thus the ritual for Nagaras and so forth has been declared. Now listen to the ritual for the depositing of the embryo (garbha).
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter [of the Aṃśumat-kāśyapa], the section on the ritual procedures for the Nāgaras and others. 24.
Now I shall explain in detail the supreme procedure for the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa). It is said that the temple is the body; its vital breath is the embryo. (1)
O Brahmin, in a house devoid of an embryo, neither I, nor the other gods, nor even the Kutkālavana spirits will dwell; we shall certainly not reside in a house that possesses a male embryo. || 2 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the ritual placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa);
for living beings, the embryo-bestowing rite bestows prosperity, while others merely bring about prosperity. || 3 ||

The placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) should not be performed; its performance leads to the destruction of the builder. It should indeed be performed above the foundation for the welfare of the Brahmins. || 4 ||

For kings, the placement of the womb (garbha) should be above the *jagatī*; for vaiśyas, it should be above the *kumuda*; and for śūdras, it should be above the *homapada*, which brings about their prosperity.
Thus has the birth-meritorious [foundation] been described; it is placed upon the first layer of bricks on the ground, as well as in temples, pavilions, enclosures, and gate-towers.
One should cause the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) to be performed in the inner sanctum of the temple;
one should deposit the embryo in that very place where the initial laying of the bricks (iṣṭakānyāsa) was performed.
The vessel for the inner contents should be made of gold, silver, or copper— best, middling, or lowest respectively— or it may even be made of bell-metal or iron.
Starting from five finger-breadths up to twenty finger-breadths,
increasing by one finger-breadth each time, the vessel corresponds in number to the *kalās*.
For the terrestrial [deities] numbering from one up to sixteen, their respective wombs, vessels, and stars are located at the root of their own feet or at the tip thereof, according to the sequence.
The width and height of the womb-vessel (*garbhabhājana*) should be equal;
one-third of the height of the vessel shall be the height of the lid (*pidhāna*). (11)
O twice-born one, the support for the lid should extend to two or three parts of the vessel;
starting from a width of one barleycorn, it should be increased by half a barleycorn at each step.
Up to a width of eight and a half barley-corns,
one should arrange the breadth of the wall for the aforementioned types of *phelās* in successive order.

O best of the twice-born, construct twenty-five squares and so forth within the interior of the vessel; the wall of the receptacle (phelā) should be half as wide as the large [area], or it may be a single line from the wall.
One should place the root mantra beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin;
outside of that, in the sixteenth square, starting from the east and proceeding in regular order.
Having inscribed the vowels in order, beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga,
one should place gems, metals, and minerals within the interior of the vessel (phelā).
One should place lumps of clay, grains, and leaves within the womb-pit;
then, reciting the Astra-mantra, one should purify the vessel with products of the cow.
One should place a ruby (māṇikya) on the peak; that is declared to be the peak-syllable (kūṭākṣara).
One should place a diamond (vajra) on Ananta, and one should place a pearl (mauktika) on Sūkṣma.
The Śivottama [liṅga] should be made of sapphire (indranīla), while the Ekanetra [liṅga] should be of crystal;
for the Ekarudra [liṅga], it should be conch-shell, and for the Trimūrti [liṅga], it should be of topaz (puṣyarāga).
One should place a sun-gem (sūryakānta) in Śrīkaṇṭha and lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya) in Śikhaṇḍika.
Having fashioned an elephant out of gold, the wise one should place it in the syllable *A*. (20)
O best of the twice-born, one should place a skull made of silver in the letter *i*,
and a jar made of copper in the letter *u*.
One should place a khaṭvāṅga made of brass at the syllable Ṛ;
having fashioned a bull out of gold, one should place it at the kūṭākṣara (the conjunct consonant). || 22 ||
One should place black pigment (śyāma) in the letter *ā*, realgar (*manaśśilā*) in the letter *ī*,
the mark of the caste (*jātiliṅga*) in the letter *ū*, and red ochre (*gairika*) in the letter *ṛ*.
One should place Saurāṣṭra upon the letter *ḷ*, añjana upon the letter *ai*,
gorocana upon the letter *o*, and haritāla upon the *visarga*.
Recalling the respective seed-syllables (bīja), one should install them in sequence:
barley, rice, millet, sesame, and mustard.
One should fill the interior of the vessel with seven types of seeds, including mung beans;
then, place a lid over the vessel and make it very smooth and very firm.
To the north and at the front of the temple, having constructed a very beautiful water-shed (prapā) measuring five, six, or seven cubits, provided with sixteen pillars; || 27 ||
Having covered the top of the lid with a wave-patterned canopy, it should be adorned with door-arches, garlands of *darbha* grass, and other ornaments. (28)
One should construct an altar in the center, occupying one-third of the pavilion's area,
with a height of either one cubit or one palm.
O best of the twice-born, there are fire-pits all around the great quarters;
they are square, bow-shaped, circular, and lotus-shaped, respectively, starting from the east. (30)
Equipped with three girdles and provided with a navel and a yoni,
fashion the sacrificial pit and altar so that they resemble the surface of a mirror.

Then, having dismissed the artisan, the Guru, after smearing [the ground] with cow dung and decorating it with flour-powders, should perform the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) above the altar, one should cover it with four droṇas of excellent rice, as well as sesame seeds, rice grains, parched grain, darbha grass, and flowers.
Having worshipped the deities of the directions with incense, flowers, and other offerings according to their respective mantras,
one should bathe them in a vessel (phelā) using fragrant water mixed with the products of the cow (gavya).
Having tied a protective cord with thread and wrapped it in a new cloth,
one should place the basket upon the sacrificial mound while reciting the "peak-syllable" (kūṭākṣara).
Having placed eight jars all around— equipped with threads,
lids, and tufts of grass, wrapped in cloth, and filled with scented water.
Having installed and worshipped those pitchers belonging to the lords of the sciences (vidyeśas) with their respective mantras,
and having performed the five purificatory rites for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
One should perform all the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
[The materials are: fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), sacrificial porridge (caru), parched grain (lāja), sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and rice. || 38 ||
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) specifically with the six limbs beginning with the Heart and with Īśāna in due order, offering eight hundred oblations for each. (39)
Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation at the end of each substance, one should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra alone;
then one should offer the *jayādi*, the *abhyātāna*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations.

Thus, one should remain awake during the night, and at dawn, during an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation, a favorable planetary conjunction, on a favorable lunar day, and on a favorable day of the week. (41)
First, one should [worship] one's own preceptor, born into a Śaiva family, initiated into Śiva,
endowed with the two baths, and whose body has been rendered complete through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
One should properly honor the preceptor, who is clad in a white upper garment and adorned with white garlands and unguents, with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
There, one should honor the artisan with garments, ornaments, and other gifts;
then, having entered the womb-chamber, the patron, together with the preceptor and the artisans, [should proceed].
One should divide the wall into eight parts; one should discard four from the outside, or three from the inside, and place the vessel in the remaining portion.
The preceptor should take eight types of earth from the heart of a riverbed, from an anthill, from the furrow of a plow, from a rat's hole, from a pillar, or from the horn of a bull.
Having filled the pit of the womb and placed the bulb upon the earth,
one should place the lotus-bulb in the center and the water-lily bulb in the east.
One should place an utpala bulb on the south and a saugandhika on the west;
one should place a kaśeru bulb on the north and deposit the seed upon it.
One should place śālī rice in the east, and indeed place *vrīhi* rice in the south;
having placed *kodrava* in the west, one should place *māṣa* beans in the north. (49)
One should place mung beans in the southeast, kangu seeds in the southwest, priyaṅgu in the northwest, and kulattha in the northeast. (50)
Having thus deposited the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra) into the womb-vessel,
it was then provided with all kinds of musical instruments and filled with dancing and singing.
Accompanied by shouts of victory and the chanting of the Vedas,
one should utter the seed-syllable of the temple and install the vessel containing the embryo.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, construct a temple in the womb-vessel (garbha-bhājana) using stones, bricks, or sand, making it very firm.
The procedure for the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) has been declared; now listen to that which consists of a single story (ekatala).
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter on the procedure for the deposition of the embryo in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kaśyapa.
Now I shall describe specifically the single-storied palace; listen. Its width and height are stated according to the measurement of the temple.
Among these shapes, there are the quadrangular, circular, triangular, bilaterally symmetrical, hexagonal, octagonal, and likewise the conical form. (2)
The small front pavilion (mukhamaṇṭapa) should measure half the height of the palace;
the best [size] is equal to the height of the palace, and that which is between these two is preferred when divided [into three parts]. (3)
I have described the length of the front pavilion (mukha-maṇṭapa) as ninefold;
its width is equal to that of the temple, and it is the best of the three types of pavilions.
O best of the twice-born! The entrance, not distinguished from the palace itself, should be one and a half daṇḍas, or two daṇḍas, measured from the central axis (mānasūtra).
The entrance should be one and a half *daṇḍas* or one *daṇḍa* from the central line (*mānasūtra*),
joined with an even number of pillars, and made beautiful in all its parts through skillful design.
Or it may have a wall with a door and a lattice, provided there is an open space between;
if there is such an open space, it should be two, three, or four cubits long.
One should construct the stairs on both sides adorned with elephant trunks;
they should be equal in width to the thickness of the temple wall, or half, or three-quarters of it.
The maṇḍapa should likewise be constructed from the width of the intermediate wall;
it may be provided with gables, chambers, and so forth, or the front maṇḍapa may be detached.
The front pavilion (mukhamaṇṭapa) should be constructed, either provided with the three goals of life (trivarga), or adorned with arches and other ornaments, and consisting of one or many stories.
In a palace, one-third of the width of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) is the extent [of the hall];
and when divided into seven parts, it is three-fifths, three-sevenths, and four-sevenths [respectively].
In the tenth part, take the portion of the elements (five); in the sixth part, divided by Rudra (eleven), take the portion of taste (six).
In the thirteenth part, take the seventh portion; in the fifteenth part, divided by the Vasus (eight), take the eighth portion. (12)
O best of the twice-born! I have described the division into seventeen parts, the nine-part division, and the half-diameter;
thus, the width of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) has been proclaimed by me as being ninefold.
The remaining wall should be wide; the wise man should arrange it all around.
In a single-storied building, there may be one, two, three, four, or five walls.
In a palace, having divided the ground, one part is raised for the floor;
the length of the base (caraṇa) is two parts, and it is joined with half a part for the entablature (prastara).

The *galocca* (neck-height) should be one part, the height of the *śikhara* (spire) two parts, and the height of the *stūpī* (finial) one part; when constructed in this manner, it becomes suitable for rites of pacification (*śāntika*). || 16 ||
In the case of pacification (śāntika), the platform (mañca) should consist of ten, eight, or seven parts;
one part is subtracted, and the remainder is the platform, or it may be exactly as previously described.
Thus has the rite for pacification (śāntika) been explained; now hear concerning the rite for nourishment (pauṣṭika).
When the sun is in its own sign, in its exaltation, or in its ninth-part (navāṃśa), the rising of the horizon occurs at the auspicious portion (śivāṃśa).
The base (caraṇa) should be two parts joined with half a part;
the pedestal (mañca) likewise one part, and the neck (gala) one and a half parts.
The height of the pinnacle (śikhara) is said to be three parts plus one-third;
likewise, the elevation of the stūpa is one part, together with the temple for nourishing rites (pauṣṭika).
In the sixth part of the ninth portion (sadanoñcadaśāṃśa), however, the auspicious base (adhiṣṭhāna) is one unit;
the pedestal (pāda) is two and a half units, and the entablature (prastara) is one unit of Śiva (śivāṃśaka). || 21 ||

The height of the neck (gala) is one and a half parts, the rise of the pinnacle (śikhara) is three parts, and the measure of the dome (stūpi) is one part; this is declared to be the "Victory-giving" (jayada) [type]. || 22 ||
In the Rudra-portion, the palace (harmya) is one part high, the ground level (dharātala) is one and a quarter parts,
the height of the base (pāda) is two and a half parts, and the entablature (prastara) is one part of Śiva.
The height of the neck (kaṇṭha) shall be one and a half parts, and the head-piece (śīrṣaka) shall be three and a half parts;
the remainder is known as the height of the stūpa, and thus the temple becomes truly wonderful.
In the height of seven parts, the base (dharātala) shall be three-quarters of a part;
the height of the plinth (pāda) shall be one-quarter of a part, and the entablature (prastara) shall be three-quarters of a part.

The measurement for the neck (gala) shall be three parts, the height of the pinnacle (śikhara) two parts, and the elevation of the dome (stūpī) likewise one part; this [proportion] fulfills all desires.
When endowed with the arising of pacification and other rites, and rising in due order within the series of palaces, it brings prosperity;
however, when reversed, it constantly brings about calamity for kings and others.
Therefore, one should cause the group beginning with Śānti and the *dudaya* (the rise) to be constructed;
in the portion of Rudra, the height of the base (*sadanotsedha*) is at the measure of one part for the floor (*talama*).
The height of the base (caraṇa) should be two parts, while the entablature (prastara) should be one part of Śiva (one-fourth).
The neck-base (upagrīva) should be one and a half parts, and the height of the entablature (prastarodaya) should be three-quarters of a part.
The height of the neck is one and a quarter parts, the head-piece (śīrṣaka) is two and a half parts, and the measure of the stūpi is one part; thus indeed is the wonderful [form] remembered.
Alternatively, there may be eight, or twice eight, or nine, seven, and eight;
[these constitute] the wing, the supporting foot, the bedstead, the neck-piece, and the couch. (31)

At the top of the neck, the measurement of the crest (śikhā) is one part of the king (nṛpa); it is surrounded on all sides and is equal to the collar (upagrīva), and these two together exist as a single unit.
Alternatively, having fashioned a base consisting of eight, twice eight (sixteen), and seven times eight (fifty-six) parts made of wood,
one should construct a pedestal, a neck-piece, and a bedstead.

O observer of noble vows! At the top of the neck, the measurement for the crest (śikhā) should be equal to eight or nine parts; above that, on the upper platform, there should be [ornaments] at the four corners.
One should fashion all the parts, beginning with the base (adhiṣṭhāna), exactly as before, whether it be provided with ear-lobes (karṇakūṭa) or specifically lacking them. || 35 ||
It is endowed with a rounded neck and likewise has a pinnacle and a pitcher;
on the pinnacle there is a great nose, and four [faces] in the cardinal directions.
When it is joined with Diśibhadra, it is called Mañcālpānāsikā;
when on a stone slab, it is called Alpanāsī or Vijaya—thus it is described. || 37 ||

That very [structure], enriched with pinnacle-ridges (karṇakūṭa) and bent by a fifth part of its width, should be fashioned into the form of a pinnacle-ridge suitable for the Nāgara and other styles. || 38 ||
The center of the karṇakūṭa is the bhadra; that same [measure] is the bhadranāsikā, and the antarāla is equal to that, joined with small pañjara-windows.
The *subhadra* has a prominent ear-tip (*karṇakūṭa*), while the *pañjara* has a small nose;
the *madhyama* has a broad nose, and the *viśāla* has a broad middle part, being both auspicious (*bhadra*) and expansive (*viśālaka*).
The width of the hall may be three, four, five, six, or seven parts;
the *kūṭa* (pinnacle) may be one or two parts, being broad in the middle and auspicious. (41)

The staff should be one and a half times the length of the hall, or it may be the supreme measure suitable for all deities; that same [staff] should be placed outside the building, or it may be joined with the central auspicious [portion].
That [portion] ending with the lattice-work (jālaka) is declared to be Śrīśaila;
that same part likewise constitutes the altar-base (vedikā), the neck (kaṇṭha), the pinnacle (śikhara), and the dome (ghaṭa).
It is adorned with cloth strips at the base and possesses auspicious "noses" (projections) in the four cardinal directions;
the four inauspicious noses, however, are situated on the peaks in the intermediate directions.
When the feet are raised slightly and the seat is richly adorned, that is called the Svastika bandha;
it is likewise auspicious when the middle is thus formed and the ear-protrusions are absent. (45)
It is renowned as bringing great beauty and is dear to all the gods;
on the peak, there should be a large nose, measuring eight or sixteen [units] in width.
The four-cornered pinnacle, the neck, and the altar-platform are indeed the source of prosperity;
that very same [structure] on the pinnacle is endowed with eight small noses.
That which is endowed with four great nostrils is declared to be Śrīkaṇṭha; those [nostrils] are said to be shaped like a horse's chest, a triangle, a circle, and the back of an elephant. (48)
One should fashion a hexagon for the neck and the top of the pedestal;
one should then design the fillet (paṭṭa) as the great nose, ending at the shoulder.
Joined with the *madhyabhadra* [moulding] and provided with the *karṇakūṭa*, the *śīrṣaka* (dome) shall be constructed, joined with a chamber (*koṣṭha*) above the great opening (*mahānāsya*). (50)
The nose should have a wide staff-like projection, either double or triple;
it is described as being as long as the interior cavity, and its height should be equal to that of the nose.
In the intermediate directions, one should fashion a pinnacle (śikhara) rich with auspicious faces;
its top may be circular, its ears and face [shaped accordingly], and its neck and head may be octagonal.
The *vṛttakesara* (round-keśara) is declared to be octagonal, while the *rājakesara* (royal-keśara) is [also octagonal];
one should divide the width of the temple by five, seven, or eight.
It may be two parts, or three parts, or as before, the "middle-bhadra" (madhyabhadraka);
or it may be one staff (daṇḍa), or one and a half staffs, or two staffs, or three staffs.
Emerging from the middle Bhadra is the Bhadrāveṣṭita harmya,
which is provided with four great nostrils (nāsikas) and has a long, circular pinnacle (śikhara).
With a base richly adorned with small mouths, and a neck shaped like a headpiece, it is known as the Kalyāṇasundara; it shall be worthy of all the gods.
O best of the twice-born! That very same [mark] on the forehead and nose is auspicious and abundant when it appears on both the left and right sides, O most excellent of the twice-born! (57)
Whether square or rectangular, the layout should be designed with skill;
now the orientation of the vimānas according to the directions will be described.
One should indeed place Skanda in the eastern quarter, Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the south,
Viṣṇumūrti in the west, or else the Liṅgodbhava.
O sage, one should avoid placing Dhātṛ in the northern doorway;
however, one should install Vināyaka in the auspicious southern pavilion.
To its east and west, one should fashion the form of Nṛtta;
likewise, Durgā in the northern quarter and Kṣetrapāla as well. (61)
One should fashion the station, the abode, or the form of the directions;
thus, O best of the twice-born, it should be performed above the surface of the earth.
Or Skanda in the eastern quarter, or Śakra with the elephant Rohita;
the elephant without the lotus, the nose, and the extent of Agni. (63)
In the south, one should worship the Dakṣiṇāmūrti or Vīrabhadra;
in the west, however, Nārasiṃha or the Saumyamūrti.
But to the north, O best of the twice-born, one should place the creator Dhanada upon a stone slab, likewise on one, two, or three stories.
In the great scriptures such as the Caturbhūmi, the Great Lords (Maheśas) are described according to their respective desires;
the Great Lords are proclaimed to be accompanied by Umā, Skanda, and others. (65)

Furthermore, the other gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and the hosts of Maruts [are located] up to the end of the Kalā; and the Yugas, the Earth, and so forth, are on the neck up to the end of the Prastara.
The best of those skilled in ritual procedures should fashion the eightfold form within these eight [squares]; place the syllable *maṃ* below the throat and the bull in the upper corners.
At each corner, place either two or one bull as a bed;
or else, in the four corners, place a Bhūta joined with a heart-añjali.
One should visualize [the deity] with a large body seated upon a lotus throne;
Āmoda should be in the southeast corner, and Pramoda should be in the southwest. (70)
Durmukha is at the air corner (northwest), while Pramukha is at the Īśa corner (northeast);
they are white, red, yellow, and black, respectively, starting from the southeast (Agni) and proceeding in order.
"Perform the marriage for me alone with those men and those women, [providing] a thick coating of a paste of *karāla* beans, parched grain, and *kulmāṣa*. (72)
Adorned with various ornaments, endowed with various graceful gestures,
and engaged in various sports, [it was constructed] with lime and likewise with timber.
The wise man should fashion it appropriately; the sacrificial pap (caru), the wood, and the brick may serve as the base.
Thus is known the single-story [temple]; thereafter, they know the two-story [temple].
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter [in the section] on the rules for the single-surface [mandala] within the Āṃśumat-kāśyapa [tantra]. || 26 ||

Now I shall specifically describe the characteristics of the *dvitala* (two-storied) temple; its width, height, and projection should be made according to the proportions of the base of the main temple. || 1 ||
One should divide the width between the two layout-lines (vinyāsa-sūtra) into seven or six parts;
