one part shall be the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa), and the cell (koṣṭha) shall be twice that in length.
O best of the twice-born! A chamber equal in width to the total span of the peak (kūṭa) should be made in the extent;
the remaining space between the garlands (hāra) on both sides should be a chamber provided with a lattice-work (pañjara).
Whether it be an entire interval between necklaces, or three-quarters, or even half,
it is declared to be the width of the cage, extending outwards from the summit.
Either slightly entering from the peak, or reaching as far as the end of the mental cord (mānasūtra),
the cage (pañjara) should resemble the peak of the ears or indeed have the shape of a nose.
O Brahmin, one should divide the height of the temple into twenty-eight parts, whether it be shaped like a needle or resembling the trunk of an elephant.
The height of the ground surface shall be one-sixth part; the elevation of the base (caraṇa) shall be one-sixth part;
the height of the stone slab (prastara) shall be one-third part; and the elevation of the base shall be one-fifth part.
The height of the entablature (prastara) shall be two parts, the elevation of the pedestal (vedikā) one part,
the measurement of the neck (gala) two parts, and the capital (śīrṣaka) three and a half parts.
The height of the stūpa should be divided into thirty-four parts; thus arranged, it shall be suitable for rites of pacification (śāntika) and the arising of the celestial abode.
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be one and a half parts; twice that is the height of the pedestal (caraṇa).
The height of the plinth (prastara) shall be three parts, and the fillet (talipa) shall be six and a half parts.
The height of the pedestal (mañca) is one part of the [total] width; the elevation of the altar (vedikā) is one part of the sky-portion (vyoma);
the height of the neck (gala) is two and a half parts; and the elevation of the spire (śikhara) is five parts.
One and a half parts shall be the measurement of the crest (śikhā); this shall constitute the abode for prosperity.
One should likewise determine the measurement of the neck (gala) as two and a half parts.
The remainder is exactly as before; thus, when the emergence of the thirty-three [deities] has been performed, this abode is indeed victory-bestowing and brings delight to all the gods. (13)
One should divide the height of the palace into thirty-six parts;
the floor level (dhārātala) shall be two parts, the measurement for the foot (pāda) shall be eight parts, and the entablature (prastara) shall be three and a half parts.
The height of the *caraṇocca* (pedestal) shall be seven parts; the height of the *mañcamānaka* (platform) shall be three parts;
the height of the *vedikā* (altar-base) shall be one part; and the rise of the *gala* (neck) shall be three parts.
The height of the pinnacle should be one-sixteenth part, while the height of the stūpa should be one and a half parts;
thus indeed should the most skilled knower of ritual procedures fashion the wonderful temple.
The height from the base to the top should be divided into forty parts;
the height of the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be four parts, and the pillar (staṃbha) shall be twice that in length.
The base (talipa) should measure one-eighth of a yuga and seven and a half [units];
the height of the entablature (prastara) should be three parts, and the elevation of the altar (vedikā) two parts. || 18 ||
The measurement of the neck is three parts, while the pinnacle (śikhara) is seven parts;
one should know that the remainder is the height of the pinnacle for this vimāna which fulfills all desires.
One should conceive of the structure as being quadrangular, extending from the sacrificial fire-altar (homādi) up to the stūpa;
it should have four peaks, four halls, and be joined with eight pavilions (pañjara).
One should arrange six or eight small noses for each quarter;
however, on the summit, it should be provided with large noses in the four directions.
Adorned with various colorful designs such as altars and so forth, this is called the Svastika; it brings delight to all the gods.
That very [structure], with small *nāsikās* on the sides at the corners of the pinnacle, is known as the *Svastibhadra*; it shall be pleasing to me. (23)
That very [structure] is the *natakūṭa*, with elevated chambers and level benches, joined with a curved framework; this is vast and beautiful. (24)
That very space is especially enriched with upper galleries (mañca) and peaked chambers (kūṭakoṣṭha),
joined with a curved lattice-work (natapañjara) and a pinnacle (śīrṣaka) of desired form.
Likewise, the *stūpīghaṭa* and *gala* types are proclaimed as *śrīkara*;
these same [types] may have nine halls (*navaśālā*), with their peaks (*kūṭa*) being equal in height to the base (*unnata*).
That which is joined with a lower penthouse (nimnapañjara) is called Kailāsa;
that very same [structure], when devoid of both the upper peak-chamber (kūṭa) and the inner cell (koṣṭha), as well as the lower and higher [projections], is likewise designated.
Provided with an inner layer of masonry, level and elevated along the same alignment,
and especially distinguished by an interval for necklaces, it is either a pair or a double lattice-work.
It has four peaks and four halls, with six or eight small nose-projections; it is endowed with a vedikā having eight corners, and its dome and neck are circular.
The pinnacle is enriched with jewels, and there are four auspicious [shrines] each; abounding in altars and archways, this supreme form is beloved by Rudra.
One should fashion that very pinnacle as the neck with eight corners;
this is known by the name Viṣṇukānta and is worthy of all the gods. || 31 ||
That very [structure] is circular, with a pedestal-neck (*vedīkandhara*) and likewise a pinnacle (*śikhara*);
it is enriched with four halls (*catuśśālā*) and eight peaks (*aṣṭakūṭa*), and possesses seven or eight small noses (*alpanāsikā*). (32)
This vimāna, called Parvata, which is the abode of prosperity,
extends from the peak of the koṣṭha by one daṇḍa or one and a half daṇḍas.
The exit from the false treasury shall consist of two or three pillars, joined with various foundations and provided with various columns. || 34 ||
For all those previously mentioned [types of temples], however, one may choose either the *kalpita* or the *vihīnaka* [measurement];
that very same [measurement] is for the four cells (*koṣṭhaka*) situated at half the height of the pinnacle (*śikhara*).
Endowed with a square summit and possessed of four peaks, and provided with six or eight spires—this is known as the Svastibandha [temple]. || 36 ||
There are two *kūṭakoṣṭhas*, four provided with intermediate *prastaras*,
joined with *hāras* and *pañjara*s, and nine or eight small *nāsikā*s.
Adorned with all ornaments and beautiful with various auspicious features, that very [structure] on the summit should be made with half a cell (ardhakoṣṭhaka), but one should avoid [the other].
One should fashion a pinnacle provided with four nostrils and adorned with various ornaments; this is intended as the Pāñcāla style. || 39 ||
That very [structure] consists of an eight-sided altar, a neck, a pinnacle, and a dome;
on the pinnacle there are eight great noses, and it is indeed joined with the Viṣṇukāntaka.
With an interval between them, there are four by four corner chambers provided with a prastara;
it is joined with eight penthouses (pañjara) and has a circular head and neck.
One should design the *daṇḍa*, or one and a half *daṇḍas*, or two *daṇḍas*, or three *daṇḍakas* as extending out from the corner (*karṇakūṭa*) and the cell (*koṣṭha*). (42)
Endowed with six, eight, or a small nose, or even four in a row—this is the "Beloved of Īśvara," which brings pleasure to Īśvara. (43)
That same [base] should be made into a square with a length increased by three or four parts;
likewise, one should fashion the head (śīrṣaka), the neck (kaṇṭha), and the altar-platform (vedikā).
A stūpa joined with three [domes] is called this auspicious [type]; that same form, appearing elongated and circular, is known as Gāndhāra. (45)
Its length should be one and a half times [the width], and it may be rectangular or square;
it should have two corners rounded and be provided with a head-piece (śiras), as well as a pedestal (vedikā) and a neck (gala). || 46 ||
This supreme *hastipṛṣṭha* has the form of the front of a hall with windows;
it is fashioned with two ears, a rounded base, and so forth, or indeed that very same [structure]. 47.
One should construct [the temple] outside with four equal sides or a quadrangle,
provided with a circular inner sanctum and joined with gabled chambers and the like.
One should fashion the śrīkara, which resembles a circle, at the tips of the ears;
one should then construct the kūṭakoṣṭha and the nīḍa along the same perpendicular line.
A supreme palace named Manohara, worthy of all the gods, was built,
circular from its base to its pinnacle, becoming increasingly wide as it went outward.
The remainder is indicated as being as before; this supreme [mandala] is beloved by Śiva. The square base and the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) are likewise [to be constructed]. (51)
Above the base (adhiṣṭhāna), however, up to the end of the dome (stūpa), it should be circular in shape;
all its parts, such as the pinnacle (kūṭa) and the chambers (koṣṭha), should be joined so that the structure is circular. || 52 ||
The foundation may be square or even oblong;
it should be provided with a pinnacle having six corners, a neck, and joined with small towers, chambers, and so forth.
Having appropriately conceived [the design] by name as Kauberakāntaka, it is thus suitable with two stories (dvitala); eighteen varieties are recorded.
A mansion constructed and built up with bricks or stones, beginning from the sacrificial altar (homa) and ending with the pinnacle (stūpikā), is indeed a person made solid.
Indeed, that very same palace may be mixed with stone and brick;
in such mixed structures, the work of stone should first be performed, and above that, the work of brick.
A collection of women is known as *saṃcitā*, and what is remembered as *ghanāghana* is [a structure] made of bricks or wood; that which is a mixture of these is called a *ṣaṇḍa*.
That very same [state] when accumulated is known as the "dense-mass" (ghanāghana);
it is declared that the effect, when devoid of its constituent parts, exists as the accumulated [state] in memory.
And that which is known as Aghana is for the male, the neuter, and the female;
its measurement is that of the vestibule (vaktra-maṇṭapa), and it is spacious like the inner sanctum (garbhageha). || 59 ||
And all of them [should have] the same width as the wall, like that of a single-story [temple] as described before;
however, O twice-born one, on both sides of the door, within the space between the two bases (pādas).
One should construct the cave for the door-keeper (dvārapāla) with its northern boundary starting from the base;
it should be as wide as the [central] image and extend for the length of a staff (daṇḍa). || 61 ||
And in every chamber, it should be constructed without an entrance;
thus is the two-storied [structure] described, and they likewise know the three-storied one in that same way.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Two Stories," in the *Aṃśumat* section of the *Kāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe in detail the three-storied [temple]; listen, O observer of noble vows!
Its width and height are as previously stated for the *harmya* class of buildings.
Within the two layout-lines (vinyāsasūtra), when divided into eight parts,
one part is the width of the kūṭa, while its length is twice that.
The width of the cage (paṃjara) is said to be equal to, three-quarters of, or half [the total width];
the remainder is known as the space for the necklaces (hārāntara). The projections (niṣkrānta) and so forth are as described previously.
In the upper storey, one part out of six parts is declared to be the width of the kūṭa;
in the hall, it shall be two parts, and the remainder shall be the space between the garlands (hārāntara).
The *pañjara* (penthouse) should be equal to the interval between the *hāras*, or it may consist of two and a half parts;
in the middle of one part of the upper floor, a *bhadra* (central bay) is prescribed.
The *nīvra* (pedestal) of the *madhyabhadra* [type of temple] shall be one *daṇḍa* or one and a half *daṇḍas*.
When the height of the temple (*prāsāda*) is divided into twelve parts, [the *nīvra* should be] two parts. (101:6)
The height of the base (dharātala) should be two parts, the elevation of the plinth (caraṇa) one-fourth part,
the measurement of the platform (mañca) two parts, and [the remaining height] three-quarters of four parts.
The height of the plinth (prastara) is declared to be one and a half parts;
the height of the base (pāda) is three and a half parts, while the couch (mañcaka) is one and a quarter parts.
The measurement of the pedestal (vedikā) is half a part; the measurement of the neck (gala) is one part of Śiva (one-third);
the pinnacle (śikhara) is three and a half parts; and the height of the stūpa is indeed one part.
Thus, this constructed house is known as the *śāntika* (pacifying) type;
it is twenty-four *vimāna*-units in height, with its upper portion being two *bhāga*s high.
One-sixteenth part [of the total height] is the measurement for the base (caraṇāyāma), one-eighth part is the measurement for the wings (pakṣa),
and one-fourth minus one-quarter (three-eighths) is desired as the height of the pedestal (talīvodaya).
The height of the stone slab (prastara) shall be one and a half parts; the elevation of the pedestal (aṅghri) shall be three and a half parts;
the height of the mañca shall be one and a half parts; and the elevation of the vedī shall be half a part. || 12 ||
The measurement of the neck is eleven parts, the height of the pinnacle (śikhara) is three parts, and the measurement of the crest (śikhā) is one and a quarter parts;
this is declared to be the Pauṣṭika [type].
Having divided the height from the ground to the top of the temple into twenty-seven parts,
two parts shall be the elevation of the ground level, and four parts the elevation of the base (caraṇa).
The height of the base (caraṇa) should be two parts out of the three parts of the mañca;
the mañcas themselves should be one and three-quarter parts, and the height of the pedestal (talīpa) should be twice that.
The height of the *prastara* (moulding) shall be one and a half parts; the elevation of the *vedikā* (pedestal) one part;
the measurement of the *grīvā* (neck) two parts; and the *śīrṣaka* (head-piece) four parts.
The remainder is known as the emergence of the stūpa, which is declared to be the bestower of victory.
Having divided the height of the base into forty-two parts, [one should determine] the height of the dome (gṛha).
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) is three and a half parts; the elevation of the plinth (caraṇodaya) is seven parts;
the height of the floor (talocca) is equal to that; and the height of the platform (mañcatali) is six and a half parts.

One part of the total height is for the pedestal (prastara), six parts for the upward-facing base (ūrdhvapāda), two and a half parts for the height of the platform (mañca), and one part for the elevation of the altar (vedikā). || 19 ||
In the Adbhutaharmya [temple], the height of the neck (galamāna) shall be two parts, the rise of the spire (śikhara) one part (the portion of the elements),
and the height of the dome (stūpī) is said to be two parts.
When the height of the palace is divided into sixteen parts, the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna) shall consist of four parts, and the elevation of the base (caraṇodaya) shall consist of eight parts.
The base (talipa) should be one-fourth of the bed (mañca), and seven and a half parts;
the height of the bed (mañcocca) should be three and a half parts, and the rise of the legs (caraṇodaya) should be seven parts.

The height of the *prastara* (plinth) shall be one part, the elevation of the pedestal (*vedikā*) shall be eleven parts, the measurement of the neck (*gala*) shall be two parts, and the spire (*śikhara*) shall consist of six parts. || 23 ||

The measurement of the crest (śikhā) should be two parts; thus it becomes "fulfilling all desires" (sārvakāmika), possessing eight peaks and eight halls, and joined with a lattice-work cage (kalāpañjara). || 24 ||
It is rich with ninety-six minor faces, its birth-place being the foremost, shaped like a fourfold yoke (a square), joined with various foundations, and adorned with various pedestals. (25)
On the summit, it should be enriched with the sun (the pinnacle), whether large or small, consisting of four or eight [parts];
features such as the spire, the chamber, and the plinth should be appropriate for the Nāgara and other styles.
O twice-born one! That very same [structure] on the summit is known as the Svastika mansion;
it is endowed with four great nostrils and is devoid of the eight minor ones.
This is known as Svastibhadra, which brings delight to all the gods;
its pinnacle is circular, and its neck and pedestal are likewise so.
This [structure] named Rudrakānta shall be pleasing to me;
it should have two small noses at the corners of the top. || 29 ||
The constructed house, beloved of Śiva, shall be pleasing to Śiva;
it likewise consists of the pedestal (vedikā), the neck (kaṇṭha), the capital (śīrṣaka), and the dome (ghaṭa).
That which is fashioned as the *vasvaśra* (octagon) is this supreme *viṣṇukānta*;
it is formed within the two lines of demarcation when divided into nine parts.
One part shall be the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa), and two parts the length of the bay (koṣṭha).
For each bay, there should be two bays, and the lattice-work (pañjara) shall extend over half a part.
The best of those skilled in ritual design should fashion the remaining portion as another series of pendants;
it consists of four peaks, eight halls, and is joined with a solar cage.
One should proceed thus for the first floor, with twenty-four *hārāntaras*;
one should divide the portion into seven parts, and the width of the *kūṭa* shall be one part.
The width of the hall (koṣṭha) should be two parts; one should arrange this in the middle of the temple.
Half a part shall be the width of the lattice-work (pañjara), and the remainder shall be the space between the decorative garlands (hārāntara). || 35 ||
Construct a second ground floor with four peaks, four halls, joined by eight balconies, and provided with an inner corridor.
The expansion of the upper floor is one-third [of the total], with a central bay (madhyabhadraka);
it consists of eight peaks (kūṭas), a hall (śālā), and is joined by twenty pinnacles (pañjaras). || 37 ||
O best of the twice-born! The head and neck should be octagonal, provided with one hundred and eight nostrils;
the pinnacle (śikhara), however, should be endowed with eight great nostrils.
By name it shall be Śuddhavimāna, which will bring me great delight;
its altar is octagonal, while its spire and neck have the appearance of a circle.
That which is named Vimalākṛti brings benefit to all the gods;
that very same [structure] with a pinnacle and a neck, having eight corners, is the Brahmakāntaka.
That same [shape], however, when elongated, has a length of three and one-quarter parts, a width of eight parts, and its extension shall be tenfold. || 41 ||

One part shall be the width of the kūṭa, extending to the end of the hall and twice as long; the remainder is known as the interval between the garlands (hārāntara), which one should arrange just as before.
In the upper storey, the width and length [of the hall] should be six and eight parts respectively;
the pinnacle (kūṭa) should be one part each, and its length across the chamber (koṣṭha) should be two parts.
Half a part shall be the width of the cage (pañjara), and the remainder shall be the interval between the necklaces (hārāntara).
The width of the upper base shall be one part of three, and the central auspicious section (madhyabhadraka) shall likewise be one part.
It has two corners, a circle, an altar, a neck, and likewise a head;
it possesses four peaks and eight halls, and is joined with a cage of suns.
One should plan twenty-four intermediate necklaces (hārāntara) on the primary ground;
it shall consist of four kūṭas, four śālās, and be joined with eight pañjaras.
Combined with sixteen internal [parts], there are one hundred small nostrils;
the forehead and the nose, the face, and the auspicious nostrils on both sides.
In the same manner, one should fashion the nose, the front part, and the head;
it should be joined with various pedestals and provided with various bases.
Adorned with all ornaments, this shall be another type of necklace;
it is divided into nine times nine parts, ending at the line of the forehead.
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of one part of the [total] dimensions, while the thickness of the wall shall consist of one part of Śiva.
The surrounding veranda (alinda) shall be one part, and the width of the frieze (hāra) shall be one part of Śiva.
Thus, among those [elements], the *karṇakūṭa* is conceived as a portion of Śiva;
the central cell (*koṣṭha*) shall consist of three parts, and likewise the *pañjara* consists of one part.
Likewise, one should conceive of the interval between the necklaces as half a part on the first floor;
alternatively, it is prescribed as six parts for the *pañjara* (latticed pavilions).
The remainder is called the *hārāntara*; one should perform it all around that very [space]. (p.
106) By means of three staffs from the center of the square, the *mahānāsī* emerges. || 53 ||
In the upper level, one-sixth of the portion should be for the kūṭakoṣṭha;
half a portion should be the width of the pañjara, and the remainder shall be the space for the hāra.
The upper portion extends to the width [of the base], with an exit through a staff in the middle;
the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) is square, while the capital (śīrṣaka) and the neck (gala) are octagonal.
First, on the ground level, one should construct a pinnacle with four corners and a square top;
from the center, one should fashion a pinnacle with an octagonal top on the upper floor.
It possesses eight peaks and eight compartments, joined with a cage of decorative elements,
endowed with a hundred small spires, and is exceedingly great upon its summit.
This supreme [structure], worthy of all the gods, is named Bhadrakoṣṭha;
it is the very same as the circular-shaped pinnacle (śīrṣaka) of the Karṇakūṭas.
One should fashion the neck of the temple spire in a circular shape;
at the summit, it should be provided with auspicious pediments on all four sides.
In the intermediate directions, this supreme circular pinnacle is enriched with small nāsas;
that very same structure at the corner is provided with eight small nāsas.
The pinnacle of the corner-turrets (karṇakūṭas) is octagonal, while the crest (śīrṣaka) is circular in shape;
the remainder should be constructed as before—this is declared to be the Śrīkaṇṭha [temple].
That same length increased by one-eighth should be made square;
one should arrange a great throne (mahānāsī) in the middle of the hall, excluding the *bhadra* [projection].
The neck should have the appearance of a hall, being either circular or elongated;
it is joined with three *stūpis*, and by this name it is known as *Sumaṅgala*. (68)

O best of the twice-born! Having divided the space between the mental lines into parts for the religious elements, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of four parts, surrounded by the mass of the temple structure.
One should arrange one part around the *alinda* using the portion of the *hāra*;
among those, there should be the width of one *kūṭa* in the middle, and two [parts] extending the length of the *koṣṭha*.
The width of the *pañjara* (lattice-work) is said to be one part between those two;
then, the interval for the *hāra* (necklace-moulding) on both sides of the *pañjara* is by one part.

Having made the upper floor one-eighth [of the total height] and the width of the kūṭa one part, the hall (śālā) shall have a length twice that; between these two, however, is the penthouse (pañjara).

One part alone should be made [the base]; the remainder shall be the intervening neck (hārāntara). The upper platform (ūrdhvamañca) is four parts, and the central auspicious section (madhyabhadraka) is two parts.
The *daṇḍa*, or the *adhyardhadaṇḍa*, or the *dvidaṇḍa* should be the projection;
likewise, the pedestal (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the corner (*karṇa*), and the capital (*śīrṣaka*) should be quadrangular.
It has eight halls and eight peaks, a cage provided with sixteen [features],
endowed with a hundred small spires, and furnished with a pedestal for the bull.
It is joined with various foundations and adorned with various bases;
it has two elevated towers and upper chambers provided with intermediate floors.
The neck and head are renowned as "Gāndhāra" and are octagonal;
the neck of the pedestal is circular and renowned as "Śrīviśāla. (72)
The head-piece (śīrṣaka) should indeed be fashioned, and the remainder should be executed as before;
this is renowned as Śrībhoga, the supreme [form] worthy of all the gods.
One should fashion the circular, the oval, the two-sided, the circular-octagonal, and the hexagonal [mandalas];
likewise, all parts such as the peaks (kūṭa) and the cells (koṣṭha) should be constructed exactly as previously described.
One should avoid the *vṛṣasthala*, the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), the *karṇa*, and the *śīrṣaka*;
however, for those [temples] devoid of the *vṛṣasthala*, the *karṇa* and *śīrṣaka* may be included.
The gabled roofs, storehouses, and all other parts should be appropriate for the Nāgara and other styles;
they should be endowed with various ornaments and variegated with diverse paintings. || 76 ||

The sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be spacious, and the main hall (maṇḍapa) at the front of the building should be constructed according to the prescribed rules as either single-storied or, specifically, two-storied.

Thus the three-tiered [temple] has been described; now the four-tiered is being discussed. Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter on the rules for the three-tiered [temple] in the *Aṃśumat* of the *Kāśyapa*.
Now I shall specifically describe the characteristics of the four-storeyed temple; its width and height have been declared according to the proportions of the palace.
In the Kṛta [Yuga], the solar portion up to the end of the central line constitutes the womb-chamber (garbhagṛha), which is six [parts];
the mass of the hall, the portico, the archway, and so forth, each consist of one part. (2)
One should divide the space between the two layout-lines (vinyāsasūtra) into eight equal parts;
the corner-pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) shall consist of one such part, while the central chamber (koṣṭha) shall be twice that length.
The remainder, equal to a portion of the width of the cage, shall be the interval between the necklaces;
again, the upper ground [should be] divided into eight parts.
The *karṇakūṭa*, the *koṣṭha*, and the *pañjara* should be as described previously.
Above that, at the eighth division, the width of the *kūṭa* shall be one part of Śiva.
One should take one-eighth of the height of the inner chamber for the *āśvanī* (the upper molding), and half a part for the *pañjara* (the cage-like structure);
the remainder is declared to be the space for the *hārāntara* (the interval between decorative bands). One should avoid making these proportions either deficient or excessive.
In the upper portion of the fire-sector, however, the sky-portion is the central auspicious part;
it extends outward by one cubit, or one and a half cubits, or even two cubits.
One should divide the height of the palace into thirty parts;
the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be eight and a half parts, and the elevation of the plinth (caraṇa) shall be five parts.
O best of the twice-born! One should fashion the platform equal to the base, the pedestal at three-quarters of that, and the height of the throne at one-sixth part.
The height of the base (pāda) is one and a half parts of the Vedas (four); the height of the entablature (prastara) is one-fifth;
and the height of the pedestal (caraṇa) is desired to be one and a quarter parts of the Vedas.
The height of the *ucca* (pedestal) shall be three-quarters of a *pakṣāṃśa*, the height of the *vedikā* (platform) shall be one-eighth of that,
the height of the *karṇa* (corner pillar) shall be two parts, and the *śīrṣaka* (capital) shall be four and a half parts.
The height of the stūpa should be two parts, and the temple for pacificatory rites (śāntika) should be [the remainder].
Having divided the height of the house into forty-two parts, [the proportions are established]. (12)
The portion for the *guṇa* (three) is the measurement of the base (*tala*), while the portion for *rasa* (six) is the height of the pedestal (*caraṇa*);
the *prastara* (moulding) is by the part of fire (three), and the *talipa* is five parts in length.
The height of the base (mañca) should be three-quarters of the fire-portion (pādonāgnyaṃśa), and its projection (caraṇodaya) should be five parts.
The height of the pinnacle (ucca) should be two and a quarter parts, and its projection (udaya) should be four and a half parts.
The height of the pedestal (mañca) shall be two parts, while the elevation of the altar (vedikā) shall be one part of Śiva;
the height of the neck (gala) shall be one and a half parts, and the elevation of the spire (śikhara) shall be four parts. || 15 ||
The measurement for the crest (śikhā), which is conducive to nourishment (pauṣṭika), is said to be two parts;
one should divide the height of the temple, ending with the stūpa, into fifty parts.
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) is thirty-five parts; the rise of the plinth (caraṇa) is seven parts. Half of that is the measure of the pedestal (mañca), and the rise of the plinth is six parts.
The portion for the *guṇa* (moulding) is one part, while those two [the *mañca* and the *ūrdhvapāda*] are each two parts;
the height of the *prastara* (beam) is three parts, and the height of the *pāda* (base) is five and a half parts.
The height of the prastara (cornice) shall be three parts; the elevation of the vedī (pedestal) one part;
the measurement of the gala (neck) two parts; and the elevation of the śikhara (spire) five parts. || 19 ||
The measurement of the stūpa, including one and a half parts, is declared to be victory-bestowing;
a wise man should divide the structure from the base (upāna) to the pinnacle (sthūpi) into fifty parts.
The height of the base (talocca) should be one and a half parts of the fire-portion (three-sevenths), while the rise of the plinth (caraṇodaya) should be seven parts.
The platform (mañcatalīpa) should be equal to the height of the base and measure six and a half parts. (21)
The measurement of the platform (mañca) is declared to be three and one-quarter parts;
the height of the base (pāda) is six parts, and the height of the entablature (prastara) is three parts.
The height of the pedestal (mañca) should be five and a half parts; the base (aṅghri) should be two and a half parts;
the measurement of the altar (vedikā) should be one part; and the emergence of the neck (galodaya) should be two parts.
The pinnacle should be five parts high, and the rise of the pinnacle one-quarter of that;
thus should the most excellent knower of the ritual fashion this wonderful abode.
Having specifically divided the height of the temple into fifty parts,
the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall consist of three and a half parts, and the emergence of the plinth (caraṇodaya) shall consist of four parts.
The height of the prastara should be three parts, and the caraṇa should be six and a half;
the mañca should be three and a quarter, and the talipa should be six and a half.
The height of the entablature (prastara) shall be three parts; the height of the base (pāda) shall be five and a half parts;
the height of the neck (mañca) shall be three-quarters of a part; and the elevation of the pedestal (vedikā) shall be one part.

The height of the neck is two parts, the elevation of the pinnacle (śikhara) is one-quarter part, and the measurement of the crest (śikhā) is one-sixteenth part; this is the temple design suitable for all regions.
One should fashion a four-cornered [mandala] beginning with the *homādi* and ending with the *stūpivarga*;
likewise, the *bhānukūṭa*, the *koṣṭha*, and the *bhānudviguṇapañjara*.
On the summit, however, there are four *bhadranāsī* (auspicious noses) in the four directions;
each foot is enriched with small noses, and the summit has eight small noses.
Construct all parts, such as the gables and the inner chambers, in a manner suitable for the Nāgara style and others;
that which has pillars of a uniform shape at the base is known as Subhadra. (31)
That very same [structure], when devoid of the small nose on the summit, becomes known as Brāhmya; it brings delight to all the gods. || 32 ||
Thus, a pinnacle with a circular neck is called Śrīkānta;
a pinnacle with an eight-sided neck is declared to be Śrīmaṇḍana.
That very [structure] on the peak, provided with eight great nāsīs,
is known as Śrīvanta, or it may be endowed with Śālābhadra.
Alternatively, a Vibhadra layout should be made for all the temples;
it may have eight small shrines on the summit, be richly adorned with faces, or be the Śrīviśālaka type.
They are joined with various pedestals and proclaimed by their respective names;
the pinnacle (śīrṣaka) is in the form of an assembly hall, with its length being one and a half times its width.
It is said to be the abode of prosperity, supreme and worthy of all the gods;
having specifically divided the space between the mental lines into nine parts (nandabhāga). || 37 ||
The inner sanctum (garbhageha) shall consist of one part, the pedestal of the temple (gṛhapiṇḍikā) one part,
the vestibule (alinda) should be made with one part, and one should arrange the archway (hāra) with one part.
Then, when the site has been divided into nine parts up to the end of the layout-lines (vinyāsasūtra),
one part is the width of the peak (kūṭa) and three parts are the length of the chamber (koṣṭha).
One part shall be the width of the cage (paṃjara), and one and a half parts the interval between the arches (hāra).
In the middle of the hall (śālā) is the great throne (mahānāsī), and its pedestal (nīvra) is made with half that portion. (40)
One should design the pinnacle (kūṭa) with one-eighth part of the upper floor;
the hall (śālā) shall have a length double that, and the cage (pañjara) shall consist of one Śiva-part.
The remainder and the other weight above, being a portion of the elements divided by the essence (rasa), should be made into a peak with one [unit]; that cell should be twice as long.
Half of the width of the cage (paṃjara) shall be the [width of the] neck, and the remainder shall be the interval between the necklaces (hārāntara).
Above that is the base (bhūmi), half of which is the protrusion (nirgati) in the middle by means of a staff (daṇḍa).
The pinnacle of the spires (kūṭa-śīrṣaka) is respectively quadrangular, octagonal, and circular;
the chamber (koṣṭha) is like the handle of a water-pot (kakarī), and the palace pinnacle (harmya-śīrṣaka) is octagonal.

One should fashion a head-piece (śīrṣaka) provided with eight great nostrils (mahānāsya), a peak (kūṭa) consisting of twelve squares (ravi-koṣṭha), and a lattice-work (pañjara) double that number of the sun (twelve).
This supreme Bhadrakoṣṭha, however, is like the previous one, but with the upper portion increased;
having divided the width of the house into seven parts, one should take four for the Nālīgraha.
One should fashion the *alinda* with a measure of one part according to the total parts of the planetary units,
and the width of the *hāra* (projection) all around with nine parts.
When the distance between the two layout-lines (vinyāsasūtra) is divided by twice the width (vyāsa),
one part thereof is the ear-ridge (karṇakūṭa), while the length of the cell (koṣṭha) is twice that.
Half a part shall be the width of the cage (paṃjara), and the remainder shall be the interval between the necklaces;
the cage consists of four tiers and eight compartments, numbering twelve.
(114) One should arrange twenty-four *hārāntaras* on the first floor;
the *alinda* is made solid up to the end of the *prastara*, enriched with water-pipes (*jalapāda*).
Above, however, in the eighth part, the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa) is one part of Śiva;
its chamber (koṣṭha) is twice that in length, and the cage (pañjara) measures one part.
The remainder is known as the interval between necklaces (hārāntara);
when divided by eight, the portion above should be made into a peak (kūṭa), and the cell (koṣṭha) should be twice that in length.
The remainder is known as the *hārāntara*, joined with small cages (*kṣudrapañjara*);
the upper floor consists of one-third [of the height], with a projection in the middle by means of a staff (*daṇḍa*). (53)
The base is square, the head and neck are octagonal;
at the pinnacle are eight great nostrils, and on each foot is a small nostril.
The *karṇakūṭa* (corner pinnacle) should be one *bhānu* (twelve units), while the *koṣṭha* (cell) is joined with sixteen [units].
The *nata* (recessed part) and the *kūṭonnata* (elevated pinnacle) are cells provided with an internal *prastara* (layer).
The twenty-eighth [type] is Kṣudranīḍa;
it has various masūraka bases and is endowed with various ornaments, lattices, and archways.
The various and diverse sections of the gourd, however, are as before;
this is known as the "Victory-bringing" (Jayāvaha), which is supreme and worthy of all the gods. || 57 ||
That very [structure] with rounded corners is the *śīrṣaka* (head-piece) that fulfills all desires;
that same [structure] may be an *antaramañca* (inner terrace), a *kūṭakoṣṭha* (gabled chamber), or a *pañjara* (cage).
The pinnacle of the spires (kūṭas) shall consist of a dome (śīrṣaka), a finial (stūpī), a pitcher (kumbha), and a circular eave (karṇa).
Thus should it be; however, on the middle floor, the base ground should be octagonal.
One should fashion the corner-ridge (karṇakūṭa) on the upper level as a quadrilateral;
this is known as the "Bringer of Happiness" (Sukhāvaha), which is supreme and worthy of all the gods.
That very same peaked hall (kūṭakoṣṭha), without an intermediate floor and with its sides aligned on a straight line, becomes that imperishable house (avyayagṛha). || 61 ||
That very pinnacle is the ear, four-cornered, the creator and the destroyer.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter on the construction of the four levels in the *Aṃśumat* of the *Kāśyapa*. 29.
I shall here describe the characteristics of the kūṭakoṣṭhas and pañjaras;
they are proclaimed to be equal [in their proportions], ranging from two stories up to ten stories. || 1 ||

The floor should be a square with equal sides as specified by Vyāsa; the *karṇakūṭaka* (corner-turret) should be triangular, while the *koṣṭha* (central chamber) should be rectangular, having four sides and a single wall.
It consists of the base-pillar section, the entablature, the neck, and the capital;
it is further endowed with the dome-section, and specifically with the pinnacle and the chamber.
In this manner, one should construct the foundation level at the very bottom; above that, the floor of the main structure (dharātala) should be made.
The gabled halls (kūṭaśālā) and the balconies (pañjara) should likewise be constructed according to their proper height.
One should specifically divide the height of the *ūrdhvapāda* into seven parts:
one part shall be the height of the pedestal (*vedikā*), and one and a half parts shall be the measurement of the neck (*gala*). (5)
The *śīrṣaka* (dome) should be one part of the [total] proportions; the remainder shall be the height of the *sthūpī*.
In this manner, one should fashion two *kūṭakoṣṭha*s for each floor.
Alternatively, I shall now describe the rising [measure] of the false storehouses (kūṭakoṣṭha):
from the upper limit of the northern face to the upper limit of the Haṃsamāla.
Alternatively, one may first mark off the portion ending at the *kapotālamba*;
however, if there is an intermediate layer (*sāntaraprastara*), it should be the upper limit of that layer.
The altar (vedī) may be above [the base], level with it, or provided with an intervening prastara;
having divided that height into eleven parts, one part is the elevation of the altar.
The height of the base (caraṇa) is one part; the bedstead (mañcaka) is one and three-quarter parts;
the height of the neck (gala) is one and a quarter parts; and the head-piece (śīrṣaka) is one and three-quarter parts.
One should calculate the height of the stūpa as one and a quarter parts;
in this manner, the best of those skilled in ritual should fashion two kūṭas and two koṣṭhas.
The self-nose (svanāsī) should be one-third of the width of the kūṭa;
on that width, at the third, fourth, or fifth part, there should be a niche (nīvraka).
From the elevation of the ear-ridges and the peak, the emergence of the nose should occur;
one should fashion four noses for the peaks in the four directions.
It should be provided with a single stūpa, having a narrow entrance like a celestial chariot (vimāna),
and its neck and head should be either quadrangular, octagonal, or circular in appearance.

(117) O Brahmin, one should especially design the *karṇakūṭa* (ear-ridge) as is appropriate for the *nāgara* and other styles; on both sides of the *śālās*, there should be [projections] called the forehead (*lalāṭa*) and the nose (*nāsikā*).
The jeweled front-frieze of the hall (śālā) should be broad;
its limit at the front of the face is said to be equal to the top of the stūpa (sthūpī).
One-third of the length of the hall shall be the width of the face and nose;
one should describe the *nīvra* (ridge) of the *kūṭas* as the great nose (*mahānāsī*).
O twice-born one! In the Nāgara style of architecture, the temple is provided with three *sthūpis*;
however, in the Drāviḍa style, there are twenty-seven *sthūpis* for the halls.
For halls and porticoes, there should be one or four *sthūpīs*;
on the neck-section (*galāṃśa*), one should arrange the *kūṭakoṣṭhas* and the deities and so forth. || 19 ||
Thus indeed is the kūṭakoṣṭha; now the pañjara is described:
from the base (upāna) to the northern end, it is divided into nine parts.
Then the *upapīṭha* (sub-base) is one part; the ground level (*dharātala*) is two parts;
the length of the base (*caraṇa*) is four parts; and the middle of the platform (*mañca*) is one and a half parts.

The height of the neck (galodaya) is said to extend from the edge of the pigeon-cornice (kapota) up to the limit of each successive molding (vājana), with the measurement of the altar (vedikā) being one-and-a-half parts. || 22 ||
And outside the temple, there should be an exit according to the proportion of the ornamentation;
it may take the form of a cage-like nose, or the shape of a gabled chamber.
Or else, it may have the appearance of a peak on an elephant-back palanquin;
thus, in its many varieties, the cage-like form is described. (24)
One may construct there as desired on multi-storied mansions;
likewise, one should construct on the ground floor provided with intermediate floors.
Having emerged from the mental thread (mānasūtra), one should indeed act in this manner;
specifically, the cage (pañjara) should be free from obstructions above the foundation (prastara).

One should construct the cage (pañjara) with a width equal to the pinnacle of the ear (karṇakūṭa), or one and a half times, or even three-quarters; its height should be proportionate to that width, executed according to sound design principles.
The height of the base and the feet above it should be as previously stated in the nine-fold division;
the dome (ghaṭī) should consist of three parts and be joined with a pinnacle (chatraśīrṣaka).
One-fourth of the length of the base is for the *prastara*;
one and a half parts is for the *vedikā* measurement; and one-half part is the measure of the *kapota*, which constitutes the emergence of the *gala*.
The emergence of the cage (pañjarodaya) is said to extend to the limit of the counter-arch (prativājana);
the remainder should be constructed as before; thus is the "emerging cage" (niṣkrāntapañjara).
And likewise, it should be without an exit above the stone slab as before;
[it may be placed] in a cage, in a peaked chamber, on a pillar, or even between pillars.
Having appointed cowherds of great strength and prowess as its guardians,
[the city] was provided with two hands and two feet, was self-controlled, strewn with matted locks, and endowed with these two.
Possessing a fierce gaze and resembling the luster of red collyrium,
having assumed the gopāna posture, the two feet are then joined together.
Or likewise, one should place the outer part of the cow-shed at the head [of the site], resembling an elephant or a swan, or indeed resembling a lion or a serpent, according to one's preference. (34)
The characteristics of the *kūṭa* and so forth have been declared, as well as the procedure for the five stages (*pañcabhūmi*).
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the section on the characteristics of the *kūṭa*, *koṣṭha*, and so forth, in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the five stages (bhūmis),
including their width and height, as prescribed according to the measurements of the temple (prāsāda).
Having divided the width into eleven parts, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall occupy three parts;
the structural wall (gṛhapiṇḍī) shall be two parts, and the veranda (ālinda) one part.
The *hāra* (necklace-moulding) should be made according to its proportion, or it may be a solid wall;
one should fashion it above the *prastara* (cornice), joined with the *varṣika* (rain-gutter) and the platform.
One should perform the installation of the deity on the ground level, or on the second, or on the third floor; thus is the worship of the deity accomplished.

At the end of the two layout-lines (vinyāsasūtra), which are divided into eleven parts (rudrabhāga), the portion of Śiva is the ear-ridge (karṇakūṭa); in the middle, the square (koṣṭha) consists of three parts (guṇāṃśaka).
The width of the cage (pañjara) is said to be one part between those two; then, the best of those skilled in ritual design should arrange the interval for the pearl necklace (hāra) with another part.
p. 120) Having divided the portion of bliss extending upward from that into nine parts, one should make the *sauṣṭika* part;
in the middle, however, there should be a portion of three cells according to the measurement of the *pañjara* part.
One should fashion the necklace (hāra) and the star (tāra) with one-eighth part in the second [section];
above that, in the world (bhuvana), the pinnacle of the eaves (karṇakūṭaka) should be eight parts.
The length of the inner chamber (koṣṭha) should be two parts; from that, the lattice-work (pañjara) is one part.
Then, having made the interval between the garlands (hārāntara) half a part, it is endowed with the proper characteristics.
In the upper storey, however, the width of the kūṭa (pavilion) shall be one part;
the length of the hall shall be two parts, while that of the *pañjara* (lattice-work) shall be half a part.
The remainder is known as the *hārāntara* or the *lambapañjara*.
The floor above that extends out by one-third [of its width], with a projection in the center formed by a pillar.
The height of the house is six and eight parts; the ground level is three-quarters of a fire-part (three and a half);
the height of the plinth is five and a half parts; and the platform is two and a half parts.
The height of the base (caraṇa) is said to be five and one-quarter parts;
the measurement of the pedestal (mañca) is two and a half parts, and the length of the base is five parts.
One part shall be the height of the base (pāda), one and a half parts the height of the seat (mañca), one part the height of the plinth (pādona-pañcaka),
two parts the height of the entablature (prastara), and four and a half parts the height of the pillar (aṅghri).
The base (pāda) is two parts; the couch (mañca) is one part of Śiva (three parts); the height of the pedestal (vedikā) is four parts;
the corner (karṇa) is three-quarters of a pakṣāṃśa; and the height of the head-piece (śiraḥ) is four and a half parts.
The measurement of the stūpa should consist of two parts, while the temple for peaceful rites (śāntika) should be made with forty-one parts as its height. (16)
The portion for the qualities (guṇāṃśa) should be as high as the sole; the portion for the elements (bhūtāṃśa) should be the length of the foot;
and the plinth (prastara) should be one-third (agnibhāga) of that, increased by half a foot. || 17 ||
The seat (mañca) should be two and one-quarter parts; the pair of upper feet (ūrdhvapādayuga) should be [two parts].
The seat should be two and one-quarter parts, and the pedestal (talipa) should be a pair plus one quarter-part.
The height of the *prastara* (pedestal) should be two parts; the *caraṇa* (base) should be one-fourth part;
the height of the *mañca* (platform) should be one-fifth part; and the *pāda* (plinth) should be one and a half times that [fifth] part. || 19 ||
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) should be one-sixteenth of the total height;
the neck (gala) should be two parts, and the capital (śīrṣaka) one and a half times four parts.
The height of the crest (śikhā) should be one and a half times [the base], accompanied by the prosperity-bestowing (pauṣṭika) structure;
having divided the height of the building into thirty-six parts, O best of the twice-born! (21)
The foundation (adhiṣṭhāna) is two parts;
the height of the plinth (prastara) is two parts and its length is one-fourth [of the total]; the length of the base (pāda) is four parts. || 22 ||
One should fashion the pedestal-measure with three parts of Śiva;
the base (talipa) should be one and a half parts of fire (three parts), and the pedestal-measure should be half of that.
One quarter of the fire-altar's dimension shall be the base; the middle of the platform (mañca) shall be by one and a half parts;
the length of the base shall be three parts, while the plank (prastara) shall be one and a quarter parts.
One part is the measurement for the altar (vedikā); the neck (gala) is one and three-quarter parts;
the pinnacle (śikhara) is one and a quarter parts; and the remainder shall be the height of the finial (sthūpī). || 25 ||
(122) Thus, the one most skilled in ritual procedures should design the victorious temple;
he should divide the height of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) into thirty-three parts.
The measurement of the base (dharaṇī) is two parts; the height of the pedestal (vedī) is one-fourth part;
its length is one-fourth part; the height of the plinth (prastara) is two parts; and the height of the base (aṅghri) is three and a half parts.
The base (prastara), which is devoid of feet, is prescribed as two parts;
the height of the feet is three parts, and above that is the measurement for the dais (mañca). || 28 ||
The height of the base (pāda) is two and a half parts; the bedstead (mañcaka) is one and a quarter parts;
the pillar (stambha) is two parts plus a quarter; and the measurement of the bed (mañca) is two and a quarter parts. || 29 ||
One part is for the sky-section (vyomāṃśa), which is the measure of the altar (vedikā); two parts are the measure of the neck (gala);
three and a half parts are the pinnacle (śikhara); and two parts are the measure of the finial (sthūpī).
O God, one should thus construct a wonderful dwelling worthy of the Tathāgata;
having divided the height of the dwelling into twenty-four parts, [one should proceed].
The height of the base (tala) should be one and a half parts; the measurement of the pedestal (pāda) should be three parts;
the measurement of the platform (mañca) should be half of that; and the pedestal (pāda) should be three parts less a quarter.
Half of that should be the height of the entablature (prastara), and one and a half times that should be the rise of the base (pāda).
The entablature shall be one and a quarter parts, while the pillar (stambha) shall be two and a quarter parts.
Half of that is the height of the mañca, while the pedestal (aṅghri) is two and a quarter parts;
the height of the entablature (prastara) is one part, and the elevation of the altar (vedikā) is half a part.
The neck should measure three-quarters [of the height], while the head should be one and three-quarter parts;
the elevation of the *sthūpī* (dome) shall consist of the space [above] minus one-eighth part. (35)
O twice-born one, this temple, which fulfills all desires, must be constructed in this manner;
one should fashion it as quadrangular (yugāśra), beginning from the fire-oblation (homa) up to the pinnacle (sthūpī).
The *kalā* and *śālā* are the excellence of the art; the cage consists of four and eight parts.
Each foot is enriched with small mouths, and there are two necklaces at its two nostrils.
One should fashion four Bhadranāsīs on the summit, and two Kṣudranāsīs at the corner; this is designated as the Brahmakāntaka.
The Prājāpatya [pavilion] is described as being rich with inner platforms (antara-mañca) within its peaks;
it is that same [structure], though without the peak, having platforms level with the height of the chambers.
This supreme abode of the Self-born (Brahmā) is worthy of all the gods;
its very altar is the neck, and the pinnacle is the eight-cornered dome.
One should arrange four *bhadranāsī* on the summit, and two *kṣudranāsī* at the corners; this is designated as the *brahmakāntaka*.
The Prājāpatya type is described as being rich with gabled roofs, internal galleries, and balconies;
that same type, when its gables are bent inward and its chambers have elevated, level balconies, is [known as another variety].
This supreme abode of Svayambhū is worthy of all the gods;
its altar-neck and pinnacle consist of eight corners.
The projection [of the portico] is measured by one-eighth of the hall's width according to the measure of the staff;
this is known as the Bhadrakānta, in which two kūṭas and two koṣṭhas are equal.
Whether it be square or rectangular, the temple of Janārdana may be situated in the center of that very [site], whether it be of the *bhadra* type or devoid of the *bhadra*. (45)
Alternatively, a mandala joined with a medium-sized *bhadra* at the head, the crown, and the neck is known as the *atibhadra*; it is supreme and worthy of all the gods. (46)
That very [structure]—the kūṭakoṣṭha, the pañjara, the samañcaka, the sonnata, and the sarvatobhadra—shall be pleasing to me. || 47 ||
The celestial chariot has peaked chambers and a cage-like structure with perfectly aligned lines;
it is joined with various pedestals and adorned with diverse pillars.
Adorned with various ornaments and joined by twin cages,
it was enriched with small-faced figures on its peaks and possessed four great noses.
That which is renowned as Vibhadra brings delight to all the gods;
it is enriched with eight halls on the ground floor by means of two parts.
One should arrange the remainder, joined with a cage of suns, as previously described;
one should assign the names mentioned before to those [deities] according to one's preference.
The five-fold ground has been fully described; now hear concerning the six-fold terrace.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the section on the procedure for the five-fold terrace, in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme procedure for the six stages (ṣaḍbhūmi);
its width and height should be according to the proportions of a temple.
Having divided the width into eleven parts, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of three parts;
the wall-pediment (gṛhapiṇḍī) shall be two parts, and the portico (aliṃda) one part.
The area for the courtyard should be measured by one *hāra* and one *śiva*-part;
the ground level should consist of two or three stories, and the installation of the deity should take place there.
Wherever the installation of the deities is to take place, it should be very firm and solid;
externally it should have the shape of three peaks, while the interior should be like a dwelling.
One should first design on the ground a square of four peaks with eight compartments, joined by a lattice of suns, with twenty-four necklaces in between.
The *pañjara* should be in the middle of the *harmya*, while the *sauṣṭika* should be at the corner;
one should arrange the *pañjara* on both sides of the corner-pinnacle (*karṇakūṭa*).
One should specifically design [the structure] between the interior chamber (koṣṭha) and the cage-like framework (pañjara);
above that, at one-tenth of the height of the ground, there should be a sky-portion (vyomāṃśa) for the pinnacle of the corner (karṇakūṭaka).
In the middle, one part shall be for the *pañjara*, and likewise the *karṇakūṭa*;
the length of the cell (*koṣṭha*) shall be two parts, while that of the *pañjara* shall be half a part.
The remainder is known as the interval between necklaces (hārāntara); their number is highly adorned. Above that, however, is the broad base (bhūviśāla), divided into nine parts.
Then, the *karṇakūṭa* is one part; in the middle, the *śālā* is three parts;
the width of the *pañjara* is one part; and the *hāra* above it is half a part.
Above, in the portion consisting of two units, one part is for Śiva, extended as a peak (kūṭa);
in the center, the chamber (koṣṭha) occupies two parts, and likewise, the cage (pañjara) occupies one part.
Then, the best of those skilled in ritual procedures should fashion an interval of laughter measuring half a part;
above that, one should divide the width of the ground into six equal parts.
The pinnacle (kūṭa) should be one part in measurement; the length of the chamber (koṣṭha) should be twice that;
the width of the lattice-work (pañjara) should be half a part; and the remainder shall be the space for the garland-mouldings (hārāntara). || 13 ||
Above that, the central *bhadra* should be half a part in width;
its *nīvraka* (projection) should be one staff (*daṇḍa*), one and a half staffs, or two staffs.
The preceptor, having divided the height of the pinnacle (tuṅga) everywhere into fifty parts,
shall make the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) six parts and the elevation of the plinth (caraṇa) three parts.
The measurement of the pedestal (mañca) is declared to be one-fourth less than the portion of the fire (three parts);
the height of the pedestal is five and a half parts, and it is [further] increased by one and a half parts.
The height of the base (pāda) is recorded as five parts plus one-quarter;
the height of the pedestal (mañca) is two and a half parts, and the rise of the plinth (caraṇa) is five parts.
The height of the *prastara* (the cornice) is said to be two parts plus one-quarter;
the height of the *talipa* (the base-moulding) shall be five parts minus one-quarter.

The *prastara* (bedding) is known to have two parts; the *mañcaka* (bench) has one and a half times the four parts [of the bed], while this is known to have a length of one quarter and a width of one and three-quarter parts.
One should fashion the neck (gala) as three-quarters of the measure of the altar-platform (vedikā), which is one part of the sky (vyomāṃśa),
and the head-piece (śīrṣaka) as four and a half parts.
On the pinnacle, however, one should fashion four great noses;
this is declared to be the "Lotus-Seated" (ambujāsana), which brings delight to all the gods. (21)
One should conceive that very pinnacle as the neck, having eight corners; however, the head of all auspicious structures is indeed square.
Whether it be elevated or depressed, auspicious or with an auspicious courtyard,
provided with an intermediate floor, or even inferior or uniformly level.
This is known as the auspicious Sauṣṭika-śīrṣaka;
it should be made circular in shape and is called by the name Bhadravalīnaka.
That same [shape], with eight [projections] on the peak and arising from a pair of small noses, is known as this Śivabhadra, which is supremely pleasing to Śiva. (25)
That very same [shape], appearing like two coils joined at the neck, with the face enriched by the forehead and nose, is designated as "Nāgendra. (26)
Thus the six levels have been fully described; now, furthermore, the seven levels above them.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter [of the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*], the section on the arrangement of the six levels.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the seven storeys; one should determine the arising of the residence according to the rules for the measurement of palaces.

One should divide the bright portion (ravi-aṃśa) for the spire (tāra), the fourfold portion (veda-aṃśa) for the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), the fortnight-portion (pakṣa-aṃśa) for the wall and the cross-beam (viṣkambha), and one part is desired for the porch (alinda). || 2 ||
Then, one should arrange another necklace around it by means of a fractional part; one should divide the space between the two layout-lines equally into twelve parts.
One part shall be the width of the pinnacle; the chamber (koṣṭha) shall be three times as long [as that];
one part shall be the width of the cage (pañjara); the remainder shall be the space for the necklaces (hārāntara). || 4 ||
It has four peaks and eight halls, and its cage consists of twelve parts;
above that, the extent of the floor is divided into nine sections according to the divisions of the Dharma.
One should fashion the *karṇakūṭa* and the *koṣṭha* as before;
half a part shall be the width of the *pañjara*, and the remainder shall be the space for the *hāra*.
The expansion of its upper floor is divided by the same number as before;
the cage and the peak-chamber are likewise constructed in that same manner.
In the upper section, within the nine parts, the hall occupies five parts;
the corner pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) shall consist of one part, and the lattice-work (pañjara) shall extend over one part.
Then, another necklace [of one unit] and half a part above it;
when that is divided by eight, there is a hall in the middle occupying two parts; the remainder should be treated as before.
Above that, the width of the floor should be divided into six parts;
it is said that the *kūṭa* (pinnacle) occupies one part, while the *śālā* (hall) has twice that length.
Half of the width of the cage (paṃjara) shall be the [width of the] pillar, and the remainder shall be the interval between the necklaces (hārāntara).
One part out of the thirty-six parts of the upper floor shall be the projection (nirgama) of the staff (daṇḍa) in the middle.
The rising seat (sadanodaya) should be made with sixty-seven parts;
the base (adhiṣṭhāna) should have three and a quarter parts, and its height (tuṅgaka) should be six and a half parts.
Half of that is the height of the pedestal (mañca), while one-sixth is the rise of the base (caraṇa);
that [height] is declared to be three-quarters of two parts as the measure of the pedestal.
The height of the pedestal (aṅghri) is stated to be one and a half parts; the entablature (prastara) is two and a half parts;
and the measurement of the pillar (stambha) is five parts plus a quarter.
The *prastāra* (the base) shall be four and a half parts; the *caraṇodaya* (the foot-projection) shall be five parts;
the *mañca* (the platform) shall be two and a quarter parts; and that [the *vedī*] shall be three and a quarter parts.

The height of the pedestal (caraṇodaya) is said to be two parts; the height of the plinth (prastara) is one and a half parts; the height of the base (pāda) is four and a half parts; and the height of the seat (mañcaka) is one and three-quarter parts.
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) should be one-sixteenth of the total height; the neck (gala) should be two parts less a quarter;
and the height of the capital (śīrṣaka) is desired to be four parts plus a half.
The measurement of the stūpi is known to be one-seventh of the wing;
the *pañjara*, *kūṭa*, and *koṣṭha* are likewise arranged along the same axis.
The *homādagra* is a quadrangular [temple], while the *śikhara* has four nostrils (*vedanāsikā*).
The *śālā* is joined with thirty-six [parts], and the *kūṭaka* is twice the number of the sun (twelve).
The foot is joined with the sixty-fold cage (ṣaṣṭipañjara), and the nose is very small;
it is joined with various bases, or else it is of a single form.
The form of one or many is declared to be the *vāṅghrisamujvalana*;
that same [form], when provided with high peaks and accompanied by internal layers (*prastara*), becomes [the next type]. (21)
(130) Known as the *Śrīcchanda*, it is supreme and worthy of all the gods;
that very same [structure] is the *Natakūṭa*, with its cells being equally elevated. (22)
That which is known as Śrīviśāla brings delight to all the gods;
it is the very head and ear, extending as wide as the altar (*vedikā*).
That which is renowned as Śrīkānta, or equal to Kūṭakoṣṭha, or having level or elevated peaks, is declared to be the bestower of prosperity. || 24 ||
That same [shape] with a rounded pinnacle and likewise a thick finial (sthūpī) and neck is known as Rudrakānta; it is supremely pleasing to Rudra. || 25 ||
That very [mandala] has ears as its peaks, with four corners and eight squares;
having been fashioned in sequence from the base, this is known as the Vṛttabhadra.
That same [shape] with its peak elevated and endowed with a drooping *lālā* is known as *suvṛtta*, wherein the tops of the peaks are circular. || 27 ||
The *sannata*, the *kūṭakoṣṭha*, the *paṃjarāntara*, and the *maṃcaka*;
the pinnacle may be of any desired shape, as well as the neck, the dome, and the pot.
One should fashion the *karṇakūṭa* (the pinnacle of the corner) provided with a four-sided crest;
this is known as the *śivabhadra*, which is supremely pleasing to Śiva. (29)
That same [structure] may be a kūṭakoṣṭha, or a daṇḍa, or an adhyardhadaṇḍaka,
or a dvidaṇḍa, or a niṣkānta, or a bhadra, or a bhadrapañjara.
Endowed with various foundations, adorned with various feet, and variegated with diverse patterns, it is proclaimed as the bliss of Śiva. || 31 ||
That very inner sanctum (garbhageha) may be square, circular, or even octagonal;
likewise, the exterior should be circular, appearing round and adorned with decorative ornaments (sauṣṭika).
The remainder is designated as before by name as the Sarvāṅgamaṅgala;
it consists of a cage (pañjara), a peak-chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha), and an interior provided with a stone slab (prastara).
With a peak shaped according to one's desire, it is called Śrīpratiṣṭhita;
thus is the seven-storied [temple] renowned, and now the eight-storied (Vasubhauma) is described.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the Section on the Arrangement of the Seven Grounds, in the *Ityaṃśumān* [Tantra] of the Kāśyapa [family]. 33.
Now I shall explain in detail the supreme ritual for the eight stages (vasubhūmi),
which should be undertaken according to the proportions of the temple and at the time of sunrise.
Having divided the width of the temple into thirteen parts,
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall occupy one part, and the pedestal of the cell (gṛhapiṇḍikā) shall occupy two parts.
One should design the *alinda* (veranda) with one part and the *hāra* (projection) with one part;
alternatively, the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) is prescribed with nine parts. || 3 ||
The main body of the house should consist of one part, and the porch (alinda) should be made with one part;
the wall should be made with one part, while the porch should occupy four parts.
O best of the twice-born, a necklace (hāra) should be fashioned by means of a lunar portion;
thus it should be calculated when the ends of the two layout-threads are divided into thirteen parts.
The peak (kūṭa) is said to consist of one part; the length of the box (koṣṭha) is two parts;
the central box should be three parts; and the remainder shall be the space between the garlands (hārāntara). || 6 ||
Half of that should be the width of the cage, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
it should have twelve compartments (bhānukoṣṭha), four peaks (catuṣkūṭa), and be joined with a lattice-work cage (kalāpaṃjara).
One should arrange thirty-two intervals of necklaces on the primary ground;
from the region of the rain-stations up to the end of the stone-work, it should be made solid.
The expansion of the upper levels, including all parts such as the towers and chambers, should be divided into thirteen parts, exactly like the first level.
Above that, the ground is broad, divided into twelve parts;
one part is for the *karṇakūṭa*, and the length of the hall (*śālā*) is two parts.
Half of the width of the *paṃjara* shall be the space between the *hāras*;
the *paṃjara*, the *kūṭa*, and the *koṣṭha* shall be according to the numerical proportions mentioned previously.
And that which is broad above it, divided into twelve parts by the sun's divisions,
with all its components such as the towers and chambers, is measured by the same numerical proportions as before.
Above that, at one-tenth of the height, there is a peak-chamber as before;
then, with an interval of a garland and half a part, it is joined with a hanging cage.
Above that, the base should be broad and divided into eight parts;
one part of that constitutes the corner-pinnacle (karṇakūṭa), and the central hall is formed by two parts.
One part of the width of the cage (paṃjara) shall be the interval between the arches (hāra), and half a part shall be the space between them;
this four-peaked (catuṣkūṭa) four-hall structure is joined with the Vasu-cage (vasupaṃjara).
p. 133) Another necklace is said to be a *kalā*; thus, when fashioned in this way, there shall be six tiers.
Above that, one should divide the width of the base into six equal parts. (16)
The kūṭa is said to be one part; in the middle, there is a cell (koṣṭha) of two parts;
the width of the pañjara is half a part; and the remainder shall extend to the end of the hāra. || 17 ||
Above that, the middle portion should be half as wide as the base; from the center, there is an outward projection by means of a staff (daṇḍa).
From the peak (kūṭa), there may be a chamber (koṣṭha) or a niche (nīvrā); the central hall (madhyaśālā), however, is a niche (nīvraka).
One should construct a special gabled chamber, or one with perfectly level lines,
having made the height of the house into twenty-one parts by dividing it into three equal sections.
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) is one and a half parts; the rise of the pedestal (caraṇodaya) is seven parts;
the plinth (prastara) is three and a quarter parts; and the height (tuṅga) is six and a half parts.
The mañca should be one-sixth of the portion of the guṇas, with its height being one-sixth of the base;
it should be three-quarters of the fire-portion (three-eighths) and have a height of four and a half units.
One should specifically fashion the height of the pedestal as two and a half parts; the elevation of the base (caraṇa) is said to be one-fourth of five parts.
The *prastara* (the base layer) shall be one and a half parts;
the *caraṇodaya* (the emergence of the foot) shall be five parts; the *mañca* (the platform) shall consist of two parts; and the *pāda* (the pillar-base) shall be four and a half parts. || 23 ||
The base (pāda) should be two parts, the height of the pedestal (mañca) one and a half times that,
the height of the main body (mañca) three-quarters of a part, and the elevation of the altar (vedikā) one-sixteenth of a part.
The neck is three-quarters [of the height], the dome (pakṣa) is one-fifth, and the capital (śīrṣaka) is four and a half parts;
the pinnacle (sthūpī) is equal to the measurement of the neck—this is declared to be the height.
One should fashion that [structure], from the base up to the pinnacle of the stūpa, as having four corners, including its plinth and so forth;
and the top of the spire (sauṣṭhya) should be eight-cornered, while the pillars should have small nose-like projections.
On the summit, however, there are four peaks which, by their arrangement, are very large;
the pillar with a uniform surface is declared to be the Śivacchanda. || 27 ||
Those very [structures] should be dance halls, equal in measure to the *sauṣṭika*;
this is renowned as Vāgīśa, the supreme [temple] worthy of all the gods. (28)
That very *natakūṭa* with elevated chambers and level benches is known as *yāgavanta*, which brings delight to all the gods. (29)
One should repeatedly fashion the vimāna-shikhara and the neck (kaṇṭha) as having eight sides, appearing square, octagonal, and circular, with beautiful compartments.
That is known as the eightfold [worship], which is supremely pleasing to me;
that very same [practice] may be performed in a secret chamber, either with equal [offerings] or without [such] distribution.
The peak is likewise elevated, with various foundations and pillars; it is variegated with diverse paintings, and thus it is known as Pārvatī.
One should fashion that very peak as a circular neck;
it is called by the name Kailāsa, which is supremely pleasing to me. (33)
Thus the eight-story [temple] is described; now, above that, is the nine-level one. Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter on the arrangement of the eight levels in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*.
Now I shall specifically describe the supreme procedure for the nine levels; the width of the house and its height should be made according to the measurement of the temple.
One should divide the *tāra* (the central span) into fifteen parts;
the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*) shall consist of three parts, the structural wall (*gṛhapiṇḍī*) shall be two parts, and the porch (*alinda*) one part.
The width of the wall should be one part of the sky (ten parts), and the veranda should be equal to that;
the best of those skilled in ritual design should determine the width of the *hārā* (the inner courtyard) using the part of Śiva (eleven parts).
Alternatively, one should then divide the temple into sixteen parts;
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of four parts, and the pedestal for the deity (grahapiṇḍikā) shall be two parts.
The *alinda* (veranda) should be made with a portion equal to that of the sky (*vyoma*), and the *hāra* (necklace-moulding) likewise;
or one may divide the space up to the laying-out line (*vinyāsasūtra*) equally into sixteen parts (*kalāṃśa*).
One part is the width of the *sauṣṭika* (the central projection), and the *koṣṭha* (the main body) is twice that in length;
one part is the width of the *pañjara* (the side wing), and it has the form of a *karṇakūṭa-śiva*.
Then, the best of those skilled in ritual design should fashion another *hāra* (projection) by means of a fractional part;
it consists of four *kūṭas* (towers), four halls, and is joined with a *kalāpañjara* (ornamental cage).
One should fashion thirty-two intermediate necklaces starting from the ground;
in this very same manner, the second level of the earth should be constructed.
The width of the third level, divided into nine parts by the sages, should have half a part as the width of the cage (pañjara); the remainder should be executed as previously described.
In the same manner, the best of those skilled in ritual procedures should fashion a four-storeyed structure,
and one that is spacious with five levels, divided into twelve parts.
136) One part shall be the width of the kūṭa; the hall (śālā) shall be twice that in length.
Half a part shall be the width of the pañjara, and half [of that] shall be the interval between the hārīs.
The Bhānuśālā has four peaks, while the Pañjara has sixteen;
the one most skilled in ritual design should arrange thirty-two Hārāntaras.
Having divided the width by six parts, one part is for the *sauṣṭika*;
the chamber (*koṣṭha*) is twice that in length, and half a part is the interval between the arches (*hāra*).
One should fashion an intermediate necklace joined with hanging clusters;
its upper portion should be broad, divided into six parts.

One part shall be the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa), and twice that shall be the length of the cell (koṣṭha). Half a part shall be the width of the cage (pañjara), and the remainder shall be the space for the necklaces (hārāntara). || 15 ||
Above that, the width of the base (bhū) should be divided according to the proportions of the qualities (guṇas);
one should determine the projection (nirgama) in the middle portion by the measure of the staff (daṇḍa).
The wise man, having divided the height of the palace into eighty-eight and two parts,
should designate three-quarters of four parts as the ground floor.
The height of the base (pāda) is seven and a half parts; the lintel (prastara) is three and a half parts;
the height of the foot (caraṇa) is seven parts; and the bedstead (mañcaka) is one and a quarter parts.
The height of the pedestal (mañca) should be six and a half units; its width should be three parts.
The measurement of the base (pāda) should be six parts, while the height of the pedestal (mañcaka) should be three and three-quarter parts.
The height of the base (pāda) is one and a half parts of the total height; the bedstead (mañcaka) is one and a half parts of a quarter-part;
and the height of the foot (pāda) is said to be five parts plus a quarter.
The height of the *prastara* (moulding) shall be one and a half parts, five parts, or four parts;
alternatively, the height of the *prastara* may be two parts plus an additional quarter-part. || 21 ||
The height of the *prastara* (the base course) shall be one and three-quarter units; the *pāda* (the first tier) shall be two parts increased by half a unit;
and the *mañcaka* (the second tier) shall be two parts diminished by one-quarter. (22)
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) shall be one part of Śiva; the corner (karṇa) shall be one and a half parts;
the capital (śīrṣaka) shall be three and a half parts; and the bud-shaped ornament (kuḍmala) shall be one and three-quarter parts.
The base (pāda) is rich with small nostrils; on the head (śīrṣaka) there is a nose-like projection;
it is even and endowed with a raised peak, and the top of the peak is square.
One should fashion the structure from the *homādi* up to the pinnacle (*sthūpī*) as a quadrangle;
the middle hall should be complete, while the side chambers constitute the exit.

It may be a *daṇḍa* or an *adhyardhadaṇḍa* in length, known by the name Lambitabhadra; its elevated sections (*unnata-koṣṭha*) should be like that very [form], or it may have elevated peaks (*unnata-kūṭaka*).
This [mudrā] is named Brahmakānta; it brings delight to all the gods.
Whether with the thumbs joined or the thumbs separated, both the index fingers and the little fingers are raised. (27)
That which is renowned as the "Prādeśa" is the supreme benefit for the gods;
that very [structure] is the peak and the throat, eight-cornered and possessing eight nostrils.
One should repeatedly fashion a quadrangular shape with eight compartments and a circular one;
or, using a quarter-part of that circle, one may make it quadrangular—this is the supreme Śrīvardhana [mandala].
The two kūṭakoṣṭhas should be equal, or the two vimaṃcas should likewise be similar;
it should be provided with a rounded neck and crest, and auspicious nostrils on the four directions.
In the intermediate directions, there should be one or more pairs adorned with auspicious noses;
when joined with a pair of enclosures, it is known as the Supadma.
