That very same [structure], characterized by supreme beauty and increasing the merit of the sacrifice, is called the *pratisauṣṭyagra*;
that very same [structure] is the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*), and when it is circular, it becomes a circular temple. (32)
Thus the nine levels are described; now, above that, are the ten bhūmis.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the section on the arrangement of the nine grounds, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kāśyapa. 35.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the ten stages (daśabhūmi),
as well as their elevation according to the same method previously stated for the measurement of the temple.
Having fashioned that central point (tattāra) according to the division prescribed by the sages,
the body of the temple (gṛhapiṇḍī) should consist of three parts, with the inner sanctum (garbhageha) occupying one part of the Vedas (four parts).
The *alinda* (veranda) occupies one part, while the *hārātāra* (the space between the garlands) is a portion of Śiva (eleven parts);
this is the interval between the two layout-lines when the area is divided into parts by the sages (seven).

Among those, one [part] shall be the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa), twice that the length of the hall (śālā), one part the width of the window-lattice (pañjara), and a quarter shall be the interval between the decorative bands (hārāntara). || 4 ||
One should fashion four peaks, a hall, and a cage provided with sixteen [elements],
along with thirty-two intervals between the necklaces, upon the primordial ground.
Above that, the width of the floor is divided into thirteen parts;
one part constitutes the corner-ridge (karṇakūṭa), while the hall (śālā) is twice that length.
Three-quarters of the width of the cage (pañjara) should be the width of the foot (pāda), and the interval between the necklaces (hārāntara) should be one quarter;
furthermore, the number of kūṭas and other elements should be equal to that of the first floor.
Having divided the upper portion of the width by twelve, one should make the *sauṣṭika* part double the length of the cell; the *pañjara* is spread over half a share.
The width of the base is one quarter [of the total], while their number remains as before;
its upper surface width, when divided into eleven parts, is as follows.
The width of the base (pāda) is equal to the extent of the cage (pañjara); the remainder is exactly as before.
The width of the upper floor is one part of the void (vyoma), and the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa) is likewise.
The inner chamber (koṣṭha) is known to be twice that [measure]; the remaining space is the equal interval between the garlands (hārāntara).
One-third of the interval between the garlands is said to be the width of the lattice-work (paṃjara). || 11 ||
In the upper portion of that [structure], the part belonging to Śiva shall be the *sauṣṭika*;
the *koṣṭha* shall be one and a half parts, and the remainder shall be the *hārāntara*, equal [in measure].
One-third of the space between the necklaces (hārāntara) is said to be the width of the lattice-work (pañjara).
Indeed, the number of kūṭas and so forth is likewise [one-sixth], as before. 13.
One should divide the width of the seven stories into eight parts;
the pinnacle (kūṭa) shall measure one part, and the central hall (śālā) two parts.
One part is for the expanse of the *pañjara*, and the space between the necklaces (*hāra*) is half of that;
it consists of four *kūṭas* and four halls, joined with eight *pañjaras*.
The number of *kalās* should be conceived as the intervals between the necklaces; thus is the seventh floor [described].
One should divide the width of the eight-fold floor (*aṣṭabhūmi*) into seven parts. (16)
As before, there is the peak (kūṭa) and the chamber (koṣṭha); the remainder shall be the space between the garlands (hārāntara).
One part out of three parts of the space between the garlands is the width of the central lattice (madhyapañjara).
One should divide the extensive area of nine bhumis into six equal parts;
as before, one should fashion the kūṭa, the koṣṭha, and the pañjara.
When the expansion of that upper floor is divided into nine parts,
the *bhadra* in the center occupies one part, and its projection is measured by the length of a staff (*daṇḍa*).
The height of the palace, divided into one hundred parts,
has its foundation occupying four parts, and the length of the base (the plinth) occupying eight parts.
The measurement of the pedestal (mañca) is declared to be three-quarters of a Veda-part;
its height is seven and a half parts, and the entablature (prastara) is three and a half parts.
The height of the base (caraṇa) should be one-sixteenth part of the diameter; the height of the pedestal (mañcaka) should be one-thirty-second part;
and the height of the platform (prastara) should be six and a half parts, while its width should be three parts.
The height of the base (pāda) should be one-sixth [of the total height], while the height of the bedstead (mañcaka) should be three-quarters of a fire-part (three-sevenths).
The height of the base should be five and a half parts, and the height of the bedstead should be five and a half parts. || 23 ||
The height of the base (pāda) is said to be five parts plus one-quarter;
the height of the pedestal (mañca) is four and a half parts, and the length of the base is five parts.
The measurement of the couch (mañca) is declared to be one and a quarter parts of the side;
its length is declared to be three-quarters of that [side] plus two parts. || 25 ||
The height of the *prastara* (the entablature) shall be two parts; the *aṅghri* (the base) shall be four and a half parts;
the *añca* (the cornice) shall be one and three-quarter parts; and the *vitardikā* (the frieze) shall be one-eighth part.
The neck (*kaṇṭha*) is one and a half parts, and the head-piece (*śīrṣaka*) is two and a half parts; the height of the pinnacle (*sthūpī*) is declared to be one and three-quarter parts.
The Agnākāra has eight corners, while the Śikhara has two nostrils;
the Pāda is rich with small mouths, and the Rasātala has various feet.
When that same [structure] is joined with the ultimate form (atyantākāra) and brings delight to all the gods, it is known as Indrakānta if its summit is elevated. || 29 ||
That same [structure] with a raised interior chamber is called *unnata-koṣṭha*, while one that is bent or has a raised *sauṣṭika* is called *nata-unnatasauṣṭika*.
A *pakṣaśālā* is situated in the middle, and a *daṇḍa* is a hall that is low.
The neck has eight corners and peaks, and upon those peaks there are eight nostrils;
likewise, this [structure] consists of four mounds and is adorned with various ornaments.
That very same [structure] is a peaked chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) with an internal floor-level (sāntaraprastara), level;
it is joined with the peaked chamber and other elements, and possesses equal lines above.
One should fashion that very pinnacle as the neck, circular in appearance, known as the "Mantra-purified" and extending over all regions. (33)
The temple renowned as Śrīkānta is a dwelling worthy of all the gods;
it likewise serves as the pinnacle, the crest, and the neck for the Karṇakūṭas.
That which is circular in shape should be made; it is called the beloved of Īśvara.
Thus the ten levels have been described, and after that is the eleventh level.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Ten Stages," in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*. 36.
Now I shall describe specifically the Vimāna-type temple for Rudra;
one should then collect the materials according to the rules for the measurement of a Prāsāda.
One should divide that [area] into fifteen parts;
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of three parts, the structural body of the house (gṛhapiṇḍī) shall consist of five parts, and the porch (alinda) shall consist of one part.
One part shall be the width of the wall, while the porch (alinda) shall be one part of Śiva;
then, one should fashion the space between the friezes (hārāntara) by means of one part, according to the sequence.
An *alinda* (veranda), or another *alinda*, or even a thick wall;
or a solid [structure] up to the roof-level, or an *alinda* above that. || 4 ||
The internal width between the two layout-lines (vinyāsa-sūtra), divided into five parts,
should have one part for the corner-ridge (karṇakūṭa) and two parts for the wing (pakṣa) by means of a double division of the hall (śālā).
The middle hall should consist of one part of the fire (agni), and the lattice (pañjara) should be half a part;
the interval between the garlands (hārāntara) should be equal to that—thus it should be arranged on the ground.

Above that, the area should be made extensive; when divided into fourteen parts (manvaṃśa), the portion for Śiva is the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa), while the length of the cell (koṣṭha) is twice that.
The distance between the two [pillars] is the width of the cage (pañjara), and the interval for the necklace (hāra) is likewise;
it consists of twelve squares (bhānukoṣṭha), four peaks (catuṣkūṭa), and is joined with a kalā-pañjara.
The interval between the necklaces is eight [units], as is the second, which is the foundational ground;
above that is the broad ground, divided into thirteen parts.
The width of the pinnacle (kūṭa) should be one part of the sky (vyomāṃśa); its length should be two parts, equal to the length of the cell (koṣṭha).
The width of the cage (paṃjara) should be half a part, and the remainder shall be the space for the necklace (hārāntara).
The measurements for the kūṭas and so forth should be as they are on the first level;
above that, the width of the level is divided into twelve parts. (11)
One part shall be the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa), while the chamber (koṣṭha) is twice as long;
the remainder is known as the interval between the garlands (hārāntara), with a lattice (pañjara) consisting of one part out of three.
The cage and the peaked chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) are indeed to be numbered as before;
above that, the width of the floor is to be eleven parts, as previously stated.
One should determine the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa) for the portion of the ground above that;
having divided the extent of that upper ground into ten parts, [one should take one part]. || 14 ||
The pinnacle (kūṭa) and the inner chamber (koṣṭha), as well as their proportions and measurements, are as described previously.
Above that, in the ninth part of the height, the width of the pinnacle is one part of Śiva (eleven parts).
One and a half parts shall be for the central bay (koṣṭha), and the remainder shall be the space between the arches (hārāntara).
One-third of the space between the arches is desired as the width of the lattice-work (pañjara). || 16 ||
The number of kūṭas and so forth should be as before; the one most skilled in ritual design should conceive them.
One should divide the width of the eight-storeyed structure into eight parts.
One part [of the total width] is for the extension of the kūṭa; the central hall (madhyeśālā) is made with two parts;
the width of the pañjara is one part, and the interval between the hāras is half of that.
The four-peaked [temple] consists of four halls and is joined with eight *pañjara*s;
the *hārāntara* is said to be endowed with eight parts, numbering as many as the *kalā*s.
One should divide the area of the nine bhumis into seven equal parts;
the width of the central peak (kūṭa) shall be one part, and the length of the cell (koṣṭha) shall be two parts.
The remainder is known as another type of *hāra*, which has a single *pañjara* occupying one-third of it;
its width across the ten stories (*daśabhūmi*) is divided into six parts. (21)
One should fashion the peak and the chamber as before,
and likewise arrange [the structure] from the first up to the fifth level, joined with the auspicious lattice (bhadrapañjara).
Above the five levels, however, there is either the Bhadra or the Bhadrapañjara;
it is expansive on the upper level and divided into sections according to its qualities.
In the center is the *bhadra*, which is one part; its projection is according to the measurement of the *daṇḍa*.
The height of the temple, however, is thirteen parts out of a hundred.
Having made the base of the ground consist of one and a half *yuga* parts,
the height of the pedestal (*pāda*) is eight and a half parts, and the fifth measurement is one *yuga* part.
The length of the foot is one-eighth [of the total], the yuga is five parts less a quarter,
the foot is seven and a half parts, and the prastara is three and a half parts.
The length of the legs should be one-seventh [of the total height], while the bedstead (mañcaka) should be three and a quarter times the length of a leg;
the height of the legs of the bedstead should be six and a half parts.
The height of the base (pāda) is six parts; the bedstead (mañcaka) is three-quarters of a fire-part (three and a half parts);
and the length of the base is said to be one and a half earth-parts (five and a half parts). || 28 ||
The height of the *prastara* (the uppermost tier) should be two and a half parts;
its length is praised as being five parts plus one-quarter of a part. || 29 ||
The height of the pedestal (mañca) is one and a half parts; the rise of the base (caraṇa) is one part;
and the measurement of the pedestal (mañca) is stated to be one and a quarter parts.
One-quarter less than five parts is declared to be the height of the base (caraṇa);
the pedestal (mañca) is two parts, and the foot (aṅghri) is four and a half parts.
The height of the pedestal (prastara) shall be three-quarters of a part;
the measurement of the altar (vedikā) shall be one-sixteenth of a part, and the height of the neck (kaṇṭha) shall be one and a half parts.
The rise of the spire (śikhara) is desired to be one and a half parts of the Vedas (four parts);
the rise of the pinnacle (stūpī) is desired to be two parts less a quarter.

One should conceive of the shape as a quadrangle, beginning from the sacrificial fire (homa) and ending at the stūpa; and upon the pinnacle, it should be provided with great archways (mahānāsī) in the four directions.
A foot that is not too short nor too long is called *dhātṛ*;
when it ends with *sauṣṭika*, it is declared to be *vijaya*. || 35 ||
That very [structure] has its peaks elevated and its platforms raised evenly;
this is known as the "All-Souled" (Sarvātmaka), the supreme [form] whose essence is all the gods. || 36 ||
That very [structure] with a pinnacle, having eight corners and eight noses, is declared to be Viśālabhadra, the supreme [temple] worthy of all the gods. (37)
That same [structure] is enriched with a central bay; the gables and the inner chambers are equally elevated, whether symmetrical or asymmetrical, and there is a gabled hall and a penthouse.
The *gaṇikā* is said to be *viśālaka*, worthy of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
its very summit is the neck, circular with an eight-sided pedestal. (39)
The celestial chariot known as Indrakānta is universal;
that same [structure], when provided with a pinnacle at the corner and joined by a Bhadra, is called Karṇabhadra.
That very same [structure], when circular in shape, is for the *sauṣṭikas*;
by name it is the *karṇaviśāla*, which brings delight to all the gods. (41)
Thus, the eleventh characteristic of the stages has been fully proclaimed.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, the section on the rules for the Rudra-stage, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kāśyapa.
Now I shall specifically describe the supreme ritual for the Sun and the Earth;
the measurement of its width and height is declared to be according to the proportions of the temple.

Having divided it into seven parts for the distribution of the elements, the sanctum (garbhageha) shall occupy one part, while the pedestal of the temple (gṛhapiṇḍikā) shall occupy two parts; thus the temple is expanded.
The porch (alinda) shall be one part, and the wall (kuḍya) shall be measured at one part;
the porch shall be nine parts, and one should fashion the drip (dhārā) as one part.

Alternatively, one should have the inner sanctum (garbhageha) constructed with only a portion of the [total] dimensions; or it may be as wide as the entire mass of the temple building, equal to the inner sanctum itself.
The remainder should be performed as before; the *alinda* is formed by the line of the wall, once the layout has been divided into seventeen parts at the end of the two threads.
The middle hall (madhyaśālā) shall have a portion of six units (guṇāṃśa), and the corner pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) a portion of eleven (śivāṃśaka).
Between those two, the length of the hall (śālādīrgha) is declared to be seven portions (pakṣāṃśa).
Within the peak-chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha), or even between two chambers, the width of the cage (paṃjara) should be one part of Śiva, having a form like the peak of an ear (karṇakūṭa). (7)
The interval between the necklaces (hārāntara) should be half of that measure, joined with small cages (kṣudrapañjara);
one should construct the first floor in this manner, and the upper floors as described for the Rudra-floor.

O best of the twice-born! Having divided [the height] into one hundred and twenty-seven parts, the height of the temple (harmya) consists of one part; the elevation from the ground surface consists of nine parts; and the elevation of the base (caraṇa) consists of nine parts.
The height of the pedestal (mañca) is one and a half parts; above that, it is like the Bhānutala.
Thus the Bhānutala has been described; now hear about the Trayodaśatala.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Sun-Ground," in the section concerning Aṃśumat within the Kāśyapa [Tantra].
Now I shall describe in detail the thirteen-storeyed [temple]; listen. Its width and height are like those of the house according to the measurement of the temple. (1)
The extent of the temple should be made with nineteen parts;
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be three parts, and the pedestal of the house (gṛhapiṇḍikā) should be five parts.
The *alinda* should be one part of that auspicious [structure], and one should fashion the *hārā* with one part;
outside of that, O Teacher, the *alinda* is one part and the *hārā* is one part.
The *vyomabhāga* shall be the *alinda*, and the width of the *hāra* shall be equal to that;
within the two lines of demarcation, there are nineteen parts.
The *karṇakūṭa* should consist of one part of Śiva; in the middle, the hall (*śālā*) is three parts;
the wing-hall (*pakṣaśālā*) is equal to that; and the *pañjara* is one part. (5)
The interval between the necklaces (hārāntara) should be half that measure and joined with small cages (kṣudrapañjara);
the cage should resemble the pinnacle of the ear (karṇakūṭa), and the small cage should have the same appearance as it.
Thus has the first floor been described; the upper floors are like those of the Sun, with the rising of the abode occurring at one hundred and forty-two degrees.
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be five parts; the plinth (caraṇa) shall be ten parts; the height of the pedestal (mañca) shall be five parts;
and the remainder shall be like that of the twelve-storey [temple].
Thus, indeed, there are thirteen levels, and above that is the stage of the digits (*kalā*).
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the section on the rule of the thirteen stages, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kāśyapa.
Now, the characteristics of the sixteenth ground (bhūmi) will be described;
having thus conceived it in sequence, together with the fivefold group (pañcālī) and the meters (chandas).
The outer structure of the house is joined with five parts of food (breadth), while the inner sanctum is one-sixth part;
the base of the house is one-fourth part.
The remainder is indicated as before, O best of the twice-born:
the *alinda* and so forth, on one, two, three, four, or five levels, or even upon the surface of the earth.
One should perform the installation of the deity upon the sixteen-storied palace;
construct it with solid mass up to the ground level where the deity is to be installed.

On the exterior, however, one should construct a variegated ornament with a thick ground surface; it may be a porch (*alinda*), a *lajapāda* structure, or covered with beams (*tulā*) and other such elements. (5)
It may be solid up to the level of the sacrificial grass (prastara), or solid up to the level of the necklaces (hāra);
when the diameter is divided into thirty parts, the corner-pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) occupies eleven parts.
In the center of the palace, the length of the hall is declared to be one-fourth [of the total];
the length of the hall between those two [side-wings] is declared to be two parts.
And between those two, one should construct a hall (śālā) with a portion equal to a wing (pakṣa);
and between those two, one should make a penthouse (pañjara) with a portion of three parts, like a corner-pinnacle (karṇakūṭa).
One should arrange a *hārāntara* between those two with exactly half a share;
in this manner, one should indeed arrange twenty-eight ground floors and halls from the beginning.
The ear-lobes (karṇakūṭa) should be four [units], and the cage (pañjara) should be thirty-two;
O best of the twice-born, the interval between the necklaces (hārāntara) should be sixty-four in number.
Thus the first floor is described; in the second, which consists of thirty-two parts, the central hall should occupy two parts, while the remainder is exactly as before.
The second [level] has indeed been described in this way; now the third is being discussed.
Having divided the third level into thirty parts, [one should proceed]. (12)
The *karṇakūṭa* should be situated at the side, and the *pañjara* by half that portion;
the space between the necklaces (*hārāntara*) should be half of that, and the remainder should be like the second floor.
The fourth level, however, is broad; when divided into twenty-eight parts, the pilasters on both sides of the hall are equal in height to the corner-ridges.
The width of the cage (paṃjara) is half a part; the remainder is conceived as before.
In the fifth story (tala), the width is divided into twenty-six parts. (15)
The central hall (madhyaśālā) shall be one-fourth [of the width], and the corner pinnacle (karṇakūṭaka) one-sixteenth;
the hall situated between those two, and the chamber (koṣṭhaka) in the middle of those two.
The best of those who know the ritual procedures should fashion each [of these] with two parts each;
between those two, one should make a cage with half a part, like a corner-peak (karṇakūṭa).
The interval between the necklaces is half of that, and their number and so forth are like those of the levels;
and the sixth level has a width divided by twenty-four.
In the middle, the remaining portion should indeed be divided into two compartments as before;
one should divide the seventh ground's width into twenty-two parts.
The pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) should consist of one part of Śiva; in the middle, the hall (śālā) should be two parts.
Between those two, one should fashion a small chamber (kṣudrakoṣṭha) using one part of Śiva.
Between those two, one should specifically construct a hall occupying two parts;
the width of the *pañjara* should be one and a half parts, and the interval between the *hārīs* should be half of that.
The cage (pañjara) and the peaked chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) are indeed to be numbered as before;
the eighth is the ground width, divided into twenty parts.
The ear-ridge (karṇakūṭa) should be one part of the sky (vyomāṃśa); in the middle, by means of two parts of a cell (koṣṭha), and between those two, the length of the cell is declared to be two parts.
Between those two, one should fashion a small cell by means of a portion of Śiva;
the remainder should be made as before, and their number is as previously stated.
The nine-fold ground, divided into thirty-six parts, should have the portion for Śiva as the corner-ridge (karṇakūṭa); in the center, the hall (śālā) shall occupy two parts.
Between those two, one should fashion a *pañjara* (lattice-work) using half a part;
by half of that again, there should be an interval of a *hāra* (necklace-moulding) on both its sides.
One should specifically construct a chamber occupying two parts on both sides of that;
it may be situated either between two peak-chambers (kūṭakoṣṭha) or even between two ordinary chambers.
O observer of noble vows! the wise one should fashion the cage with exactly half a part;
the best of those skilled in ritual design should fashion the space between the necklaces with half of that part.
That peak consists of twenty compartments, and the cage is composed of twelve [squares] by means of the suns;
thus it should be arranged on the ninth level, while the extent of the tenth level is tenfold.
The width of the ten-fold base (daśabhūmi) should be divided into sixteen parts;
the corner-pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) shall consist of eleven parts, and the cage-like structure (pañjara) extending from it shall be equal to that.
The length of the hall is divided into two parts, while the interval between the columns is half a part;
the hall of the Sun consists of four kūṭas and is joined with a kalāpaṃjara.
One should arrange thirty-two *hārāntaras* on the tenth level;
the width of the eleventh level is divided into twelve parts.
The pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) should be one part of Śiva, while the hall (śālā) in the middle should be two parts;
between those two, one should arrange three parts for the platform (sthalāṃśa).
Half of that [measurement] is the width of the *pañjara*, and half of that again is the interval between the *hārīs*.
The hall (*śālā*) consists of four *kūṭas*, and the *pañjara* is endowed with sixteen [parts].

Furthermore, another necklace (hārāntara) of thirty-two [units] should be conceived both at the base of Rudra and on the ground of the Sun; its width is that of the solar ground, divided into twelve parts.
The cage and the peaked chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) are numbered according to the system of the Rudra-taloka;
for all the chambers, one-fifth is prescribed.
With a width of thirteen stories divided into ten parts,
the *karṇakūṭa* (corner turret) is made with one part of Śiva, and the central hall (*śālā*) occupies two parts.

One should fashion the shape of a pillar with one part from the middle of those two; in the space between them, one should construct a cage-like structure like a pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) using a division of that same measure.
Half of that [measurement] for the inner necklace (hārāntara) is the number [of parts], like the twelve stages (bhūmi);
its width across fourteen stories is divided into eight parts.
The *karṇakūṭa* (corner turret) is made with one part of Śiva; the central hall (*śālā*) occupies two parts;
the width of the *pañjara* (lattice window) is half a part, and the interval between the *hārīs* (mouldings) is half of that.
A four-peaked structure with four halls, provided with sixteen pavilions,
and twenty-four inner courtyards (hārāntara)— it should be designed in this sequence.
One should divide the width of three or five bhumis into six equal parts;
the corner pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) occupies one space, while the central hall (madhyeśālā) occupies two parts.
The interval between the necklaces, however, should be one-sixteenth part [of the width], joined with a pair of cages;
this is the extent across the entire upper surface when divided into four parts.
Having made the middle *nīvraka* (pedestal) two parts wide and equal in measure to the staff (*daṇḍa*),
the height of the temple (*prāsāda*) should be two hundred [units] consisting of two parts.

The ground level (dharātala) consists of seven parts; the height of the base (caraṇocca) is thirteen; the height of the pedestal (mañcocca) is six and a half; and the height of the plinth (pādocca) is equal to the number of the sun (twelve). (45)

The height of the *prastara* (pedestal) shall be one-sixth [of the total height], the *caraṇodaya* (rise of the base) one-eleventh, and the *aṃca* (plinth) one-fifth and a half; the *caraṇodaya* shall be one-tenth.
The best of experts in ritual design should fashion the height of the pedestal (mañca) as three and a half parts;
the height of the base (pāda) as six and a half parts, and the measurement of the pedestal itself as four parts.
The base (vasvaṃśa) and the height of the pillar (caraṇocca) are equal; the platform (mañca) is three-quarters of that, and the pair (yuga) is likewise.
The pillar (caraṇa) is seven and a half parts, and the lintel (prastara) is three and a half parts.
The fire-altar (agni-mañcaka) may have its length equal to seven parts or one and a quarter times the length of the foot;
its height, however, is six and a half parts. || 49 ||
The measurement of the foot is one-sixth [of the total]; the couch (mañcaka) is three-quarters less than that;
and the length of the foot is declared to be five-eighths plus a half.
The height of the prastara should be two and a half parts;
its length is declared to be five parts plus one-quarter. || 51 ||
The height of the pedestal (mañca) is one and a half parts; the height of the base (caraṇa) is four parts;
and the length of the pedestal is said to be one and a quarter parts.
The rise of the base (caraṇa) is said to be three-quarters of the width of the wall (pakṣa);
the height of the pedestal (mañca) should be two parts, and the pillar (aṅghri) should be four and a half parts.
The height of the pedestal (prastara) shall be three parts of Śiva;
the measurement of the altar (vedikā) shall be one part of the moon (śaśi); and the height of the neck (kaṇṭha) shall be two parts.
The height of the spire (śikhara) is said to be one and a half parts of a yuga;
one should then determine the measurement of the pinnacle (śikhā) as one and a quarter parts, following the sequence.
One should conceive of the shape as having eight corners, extending from the base of the fire-offering (homādi) up to the pinnacle (sthūpī);
and at the summit, it should be provided with great spires (mahānāsī) in the four directions.
A quarter [of the verse] with short syllables at the beginning is called *brahmakānta*;
that same [quarter], when separated by an interval, is called *mañca*, *sauṣṭika*, or *natakoṣṭhaka*.
This is known as the Sārasvata house, which brings delight to Śiva;
it has a curved peak, elevated corners, and high couches.
That which is renowned as the "span" (prādeśa) is the cause of prosperity for all;
one should fashion that very [measurement] as the peak and the neck, having eight corners.
When it is provided with eight great nasal projections on the summit, it becomes the Śrīkara;
that same [type], when enriched with a central *bhadra* and endowed with a *kūṭa* and a *koṣṭha*, [is likewise]. (50)
O best of the twice-born! Whether level or uneven, this peak-shrine known as Pārvatīka shall be conducive to the attainment of one's goals.
That very pinnacle is the neck; it may be circular or eight-sided, with a pedestal (vedikā).
Above that pedestal, it is indeed endowed with a circular shape.
This is known as the excellent Śāmbhava [mandala], dear and beneficial to Śaṅkara;
it consists of the cage (pañjara), the peak-chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha), the pinnacle (śikhara), and likewise the jar (ghaṭa).
Perform all these [rites] appropriate for nagas and so forth;
or else, one may perform them with this very [mantra] in a temple consisting of one or more stories.
Indeed, this foundation (tala) must be prepared;
its first bed (mañcaka), as well as the interior chamber (garbhaka), should have a height and wall [thickness] appropriate to each respective [requirement]. || 55 ||
This should be performed according to this rule, adorned with the syllables *gaṃ* and *laṃ*,
just like the ascent of the stairs for houses provided with verandas.
In those various places, one should construct what is appropriate with stones, bricks, or wood;
at its summit, one should construct a mandala, either single-storied or multi-storied.

One should fashion it according to the previously mentioned procedure, adorned with all ornaments, and possessing the qualities of being formidable, raised, rounded, smooth, soft, and glossy. It should be made variegated with various colors as prescribed by the ritual injunctions.
Thus, he who builds a mansion that is impossible to maintain or attend to; || 59 ||
Right here he becomes wealthy, illustrious, possessed of sons, grandsons, and a wife, along with female and male slaves and others, living in joy under his own control and with contented minds. (60)
At the end, he shall joyfully cause twenty-one generations of his lineage to cross over.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, the section on the ritual procedure for the sixteen stages, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of the *Kāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme rite for the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā),
either above the emergence of the spire (śikhara) or at the conclusion of the great nose (mahānāsī).
Or, at the conclusion of the Śaktidhvaja [section], one should place the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā);
indeed, upon the completion of that Vidya [section], one should then place the crown-brick.

One should perform [the rite] during the auspicious conjunctions of the month, fortnight, lunar mansion, and day of the week, as well as at a favorable moment (sulagna); for a temple of stone, one should use stones, and for a temple of brick, one should use bricks.
One desiring auspiciousness should construct a wooden temple using wood;
however, in a temple made of mixed materials, it should be constructed with whatever material was used for the pinnacle (śikhara).
O best of the twice-born, the head-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā) should be fashioned from that same material,
especially for mansions with one or more stories.
O Brahmin, one should fashion the bricks so that their width, length, and thickness are like those of the first brick; thereafter, one should begin the installation.
To the east or north of the front of the temple, within the vicinity of the palace,
one should construct a pavilion measuring nine, eight, seven, six, or five cubits.
The Guru should construct a pavilion (maṇṭapa) or a water-shed (prapā), square in shape, with its length and breadth equal to that [of the mandala], and provided with sixteen pillars.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways, surrounded by a moat and a rampart,
and equipped with canopies and banners.
Having especially adorned [the area] with garlands of pearls and darbha grass,
one should construct a small altar in the middle of one-third of the pavilion.
At the end of four finger-breadths from that enclosure, one should construct a quadrangular altar;
the remaining width of the altar, however, should be equal to twelve finger-breadths.
It should be two finger-breadths high and shaped like the surface of a mirror;
one should fashion the great sacrificial pits for the Śāstras as being square. (12)
Alternatively, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with coarse sand;
having performed the smearing with cow-dung, one should then dismiss the artisan.
One should feed Brahmins there and then dispose of their leftovers;
having smeared it again with cow dung, one should then have the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) proclaimed.
The wise one should have a sacrificial mound prepared with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice;
it should be adorned with half that amount of *taṇḍula* rice and half of that again with sesame seeds.
Having strewn parched grains (lāja), one should arrange a white lotus;
the wise practitioner, having strewn various flowers, kuśa grass, and darbha grass, [should proceed]. || 16 ||
Having specifically worshipped Manonmanī in the pericarp and Vāmā and the others on the petals with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using their respective mantras.
One should have the stūpa-pole made either of metal or of wood—
specifically from the wood of the jackfruit tree, the khadira, the sāla, or the heartwood of the tamarind.
The Madhūka flower-cluster and these six [other materials] are made of heartwood;
they may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even mixed with iron.

The height of the base should be equal to the upper level, and the length of the stūpa-shaft (stūpīdaṇḍa) should extend from the top of the stone dome (śaila) up to the end of the stūpa; or alternatively, it may be as long as that [upper level].
The wood for the stūpa (stūpidāru) should have a broad base equal to the width of the feet of the upper story;
its width at the top should be one finger-breadth, becoming gradually thinner from the base to the tip.
In the elevated portion consisting of nine parts, one should perform the Lord's [mandala]; at the base, one should practice the fourfold hermitage (vedāśrama).
In the middle portion consisting of eight parts, one should fashion a circular shape at the front. (22)
Above, it should be either square or entirely circular;
at its base, however, one should properly join the "peacock-foot" (śikhipāda) motif.
The width [of the base] is equal to the root of the staff, and it is three times as wide and three times as long;
provided with a thickness equal to half that width, it should have its tip pointing eastward and its other end pointing northward.
Having tied it within the middle opening, one should properly join the base of the staff;
the width of the crest should be one-third of the base of the staff, serving as its support.
One should firmly join the thick portion at the feet of the flame to its long part;
the wise man should also fix an iron band at both the base and the tip of the staff.
Having washed both the staff and the brick with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should place the staff upon the pericarp and [the bricks] upon Indra and the other deities in their proper order.
Having placed four bricks, the wise man should, at the end of the staff, draw the seeds beginning with earth using water mixed with rice-flour paste.
Starting from the eastern direction, one should worship the staff with flowers and other offerings,
using threads made of gold, silver, copper, or even cotton.
The wise one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) while reciting the respective seed-syllables of Brahmā,
Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśāna, and Sadāśiva.
One should worship the presiding deities in sequence, beginning with Śakra and Iṣṭakā and ending with Daṇḍa;
one should cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented to them and offer betel leaf (tāmbūla).
One should cover each [vessel] individually with a cloth together with a *kūrca* [bundle of grass];
likewise, one should place eight jars around [the central one], equipped with *kūrca*s and lids. (32)
He [should place] the eight lords of the Vidyās, filled with scented water, provided with cloth, gold, and flowers, accompanied by threads and endowed with sprouts.
Having established [the deity] with one's own root mantra, one should worship until the offering of food (naivedya);
thereafter, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed; carry out the rites beginning with the installation of the fire (agnyādhāna).
The wise one should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, and barley with the Savya-mantras and others,
one hundred times, fifty times, or twenty-five times for each, in due order.
Reciting the seed-mantra of the *kṣurikā* along with the five Brahmans and the six limbs,
the wise one should offer oblations of clarified butter twenty-five times for each.
One should perform the oblations with the Jaya and other mantras, the Abhyātānas, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛts;
and with the seed-mantras of Brahmā and the others, one should offer ten individual oblations while touching [the respective parts]. (37)
Thus, having kept watch during the night, at the clear and auspicious dawn,
the preceptor, together with the image-keepers, shall perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
Wearing a new garment and a turban, bearing ashes and rudrākṣa beads, he was adorned with a white sacred thread, white garlands, and white unguents. || 39 ||
Adorned with golden rings, bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments,
one should decorate the artisan with these ornaments along with a sacred thread.

The preceptor, having gone to the pavilion, having worshipped the pillars, bricks, and the striking-sticks with scents, flowers, and other offerings, and having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with the Jayā and other mantras; || 41 ||
One should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," whether at the rising of a fixed zodiac sign (sthirarāśi) or even at the rising of a dual sign (ubhayarāśi). (42)
Or the *jīva* conjoined with *Śukra*, or by the aspect of those two;
the preceptor, together with artisans, [should construct] upon a stone house according to the requirements. (43)
Having observed that the position of the bricks at the base is neither deficient nor excessive,
and having adorned it with a broom, one should then [sprinkle] it with the five products of the cow and water infused with kuśa grass.
One should sprinkle [the site] with the Śiva-mantra and then begin the installation;
the hollow at the peak of the architect's [image] should be the size of a finger-joint.
Then, O Brahmin, one should cause the head-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā) to be placed;
likewise, the bricks, the stūpika, and the kumbha should be arranged clockwise around the fire-sanctuary.
Having adorned it with various ornaments,
the preceptor, who is knowledgeable in the mantras, should then place it upon the palace while facing north.
Having meditated upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśāna, and Sadāśiva, one should place the bricks in the four corners with their respective mantras.
The wise man, having established the stone consisting of the earth element with its tip facing north in the Śāṅkara [mandala],
should fix it upon his own body, extending from east to north, consisting of the water element.
In the southwest, it is characterized by Nairṛta and Soma;
in the north, resting upon Vāyu, it is characterized by the Maruts and extends toward the northeast. || 50 ||
In this manner, one should gradually place [the gems] upon the stone; one should ensure it is without holes or defects.
[The gems are]: ruby, emerald, lapis lazuli, and sapphire. (51)
Having placed pearl, crystal, ruby, coral, and diamond in the middle and the other positions, one should recollect the seed-syllable of Śakti. (52)
Above that, one should place the *sthūpī* (finial) supported by the staff (*daṇḍa*) which rests upon Īśāna;
having sprinkled both the staff and the stone with the water from the jar.
Having worshipped the image in the pit with perfumes, flowers, and incenses, and having fixed the pinnacle (sthūpī) immovably with molasses-water and lime; || 54 ||
Then the remaining five [parts] should be executed as previously described;
moreover, the *sthūpī* should be placed upon the summit according to the method stated before.
One should then cause it to be covered with lime and other materials so that it becomes steady and very firm; one should then cover the house with gold, silver, or copper.
One should cause a cow fashioned from gold to be given to the preceptor;
one should also cause a sacrificial fee of ten niṣkas of gold to be given to him.
One should cause all the implements of the sacrifice to be given to the preceptor;
thereafter, one should honor the artisan with cows, land, gold, and other such gifts.
Thus, the mortal who performs this attains the fruit of prosperity.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, concerning the ritual for the bricks on the head of the Sun-god, in the *Kāśyapa* [Śilpaśāstra]. 41.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the enclosures (prākāra),
for the purpose of protection and for the sake of beauty, as well as the hall (śālā) belonging to each [enclosure].
Half of the width of the palace, divided into three parts, [should be used];
the extent of the inner mandala should be one part out of four, or one part out of three. (2)
The width of the inner necklace (antarhāra) is indeed double that [of the previous];
the width of the middle necklace (madhyahārā), however, is outside that—such is that triple mandala.
The extent of the *viśālā* boundary is four times that of the *ādi*;
the extent of the *mahāmaryādā* boundary shall be five times that of the *ādi*.
The Brahmins [ascend] by the steps of the palace, or from the first *āhoma*;
the second *nīvra* is from the first, and the third *nīvra* is from the second.
The third [enclosure] extends four [units] outward from that; the fifth, however, is the *nīvra*.
It is stated that they extend toward the wall (*prākāra*), having the wall as their boundary.
It is prescribed that [the fire] should end halfway on the wall, or even outside the wall;
or else, for the remaining Brahmins, it is performed starting from the grain-oblation (nīvrahoma).
First, the base should be equal to the *prakṛti*; from that, the *guṇāṅgula* [measurement] follows.
Then, the second part is bent, and likewise, it is bent sequentially in that same manner.
Having thus described the measurement by *harmya*, the measurement by *hasta* is now stated:
the first [type of temple] shall be of three kinds, measuring three, five, or seven *hastas*.
Nine and eleven cubits, thirteen for the second,
fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen cubits.
The middle necklace is said to be of three kinds; now hear about the *maryādī* and others:
they consist of twenty-one, twenty-three, or twenty-five strings. (11)
By means of twenty-seven, nineteen, and thirty-one [units],
the extent of the Mahāmaryādī is thus said to be threefold.
In this manner, one should conceive of the luminous palaces and the conceptualizations,
beginning at seven cubits and ending at thirty-five.
For each of the first [categories] of halls, three measurements each are prescribed;
these are declared to be the designations for the five types of mansions.
Beginning from nine cubits and ending at thirty-seven,
the number of stories for the palatial mansions known by their respective classes shall be as previously stated.
The enclosure wall (sālā) is considered to be of the same proportions as the previously mentioned palace; thus, there are five enclosures, and now the three-enclosure system is described.
Let the second, third, and fourth walls be taken up;
the remainder [should be] inside, while the outer three walls are excluded.
Excluding those within and outside, one should take either the second or the third of those three sāla trees; the remaining ones are to be avoided. || 18 ||
O best of the twice-born, a mansion provided with one hall is likewise [described];
that which is joined with two halls in a favorable manner is proclaimed as "dvisāla" (two-halled). || 19 ||
Wherever one observes that a particular tree is suitable for a palace or a mansion,
the most skilled in ritual procedures should designate a watch (yāma) at each such opening.
The foot [of the mantra] may be one-fourth, one-half, three-quarters, or equal to that;
or it may be double, triple, quadruple, or even fivefold. || 21 ||
O best of the twice-born! One should fashion the width of the opening at the top of the seed-syllable;
its extension from the wall of the inner circle should be one *vyoma-hasta* (four cubits). (22)
Therefore, one should increase it by three *mātrās* at a time, or else increase it by six *mātrās*,
up to the limit of two and a half cubits or even one cubit, ending at the great boundary-mark (*mahāmaryādā*).
The width of the wall has been fully described; now hear, O observer of noble vows, concerning its height: the height of the wall should be three, four, or five times that width. || 24 ||
Alternatively, the *sālā* is described as being as high as the northern boundary, or the end of sleep, or the end of people, or the end of a stone slab, or the end of the throat. (25)
Having constructed the pinnacle (vājana) with straight walls and provided with a top-ornament (chatraśīrṣaka),
and having installed the bulls according to the prescribed rite, one should place the crest-ornament (śīrṣaka).
Alternatively, it may be outside the wall, provided with a gabled chamber and so forth;
or it may be situated on the ground level, being external yet adorned within.

O best of the twice-born, the width at the base of the wall should be divided into ten parts, and its width at the top should be reduced by one part; thus, from the base to the top, it gradually diminishes by one-eighth part.
Alternatively, the height of the enclosure wall is prescribed according to the measurement of cubits,
starting from three, five, or seven cubits, or from nine (Nanda) or eleven (Rudra) cubits and so forth.

Alternatively, by increasing two cubits at a time, each of the five types of *pañcaśālā* (five-hall temples) has three varieties; thus, from the first onwards, there are indeed nine varieties for their height.
Alternatively, the height of the *sāla* is prescribed in another manner:
by increasing it by two cubits at each stage, there are three varieties for each.
The first [stage] ends with the water-pot; the second ends with the wooden plank;
the third ends with the *bodhikā*; and the fourth ends with the northern boundary. (32)
The fifth, however, ends with the Kapota and consists of the gradual rise of five salas;
among those [types] with one, three, and five salas, they know the muktodaya (frontal elevation) to be as follows.
It may be enclosed by a garland-like wall, or in the shape of an assembly hall, or in the form of a pavilion, or even with straight walls. || 34 ||
On the fifth day, having performed the rite with the qualities of the elements and the Vedas, or even on the day of the sky (the tenth),
there should be a wall upon the wall and a pillar upon the pillar.
One should make the base (tala) for each layer (pratiprastara), and the quarter-measure (pāda) for the small nose (alpanāsikā);
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the measurement of the quarter-measure (pādamāna).

In the main temple, that which rises from the beginning of the fire-oblation (homa) up to the end of the northern rite— having divided that measurement into seven parts, one part is the ground level (dharātala).
The base (pāda) should have five parts and a length equal to its own width; it should be provided with all its constituent members.
One should fashion that base as either level or according to the prescribed [architectural] form.
In the main temple, however, from the fire-oblation (homa) up to the northern limit, there should be nine divisions;
the ground level shall consist of two parts, and the elevation of the base (caraṇodaya) shall consist of seven parts.
The northern end, however, beginning with the *homa* and so forth, should be divided into the portion for Rudra;
the *adhiṣṭhāna* shall consist of a share of the qualities (*guṇa*), and the remainder shall be the emergence of the base (*pādodaya*). || 40 ||
Alternatively, it may have four levels equal in height to the main temple;
one should divide the measurement of the base's elevation into six, seven, or eight parts.
One part of the width of the base should be made of wood or stone;
it may be one-third, two-thirds, three-quarters, or even half [of that]. (42)
One should determine the width of the wall at every part of the base;
however, the width of the main base itself should be divided by eight according to the Dharmananda system.
The tip should be devoid of one part; from the base to the tip, it should gradually taper.
That which is wide at its tip by one-quarter is designated as a *daṇḍa*.
The staff (daṇḍa) is said to be one-third, one-quarter, or one-half [of the height], corresponding respectively to the best, intermediate, and lowest types;
its height is declared to be the same as the width of the base pillar.
The northern width is declared to be either equal to the middle foot or equal to the front foot; these are considered superior, middling, and inferior respectively.
The height of the *vājana* and the *nīvraka* is one-third of the height of the *uttara*;
the *tulānīvraka* is declared to be equal in height to the *uttara*.
Its width should indeed be half or three-quarters of that;
one should perform the installation of the balance on the top of the *vājana* or the *vallī*.
Above the *tulā*, there should be the *jayantī* with a width of half a *tulā*;
the height and breadth of the *jayantī* should be half [of that], and this is declared to be the path of Manu.
The interval between the scales (tulāntara) is the height of the scales (tulocca), and the interval between them is the height of the Jayantī;
likewise, the measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) and the interval between the bricks (iṣṭakā) should be conceived according to the path.
One should construct the pigeon-cot and all other parts exactly as described for the temple;
or alternatively, one may place a layer of bricks upon the top of the *tula*.
O Brahmin, you should construct the brick-layering (iṣṭakāstaruṇa) with the height of the Jayantī festival;
you should construct the brick-layering with lime and molasses-water.
One should perform the smearing with a paste of Karāla, Mudga, and Guḷma, making it smooth;
for this is the method for making bricks when the stones are placed one above the other.
One should especially cover it with stone slabs;
above the frieze (vājana), one should perform the plastering work (sudhākarma) for the covering.
Thus has the ground level been described; now I shall speak of the upper levels.
One should divide the height of the pillar, from its base to its top, into eight parts according to the Dharmananda system. (55)
One part should be lower, the feet higher, and likewise the upper parts;
the floor and the platform should be made in this manner, whether on a single or multiple levels.
It should be constructed upon a foundation with a wall one cubit high, shaped like a parasol with a pinnacle, or else in the form of an assembly hall. || 57 ||
O twice-born one, having resolved upon a boundary either as far as a cow-pen or a plough-furrow, [one should construct it] within that space using clods of earth,
lumps of iron, or pieces of solid wood.
One should construct the roof-covering over the *lūpā* (ridge-pole) provided with a pinnacle;
this is known as the *sabhākāra* (hall-shaped) style, which is devoid of a *vāra* (projecting eaves).
It is specifically stated that the shape above the stone slab is that of a pavilion (maṇḍapa);
it is adorned with the form of a pavilion, though devoid of external walls.
This is known as the umbrella-shaped [mandala]; one may arrange them among those as desired.
The *jāti* is known to have five stories, while the *chanda* shall consist of four stories.
One should know that the *vikalpa* has three stories (*tritala*) and the *ābhāsa* has one floor (*ekabhūmika*);
for the palaces of the [deities] such as Jāti and the others, construct an intermediate wall (*sālātara*) as is appropriate. (62)
Relying on the boundary wall, one should construct the kitchen to the side;
or else, the kitchen should be in the southeast, within the middle courtyard.
The armory should be in the southwest, the sleeping quarters in the northwest;
the sacrificial hall should be in the northeast, or else, O wise one, in the portion designated for waste.
The temple of Maṇḍana should be constructed between the southeast and the south,
or alternatively, between Indra and Śaṅkara (the northeast and the north).
The place for musical instruments should be at its side, or even in the position of Bhṛṅgarāja;
between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, there should be a pavilion for hearing the Dharma.
Between Varuṇa and Vāyu, however, one should construct the temple for the worship of the Book;
on its two sides, an excellent temple of ornaments should be made.
The kitchen should be constructed either beside the storehouse;
establish the armory between the north and the northwest.
Between Soma and Śaṅkara, one should fashion the dwelling of Gaurī;
at its side, a place for a bed provided with a couch.
Then, O best of the twice-born, one should construct a flower-pavilion for Maheśa as part of the floral rites; and during the lunar mansion of Puṣya, one should build a granary.
One should arrange it in this very same manner all around the garland;
and within the garland, in the northeast, the location for the well is prescribed.
Alternatively, I shall describe the determination of the regions in another manner:
the location of Śāli is said to be between Śakra and Śaṅkara. (72)
Between Śakra and Anala, Dhanavatī is proclaimed; between Yāmya and Pāvaka, Puṣpamaṇḍapa is said to be located.
Between the southern (Yāmya) and southwestern (Nairṛta) directions, the bathing-water tank is said to be located;
between the southwestern (Nirṛti) and western (Varuṇa) directions, the pavilion for hearing the Dharma is situated.
The place for weapons is said to be between the directions of Varuṇa and Vāyu;
the place for the bed is said to be between the directions of Vāyu and Soma. || 75 ||
Between the directions of Īśāna and Soma, construct a pavilion for the purpose of sacrifice;
let there be a hall for applying collyrium toward Jayanta, and a kitchen in the south-eastern quarter.
In the garland surrounding [the temple], all the locations are described:
the dancing form of Śaṅkara and the one who has the bull as his vehicle in the southeast.
O Brahmin, one should place [the deity] together with Umā and Skanda in the southwest;
Kaṅkāla in the direction of the wind (northwest), and Bhikṣāṭana in the northeast.
In the Satyāṃśa [Kalpa], the [deity] is Sukhāsana; in the Vitatha, Tripurāntaka;
in the Sugrīva, Harirardha; and in the Gandharva, Candraśekhara. (79)
In the remaining portion, one should worship Madanāri; in the primary [portion], Kālārimūrti;
in the south, Ardhanārīśa; and in the east, Kalyāṇasundara. || 80 ||
Kṣetrapāla is in Parjanya; Dakṣiṇeśvara is indeed in the south (Yāmya);
the manifested Liṅga is in Vāruṇya; and Gajahārin is in the north (Saumya). || 81 ||
(170) Above this, one should designate the ālaya; one should arrange it within the intermediate spaces.
Having carefully inspected the root edifice, perform the installation of all [the deities]. 82.
One should arrange the beauty of the gates and other features on the four sides of the walls;
in the middle of the series of walls and in the middle of the length, there should be an entrance.
Alternatively, O twice-born one, there may be a single principal door in the middle of the main building, or others, or latticed windows.
Thus the enclosure wall has been described; outside of it, the pathway (vīthi) is prescribed, with an extent of one, two, three, four, or five staff-lengths (daṇḍa), according to the ritual rule.
Outside of that, construct a row of houses according to the prescribed measurements;
the residence for the attendants of the Śaivas is said to be in the east.
A female teacher is prescribed for the eastern or southern region;
for astrologers, Ambaṣṭhas, physicians, and musicians, she is prescribed in the south.
For those who live by the sale of books, it is prescribed in the west;
for all devotees, however, their residence is on the northern side. (88)
In the southeast is the site of Mahāvrata; in the south is the abode of Pāśupata;
in the southwest is Kālāmukha; and in the west is the abode of the Buddhists.
One should construct a great hall in the northwest, a residence for Brahmins in the north,
and especially a dwelling for the practice of knowledge in the northeast.
Externally, however, one should have a reservoir excavated in the direction of Indra;
between the south and the southeast, establish a water-giving shed.
One should construct a cowshed between the southern and southwestern directions; or, a maternity chamber is prescribed between the western and southwestern directions. (92)
Between Varuṇa and Anila is the dwelling for those afflicted by disease;
between Saumya and Anila is the pavilion for the instruction of children.
Between Soma and Śaṅkara, there should be a pavilion for the singers;
outside of that, O Brahmin, all around, [there should be space] for the groups of female servants, courtesans, and so forth.
[The same applies] to those who live by dancing, singing, and eating; those who live by buying and selling;
to cart-drivers, those who live by flowers, and likewise to potters. (95)
For those who live by fish and meat, there shall be a weaver's workshop; for barbers, shavers, cowherds, and artisans, [there shall be separate quarters]. (96)
The wise man should arrange a row of houses for the guards around the Cāpavatsa and Meṣa, as a dwelling for those starting from the east.
Outside of that, however, in the northeast or the northwest direction is the cremation ground;
and to the south and outside to the north are the dwellings of the leather-workers and others.
Because of their residence, the dwelling place for washermen should be established;
at a distance of one krośa outside of that, however, the settlement of the Caṇḍālas is prescribed.
"O best of the twice-born, this indeed is declared to be the characteristic of the enclosure wall.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, the section on the rules for the characteristics of the enclosure wall, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kāśyapa. 42.
One should join the head with Īśāna, the crown with Kavaca,
the hands with Astra, and the feet with Sadyojāta.
One should conceive of all the limbs, beginning with the feet, as being like oneself;
first and then subsequently, one should perform the reintegration in due order until it is complete.
Then one should perform the *upāṅga* placement, and then perform the *pratyaṅga* placement;
the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās* is declared to be the *sthāna-aṅga*.
Clothing, ornaments, weapons, and thread are considered the secondary limbs (upāṅgas).
According to the nature of the *tāla*, from the *tritāla* up to the end, they are of three kinds: superior, intermediate, and inferior.
The supreme ten-tāla measure is known to be two hundred and forty finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
the middling ten-tāla should consist of one hundred and ninety-two finger-breadths.
The lowest ten-tāla measure consists of one hundred and sixteen finger-breadths;
the highest nine-tāla measure shall consist of one hundred and twenty-four parts.
The middle [type] consists of one hundred and eight parts with nine tālas;
the smallest should consist of nine tālas and one hundred and four [parts].
In the case of the *tāla* measurement, one should likewise subtract four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) successively;
the supreme [image] for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara is made with ten *tālas*.
Umā and Sarasvatī should likewise be ten tālas in height;
so too Uṣā, Bhūmi, Durgā, Lakṣmī, and the Mothers.
O best of the twice-born! One should have Guha, Śatamakha, Caṇḍeśa, and Kṣetrapālaka made with a height of ten tālas in their smallest form.
The Vasus, the eight Mūrtīs, the Vidyeśas, the Lokapālas, and other deities likewise [are to be represented] according to the excellent nine-fold measurement (navatāla). (11)
The wise man should have Vighneśa fashioned according to the excellent Pañcatāla measurement, along with hosts of Yakṣas and Apsaras, the eight forms (of Śiva), and the Maruts.
With that same medium-inferior [tempo], make all the hosts of beings;
the children [should be performed] with the Vedic tempo, and the Kinnaras with the triple tempo.
One should likewise have the Puruṣas and others fashioned with a triple time-measure (tritāla). Thus has the sequence of time-measures been declared, which is conducive to the success of the images.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of pavilions (maṇṭapa). In a temple with a single story, the front pavilion (mukhamaṇṭapa) is prescribed.
One should likewise contemplate the classes [of mantras], the variations of will, and the manifestations, facing the temple in the cardinal and intermediate directions. || 16 ||
In the midst of villages and the like, or in the cardinal and intermediate directions, or in a garden, or on a riverbank, or indeed at the edge of a lake. (17)
One should construct a pavilion for the sake of the deity according to one's desire, provided with a proper entrance;
one should build a square pavilion in front of the temple.
First is the hall for the face (mukhamaṇḍapa), then the hall for the image (pratimāmaṇḍapa);
the third is for the purpose of bathing, and the fourth is for dancing.
Among those, the first is as before; now the second and subsequent ones are described here:
perform [the arrangement] starting from the garland of the inner maṇḍala and ending with the inner necklace, or vice versa.
One should arrange three pavilions (maṇṭapa), while the remainder [of the structure] is outside in whichever direction is desired;
[the arrangement may extend] from one pavilion to another, or from a hall (sālā) to the end of a pavilion. || 21 ||
Now listen to the characteristics of that which is known as the *antarāla* at the beginning:
it may consist of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight cubits.
Alternatively, it may have nine dharmas or even the "hand of Rudra" (rudrahasta);
however, those with a wide interior space are proclaimed to be of the number of Rudras (eleven).
In whichever pavilion one should construct [the shrine],
there one should especially prepare the inner chamber with devotion, consisting of one, two, three, four, or five [sections].
Or it may have an open space in the middle, or even a wall-enclosure;
if it is a wall-enclosure with an opening in the middle, it should be joined with a vestibule on both sides. || 25 ||
One should construct a vestibule (veśa) consisting of one, two, three, or four bays;
or, one may arrange a door or a lattice window on either side or in the middle. || 26 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should arrange a stream of water for the purpose of bathing on the northern side, or an uneven wall, or the inner space.
All parts of the pavilion, beginning with its foundation, should be symmetrical;
or else, the pavilion may be symmetrical even if it lacks an entrance.
The intermediate space is thus described; listen now to the measurement of the pavilion (maṇṭapa).
Starting from three cubits, it should be increased by two cubits at a time. (29)
Up to the nineteenth [section], the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is extended in nine ways;
these pavilions are indeed the manifestation of the abodes of manifestation.
From twenty-one cubits, increasing by two cubits at a time up to thirty-seven cubits, there are nine varieties. (31)
For the [deities of the] Ābhāsa worlds, however, it is appropriate for them, or else suitable for each individually;
beginning from thirty-nine cubits, it increases by two cubits at a time.
A chanda measuring fifty-five cubits is said to be the Karānta;
beginning from fifty-seven cubits, it increases by two cubits at each step.
A structure measuring seventy-seven cubits in width is called a *jāti*;
it should be a square pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with a length equal to that width. || 34 ||
Starting from one and a half cubits and increasing by six finger-breadths at each step,
up to a limit of five cubits, the width of the base (bhakti-vyāsa) is divided into three or five parts.
Beginning from half a cubit (ardhahasta) up to five cubits,
one should determine the width of the wall by increasing it in increments of one guṇāṅgula.
Starting from two and a half cubits and increasing by six finger-breadths each time,
there are twenty-three varieties of feet, extending up to a limit of eight cubits.
The height of the pillars is determined by increasing the measurement of one's own cubit (guṇāṅgula) from the upper edge of the base;
now the width of the pillars is described.
Beginning from eight finger-breadths and increasing by half a finger-breadth,
up to nineteen mātrās, the width of the foot is twenty-three [mātrās].
The height of the base (pādocca) should be divided by twelve, ten, nine, or eight parts;
the root-star (mūlatāra) shall be one part of that, and each of those parts shall be nine units at the top.
The general rule for all pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) is that they should have a height equal to half the base-height;
however, the height of the base may be two parts out of nine parts of the total height, or the rise of the base may be two parts. (41)
The *masūraka* may consist of one part of three or four parts of the height of the pillar-base (*aṅghrituṅga*),
or the pedestal (*adhiṣṭhāna*) may be provided with a base (*upapīṭha*), or it may be a *masūraka* alone.

The height of the *upapīṭha* (subsidiary pedestal) is known to be equal to the surface of the earth, or twice, or even three times that; or it may be the same as the height of the *upapīṭha* itself. || 43 ||

The secondary pedestal (upapīṭha), the base (adhiṣṭhāna), the foot (caraṇa), and likewise the plinth (prastara), as well as the enclosure (nīvraveśa) and the ornament (alaṃkāra), are to be counted as existing as before. 44.
It should be endowed with the three types of devotion (bhakti), joined with sixteen pillars,
provided with a small nose-like projection (nāsikā) for the kalā, and having a pinnacle (kūṭa) in the center.
It may be adorned everywhere, or provided with four gates;
likewise, it may have its desired gate in one direction, or consist of two lattices and compartments.
On the exterior, it should be provided with stairs and adorned with various arches and the like; or, even if devoid of arches and such, it should first be fashioned in this manner. (47)
The large [mandala] should have four bays and be provided with doors toward the desired directions;
the front and back [sections] should each have two bays, and the *nīvraka* should be one bay wide.
Leaving aside the middle foot, there are two divisions above;
it is joined with feet numbering twice the sun (twelve), and possesses twenty noses. 49.
In the directions of the doors,
there should be a second pavilion with stairs, having a plough-shaped wall at the corner and joined with a cage of eight [pillars].

With five divisions, one should construct a quadrangular [mandala], with a *kūṭa* (pinnacle) in the center occupying three parts; the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) surrounding it, consisting of one part, is provided with thirty-two pillars. (51)
It is enriched with twice the number of suns (twelve) as noses, joined with eight cages,
provided with doors in the desired directions, and the walls are located right there at the doors.
At the location of the door, there should be a staircase adorned with all ornaments;
the third part, however, is the wall decorated with water-pots, creepers, and other such motifs.
The square [pedestal] is divided by six lines, with a central pinnacle (kūṭa) occupying two parts;
that pinnacle is provided with eight feet and joined with a courtyard (raṅga) in its center.
It should be provided with four doors, or even with a door facing the desired direction;
it should have a width of two bays and be joined with a *nīvr* (roof-structure) consisting of one bay.
One should employ there either a division of the directions according to one's preference, or simply a four-directional division,
or one consisting of forty-eight parts.
The fourth [section] consists of a wall enriched with twenty-four small windows, adorned with pitcher-creepers,
joined with eight archways, and provided with a pavilion.
The square [pedestal] should have seven parts and be joined with sixty-four units;
in its center, there should be a pinnacle (kūṭa) or a decorated knob (maṇḍitāgra) consisting of nine parts.

It is endowed with thirty-two minor projections (nāsā), joined with auspicious projections (bhadraka) on the four directions; its width is one-third of the total, and the front projection (mukhabhadraka) extends outward by one part.
The fifth is proclaimed as being provided with a central stage, joined with walls in the desired directions, and endowed with all ornaments. || 60 ||

By dividing [the height] into eight parts according to the four ages (yuga), one should fashion the upper pinnacle (ūrdhvakūṭa) in the middle of that [structure], consisting of eighty cubits and possessing a fourth part [of the total height].
The sixth pavilion shall be provided with doors on all four sides, a peaked roof in the center occupying one part, and adorned with every ornament.
With ninefold devotion, the quadrangular [mandala] consists of one hundred parts including the feet;
the Nīvrabhadra has twenty parts, with each part divided into three. || 63 ||
It should be provided with four doors, or else with doors facing the desired directions;
at the entrance, there should be a staircase consisting of fire-parts (three parts), endowed with the appropriate width and length.
The seventh pavilion should be provided with a central stage, endowed with six or eight pillars and a nose-projection, and adorned with all ornaments.
It should be square, with a tenth part [of the side] increased by a tenth part of the sun (twelve);
and it should be provided with nine peaks in the center and in each of the eight directions.
One should arrange the intermediate space by means of the portion that covers the peak;
the staircase, as before, should face the entrance and be provided with a *bhadra* in that direction.
The eighth pavilion should be adorned with all ornaments;
it should be quadrangular due to devotion to Rudra, while the central pinnacle (kūṭaka) is formed by one-third of that area.

At the entrance, it should be provided with a flight of stairs and endowed with auspicious divisions according to the desired directions; the doors or the walls therein should terminate at the desired sections.
The ninth pavilion should be adorned with all ornaments;
in the twelfth part [of the area], it should be quadrangular, with a pinnacle (kūṭaka) in the center occupying two parts.
Outside the pavilion, however, a porch (ālinda) is desired, measuring one part [in length];
its width should extend four or two parts, projecting out in all four directions. (71)
One should fashion the pedestal in the central area with one hundred and sixty-eight parts;
adorned with all ornaments, it shall be the tenth maṇḍapa.
In the center, a peak (kūṭaka) is formed by a thirteenth part of the quadrangular [base] and a fire-part (three parts);
it is joined with walls toward the desired directions and provided with portals (bhadra) in the four cardinal directions.
One should fashion the Mukhabhadra in the eastern direction according to the Nanda-portion, provided with two [units], ninety [units], and endowed with the quarter [unit]. (74)
Adorned with archways, small lattices, and other ornaments, and endowed with every kind of decoration, the pavilion should be a portion of Rudra. (75)
With portions of one *manu* (14), it is a quadrangular [structure], while in the center, with two parts (*dvaṃśa*), is the *kūṭaka*.
There is an increase of four [parts], twenty parts, two hundred, and accompanied by the *caraṇas*. 76.
The pavilion should be provided with walls and endowed with auspicious openings on the four sides;
it should be especially adorned with the Nanda and other auspicious designs according to one's devotion.
The twelfth pavilion should be adorned with all ornaments;
it is square in shape, five cubits wide on each wall, and equal in length. || 78 ||
In the middle, there is a pinnacle (kūṭa) with a third part [of the width], provided with an upper pinnacle;
its width and length are each a third part, and it is provided with a frontal auspicious projection (mukhabhadra). || 79 ||
It should be joined to a wall on the desired side, while elsewhere it is provided with pillars;
it is adorned and equipped with arches, lattices, and other such ornaments.
Two hundred and fifty-two, accompanied by four feet [verses], endowed with all ornaments, and consisting of thirteen maṇṭapas. (81)
Thus, through the differentiation of pride (māna), they know the pavilion (maṇṭapa) to be quadrangular;
from this point upward, it consists of thirty-four [units] and terminates at the ten boundaries.
One should construct a square pavilion endowed with all ornaments; the walls and pillars should be fashioned around it according to the desire of the builder.
One should construct a square pavilion for the hermitage; it is also said that the length may be equal to the width of the walls, or the width may be equal to the length of the walls. (84)

The width and the devotion [of the base] should be increased by one finger-breadth for each quality (guṇa), up to twenty-seven finger-breadths; it is said that this is done by means of a quarter-measure.

If, however, it is diminished by the increase [of the previous measurement], one should fill up the hand-measurement as prescribed for the pavilions (maṇḍapas) and then construct the pavilion. || 86 ||
One should perform the calculation of the *āya* (fortune) and other factors as before, using the number of desired parts;
then, the length of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be endowed with the auspicious *āya* and other such qualities.
Having made the appropriate divisions for it, construct the pavilion,
which is broad with three bays and possesses a length of five bays.
One should arrange the door on one side of the city or at a corner;
if it is on the side, it should be provided with thirty units (aṅghris). || 89 ||
One should construct the *lūpārohaṇaka* (the structural framework) for the interior of the pavilion all around that very [area], consisting of twenty-eight feet.
If it consists of twenty-eight feet preceded by the syllable *vāra*, or else if it is devoid of *vāra* and endowed with twenty-four feet; (91)
The first [section] should be fashioned with small altars at its feet, a network of altars, and archways, along with various water-jars, creepers, and other ornaments.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be four bhaktis wide and six parts in length;
on all sides, one part should be for the kūṭas, alternating internally.
The second [type] of the pavilion has a front face that is two modules wide and one module long, and it is provided with thirty-two pillars. (94)
In the large [type], there should be five divisions in the width and seven divisions in the length;
with a width of three and five divisions, there shall be an assembly hall in the middle of the long [portion]. (95)
The pavilion (maṇṭapa) should be surrounded by a portion [of the ground] and provided with auspicious openings (bhadra) in the desired directions;
it should be forty cubits in size or [smaller], and endowed with all ornaments.
The third pavilion should be provided with railings and other features;
it should be as wide as six parts (rasa-bhakti) and have eight corners (vasu-bhakti).

The pavilion (maṇṭapa) should have a width of two or four bhaṅgis, with its length increased by one in the middle; it should extend for six parts (ṣaḍ-aṃśa) all around and feature auspicious doors (bhadra) facing the desired directions.
The fourth pavilion should be joined with sixty pillars, adorned from the nose [pediment] upwards, and endowed with various ornaments.
In the case of the *tāra* [mandala], it should have seven divisions;
the *sabhāṅgaṇa* (the assembly courtyard) should be nine parts in length, three parts in width, and five parts in depth.

Around the pavilion (maṇḍapa), one should construct an enclosure wall occupying one-sixteenth part [of the area], provided with auspicious projections (bhadra) toward the desired directions; it should have a width of three parts and a length of one part, featuring an auspicious projection at the entrance.
Seventy-two [units] plus two more is designated as a "quarter" (pāda);
the fifth pavilion (maṇṭapa) shall be endowed with all ornaments.
It should be broad with eight parts, extended by ten parts,
