and have a width of two or four parts, being long in the middle and possessing an elevated assembly hall.

O observer of good vows! The pavilion should be surrounded [by a wall], excluding the central pillar from the portion of the fire; it should have its auspicious sections facing the desired directions, consisting of four and two parts respectively.
Endowed with ninety-six pillars and adorned with all ornaments,
this sixth pavilion is indeed declared to be worthy of Śiva.
The assembly hall (sabhā) should be nine parts wide, eleven parts long due to devotion to Rudra, and one part in width at its middle for the sake of devotion. 106.
One should construct the pavilion (maṇḍapa) surrounding the portion of the Veda;
the front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) should have a width of three or four parts and its length should be greater.
The seventh pavilion should be adorned with all ornaments;
it should be ten parts wide and two parts longer.
The width [of the structure] is two or four parts long; between those two is the courtyard (sabhāṅkaṇa);
on all sides is a veranda (linda) of one part, and outside the pavilion (maṇṭapa) it is two parts.

Outside of that, an *alinda* (veranda) occupying one part, joined with internal pillars and provided with auspicious openings (*bhadra*) in the desired directions, shall constitute the eighth, the *maṇḍapa*.
That same [area], increased by a portion of Śiva, has its width and length [determined] such that the courtyard of the assembly hall (*sabhāṅkaṇa*) occupies five parts;
the surrounding veranda (*alinda*) occupies one part, and the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) is two parts on the exterior. (111)
Outside of that, one part shall be for the porch (alinda), and the ninth part shall be the pavilion (maṇṭapa);
it should be as wide as twelve parts and twice as long, plus two additional parts.
In the middle of the four or six parts, there should be a hall (sabhā) or a pinnacle (kaṇa);
on the exterior, a porch (alinda) of one part, and in the pavilion (maṇṭapa), two parts on the exterior.
The tenth part of a *sāntatālīndra* should be the *maṇṭapa*;
when the *jagatī* is wide, its length should be two parts more than that.

In the middle of the assembly hall, occupying three-fifths of the space, there is a pavilion (maṇṭapa) enclosed by a portico (alinda); within this pavilion is the vimāna, and outside it is a portion for the portico.
Alternatively, even without an *ālinda* (veranda), a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) consisting of eight parts is called the *Bhadra-maṇṭapa*,
provided it is joined with auspicious projections (*bhadra*) toward the desired directions.
In the Manu lineage, however, the width is increased by two parts, while the length is twice that;
with a width of four parts, there is a courtyard for the assembly hall in the middle.
Outside of that, one part is for the *alinda* (veranda), and a square *maṇḍapa* (pavilion) is formed; outside the *maṇḍapa*, an *alinda* is likewise prescribed as one part.
The fourteenth is known as the Maṇṭapa, provided with auspicious openings toward the desired directions;
it is wide by five parts and three-fifths, and its length is two parts greater than that.
One-twelfth part in the center is for the pavilion (maṇṭapa), and the courtyard (sabhā) is known as the kaṇa;
one part surrounded by the courtyard is prescribed as the vestibule (alinda).
Outside of that, a square pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed;
from the portion surrounding it, there shall be an alinda, and thus the pavilion becomes thirteenfold. || 121 ||
In the sixteenth part, it should be broad by two additional parts and long;
it is provided with twenty-four corners and, on the exterior, has an *alinda* (veranda) according to the measurement of one part.
Outside of that, a pavilion (maṇṭapa) should specifically be constructed using one-fourth [of the measurement];
from one-quarter of its circumference, there shall be an alcove (alinda), making it a fourteen-fold pavilion.
One should know that the extension of the birth [sign] and so forth is called their respective arrangement;
the lattice and the door must be grasped specifically according to the proper method.
The wise one should construct a wall extending in the desired direction all around;
for they know such a structure, with its various mantra-designs and longitudinal extent, to be a maṇṭapa.
Or rather, the width of the base for all pavilions may be three, four, five, six, or seven parts; however, the width of the wall should be divided into five parts.
It should not be wide at the base, nor should it have wooden legs;
for all the Mukhabhadras, the courtyard (aṅkaṇa) takes the form of a pavilion (maṇṭapa).
On its side, it should be provided with a staircase, adorned with elephant-trunk motifs,
and its width should be five, six, seven, nine, or eight *daṇḍas*.
That [pedestal] should be one foot or one and a half daṇḍas in height, resembling the trunk of an elephant;
it should be fashioned with a central nave and a staff-like base, octagonal in shape, and shaped like an elephant's trunk.
It is slightly curved, with a face like that of a *kiṃpuruṣa*, a long tip, and the shape of a cock;
it is reduced by one-eighth from its base, and its width at the tip gradually tapers.
O Brahmin, [the distance] may be one elephant-length (hastihasta), or two, or an even number of staffs (yaṣṭi);
or it may be a staff (daṇḍa), or a staff plus a quarter-staff, or a staff plus a half, or a staff plus three-quarters. (131)
The staff and the crossbar should each have a width of two daṇḍas;
the roof should be twice that, and below it there should be a pavilion.
One part shall be for the beloved of one's choice, and one part shall be my own arising;
first, standing upon that spot while placing the left foot foremost, [one should proceed]. (133)
One should know that the ascent of the stairs is prescribed for mortals;
thus has the maṇḍapa been described—now hear about the gopura, O observer of noble vows! || 134 ||
Thus ends the forty-third chapter [of the *Aṃśumat*], concerning the rules for the characteristics of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) within the *Kāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the gate-towers (gopuras);
meanwhile, the inner maṇḍala, the enclosure wall (sālā), and so forth, are now being declared in due order.
Dvāraśobhā, dvāraśālā, dvāraprāsāda, harmyakam, and dvāragopura—these are proclaimed by name in successive order. || 2 ||
One should fashion the beauty of the gateway with one, two, or three stories;
it may also have two floors, three floors, or even four floors.
A gate-hall (dvāraśālā) should be constructed, and on the second [floor] there should be a hall;
one may begin the gate-palace (dvāraprāsāda) with three, four, or five stories.
The palace (harmya) should have four, five, or six stories;
likewise, the gate-towers (gopura) are intended to have five, six, or seven floors. || 5 ||
Alternatively, among all types of *sāla* temples, there may be one, two, or three stories;
it may include a pedestal (*upapīṭha*) and a base (*adhiṣṭhāna*), or it may be without a pedestal.
I shall describe all nine types of heights for those two [temples], beginning with the highest; the width of the main temple (mūlaprāsāda) is divided by seven, eight, or nine.
And in the tenth and eleventh parts, excluding one portion respectively, the expansion of the elements beginning with the *śobhā* and ending with the *gopura* is proclaimed in sequence. (8)
This series of gate-towers for the palaces appearing as conceptual constructions consists of four,
five, or six parts within the vastness of the root-abode.
The beauty of the *chanda* (pediment) and other features should be reduced by one-seventh or one-eighth;
it should be one-third of the main building, or one part, or even half a part.
In the first and subsequent types of *sāla* (outer wall), one should likewise take three parts, two parts, four parts, one part of the *guṇa*,
and four parts out of five.

The sequence beginning with the *śobhā* and ending with the *gopura* constitutes the temple according to its class; having thus determined the measurement of the mansion, one should then proceed according to the measurement of the cubit (*hasta*). 12.
From two cubits up to sixteen cubits, increasing by one cubit at a time,
there are three varieties each for the structures beginning with the *śobhā* and ending with the *gopura*.
Thus, regarding the manifestation of conceptual constructions within the temple of desire, it will now be explained, beginning from one cubit and extending up to seventeen cubits. (14)
By increasing by one cubit [at a time], there are three varieties each for the *śobhā* and other [elements], starting from four cubits up to eighteen cubits. (15)
The expansion of the *śobhā* and other elements exists in the *jāti-harmya*;
each has a threefold measurement, and the *chanda* is of five kinds. || 16 ||
The width of the small [shrines] and the great one should be made progressively according to the measurement of a cubit as prescribed for each;
to do otherwise brings misfortune.
Alternatively, [the dimensions] may be three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine cubits;
likewise, ten or eleven cubits—these constitute the three groups starting from the lowest.
Therefore, that [decoration] should be made for all pillars; hence it is universal.
Alternatively, there is an extensive variety of other ways for the ornaments and so forth. (19)
Beginning from five cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time,
up to thirteen cubits, the width for the beautiful [temple] is thus fivefold.
Starting from three and five cubits and increasing by two cubits each time,
the door-hall (dvāraśālā) is of five types, ending at twenty-three cubits.
Beginning from twenty-five cubits and ending at twenty-three cubits,
the width of the gatehouse and the temple is proclaimed to be fivefold.
Beginning from thirty-five cubits and extending up to forty-three,
the width of the gateway-tower (dvāraharmya) is proclaimed to be of five types.
That gateway (gopura) extends in five ways, increasing by two cubits each time, from forty-five cubits up to fifty-three cubits.
(188) Those [measures] are the width of the door and the courtyard; listen now to their length: it is one-quarter, or one-and-a-half quarters less, or double, or even double again. (25)
One-third and one-fourth [of the width] shall be the proportions, while the length shall be two parts;
thus indeed should the elements from the *śobhā* to the *gopura* be grasped.
Among them, there is a certain distinction; listen also to that distinction. Specifically, when the width is taken as one cubit (hasta), there is a particular difference.
Having determined the length as before, one should make it desiredly long among many [options];
or, having increased it by a cubit, one should multiply it, or else one should perform the previous [measurement]. (28)
It should be provided with auspicious features such as the *āya* and measured by the length of a cubit;
for, without those two, it would fall under the influence of the base of the palace as originally intended.
The length has been fully described; now their height is being stated.
Having divided the width into seven parts, the height of the ornament (śobhā) is one part of eleven (rudra).
The height of the door-lintel (dvāraśālā) should be one and a half times the height of the Tārā;
in the third [type], it should be seven parts, eleven parts, or twelve parts [of the height].
When the width is divided into nine parts, the height should be four parts;
the great gopura is desired to have a height that is double its width.
The height from the *homādi* (the base of the fire-ritual) up to the *sthūpī* (the pinnacle) has been declared; let that be grasped.
The measurement for the width and length is said to be one-quarter outside the [central] cord.
Outside of that, the roof-structure (nīvr̥), such as the gabled chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) and so forth, should be like a temple;
it should be one-third or one-fourth of the width.
In a five-part division, the projection outside the hall should be two parts; starting from one and a half cubits, it increases by six finger-breadths at each step. (35)
The width of the door for small [temples] is said to extend up to five cubits;
it is declared to be threefold for those that are very small, so now hear concerning those of intermediate size.
Starting from three cubits up to a limit of seven cubits, the width of the door is proclaimed to increase by six finger-breadths [at each stage]. (37)
Beginning from four cubits and extending up to nine cubits,
the width of the door should be increased by two parts (rasa) for each respective measurement.
The *tāra* should be five parts, seven parts, or, in the case of seven parts, ten spans; it may be one and a half times, less by a quarter, double, or double in height. (39)
The height of the door should be divided into seven parts, consisting of one and a half parts or one part;
I shall now describe the middle door for the middle-sized liṅga.
Having specifically established the nine-finger measurement for the Śiva-fire element,
one should fashion the middle of the door to the left of the center of the liṅga.
The wise know that from the base (śobhā) up to the gate-tower (gopura), the middle of the door is determined in sequence;
from the center of that, the length of the gate-tower is equal on both sides.
Construct the door-junction and the door-panel according to the characteristics of the door;
beginning from one division (bhakti) up to nineteen.
One should arrange the width of that row in this very manner;
as long as the width of two rows is, so long should the length of those rows be.
When the width is divided into five parts, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall occupy three parts;
the remainder shall be the thickness of the wall, which may be half the height or one cubit. (45)
O best of the twice-born, the remaining portion should be extensive for the hall of devotion on a single floor;
one should determine the extent of the surrounding wall by this very measure.
Thus the single-storied [temple] is described; now the two-storied is likewise explained:
it should have five parts in width and likewise in length. (47)
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of two parts, the thickness of the wall one and a half parts,
the corner pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) one part, and the length of the cell (koṣṭha) three parts.
The space between the necklaces should be a portion of Śiva; one may likewise arrange it in this manner.
The width should consist of seven parts, and its length nine parts. (49)
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall be one part of the yuga (four parts), while the thickness of the wall shall be one and a half parts.
The corner pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) shall be one part of the span (tāra), and the length of the hall (śālā) shall be three parts.
The interval between the pendants (hārāntara) should be one part in width, or it may be the same;
the length of the hall (śālā), however, should be calculated as five parts. || 51 ||

One should design the intermediate neck (hārāntara) and the pinnacle (kūṭa) each with one part; the remaining length, equal to the interval between the pinnacles, should be provided with the necks. || 52 ||
A *bhadra* or a *bhadrapañjara* should be made with a measurement equal to half the length of the *hāra*;
thus has the two-storied structure been described, and now the three-storied structure is being explained.
One should divide the width and likewise the length into nine parts;
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of three parts, and the pedestal of the shrine (gṛhapiṇḍikā) shall be one part.
The *ālinda* (veranda) occupies one part; the width of the *hāra* (projection) is one part of Śiva (three parts);
the *karṇakūṭa* (corner turret) is one part of Śiva (three parts); and the length of the *śālā* (hall) is three parts. || 55 ||
One part shall be the width of the cage (pañjara), and half a part the interval between the necks (hāra);
having thus fashioned the base floor, the wise know this to be a two-storeyed structure as described previously.
Alternatively, O observer of noble vows, listen to another method for the three-storied [temple]:
the width of the door-ornament (dvāraśobhā) should be eleven parts, and its length should be eleven parts as well.
One part of the total width is the inner sanctum (garbhageha), and it is said that one part constitutes the body of the house (gṛhapiṇḍya).
The vestibule (alinda) is known to be equal to that, and one should arrange the entrance porch (hāra) with one part.
Whether it be the portion for the porch or the wall, provided with an inner chamber,
one should determine the length of the cell by dividing the total length into five parts.
The remainder is indicated as before; the second is like the two-storied world. Thus the three-storied is described, and this is the supreme four-storied [temple]. (60)
In the width, there are ten parts; likewise, there are rows along the length.
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) consists of three parts and so forth, while the thickness of the wall is one and a half parts.
One should design the *alinda* with a portion of Śiva, and likewise the *hāravyāsa*; one should also fashion the *pañjara* and the *karṇakūṭa* each with a single portion.
The measurement of the kūṭa and tāra should be equal, while the remainder is provided with intervals for the hāras;
in the length of the hall (śālā), one-fourth part is for the [central] element, and half a part is for the interval between the hāras.
Thus has the first stage been described; from this point upward, one should proceed as before.
In its width, it should be one-tenth [of the whole], and its length should be twelve parts.
One should divide the front and back of the hall into five parts;
the remainder is prescribed as before. This is the supreme four-storeyed [temple]. (65)
The height and likewise the width shall be eleven parts;
on the eastern, western, and side faces, the hall shall be five parts in length.
One part for the width of the cage, one part for the width of the pinnacle, and one part for the Śiva-section;
likewise, one part for the interval between the necklaces—thus should the first floor be designed.
One should visualize all its upper levels as before;
the letter *Tāra* occupies one-eleventh part, while its long form occupies thirteen parts.
The inner sanctum (garbhageha) should be one part, the thickness of the walls two parts,
the veranda (alinda) one part, and the decorative frieze (hārā) should be fashioned with one part.
One should fashion all parts, such as the gabled roof and the chambers, exactly as before;
this has been described as the five-fold earth (pañcabhūmi). Now listen to the description of the six-tiered (ṣaṭtala) temple.
In the Tāra [style], however, the platform (mañca) is twelve parts long;
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) is four parts, and the base (bhakti) is two parts wide.
One should arrange the *alinda* (veranda) with one part, and the *hārā* (architrave) with one part;
the side hall (*pārśvaśālā*) shall take four parts, while [the space] at the front and back shall take six parts.
The interval between the necklaces (hārāntara) should be a portion of Śiva; the space (vyoma) should be at the two peaks of the cage (pañjara);
the remainder is prescribed as before, and likewise for the six earths (rasabhūmi).
In the thirteenth part, both the width and the length are likewise [divided];
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) occupies five parts, while the temple plinth (gṛhapiṇḍī) consists of two parts.

The *alinda* (veranda) is one part of Śiva; the *khaṇḍaharmya* (pavilion) is one part of Śiva; the length of the *koṣṭha* (cell) is five parts; and the *pañjara* (lattice) is everywhere by one part. (75)
The peak (kūṭa) should be made with one part, and likewise the intervening necklace (hārāntara);
or else, the width may be thirteen parts and the length fifteen parts.
At each opening, one should arrange large halls with a width of seven parts;
the length of the side wings should be made with five parts.
The remainder is specified as before, endowed with all ornaments;
this is declared to be the seven stories, and that shall be the great gateway (mahāgopura). || 78 ||
The one most skilled in ritual design should fashion it either with a veranda or without a veranda;
if it is made without a veranda, it may be a cell within the wall.
O best of the twice-born, having joined the portion for the porch (alinda), one should have it constructed;
thus has the first floor been described, and above that, there should be six stories.
The seven stages have been fully explained; now their enumeration is stated:
the height from the base of the main temple to the foot-plate (pādādhiṣṭhāna) is [the first]. || 81 ||
Or one-fourth, one-fifth, or one-sixth; or indeed seven, eight, or nine parts; or ten, eleven, or even seven, eight, or nine parts. || 82 ||
Or, having divided [the height] into ten or eleven parts, one part is for the pedestal (upapīṭhaka);
the remainder is divided into three parts, and one part is for the base (dharātala).
The best of those skilled in ritual design should fashion the height of the pedestal (caraṇa) as two parts;
likewise, the height of the sub-pedestal (upapīṭha) should be as prescribed in the rules for the upapīṭha.
Alternatively, the measurement of the door may be appropriate according to the measure of a cubit;
its height shall be four, five, six, seven, or eight [cubits]. (85)
Alternatively, having divided [the height] into nine parts according to the Rudra-proportion, one part is for the pedestal (upapīṭha);
the height of the pedestal is thus declared, while the remainder is divided by three.
The foundation (adhiṣṭhāna) is one part; twice that is the length of the base (caraṇa).
The measurement of the door is prescribed as extending from the fire-offering (homa) to the northern boundary. || 87 ||
Construct the base for the foot-binding (pādabandha) with the door-ornaments and so forth;
then, when divided into six parts, the section beginning from the north should extend up to the pinnacle (stūpī).
The *prastara* (pedestal) shall be one and a quarter parts; the neck-measure shall be one-eighth part;
the head shall be three-quarters of a part; and the remainder is the height of the *śikhā* (finial). || 89 ||
Thus the single-storey [temple] has been described; now hear about the two-storey one, O observer of noble vows!
When the space from the north to the crest is divided into nine parts, [the following occurs].
The height of the *prastara* (pedestal) shall be one-quarter [of the total]; the rise of the *caraṇa* (base) shall be two parts;
the measurement of the *mañca* (platform) shall be one-eighth; and the rise of the *kandhara* (neck) shall be equal to that.

The pinnacle (śikhara) should be one and a half parts, and the height of the spire (śikhodaya) one and a quarter parts; thus the two-storeyed structure is described. Now listen to the description of the three-storeyed structure.
Dividing the space from the north wall to the top of the *śikhā* into twelve parts,
the height of the *prastara* (cornice) shall be one and a quarter parts, and the height of the base (*aṅghri*) shall be two and a half parts.

The *prastara* (pedestal) shall be one part, the rise of the base (*caraṇodaya*) two parts, the height of the platform (*mañca*) eleven parts, and the rise of the neck (*grīvodaya*) one part. || 94 ||
The pinnacle (śikhara) is one and a quarter parts, and the measure of the finial (sthūpī) is one part; thus is the three-storied [temple] described. Now, the four-storied [temple] is explained. (95)
Dividing the space from the north to the crest into twenty-seven parts,
two parts less a quarter is the height of the base, three parts is the height of the plinth, and one part is the rise of the pedestal.
Half of that is the height of the cornice (prastara), and one and a half parts is the rise of the base (aṅghri).
Half of that is the height of the cornice, and two parts is the rise of the base. || 97 ||

Half of that is the measure of the pedestal (mañca), and its neck (gala) is said to be equal to that. The height of the spire (śikhara) is three parts, while the measure of the pinnacle (śikhā) is one part of Śiva.
The four stages have been fully explained; now hear about what is considered the five stages.
From the beginning of the North up to the end of the Topknot (śikhā), when divided by twenty-three: || 99 ||
The height of the pedestal (prastara) should be two parts; the height of the base (aṅghri) should be three and a half parts;
the measurement of the dais (mañca) should be half of that; and the length of the plinth (pāda) should be three parts.
Half of that [height] is the height of the pedestal (prastara); the height of the base (aṅghri) is two and a half parts;
half of that is the measure of the dais (mañca), and the elevation of the foot (caraṇa) is two parts.
The height of the pedestal (prastara) shall be one-eleventh part [of the total], and the height of the neck (kandhara) likewise;
the height of the head (śiras) shall be two and a half parts, and the measurement for the pinnacle (sthūpī) shall be eleven parts.
The five levels have been fully described; now hear about the six tiers.
From the north up to the crest, there are twenty-nine divisions.

The height of the entablature (prastara) is two parts, the height of the base (pāda) is four parts, and its shoulder (aṃsa) is three-quarters of a Śiva-part; thus is the elevation of the entablature described. 104.
The height [of the base] is three and a half parts; the height of the plinth (prastara) is half of that.
The height [of the second tier] is two and a half parts; the height of the plinth is half of that. (105)
The height of the base (caraṇa) is two parts; half of that is the measure of the pedestal (mañca);
the measurement of the neck (gala) is one part of Śiva (one-sixteenth); and the rise of the head (śira) is two and a half parts.
That measurement from one quarter [of the base] up to the pinnacle (śikhā) is called the seven-storey [temple].
Furthermore, the measurement from the north side to the end of the pinnacle is thirty-six parts.
The height of the base (mañca) shall be one part; the height of the pedestal (aṅghri) shall be four and a half parts;
the height of the entablature (prastara) shall be two parts; and the height of the plinth (caraṇa) shall be four parts.
The platform (mañca) should be two parts less one-quarter [of the base]; its height should be three and a half parts;
the height of the platform (mañcocca) should be two parts less one-quarter; and the measurement of the plinth (pāda) should be three parts. || 109 ||
The height of the stone slab (prastara) should be one and a half parts; the height of the base (aṅghri) should be one and a half akṣa-parts;
the measure of the platform (mañca) should be half of that; and the length of the pedestal (talipa) should be two parts.
The *prastara* (pedestal) consists of one part of the moon; the neck-measure consists of one part of Śiva;
the head consists of three parts minus one quarter; and the remainder is the emergence of the crest (*śikhodaya*).
Thus the seven-tiered [structure] is described; now the ornamentation is stated.
O best of the twice-born, one should construct the hall for the pavilion according to the manner of the gate-hall.
O best of the twice-born! The gatehouse may be shaped like a staff, or like a palace, or it should be made in the form of a garland; such should be the gateway mansion.
One should construct the *śālākāra* (spike-shaped) form, which is called the gate-tower (*dvāragopura*);
or indeed, the best knower of ritual procedures (*kalpavittama*) may fashion all [the towers] to resemble a *gopura*.
(197) O best of the twice-born! First among those, I shall describe the beautiful gateway (dvāraśobhā), which may have one, two, or three stories (tala) and is endowed with all ornaments. 115.

O twice-born one, according to the previously mentioned rule, there should be a large nose on each face, bamboos for nostrils on the sides, and it should be enriched with small nostrils for the eight duties.
Whether it is joined with twin domes (stūpis), or has a pinnacle rising from a base (lūpāroha-śiras), or even has the form of a pavilion (maṇḍapa), that is declared to be Śrīkānta. || 117 ||
It has a pinnacle at the top, sixty-four faces on the front and back, is enriched with side-ribs and a nose, and is provided with an odd number of stupas. || 118 ||
This supreme form, known as Itikānta, is joined with four additional feet at the end;
it has sixty-four [feet] at each face, and the Vaṃśanāsikā is on both sides.

The assembly hall (sabhākāra), the head-and-shoulder (śiraskandha), and the victorious (vijaya) form— indeed, one should thus arrange the beauties of the gates according to these three types of rules.
In each opening there was a great nose, and likewise on both sides;
its cage-like structure consisted of four and a half crores [of parts]. || 121 ||
Having the form of a hall, provided with a pinnacle, odd-numbered, and constructed with a central dome, this extensive *vijaya* is indeed called the *viśālāyāma*. 122.
It has fifty million sabhārāgas, with a bhadra on each face;
it is enriched with vaṃśanāsas on its sides and endowed with a śirobhadra at the top.
A foot that is richly endowed with a short nose and possessed of all its constituent parts,
yet featuring ornaments that are misplaced, will now be described in detail.
As before, the ground portion should be provided with auspicious projections (*bhadra*) on the four directions, enriched by four great *nāsīs*, and endowed with a *śirobhadra*. (125)
Endowed with additional parts at the end of each quarter and provided with an odd number of spires, the gateway hall is of three kinds; this is called the *dvāraprāsāda*.

The door is joined with [mouldings] increasing by one-quarter [of the width] from the inner side, adorned with mandharā and other [ornaments], provided with a colored [band] above the door, and that door is endowed with the bhadra [projection]. || 127 ||
In the front and back it was broad, with a ridge-pole-like nose on the sides; it was enriched with a svastika-shaped nose and joined by four lattices.
Construct all parts, such as the gabled chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) and so forth, according to the previously stated procedure.
I shall now describe [the temple] adorned with the glorious hair-tuft (śrīkeśa); the preparation of the ground and other details are as before.
In the eastern and western halls, there were auspicious structures with beautiful noses (pediments),
featuring various pillars adorned with masūraka ornaments, along with altars, lattices, and archways.
It is joined with additional parts at the end of the foot, endowed with a middle enclosure,
enriched on both sides by staffs and faces, and adorned with small noses.
It should have a pointed tip, be provided with a handle, and be adorned with lattices and the like;
it is decorated with long hair, while the ground portion and other features are as described previously. (132)
On the two sides, at the front, and at the back, there is a set of four large pillars;
joined with an odd number of shafts (stūpis), there are three gate-pavilions (dvāraprāsādaka).
O best of the twice-born! I shall describe the characteristics of the gateway-pavilion (dvāraharmya).
O best of the twice-born! It should be constructed upon a plot of ground as previously described.

It is joined with a temple pinnacle (*sabhāśikhara*) and has a nose (*nāsikā*) in the form of a *svastika*; the pinnacle is endowed with eight noses and joined with an odd number of stupas (*stūpa*). (135)
The one known as Svastika is said to bring peace to the directions;
the Bhadrāṅga has a face upon each face, and its head is adorned with an elongated ornament. (136)
It has large nostrils in the four cardinal directions and small nostrils in the intermediate directions;
it is joined with inner [elements] exceeding the feet and is endowed with an odd number of spires.
One should arrange the ground portion of the *kūṭa* and so forth just as before;
in the supreme city, there is a great seat (*mahānāsī*) with stars, and a *nīvraka* occupying two parts.
The temple-shrine (śālākārya) should have its upper portion (śiraḥkārya) provided with an odd number of cupolas (sthūpikā);
it should be covered by the hall (śālā), well-constructed, and adorned with various ornaments. || 139 ||
The gateway-palace (dvāraharmya), endowed with various bases and steps and provided with a pedestal, is said to be of three kinds; now hear the characteristics of the gate-tower (gopura).

It is joined with *bhadra* projections on the four sides, and internally provided with northern *pāda* offsets; it has the form of a hall (*śālā*) with a *śira* (pediment), and at each entrance there is a *bhadranāsī*.
On both sides there was a great nose, and on each side were two nostrils;
this is known as Mātṛkhaṇḍa. Now hear about Śrīviśāla.
As before, the ground portion and the base are made in the shape of an elephant;
the head is likewise shaped, or it may also be in the form of an assembly hall.
It was adorned with various pillars of *masūraka* and railings;
there were great nostrils on the four cardinal sides and small nostrils in the intermediate directions.
(200) Next, I shall describe the four-faced [mandala], beginning with the site selection as before;
it is endowed with auspicious directions and joined with a central elephant. (145)
It may have various pillars made of *masūraka* stone, adorned with altars and other ornaments; it may be shaped like the roof of an assembly hall (*sabhā*) or even like a hall (*śālā*). (146)
In each mouth there is one large nose, and on both sides there are two nostrils each;
this is joined with internal [nostrils] increased by one for every quarter, according to the surface of the altar.
The gateway and the gate-tower (gopura) are threefold, provided with internal stairs;
they may consist of a wall with a cornice (alīndra), or a plain wall, or even a covered terrace (varṣasthala). || 148 ||

From the *tulā* onwards up to the *pratara*, the body of the bee-line (*alīndāṅga*) should be made appropriately, either with a straight edge (*śālākāra*), with divisions (*sabhāga*), or in the form of a garland (*mālikākṛti*). || 149 ||
In the case of two [deities], one should arrange them at the door of the desired [shrine];
or, having placed [the deity] outside each [door], one may join it with the one in the middle. 150.
One should fashion the *gṛhapiṇḍī* and the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*) exactly as before;
or alternatively, one may have it with a curved base at the measurement of the two necklaces (*hāra*).

One should fashion the structure, complete with stairs and other features, extending from the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) to the designated ground; it should be adorned with gabled chambers and the like, arranged as if situated above. || 152 ||
One should fashion the ornament for the ground portion extending as far as the neck; that which resembles a hall with a head-pole and has the form of a hall is so described. (153)
That which is called *sabhākāra* (an assembly hall) is characterized by a roof-peak (*vyoktamāṅga*) that is prone to collapse;
it is covered with a flat roof (*prastara*), adorned, and lacks a sacrificial altar (*iṣṭara*). || 154 ||
The *mālikā* is known as the *kṛtika*, while the *maṇṭapa* is [known] as the *paraspara*; thus indeed is the *gopura* described. Now hear concerning the retinue (*parivāra*). (155)
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter [of the *Aṃśumat*] concerning the characteristics of gate-towers in the *Kāśyapa*.
Now I shall explain in detail the supreme procedure for the retinue:
eight, sixteen, and thirty-two, respectively. (1)

O twice-born one, one should likewise have the retinue fashioned within the inner circle; having consecrated them, O brahmin, one should place the eight members of the retinue within the inner enclosure.
The retinue known as Kalā, however, consists of [blank spaces];
in the fourth, Madhyahārā has a retinue of thirty-two.
Whether on a rampart, in a middle enclosure, or supported by a wall of a hall,
when the site has been made square— excluding the length of the entrance— at the central seed-syllable (bīja), || 4 ||
One should divide the ninth part within the middle-middle section for the main building;
then, in the eight surrounding sections starting from the east in successive order— || 5 ||
Having established Vṛṣabha in the east and Anala in the southeast,
one should place Agni, Durgā, or the Seven Mothers in the south.
To the right of the Mothers is Vīrabhadra, and to the left is Vināyaka;
or, if there is only a single image, Vināyaka should be placed to the south or the southwest.
One should place Kumāra in the western region, Jyeṣṭhā in the northwestern quarter, Keśava in the northern region, and Kātyāyanī there as well. (8)
In the region of the Bhāskarīśa-pada, there is either a sacred seat (pīṭha) or an image;
if it is an image, it is accompanied by a temple, whereas if it is a sacred seat, it is without a temple.
Those who abide as portions of Indra, Anala, and Śiva, standing facing the west,
should fashion either a garland for Gaurī or a celestial chariot (vimāna).
For other deities as well, the pavilion or celestial chariot (vimāna) should be three-quarters, half, or even one-quarter of the height of the main temple structure.
The extent of the abode for the retinue should be equal to the inner sanctum, or half the size of the inner sanctum, or three-quarters; or it may extend to three, four, or five cubits.
One should perform [the rites] by that very path which leads to the abodes of the manifestations;
for in rites such as pacification (śāntika) and others, the house that serves as their root is indeed that very one.
One should have it constructed without transgressing these rules, for to do otherwise brings misfortune;
it should be shaped like a pavilion for the three aims of life (trivarga) and be provided with four gates.
Or a pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed for the remaining [deities] as is appropriate; this has been declared as the abode for the retinue. Now hear the characteristics of the images. || 15 ||

The door in the surrounding hall may be [constructed] according to the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha), or else one should adopt that measurement which has been prescribed for all [the deities]. || 16 ||
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, whether standing or seated,
it is fashioned within the palace of the web-like lattice, accompanied by a retinue of thirty-two.
But according to one's desire, sixteen [parts] are declared; the remainder shall be for the Sviṣṭakṛt. Or else, in all temples, one may arrange everything [according to this rule]. || 18 ||
The proportions for the limbs and so forth of Kātyāyanī’s images are as described in the section on iconographic characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
First, however, I shall describe the characteristics of the bull that serves as her vehicle.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter [of the *Aṃśumat*], titled "The Chapter on the Rules for the Characteristics of the Retinue" within the *Kāśyapa*.
When the height is fifty parts, one part shall be one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
from the neck to the end of the back, the length shall be forty fingers.
From the crown of the head down to the throat, it is declared to consist of pure dharma alone.
From there, the neck is one-eighth higher, and from the neck to the end of the chest is sixteen finger-breadths. (2)
Therefore, the length of the thighs is proclaimed to be six mātrās;
the measurement of the knees should be two mātrās, and the measurement of the shanks is six aṅgulas.
The *khuramāna* should be two *mātrās*; one should thus fashion the *tuṅga*.
The *śṛṅgāra*, however, consists of eight parts, while the height of the *śṛṅga* is four *aṅgulas*.
The base of the prong should be broad, measuring four finger-breadths;
its tip should be half a finger-breadth, becoming gradually thinner from the base toward the tip.
The wise should fashion some horns joined with two sides, or [the space] within;
the width of the forehead is one part out of nine, and the width of the face is five parts.
It is known to be solid and equal [in width], with a length of two fingers;
its height is one and a half fingers, and it is fashioned in the shape of a śaphara fish.
The length from the middle of the eye to the mouth is declared to be eight fingers;
from there to the end of the back of the neck, it is proclaimed to be six mātrās.
Likewise, the distance from the eye to the end of the neck is five parts;
the length of the ear is [the same], while the width at the base of the ear is known to be two measures.
The middle section is four finger-breadths long and one finger-breadth wide;
its thickness is known to be half a finger-breadth, and the nostril is one and a half finger-breadths in length.
The width of the nose is known as one *aṅgula*; that which is equal to it is called "firm" (*gāḍha*). The height above the nose is designated as "tall" (*tuṅga*). || 11 ||

One should fashion the mouth with a length of five finger-breadths; the lower lip should be two mātrās in height, and the upper lip three mātrās, arranging them in due order according to the proper proportions.
The tongue is said to be three, two, or one finger-breadth in width and height;
the circumference of the neck should be ten parts, and its base twelve finger-breadths.
The width at the base of the neck on the back should be eight finger-breadths;
the width at the top of the neck on the back is declared to be six finger-breadths. (14)
The height of the hump is four mātras, its width is six aṅgulas,
and the thickness at the front of the neck is said to be one and a half aṅgulas.
The hump (kakuda), however, is said to be nineteen finger-breadths in height;
the width at the middle of the body should be fourteen finger-breadths. || 16 ||
One should determine the width of the other parts through logical reasoning;
the width at the base of the thigh of the first quarter-measure shall be five finger-breadths.
The tip of the thigh (ūrvāgra) shall be four mātras, and the root of the knee (jānumūla) is equal to that;
the tip of the shank (jaṅghāgra) shall be three mātras, and the extent of the hoof (khura) shall be one and a half parts of fire (three mātras).
Others say that the width at the base of the tail should be ten units;
the remainder should be made as for the front thighs, extending from the end of the shank to the limit of the tail.
The width of the tip of the handle, including the hair-tuft, should be four finger-breadths.

At the root and the tip, it should be half a mātrā; the length of the hair [of the seed-syllable] should be four finger-breadths (yuga-aṅgula); and the length and breadth of the seed-syllable itself should be four and three finger-breadths respectively. || 21 ||

It is said that the thickness [of the base] is two mātrās; the length of the testicles is four fingers (yuga-aṅgula); and the remaining thickness from the belly is called one finger (aṅgula). || 22 ||
Whether it be standing or reclining, [the image should be placed] upon a lotus or an auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha),
made of plaster with a core of brick, or even fashioned from stone or metal.
O Brahmin, whether it be solid or not solid, or made of iron, fashion a bull; even if its measurements of weight, height, and circumference are slightly deficient or excessive. (24)
One should not act in such a manner; therefore, that which possesses the [proper] characteristics should be performed.
If it is done contrarily, it yields contrary results. (25)
The characteristics of the bull have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the fire-altar.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the Section on the Characteristics of the Bull, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kāśyapa.
One should fashion the deity Vaitvanaleśvara ten tālas in height;
he has two faces, one heart, two nostrils, and six eyes.
It has three girdles and three feet, and is surrounded by seven tongues;
there are four tongues on the right face and three tongues on the left face.
Mounted upon a ram, possessing four horns, and endowed with a crown of matted locks;
he has four hands on his right side and three hands on his left side.
The Śakti, the fire, as well as the sruk and sruva ladles are indeed in his right hand;
in the left are the tomara and the fan, and especially the vessel of clarified butter.
His body is renowned for being like gold, and his eyes are tawny;
he is endowed with a halo of light and stands upon a lotus pedestal. || 5 ||
One should fashion Analeśvara as being clothed in fine linen;
likewise [one should fashion] Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the seven Mothers;
Vīrabhadra is in the south, while Vināyaka is in the west.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted hair, endowed with all ornaments, white in color, and having the bull as his emblem. || 8 ||
The two right hands hold a trident and the gesture of granting fearlessness,
while the two left hands on the left side hold a mace and the gesture of bestowing boons.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, taking refuge beneath a banyan tree,
endowed with four arms, and possessing a golden complexion.
In his right hands, he holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a trident, the gesture of granting boons (varada), and a rosary;
he is seated upon a red lotus throne, with a swan as his vehicle and emblem.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, wearing yellow garments, and holding a lotus,
he is described as having the form of a Brāhmaṇa, seated upon the Brahmavṛkṣa tree.
She has four arms and three eyes, with a complexion of intense red;
her right hands hold a trident and display the gesture of fearlessness, while her left hands grant boons.
Adorned with a water-pot, a rosary, and a crown of matted hair, she is comparable to Īśvara;
thus she is celebrated as Īśvarī.
She has four arms and three eyes, possesses a complexion resembling the color of blood, is adorned with all ornaments, and wears a crown of matted locks. 15.
She holds a spear and a cock in her hands, while her other two hands grant boons and protection;
she rides upon a peacock or indeed the udumbara tree.
The goddess holds a conch and a discus; her hands grant boons and fearlessness.
She has beautiful breasts and a lovely face; her body is dark-complexioned and her eyes are beautiful. (17)
The goddess, wearing yellow garments and adorned with a crown and diadem,
took refuge at the rājavṛkṣa tree while riding upon the Garuḍa-bannered vehicle.
In this manner, one should have an image of Vaiṣṇavī fashioned, adorned with the ornaments of Viṣṇu;
and Vārāhī, four-armed, peaceful, and adorned with all ornaments.
One should perform the consecration joined with the Karaja tree;
she is wearing yellow garments and adorned with all ornaments.
Adorned with a crown and diadem, possessing the luster of coral,
she holds in her right hands the goad and the gesture of fearlessness, and in her left hands the boon-granting mudrā and the spear.
Resorting to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma), she who has an elephant as her emblem and a beautiful vehicle,
possesses four arms and three eyes, is red in color, and has hair standing erect.
She wears a garland of heads as her sacred thread, stands upon a lotus throne,
is clothed in a tiger skin, and possesses breasts resting upon the shoulders of lordly serpents.
With a face made terrible by fangs and resting upon a banyan tree—
such indeed is the characteristic of Cāmuṇḍī, and her image should consist of a single body.
All of them should be depicted lying on their left sides with their right legs hanging down;
O best of the twice-born, one should thus fashion the seven Mothers.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Mātṛkās," in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*. 47.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of Vighnarāja;
from the feet to the crown of the head, the measurement is divided into sixty-four parts.
From the crown of the head down to the indentation at the base of the skull is said to be two finger-breadths; from there down to the end of the eye-line is declared to be four finger-breadths.
From the eye-line to the jaw, the portion shall be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
from that point, the measurement of the ear is declared to be two finger-breadths.
That which extends from the penis to the navel is known as the *vasu* measure (eight units).
The thigh should be six parts in measurement, and the length of the knee should be three finger-breadths (*guṇāṅgula*).
The shanks are long like the thighs;
the quality is the elevation of the soles of the feet, measuring seven finger-breadths in length, extending from the big toe to the heel.
The big toe is two parts long; the little toe is one and a half parts.
From the index finger to the little toe, each successive finger is reduced by one barley-corn (yava).
The upper arm is thirteen finger-breadths; the forearm is nine finger-breadths;
the length of the palm is four mātrās; and the middle finger is three finger-breadths.
The space between the index finger and the ring finger is twenty-one barley grains;
the length of the little finger and the thumb is seventeen barley grains.
Twelve, eight, nine, eight, and seven in sequence—these are designated as the widths (vyāsa) of the fingers from the thumb to the little finger. (9)
The width of that [toe] should be three-quarters of the width of the nail; this is declared to be the width of the nail.
The length of the nail should be three-quarters of its width, and it should be rounded like a circle.
The span of the palm is four [units], the wrist three and a half;
the span to the end of the forearm is eight fingers, and the span of the upper arm is six and a half. (11)
The base of the arm is eight parts, the head is extended over eight parts,
it is bent seven aṅgulas, and there is a depression ten aṅgulas deep in the middle of the face.
O best of the twice-born! From the base of the hand to the navel, its length is six finger-breadths; its width at the tip of the fingers is one and a half mātrās.
Gradually becoming slender, there are two hollows in the middle of the hand; that which extends to the left tooth is designated as being "only a cubit" (vedamātra). || 14 ||
To the right of the root of the tooth, it should be two units high and level with the surface;
however, from the protrusion of the lower lip, the hanging portion should be two finger-breadths long.
The width of the eye is proclaimed to be six barley-corns;
its breadth, including the ear-ornament, is one finger-breadth, and its height is equal to that.
The base of the ear should be half an aṅgula in thickness and two aṅgulas [in width];
O twice-born one, the face should be fashioned exactly like that of an elephant-faced [Ganeśa].
The width up to the ends of the arms should be thirty-two finger-breadths;
the distance between the armpits is declared to be nineteen finger-breadths.
The space between the breasts is ten finger-breadths; the distance from the base of the neck to the breast is likewise like that of the breasts themselves.
The nipple is one barley-corn in width, and the circle of the breast is two finger-breadths.
The width of the breasts is said to be fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
while the width of the middle of the belly is known to be twenty-two finger-breadths.
The depression at the navel is said to be one and a half finger-breadths wide;
the length of the linga is three finger-breadths, and its width is half of that.
The length of the mūṣala is declared to be one *guṇa* (three) finger-breadths wide;
the root of the thigh is twelve finger-breadths, and the middle of the thigh is six and a half.
The portion of the knee should have extended fingers; the length of the shank should be equal to the fingers;
the width of the ankle should be two parts; and the breadth of the foot should be five parts.
The width of the toes of the feet, from the big toe to the little toe in sequence, is twelve, eight, six and a half, six, and five barley-corns respectively. // 24 //
The area of the three toes and nails, adorned with half that measure [of width],
should be used for either standing or sitting, especially upon a lotus-seat (padmapīṭha).
He holds a sweetmeat (svadanta) in his right hand and a wood-apple (kapittha) in his left;
he has a sweetmeat (modaka) in the trunk of the elephant and a goad (aṅkuśa) in his right hand.
In his left hand he holds either a noose, a serpent, or a rosary;
he has three eyes, resembles gold in complexion, and is clothed in garments of fine silk.
One should arrange the posture either with a slight bend or perfectly straight;
however, if it is a seated posture, one should rest the left foot [upon the right thigh]. (28)
The kuṭikāsana posture is formed by placing one foot upon the top of the opposite thigh;
the body should be slightly bent, especially toward the left side. || 29 ||
He had a serpent as his sacred thread, was adorned with a crown and tiara,
was endowed with all ornaments, possessed a massive body, and had a large belly.
(212) Thus, O Vināyaka, listen to the description of the six-faced one.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the section on the characteristics of Vināyaka, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kaśyapa. || 48 ||

One should fashion Skanda in the supreme size of five tālas, endowed with all the proper characteristics; all measurements, proportions, and so forth, as well as every characteristic, are as previously described.
He may have two, four, six, or twelve arms,
holding a spear, an arrow, a sword, a discus, and an extended noose.
In all her left hands, she holds a peacock feather,
a shield, a cock, a bow, a staff, and a plough, each grasped in a hand as radiant as the sun.
In his six right hands, he holds the sword, the shield, the spear, the thunderbolt, the rosary, and the cock; [these are] on the right side.
In his left hands, he holds the shield, the rosary, and the cock. (4)
Guha has four arms; his two right hands hold the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and a spear (śakti), while his left hands hold a cock and a rosary (akṣamālā).
She has two arms, holding a cock in her left hand and a spear (śakti) in her right hand;
whatever else is not mentioned here is as described in the Umāskandasahita.
The characteristics of Skanda have been declared, followed by the rules for Jyeṣṭhā.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of Skanda, in the *Aṃśumat* of Kāśyapa.
She has two arms, resembles collyrium in color, has long lips and a prominent nose,
with pendulous breasts and belly, and wears blue or red garments.
She holds a blue lotus in her right hand and places her left hand upon the seat;
she is seated upon an auspicious throne with two legs hanging down.
She was endowed with all ornaments, her hair tied in a topknot,
marked with the sign of a crow’s banner, and adorned with a tilaka on her forehead.
On her right side is indeed Vṛṣa, who has the face of a bull;
he is two-armed, holding a staff in his right hand and a needle in his left.
He should dangle his right foot while sitting in the utkuṭikāsana posture with the left leg drawn up;
he is white in color, possesses a massive body, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 5 ||
A bull indeed is thus [placed] on the right, and likewise a maṇa is said to be on the left;
she has beautiful breasts, a youthful body, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 6 ||
Resembling a black antelope skin, adorned with a red garment,
having two eyes, wearing a basket-shaped crown, and with her left foot hanging down.
Seated in a small hut on the left, holding a blue lotus in her hand—thus Jyeṣṭhā is described; now the characteristics of Durgā are stated.
She has four arms and two eyes, is of a beautiful dark-green hue, and is most excellent;
she is gentle, clad in yellow garments, and possesses full thighs, hips, and breasts.
Adorned with a crown and a casket, and decorated with all ornaments,
her right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness, while her left hand holds a sword.
In her right hand she holds a discus, while in her left she bears a conch shell;
standing with feet evenly placed upon a lotus pedestal, she should be depicted. (11)
Having bound her breasts with the lord of serpents and wearing a red bodice—thus is Durgā fully described; now the characteristics of Viṣṇu are stated.
Viṣṇu, adorned with a crown, a diadem, a waist-thread, and other ornaments, wearing yellow garments, gentle in appearance, and endowed with four arms. || 13 ||
In the right hand is the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and on the left hand is a bracelet;
furthermore, in the left hand is a conch, and in the right hand is a discus.
Above a lotus seat, [he is] seated or standing, with a form resembling the dark-green hue of grain, and accompanied on his right and left by Śrī and the Earth.
Whether joined with others or alone, it should be fashioned as an image of Viṣṇu,
having one face and two arms, and possessing a luster equal to that of the Jāti-flower.
Two [hands] have lotuses slightly blossoming, held up by the shoulders;
another is endowed with a basket-crown, while the others have their own mandala-crowns.
He is joined with twenty-six heroes, or else endowed with the sacred thread;
he has the appearance of being bound in red dye and is adorned with all ornaments.
One should fashion the image of Saura standing upon a lotus pedestal in the *samapāda* posture, endowed with two gentle eyes. Thus should he be conceived. (19)
Dark-complexioned, with two arms, wearing red garments, and auspicious;
endowed with a crown and tiara, and adorned with all ornaments. || 20 ||
He holds a spear (*śakti*) in his right hand and a goad (*aṅkuśa*) in his left;
he has a broad belly and a long neck, and is accompanied by Śacī. (21)
He should be depicted as having two eyes and a gentle face, seated upon a lion throne,
or alternatively, mounted upon an elephant.
Thus Indra has been fully described; now Aśvinī is likewise spoken of.
Seated upon a single lion-throne, the two Aśvins possess universal forms.
Resembling pomegranate flowers, both wear the sacred thread;
they have eyes like blossoming red utpala lotuses and are clothed in garments of yellow and blood-red.
The two Nāsatyas, the lords of heaven and the Maruts, wear crests and crowns;
they are endowed with two hands and adorned with the ornaments of women.
He holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in his right hand and a book in his left;
his right legs are pendant, while his left are in the vaikuṭika posture.
O Brahmin, the two physicians of the gods, who provide protection against whatever [diseases] there may be,
are situated on their two sides, to the right and left respectively.
Mṛtasaṃjīvinī and Saṃsthitau are the two Apsarases;
Pariviśālakaraṇī and Vaśvinyau are yellow and tawny respectively.
On the left is Dhanvantari, likewise accompanied by Mātṛkā;
they are endowed with yellow and red complexions and are dressed in black garments.
The two [deities] holding a sword and a shield in their hands, adorned with all ornaments, are thus described as Aśvinī; now the form of the Pitṛs is told.
The Pitṛs are fortunate, endowed with grey hair and wrinkles;
their limbs and hair are yellowish in color, and their heads are bound with vāsīkā grass. (31)
Adorned with sacred threads, possessing two arms, and clad in white garments,
they were decorated with serpent ornaments and their bodies were smeared with ashes.
Possessing white teeth and endowed with gentle eyes and faces,
the ancestors are seated upon fruit-seats or auspicious pedestals on great thrones.
Those who have their left hands placed upon the left knee and hold needles in their right hands are said to be the three Pitṛs.
The Pitṛs have thus been described; now hear concerning Vaivasvata:
he has two arms, is black in color, and carries a sword and a shield. (35)
With a face of terrifying fangs, adorned with red garlands and unguents,
wearing red garments, fierce, and endowed with a crown and diadem.
He had eyes like a blazing fire and was mounted upon a great buffalo;
standing at his sides were two [beings] with bearded faces, resembling Yama himself.
Citragupta and Kali are stationed at the sides of the doorway;
both resemble dark blue in complexion and are clad in red garments. (38)
Standing at the sides of the throne together with Mṛtyu,
the two women of fierce splendor, resembling Nīla and Lohita, were holding chowries.
O Brahmin! Standing before him were those known as Dharma and Adharma;
Yama was seated upon his throne, mounted upon a red buffalo.
The characteristics of Yamā have been described, as well as the characteristics of Rohiṇī;
she is red, adorned with a crown and a casket, two-armed, and most beautiful. (41)
Adorned with all ornaments, holding a hand like that of an elephant, and clad in white garments,
Rohiṇī is sevenfold in number, whether seated or standing.
The characteristics of Rohiṇī have been declared, as well as the characteristics of Nirṛti;
one should know Nirṛti to be red in color, two-armed, and of massive body. (43)
He holds a sword in his right hand and a shield in his left;
he wears yellow garments, is fierce in appearance, and has formidable, protruding fangs.
The Lord of the World, adorned with all ornaments, mounted upon a corpse, possessed of red hair, standing or indeed seated. (45)
Thus has the account of Nirṛti been told; from her, they know the Apsarases were born—exceedingly beautiful, youthful, passionate, and adorned with heavy masses of hair.
Adorned with various ornaments and decorated with diverse flowers, they all wore fine silk garments and possessed full thighs and broad hips. (47)
In the center, they are adorned with linen garments and other finery, their faces slightly smiling,
their limbs anointed with perfumes and other unguents, and seated upon auspicious thrones.
The seven Apsarases are recorded as being endowed with equal divisions;
thus have the Apsarases been described, and now Varuṇa shall be explained.
Varuṇa, however, is white in color, two-armed, and holds a noose in his hand;
he is adorned with all ornaments and wears a crown shaped like a basket.
He was born wearing yellow garments, endowed with great strength and prowess, marked by the sacred thread, and seated in the posture of a sea-monster (makara). (51)
The sages, however, are yellow in color, clad in garments of various hues;
they are aged, two-armed, peaceful, and endowed with matted locks and topknots. || 52 ||
Extending from the chin to the heart and endowed with the sacred thread (*upavīta*), they bear the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) made of ash; these may be in a standing posture or seated. (53)
They hold a staff in their right hand and an umbrella in their left;
or else, they hold a staff in the right hand, while the left hands bear the knowledge-finger-rings (jñānamudrikā).
With their left hands resting upon their left knees,
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and likewise Aṅgiras stood in an upright posture.
Viśvāmitra and Bharadvāja—these seven are proclaimed as the Ṛṣis.
He has two arms, possesses great heroism, has copper-colored eyes, and resembles smoke in hue. || 56 ||
Holding a banner in his right hand and grasping a staff with his left,
Vāyu has his feet slightly bent and is adorned with a garment hanging from his waist.
Adorned with various ornaments and with his hair disheveled,
he sat comfortably upon a throne, proceeding swiftly.
Thus Vāyu has been fully described; now the characteristics of Rudra are stated:
they have four arms and three eyes, and are adorned with crowns of matted hair. (59)
All are proclaimed to be white in color, wearing white garments;
they stand with feet even, in a stationary posture, all situated upon lotuses.

Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with all kinds of flowers, they hold the gesture of fearlessness and an axe in their right hands, and the gesture of granting boons and a black [serpent] in their left hands. (61)
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṃkara, Nīlalohita, Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, and Bhavodbhava. || 62 ||
O Brahmin, these are remembered as the eleven Rudras headed by Kapālīśa;
Soma is seated upon a lion-throne, endowed with a complexion like that of a jasmine flower or a conch shell.
Endowed with a halo of light, possessing two arms and a gentle countenance, he may be either seated or standing, his hands radiant with two white water-lilies.
With a golden sacred thread upon his body, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing white garments, peaceful, and decorated with every kind of flower.
The guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla), however, is of three kinds: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic;
he may be white, red, or black, according to his sattvic and other qualities.
The two-armed and four-armed forms are peaceful (sāttvika); the six-armed form is rajasic;
and the eight-armed form is tamasic—thus are they classified as sāttvika and so forth.
The wise know his standing posture to be upon a lotus-seat or a bhadrapīṭha;
he holds a trident in his right hand, while a skull-bowl is held in the other.
Thus the two-armed form has been described; now the four-armed form is being told:
in the right hand he holds a khaṭvāṅga, and in the other [left] hand a living being.
Alternatively, the front right hand should hold the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and granting boons (*varada*);
the two other hands are as before, and the left hand holds a bell.
Thus has the *sāttvika* [form] been described; now hear that which is *rājasa*.
In the three right hands, he holds a trident, a sword, and a bell. (71)
In her left hands she holds a shield, a skull-cup, and a serpent-noose;
in her right hands she holds a bow and an arrow, which are of the nature of tamas.
The remainder is declared to be like that of the Rājasa [type]: with red hair and an upward-pointing circle, endowed with a fierce gaze, and adorned with various serpents. (73)
One should fashion Kṣetrapāla as three-eyed and naked;
Īśa, indeed, has two arms, is peaceful, and is adorned with all ornaments. (74)
He is adorned with a crown of matted locks, always possessing a white radiance,
wearing a white sacred thread, and seated upon a white lotus.
A trident in the right hand and a skull-cup in the left hand—thus is Īśa fully described; thereafter, indeed, Bhāskara follows in sequence.
They have two arms and hold lotuses in their hands; they are seated upon red lotus thrones, resting within red mandalas, and are adorned with crowns shaped like caskets. || 47 ||
All of them hold red lotuses and are adorned with every ornament;
they are joined with the Channavīras and are indeed twelve in number, like the suns.
Vaikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi, Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama. (79)
Āditya, Mahāsūrya, Aṃśumālin, and Divākara—
these indeed are the twelve Ādityas, stationed in order starting from the north.
Thus the sixteenth [form] has been described; now the thirty-second will be spoken of:
Ananta, who is four-armed, gentle, and adorned with all ornaments. (81)
Having a form resembling a hibiscus flower, adorned with a basket-shaped crown, wearing white garments, peaceful, three-eyed, and seated upon a lotus. 82.
The preceptor has four arms, is peaceful, adorned with all ornaments, pure, and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, while holding an axe and a trident. || 83 ||
Having a luster resembling gold, clothed in fine silk garments,
he is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and holds a sword and a shield.
Well-established upon a lotus-seat, one should indeed fashion him thus:
he is four-armed, peaceful, fearless, and adorned with a crown of matted locks. (85)
Having an appearance equal to that of intense passion, adorned with all ornaments,
he should hold the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and carry a trident and a noose.
Large-bodied, endowed with two hands, with a gentle face and two eyes, she is exceedingly beautiful, peaceful, and adorned with all ornaments. (87)
Her limbs were anointed with various perfumes, she was adorned with various flowers, she wore a crown and a casket, and she stood upon a lotus seat. || 88 ||
Her belly was somewhat broad, and her thighs, hips, and breasts were full;
that excellent woman wore fine silk garments, divine raiment, and various other cloths. (89)
Her form has the luster and appearance of a green crop; her hands hold red lotuses, and her left hand hangs down to the knee with a gentle bend.
Subtle, resembling the color of blue, peaceful, wearing garments of gold, most excellent, four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with all ornaments. (91)
Holding the *abhaya* mudrā and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), as well as the *ṭaṅka* and the trident;
thus has the characteristic of Gaurī been described, together with all her defining features.
In that very manner, the wise one should have it made and install it as a solitary [image];
Śiva is four-armed, peaceful, and adorned with all ornaments.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, resembling a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon, he bestows fearlessness and boons, and wields a sword and a shield. || 94 ||
Indeed, upon a lotus seat, he stands or sits;
he has four faces and four arms, with a luster like yellow orpiment.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, tawny-eyed, and wearing all ornaments,
he had a black antelope skin as an upper garment and was endowed with a sacred sacrificial thread.
Wearing white garments, peaceful, with a waist-cord and a girdle, adorned with white garlands and unguents, and decorated with earrings; || 97 ||
In his right hand he should hold a rosary and a kūrca;
in his left a water-pot and kuśa grass; and in his right hands he should carry the sruk and sruva ladles.

O best of the twice-born! He should hold the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) and kusha grass in his left hand, while his two front hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. 99.
On the seat, however, one should cause the feet of the Lord to rest upon each other;
above the root of the penis, the left hand should be positioned with its palm facing upward.
And his left hand is raised above, likewise tasting the nectar of that forest;
in the right [hand] is a rosary, and in the left hand is a water-pot. (101)
Sarasvatī is on the right side and Sāvitrī on the left;
he is either seated or standing, positioned upon a lotus pedestal. || 102 ||
Śivottama is white in color, endowed with four arms, adorned with all ornaments, and wearing white garments and a sacred thread. || 103 ||
Endowed with two eyes, provided with a casket-crown, possessed of the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, holding a trident and a noose, and pure. 104.
Above the lotus seat, however, is the standing posture with feet even;
thereupon is Bhṛgu, resembling white in color, peaceful, and wearing white garments.
Adorned with a crown and a jewel-casket, endowed with two hands, granting the gestures of fearlessness and boons, and decorated with all ornaments. || 106 ||
Whether standing or seated upon a lotus pedestal, one should conceive of the Lord as already arisen [there], just as was previously described. || 107 ||
Having fashioned [the image] as Agastya Kauśika, the best of installers should establish it, [depicting him] with one face, four arms, and endowed with three eyes. (108)
Wearing linen garments, peaceful, with the luster of the bandhūka flower, he is adorned with a crown of matted locks and embellished with all ornaments. || 109 ||

Having fashioned the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa) as before— pure, endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and holding a chisel and a trident— the most excellent preceptor should install him.
Sarasvatī has four arms, sits upon a white lotus throne, is endowed with a crown of matted hair, is white in complexion, and wears white garments. (111)
She was endowed with the sacred thread, adorned with jeweled earrings,
decorated with all ornaments, wearing a pearl necklace, and possessed of beautiful eyes.
In her two right hands she holds a commentary and a rosary;
in her two left hands she holds a book and a water-pot; she has three eyes and a beautiful form.
Served by all the sages, headed by Bhṛgu and others, the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevī) is thus proclaimed as being endowed with these characteristics. 114.
Lakṣmī sits upon a lotus throne, two-armed, with a golden luster, and is beautifully adorned with two earrings shaped like crocodiles that shine with gold and jewels. 115.
She was in the prime of youth, with most beautiful limbs, her eyebrows gracefully arched;
she had red eyes, was anointed with yellow unguents, and her breasts were covered by a bodice.
The circle of the head [is marked with] a conch, a discus, and a lotus at the hairline;
a lotus is said to be in the right hand, and a bilva fruit in the left.
In the center, she of broad and beautiful hips was clothed in splendid garments;
adorned with a girdle and a waist-cord, she was decorated with every kind of ornament. || 118 ||
However, those resembling Ekākṣa should specifically have one eye;
having fashioned them like Paśupati, the best of preceptors should then install them.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anala, Anila, Pratyuṣa, and likewise Prabhāsa. || 120 ||
All eight Vasus are red in color and have two eyes;
they all wear yellow garments and are either seated or standing. (121)
Holding swords and shields in their hands and adorned with all ornaments, they are all proclaimed to be fierce, equipped with crowns and caskets. 122.
O best of the twice-born! Mahādeva should be fashioned like Paśupati;
O most excellent of the twice-born! the Trimūrti should be fashioned like Ekarudra. (123)
The giver of wealth, lord of all yakṣas, adorned with every ornament, resembling molten gold, and endowed with two hands. || 124 ||
His right hand displays the gesture of granting boons (varada) and his left hand holds a mace;
he is seated upon a lotus throne, possesses two eyes, and has a ram as his vehicle. 125.
Then both the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures, gentle and wearing red garments,
possessing the forms of spirits and endowed with great strength, appeared.
O best of the twice-born, they were seated upon a lotus-throne, holding lotuses in their hands,
adorned with crowns and caskets, and wearing white garments as upper cloths.
To the right and left [of the main deity], one should place the Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi treasures respectively;
and to the left of Dhanada, one should fashion the Goddess, endowed with all her characteristic marks.
For it has been declared that [the deity] is indeed Dhanada; one should likewise fashion Rudra as before.
Now, the characteristics of the form of Kālāgnirudra will be described.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with flaming hair,
he is supreme, equipped with a sword and shield, and holding a bow and arrow.
Wearing red garments, fierce, and adorned with all ornaments, he has red hair standing erect and is seated upon a lion throne. || 131 ||
Four-armed and three-eyed, with a luster like that of a blue lotus, he is adorned with a crown-case (karaṇḍa) and a diadem, and embellished with all ornaments. || 182 ||
Endowed with the boon-granting gesture of fearlessness, holding a hammer and a trident, supreme, clad in red garments, and seated upon a lotus pedestal. || 133 ||
Thus Śrīkaṇṭha has been described; now Nāgadeva is spoken of:
he is three-eyed, four-armed, gentle, red-hued, and clad in white garments. (134)
Endowed with the gesture of granting fearlessness, held in the hand of another,
it is a nāga wearing a crown and a casket, possessing five hoods.
Adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a lotus pedestal, he is formidable, four-armed, fierce, and decorated with every kind of jewelry. (136)
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and possessing a luster equal to that of a red gem,
he should hold the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, as well as a trident and a noose.
He is clad in white garments and is white himself, possessing a fierce gaze and prominent fangs;
the ground is like the sprouts of grain and is endowed with dark blue locks of hair.
Adorned with a crown and a casket, decorated with all ornaments, wearing yellow garments, and endowed with a serene countenance. || 139 ||
Holding either a lotus or a blue water-lily in both hands,
she may be seated or even standing upon a lotus throne.
The nature of Śikhaṇḍin, however, is endowed with four arms;
he is provided with a basket-shaped crown and adorned with all ornaments. (141)
Wearing red garments, peaceful, endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, equipped with a sword and shield, he stands upon a lotus pedestal. || 142 ||
The hosts of Maruts are smoke-colored, two-armed, and exceedingly beautiful;
they possess abundant hair and are adorned with all types of ornaments. || 143 ||
All of them wear red garments and are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons; they carry swords and shields, and possess full, fleshy thighs and hips.
Above the lotus seat are eight gods of the Marut host;
Ugra is four-armed, fierce, and endowed with a red complexion. (145)
Adorned with a crown and a casket, and decorated with all ornaments, he is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, as well as a chisel and a trident. || 146 ||
Standing upon a lotus pedestal, pure and wearing white garments,
one should meditate on Śanaiścara as being black in complexion, two-armed, and clad in white cloth.
Adorned with a crown and a basket, and decorated with all ornaments,
he holds a staff in his right hand, while his left is said to be in the boon-granting gesture.
The standing posture is performed upon a lotus-seat, or specifically upon a seat;
in this standing position, the body is considered to be slightly bent like a lame person and somewhat shortened in stature.
Thus has the image been described; now hear the characteristics of the pedestal (pīṭha):
its width should be two suns (twelve) finger-breadths, and its height should be one sun (six) finger-breadths.

(228) It is joined with three girdles and is as wide as one Veda-measure; its height is three finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula), while the elevation of the lotus is likewise three finger-breadths. || 151 ||
One-sixth of the lotus's width should be the height of the remaining upper tremulous canopy;
one should construct this with stone, brick, or white plaster.
Listen now to this procedure for the great seat (mahāpīṭha), which is indeed peerless in its retinue:
the width of the temple is here called the staff (daṇḍa). (153)
Starting from the main hall, it should measure six or eight *daṇḍas* in length, or ten or twelve *daṇḍas*, up to a maximum of fourteen *daṇḍas*. (154)
One should fashion the great seat (mahāpīṭha) as either sixteen or eighteen [units];
or else, the location of the seat is prescribed by another method. || 155 ||
In a temple with three halls, or indeed four or five halls up to the middle one, a great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) should be constructed; its characteristics are now described.

The height of the door of the primary sanctuary (mūladhāma) is the best when it is equal to the width of the pedestal; it is declared to be middling when it is three-quarters of that, and inferior when it is half the height of the door. (157)
The width of the pure entrance is said to be the inferior pedestal;
twice that is declared the middling, and thrice that is called the best. || 158 ||
