Alternatively, that which has a width of one cubit is the lowest pedestal;
two cubits is declared to be the middling, and three cubits is said to be the best. (159)
Having made it as high as its width, [the height] should be twenty-eight [parts];
the height of the base (upāna) should be two parts, and the plinth (jagatī) should be six parts.
The height of the *kumuda* is five parts (*bhūtāṃśa*), while the *kampa* is said to be one part.
The measurement of the *karṇa* is four parts, and the upper *kampa* is one part of Śiva (*śivāṃśaka*). || 161 ||
Or one may take a portion of the Mahāpaṭṭī's width as two parts specifically;
the height of the lotus (padmatuṅga) should be four parts, and the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be two parts.

Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be one-third [of the lotus], while the height of the lotus (padma) should be five parts; the great band (mahāpaṭṭī) should be two parts.
The height of the plinth (upāna) should be one part of Śiva; the remainder is indeed as before.
Now, O Brahmin, fashion the emergence of the pedestal (pīṭha) and the surface of the earth just as previously described.
Above that, the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be one-ninth of the measurement of the lotus;
one should perform the entry and exit according to the method prescribed for the base (adhiṣṭhāna). || 165 ||
In the case of Padmatārā, the pericarp (karṇikā) should consist of either four parts or five parts;
its shape may be square, quadrangular, circular, or even octagonal. || 166 ||
Alternatively, that pair—the lotus of the mandala—should be made with sixteen spokes;
it may be fashioned from metal, stone, or even brick.
Its interior was lined with plaster and adorned with various colorful paintings;
it was further embellished with figures of spirits, sea-monsters, serpents, and bulls. || 168 ||
One should decorate it with various colors or with gold and silver ornaments;
the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) may be divided into six, seven, eight, or nine parts.
One should fashion the height of its subsidiary pedestal (upapīṭha) according to what was stated for the subsidiary pedestal;
above that, however, is the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha), endowed with the width and elevation as previously described.
O best of the twice-born! A *pīṭha* may be constructed even without an *upapīṭha*.
O Brahmin, one should place Āmoda on the eastern petal and Pramoda on the petal in the direction of Yama (the south).
Pramukha is in the western quarter, Durmukha in the petal of the northern direction,
Tāmasa in the region of the southeast, and Rājasa in the petal of the southwest.
The *sāttvika* [deity] is in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest), while the creator of obstacles is in the direction of Īśa (the northeast).
That which is called the "creator of obstacles" is declared to be the obstacle itself. (173)
O best of the twice-born! That great seat (mahāpīṭha), which consists of the qualities of all beings on earth, in the atmosphere, and in heaven, is said to be the soul of all. 174.
For the sake of removing their suffering, one should always worship Valiyanta;
furthermore, for the removal of their distress, one should perform daily festivals and circumambulations.
Having performed the circumambulation of the earth, he then performed the second, that of the atmosphere;
thereafter, the circumambulation of heaven was performed by those who dwell therein.
For the sake of destroying the afflictions of the world, the best of practitioners should perform the ritual in this manner;
I shall now state a slight variation regarding a palace facing west. (147)
One should place Kumāra in the station of Vṛṣa, and a bull in the station of Kaumāra; in the Vāruṇa station, one should install the Mahāpīṭha, and perform the remainder as previously prescribed.
The procedure for the retinue has been declared; hereafter follows the characteristics of the liṅga.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, the section on the ritual for the retinue of Aṃśumat in the Kāśyapa [Tantra].
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the Śiva-liṅga;
in the process of dissolution, all objects of the senses go entirely to their place of origin.
Just as there is emanation, so too is emanation within it; this is called the *liṅga*.
During reabsorption, it is proclaimed as being partless (*niṣkala*) and tranquil (*śānta*). || 2 ||
The state of liberation for all living beings exists only through one’s own self;
it is all-pervading, secret, and the sole leader of all the worlds. || 3 ||
Therefore, indeed, at the time of creation, the principle of Peace (śānti-tattva) arises;
that [principle] is produced from the power of Peace, and from that, the emergence of Sound (nāda) occurs.
Therefore, that which arises from the Bindu is called Nāda, also known as Sādākhya. From the Bindu, Manonmanī is said to arise; within her, the origin of Īśvara occurs.
From Īśvara came the creation of Maheśa; from him, indeed, the Vaiṣṇava [creation];
from him, Prajeśa was born; and from Prajeśa, specifically, [the creation of Viśeṣa].
There are indeed three, thirty, three hundred, and three thousand [beings]:
gods, sages, and those born as dānavas and apsarases.

O Brahmin, among those [sixteen vowels], the first three are known as *niṣkala* (partless) when pierced by the *saṃbhava* [breath]. That which ends with the *bindu* is known as *sakala* (with parts), while that which has the *nāda* and the subsequent *bindu* is called *miśra* (mixed).
The resonance (nāda) is to be known as having the form of the liṅga, while the drop (bindu) is said to be the limb of the pedestal (pīṭha).
The liṅga is renowned as consisting of Śiva, and the pedestal is its own essential extension.
Therefore, being identical with Śiva and having Śiva as his very self, like fire and heat, he brings about the welfare of all living beings for the sake of destroying the suffering of the world. (10)
(232) For the benefit of the gods and others, the meditation and worship characterized by the *liṅga* and *yoni* forms brings forth the reality (*tattva*) known as Sādākhya. 11.
That definition of the *liṅga* is proclaimed for the sake of the manifestation of all [deities].
That *liṅga* is said to be of three kinds: mobile (*cala*) and likewise immobile (*acala*).
Having fashioned a linga made of either gemstone or metal, along with its pedestal (yoni), one should specifically install it in due order, known as the "moving and unmoving" (calācala).
Alternatively, having fashioned a linga from materials other than [the prescribed] substances, one should provide it with the characteristic of a yoni;
it should be provided with a head for anointing, yet devoid of the characteristic of a raised [pedestal].
Having made the entire [pedestal] circular in shape for the purpose of the emergence of the *liṅga*,
one should make it one-fourth or even one-eighth of the height of the emergence.
One should introduce the remaining portion of the pedestal (pīṭha), endowed with the visible [measurements];
having placed it in the desired part, one should remove the deficiency caused by the inability [of the stone] to undergo movement or removal.
That linga which is known as "moving" (cala) should be one-third the size of the stationary (acala) one;
it may be made of stone or of clay (bāṇaja), and it should be placed upon a pedestal within the sanctum.
One should thus place a mobile or immobile image upon a stable pedestal; however, a Bāṇaliṅga is uncreated and does not require connection with a thread.
Among those, the characteristics of the mobile liṅga will now be described first.
One should take up the stone on an auspicious month, lunar day, asterism, ascendant, and weekday.
The preceptor, accompanied by artisans, should commence the taking up of the stone;
he should observe the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial omens.
If a crow comes from the right to the left, and likewise from the left to the right;
and similarly on the right and left with an offering of elephant meat—(21).
The sight of a maiden and a cow, as well as a singer, a vehicle, a jar full of curd, and likewise a jar of milk; || 22 ||
O Brahmin, flowers belong to the wearer of flowers; women to their husband;
food to one who eats meat; and the state of being devoted to Śiva belongs to one who is intent upon devotion to Śiva. || 23 ||
A blazing fire, a lamp, a jar filled with water, a bull, a boar, an elephant, and an exceedingly beautiful courtesan. (24)
These divine omens are auspicious, whereas the inauspicious are the opposite:
the falling of meteors, the conflagration of the quarters, and the occurrence of portents during the day. (25)
Inauspicious [planets] situated within [the asterism] are called auspicious when they are weak and terrestrial;
likewise, those with disheveled hair and those with scattered hair are so described. (26)
Anointing with oil, being naked, wearing saffron-colored robes, seeing earthen vessels, and likewise seeing a vessel of oil; || 27 ||
There were mortals with severed noses, those with missing limbs, and those with extra limbs;
likewise, there were women who had no sons and widows as well. (28)
Likewise, one who eats excessively should avoid these terrestrial [omens];
if the movement is auspicious, one should proceed, but if it is inauspicious, one should turn back. (29)
The teacher should proceed toward auspicious places;
he may travel to a mountain, the ocean, a sacred ford (tīrtha), a field (kṣetra), or likewise to a forest. || 30 ||
Near a milk-tree, or near a temple of the gods, or on the bank of a river or a pond, the preceptor should take up a stone. (31)
If one should grasp it from another location, when it is grasped, there is the destruction of the performer.
It is of four kinds: white, red, yellow, and black.
Resembling cow’s milk, a conch shell, the kunda flower, the moon, a pearl, crystal, and the hue of a jasmine blossom—these seven varieties are recorded for the white [mercury]. (33)
Resembling the Japā and Aṃśuka flowers, possessing a luster like that of the Indragopa insect, resembling the Dāḍima flower, and having the brilliance of the Bandhūka blossom. (34)

O best of the twice-born! The red [ruby] is likewise known to be of seven kinds, possessing the characteristics and forms of its species, with a luster like that of a hare-marked moon or a precious gem.
Having a form resembling gold, like the flower of the mustard plant, similar to the *āsana* flower, and like the powder of turmeric. || 36 ||

Resembling the flower of the *kūṣmāṇḍa*, possessing the luster of the *heraṇḍa* flower, and having the appearance of the blossom of the *āragvadha*—these are the seven types of yellow [orpiment] from the mountain. (37)
Having the luster of buffalo-eyes and collyrium, with a radiance like that of a blue lotus;
with ears resembling those of a bee or a peacock, and a nose like that of a buffalo.
Resembling the appearance of rājāvarta, having a luster like that of black mung beans, and shaped like small black mung beans—these are remembered as the ten black mountains (kṛṣṇaśailas). 89.
White, red, yellow, and black [are the colors] corresponding respectively to the Brahmins and the other castes;
she constantly bestows all desires, wealth, and liberation.
Or else, for others, let that which is supreme among others and the highest among others—apart from [the usual] reverse and direct orders—be taken as suitable for the seed. (41)
Both the preceptor and the artisans shall wear white garments;
their bodies shall be adorned with white garlands and unguents, and they shall be endowed with ornaments for the five limbs.
Taking up axes and other tools, they should proceed toward the rock with concentrated minds;
having reached the place where the portion of the rock is located, they should circumambulate it.
Having examined the stone for defects and non-defects, and having specifically distinguished it,
one should wash it with milk and water if it has been scorched by wind, sun, or fire, or if it is impure.
One situated in a bad location, one standing on the edge, or one poorly joined at the end of the work;
likewise, one rich in gravel, or otherwise dilapidated and resembling something parched. (45)
One should avoid [a woman] marked by lines, dots, or blemishes;
she whose form is like the casting of a thread and who is endowed with the rays of a hero (vīra). || 46 ||
The lines are indeed remembered as being of three types, appearing like the falling of rain;
they resemble the shape of a rose-apple fruit, or are comparable to breasts or eyes. (47)
Or else, it has the form of a reversed [triangle] and consists of three bindus;
its appearance is like black iron, resembling a black bee. 48.
The four types of lunar spots are:
those resembling the shape of a peacock's tail-feather, those shaped like a date-palm leaf, and likewise those resembling a cluster of dūrvā grass. (49)
Harīkā is known to be of five types: having the appearance of a bamboo sprout, or like a spider's leg, or resembling the tip of a sugar cane. (50)
Resembling a conch shell, like gold, or possessing a luster like bell-metal (kāṃsyaloha), the form of a cave is known to be threefold; it brings about all manner of defects and fear. (51)
A white line upon a black horse bestows the abundance of all prosperity;
however, a black line on a black horse leads to destruction, and likewise, a black line on a white horse does the same.
Therefore, with every effort, let the other [variety] be accepted;
specifically, on the Black Mountain (Kṛṣṇaśaila), the white-colored variety is especially recommended. || 53 ||
One resembling a date-palm leaf and shaped like a clump of durva grass is auspicious;
another is known as inauspicious kṛtyā, which causes the destruction of cattle, grain, and wealth. (54)
A stain (kalaṅka) should be known as causing disease; a tremor (trāsa) brings about the destruction of the kingdom;
a dot (bindu) results in the loss of sons; and a fissure (darī) is the destruction of everything.
Having examined it thus in many ways, one should have [the image] fashioned with the proper characteristics;
whether it be a child, a young woman, or an old woman, and likewise male, female, or neuter.
Listen now to the method of distinguishing them by their divine forms and physical characteristics:
a stone that is short and emits a sound like a thick conch shell is known as *bālā*. (57)
She whose voice is long and resembles the sound of a bell is proclaimed as "Young"; she who is endowed with a harsh or open sound is proclaimed as "Old. || 58 ||
That long stone which has the resonance of a bell and is well-restrained is for men; that long stone which has the form of the resonance of cymbals is for women. (59)
Those who are unaffectionate, or harsh, or deficient in voice, or neuter, have been described by the gods; now the distinction according to physical form is being stated.
The square and the eight-sided [mandala] are proclaimed as the "woman-stone" (strīśilā);
those with ten and twelve corners are the oblong and the circular [mandalas], respectively. (61)
That stone is known as masculine when it is well-rounded; it is neuter when it has ten or twelve facets. One should avoid stones that are immature or aged.
The *liṅga* is fashioned from a male stone (*puṃśilā*), while the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is made from female stones (*strīśilā*);
however, the foot-support stone (*pādādhāraśilā*) is made from a neuter stone (*napuṃsakaśilā*).
If that which ought to be done is performed in reverse, it brings destruction to the agent;
therefore, the artisan, having taken up the stone with its edge pointing either eastward or northward, [should proceed].

When the tip is in the east and the root in the west, and the tip is in the north and the root in the south, the face is said to be in the lower part, while [the other] would be directed upwards. (65)
Having thus examined and accepted [the image], the wise one should wash it with cow-products while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
having bathed it with the *sadyojāta-mantra*, he should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
In that region sacred to Śaṅkara, one should cause a peace-offering (śāntihoma) to be performed;
one should carry out everything beginning with the establishment of the fire (agnyādhāna), as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
One should offer the fuel-stick with the Heart mantra, the clarified butter with the Root mantra,
the oblation of cooked rice (caru) with the Aghora mantra, and the rice grains with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should offer sesame seeds with the *Īśāna* mantra and mustard seeds with the *Kavaca* mantra;
for each, there should be one hundred oblations, or fifty, or twenty-five. (69)
Then one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "sviṣṭamagne".
Thereafter, having formally dismissed the fire (samudvāsya), one should perform the dismissal of the worship and the placement of the concluding rites.
Having cut the stone with the heart-mantra, the wise one should worship it with the weapon-mantra;
then, having recited the armor-mantra, he should perform the cutting of the stone.
Thereafter, one should carry out the work of the artisans, beginning with the master builder (sthapati),
as well as the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) and likewise the measurement of the door.
The pillar, the palm-measure, the cubit-measure, the finger-measure, and likewise the measurement derived from the liṅga— these seven are each of many kinds.
The inner sanctum (garbhageha) should be five parts; it is said that [the temple] with three parts is excellent.
O best of the twice-born! [The excellence] is declared to be of nine kinds, beginning with the "excellent-excellent" (śreṣṭhottama).
On the ground floor of the palace, however, that [measurement] should indeed be equal to the length of the pillar;
this is known as the "excellent" (uttama) type, while half of that would be the "middling" (madhyama).
O best of the twice-born! Between those two, at the eighth part, is the division called Nanda;
and when the distance between the pillars is divided into nine parts, [the ninth part is] Stambha.

O best of the twice-born! The measurement of the linga is ninefold, and the measurement of the pillar (stambha) is likewise; O Brahmin, one should perform the measurement of the pillar according to the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna).
Beginning with one cubit and increasing by one-eighth [of a cubit], the procedure extends up to nine cubits;
the total number [of measurements] is sixty-five.
A temple (harmya) may begin with a height of five cubits and extend down to a minimum of one cubit;
however, a temple below five cubits in height is not suitable for a linga, except when determined by the requirements of the pillars.
From one cubit up to ten cubits is the measurement for the pavilions (harmya) of the various conceptual forms;
however, for the *chanda* and *vimāna* types of temples, the linga should measure from three cubits up to six cubits.

The *liṅga* from six *karas* up to nine is appropriate for the various castes and planetary deities; thus has the measurement of the cubit (*hasta*) been fully explained. Now the measurement of the span (*tāla*) shall be described. (81)

From one *tāla* up to nine *tālas*, by increasing [the measurement] by one *tāla* at a time, those nine types of *liṅgas* shall exist; furthermore, there may be a variety conceived [according to specific rules]. || 82 ||
Starting from thirteen finger-breadths up to one hundred and nine finger-breadths,
that [measurement] should be divided by one less than the number of parts, according to the finger-breadth measurement of the liṅga.

One should not cause a liṅga to be made smaller than one cubit, even if it is accompanied by a third part [of its height]; a liṅga that is less than one cubit in measure, especially if it is circular in shape, [is inauspicious]. 84.
The wise one should join the portion arising from the fire of the Vedas (36) to the pedestal;
the remainder shall be visible as the appearance of the various parts in the temple structure. 85.
The Vaiśālilinga is for the pedestal (viṣṭhara), while the Vikalpa is for the enclosure (parigraha), excluding [the other];
it begins from one finger-breadth (ekāṅgula) up to the limit of eleven finger-breadths (rudrāṅgula).
It is said that [the pedestal] made of metal, gems, or cloth should be above;
however, one should not make the stone-made [pedestal] more than thirteen finger-breadths below.
Thus, the measurement of the *liṅga* is declared with its many varieties;
now I shall describe the *nāgara*, *drāviḍa*, and *vesara* types of *liṅgas*.
When the liṅga rises, one-fourth part is for the base and one part is the smallest;
when it is elevated, three parts for the height and one part for the width is said to be the best.
In the middle between those two, at the eighth part, the piercing (tāra) is said to be ninefold;
but when the rising occurs at the sixth part, the fivefold portion shall be for the purpose of pacification (śāntika).

The portion consisting of the Vedas is known as *pauṣṭika* (nourishing), while the portion consisting of the qualities (*guṇas*) brings victory. The portion consisting of the two [the *ṛg* and *yajur*] is *ābhicāra* (sorcery); thus, according to Vyāsa, it is fourfold. (91)
Thus, in the Nāgara style, a temple with thirteen bays (vyāsa) is prescribed;
when the height of the liṅga is divided into twenty-two parts, it should consist of six, five, and four parts [for its base, shaft, and capital].
In the Guṇāṃśa style, there are rites such as Śāntika; however, in the Rāviḍa style, there are four types.
The Vesara style also has four varieties, as does the pedestal (piṇḍikā) for the temple-lord (harmyaliṅga).
In the case of a tall Liṅga made of bell-metal, when it is divided into twenty parts,
its width is prescribed as eight, seven, six, or five parts.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) of the liṅga may be of four types: the Śāntika, the Pauṣṭika, the Jayada, and the Bhūtada; and the Vesara. Thus the temple (harmya) of the liṅga is of four varieties.
The stone slab serving as the base for the feet, fashioned by one's own hand, upon which the *liṅga* is installed, is declared to be the cause for increase. (96)
If there is mutual confusion [of castes], it brings fear to the king's very face; therefore, with every effort, one should not practice such confusion. 97.
Thus have the Nāgara and other types of liṅgas been described; now hear concerning the Āyādi type.
One should divide the height of the liṅga by means of the measurement-finger (mānāṅgula). || 98 ||
One should complete [the verse] by increasing or decreasing the number of syllables;
one should accept a verse that is filled with the appropriate measure, whether it be superior, intermediate, or inferior. 99.

O best of the twice-born! Having multiplied the height-measure by eight and divided by the number of the constellations (twenty-seven), the resulting quotient is the number of days starting from Aśvinī.
When seven is multiplied by nine and divided by twelve, it indicates the day of the week, beginning with Sunday;
when three is multiplied by eight and divided by eight, it is declared to be the *yonimudrā*. (101)
When increased by eight and divided by twelve, the remainder is declared to be the *āya*.
When multiplied by nine and divided by ten, the remainder shall be the *vyaya*. (102)
When divided by the increase of the yugas, the ninth part is taken away by thieves and others;
when income exceeds expenditure, it is always the abode of prosperity.

The banner, the lion, the bull, and the elephant are declared to be auspicious births; among the seven days of the week, the Sun, Mercury, Moon, and Jupiter are auspicious, while the others are inauspicious. (104)
From the birth asterism of the king-founder, [one should count] until the end of the asterism of the Liṅga;
this constitutes three births, excluding the fourth, eighth, sixth, and ninth [asterisms]. (105)
These four [asterisms] beginning with Viśākhā, joined respectively with the days starting from Sunday, bring auspiciousness; the remaining ones bring inauspiciousness. (106)
Enmity, deathlessness, destruction, and untimely death [are the results] respectively;
having grasped the remaining yoga, one should collect the auspicious measure. || 107 ||
The *samaliṅga*, the *vardhamāna*, the *śaivādhikya*, the *svastika*, the *sarvatobhadra-liṅga*, and the *sārvadeśika*. (108)
The Dhārā-liṅga, the Mukha-liṅga, and the Liṅga—thus the Liṅga is of eight kinds.
The Samaliṅga is for Brāhmaṇas, while the Vardhamānaka is for kings.
The Śaiva [liṅga] is for Vaiśyas, while the Svastika should be for Śūdras;
for all others, the other type of liṅga bestows the fruit of all desires.
In this very way, Mahādeva [established] the Liṅga for the benefit of men;
first, on a ground that was level and not too extensive, he made it four-cornered. (111)
Afterwards, having divided the rear portion into three parts according to this rule, the wise one should designate the lower square as the Brahma-portion. || 112 ||
In the center, there should be an eight-cornered [figure], which is proclaimed as the portion of Viṣṇu;
in the upper part of the circle, however, that which exists is known as the portion of Śiva.
Because no specific portion has been prescribed, it should be understood as being entirely of the nature of Śiva;
[likewise] the root, middle, and top of the tree, together with its branches and flowers. (114)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell, as well as skin and Rudra—each one is proclaimed to be a single part of the One. (115)
Nevertheless, for that which is endowed with distinct parts, no difference in the means of valid cognition exists; likewise, there is no distinction regarding each part of the Śivaliṅga. || 116 ||
Having fashioned a four-cornered figure with a liṅga at its center and ears extending halfway [along each side] in sequence,
the preceptor should then determine the corners from corner to corner using that same measurement.
Outside of that, the wise one should cut out an octagon; thus it shall be here.
Alternatively, having divided the "star" of the liṅga into seven parts, [one should proceed]. || 118 ||
The wise one should cut the middle band to a portion of nine parts on the outside;
alternatively, the middle band may be six parts when [the whole] is divided into eight parts.
One should cut it specifically into three types of eight-sided shapes; when the width of the cloth has been made into a square, [it becomes] an octagon.
One should mark from corner to corner the eight-sided figure (aṣṭāśra), which is half of that corner;
having delineated the exterior of that, it becomes a sixty-four-sided figure (kalāśra) here. 121.
By repeatedly cutting away portions of the corners, it becomes circular;
by the arrangement of eight corners and so forth, a square is obtained.
In the three parts of the length of the *liṅga*, one part is square;
in the middle is an eight-sided (*vasvaśra*) base, and at the top is a circular portion belonging to Śiva.
This is known as the *samaliṅga*, which bestows prosperity upon Brahmins and the other castes;
it has a length equal to twice the width of the sun (the base) and a square area consisting of seven parts.
The eight-cornered [figure] is made with one-eighth [of the diameter], while the circle is said to be nine parts;
or it may be six, seven, or eight parts, or indeed five, six, or seven.
The increasing [measurement] is of four kinds, being one-fourth, one-fifth, or one-sixth [of the height].
When the length of the liṅga is divided into ten parts, the square base is three parts.
The Vasvaśra is indeed equal to that; the Śivāṃśaka should consist of a portion of the Yugas.
This is known as the Śivādhika, or else there is another method.
Alternatively, there are four types of predominance of Śiva, consisting of five, five, and six parts; or five, six, and seven parts; or even four, five, and six parts. (128)
In the ninefold division of the length of the liṅga, the square is made with two parts; the octagon with three parts; the quadrangle (the four-cornered) is said to be the circle.
Thus the Svastika has been described; it is called Sarvatobhadra when it is perfectly circular from base to tip, with the height of the liṅga being one-third [of the total].
The portion for the pedestal is one part, the portion for the sky is one part, and the portion for the womb-binding is one part;
the portion for worship is one part, and indeed, the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] consists of these very parts. (131)
In the case of a universal Liṅga, however, it should be entirely circular; or, when the height of the Liṅga has been divided into five, four, or three parts, [the base should be made accordingly].
On the pedestal, one part is for the entrance and the remainder is said to be the portion for worship;
one should arrange the universal liṅga in this very same way.
Having specifically made the height of the *samaliṅga* nine parts,
its circumference should be six parts, and the circumference at the middle should be seven parts.
The lower part below the eighth portion is that which constitutes the *trairāśika*;
this supreme *trairāśika* is indeed worthy of all lineages. (135)
From the base to the top, it is indeed a quadrangular *dhārāliṅga*;
its base is equal and four-cornered, while the remainder is eight-cornered.
The lower portion should be square, the middle portion octagonal, and the worship-portion (pūjābhāga) should have sixteen sides; thus the dhārāliṅga is of three types. || 137 ||
Whether it measures half a barleycorn or a full barleycorn at the edge of its base, a steady stream with a symmetrical linga brings welfare to all living beings. (138)
The Dhārāliṅga has been fully described; now the Mukhaliṅga is being explained.
Having divided the portion for worship into three parts, the face should be located in the uppermost part. (139)
He has five heads and four faces, with a single neck;
he possesses eight ears and twelve eyes, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Below that, it has the form of a *liṅga*, and below that, it is provided with a pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
From there upwards, its portion consists of one hundred and twenty-four parts. (141)
The height of the uṣṇīṣa is declared to be one-third more than the [height of the] moon;
the part below the hairline should be recessed, shaped like a pearl or a dāmalaka fruit.
From the hairline to the end of the ear-measure, there are four parts increased by three;
from the eye-measure to the edge of the eyelid, and from the edge of the eyelid to the jaw. 143.
It is proclaimed that each [subsequent part] increases by three units; the portion for the yuga is thus described.
Furthermore, the measurement from the jaw to the neck is stated to be four *yava*s. (144)
One part less than a yuga (four) out of the total parts constitutes the height of the ear;
the remainder is known as the shape of the linga, which one should fashion according to the prescribed characteristics.
He may have four faces or one face, and two arms or four arms;
his reflection appears above the breast-thread, endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Alternatively, above the *hikkā* (neck) and the rest, the remainder may take the form of a phallus;
this is known as the "face-liṅga" (*mukhaliṅga*), which leads to the prosperity of kings. || 147 ||
Having divided the width into eight parts at the base, the middle, and the tip, one should conceive of it as being diminished by one part; this is declared to be the "thick-rooted" [type].
One should decrease the portion for Śiva and so forth; that is called the "thick-headed" (śiraḥsthūla).
Thus has been described the excellent Ārṣaka, which is honored by the sages. 149.
It has three, five, six, seven, twelve, ten, and nine corners,
and at its tip it is like the incomparable Tāra-mantra.
The board is mirror-shaped, with a single line and no other lines; it is used for rubbing the head and is provided with the correct proportions of measurement. (151)
The divine one and the self-born (Svāyambhuva) are renowned as being well-worshipped by the gods;
that which was worshipped by Bāṇa for the sake of enjoyment is declared to be the Bāṇaliṅga. || 152 ||
The gross, the subtle, and the root of the head are enumerated in sequence;
the face is known to be elevated, yet it is exceedingly cold to the touch. (153)
This is known as the Bāṇaliṅga, which is equal in color to honey;
however, regarding its entry into the pedestal (viṣṭhara), it follows the proportions of a universal (sārvadeśika) liṅga.
Treat iron and silver in the same manner as for all other regions.
The classification of the *liṅga* has been fully explained; now hear about the rubbing of the head. || 155 ||
From the base of the linga up to the end of the hair, there should be the rubbing of the head;
therefore, O twice-born one, when the linga has arisen, the rubbing of the head should be performed above it.
The first should be shaped like an umbrella; the second like a hen’s egg;
the third like a *tripuṣa* flower; and the fourth like a half-moon. || 157 ||
The wise one should divide the width of the liṅga into eight parts;
starting from the upper half-part, the first [section] is the *chatraśīrṣaka*.
One should divide the star into thirty-two parts; the upper portion should hang down.
The second part should have the appearance of an umbrella, while the third consists of seven parts.
The fourth, however, consists of nine parts and has the appearance of an umbrella; it is of four kinds.
For both the twice-born and kings, the umbrella-shaped [seat] grants all desires. (160)
Among all types of *liṅgas*, the *chatraśīrṣaka* is most excellent;
according to Vyāsa, when divided into thirty-two parts, it is formed by the portions of fourteen and one-sixteenth. (161)
The kukkuṭāṇḍa [shape] with seventeen parts is of four kinds;
it is highly recommended for a *vardhamāna* linga and is suitable for Kṣatriyas.
In the twenty-second degree of the head asterism (Śirastārā), there is likewise the portion of Dharma-Rudra;
with thirteen parts of the Sun, it forms the fourfold Tripuṣābhā.
It is highly praised when superior to Śiva, or worthy of a Vaiśya, granting all desires;
in this extensive [area], there are twenty-two or twenty-one parts in the thirtieth division.
The half-moon (ardhacandra) should be made with twenty or nineteen parts in four ways;
this should be performed on liṅgas known as svastika, which bestows prosperity upon Śūdras.
For all regional liṅgas and others specifically,
the shape of the top, such as a parasol and so forth, should be determined according to the caste of the artisan.

For divine, artisanal, and *kaliṅga* lingas, the head (*śīrṣaka*) shall be one-eighth [of the total height]; the height of the head's ornamentation (*dvartana*) shall be one-third of that [head]. (167)
One should fashion a portion from above the liṅga, provided with the curvature of the head;
this is called the uṣṇīṣa, and that is declared to be the measurement of the head.
From the center of the top [of the dome], one should gradually rotate it around until reaching the limit of its own portion;
from the center of the top, it is bent as far as the boundary of the lambā-portion.
The *chatraśīrṣaka* should be fashioned with three faces; it should be bent like a barley grain at the top, middle, and base of the *liṅgas* that have the *chatraśīrṣaka* shape. 170.
Thus, everything is stated in sequence from one *śīrṣaka* to the next. (p.
248) Regarding the *śīrṣaka*, one should not construct anything other than what is specified for the height of the *liṅga*. || 171 ||
If it is made otherwise than what has been prescribed, it brings fear to the king and the kingdom;
therefore, with every effort, one should have it fashioned according to the stated path.
The characteristics of the liṅga have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the pedestal (piṇḍikā). || 172 ||
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, concerning the characteristics of the *liṅga*, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of the *Kāśyapa* [lineage]. || 51 ||
Now, therefore, O Brahmin, the characteristics of the pedestals for the deities beginning with Nāgara shall first be described; thereafter, the wise know them for all [other types].
In a stone temple, however, the pedestal should be made of stone, or else of lime or brick;
in a wooden temple, it should likewise be made of wood or of brick.

For lingas made of gems, metals, and the like, or those fashioned from their own source-materials or iron, the pedestal should have a width equal to the height of the linga; this is considered the best.
The pedestal (pīṭha) equal to the height of the worshipper is called the "Tāra" or the smallest;
between those two, at the eighth part, are the three categories beginning with "Uttama," each consisting of three [subdivisions].

Having divided the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) into three parts, the height of the best type is two parts; the height of the lowest type is half the width; and between these two, the intermediate types are determined by dividing [the difference] into eight parts.

O Brahmin, the ninefold pedestal-height consists of three groups of three, starting from the *uttama* (best) category; these are declared in sequence as the *nāgara* style, by which one is indeed liberated.

The width of the *liṅga* at the top should be divided by nine; that which is seven parts is the best width, while that which is eight parts when divided [in the same way] between those two is the smallest. (7)
It is renowned as being expanded ninefold even for the portions of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
having divided the earth at its rising, it occupies two parts in the portion of fire.
One should especially assign one part to the area of the platform;
the remainder is known as the emergence of the pedestal (pīṭhodaya). In this manner, one should perform the Drāviḍa style.
Equal to the circumference of the portion for worship, it should be excellent and very large;
however, if it is one-sixteenth of the circumference, it is the lowest, consisting of twelve parts.
In the middle of those two, at the eighth part, the pedestal is ninefold in width;
with a height equal to the portion of Viṣṇu, the pedestal is called the smallest (kanyasa).

The best [height] is said to be one and a quarter [parts]; when the height between those two is divided by eight, the height of the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is ninefold; thus one should act in the Vesara style.
Alternatively, the width of the pedestal should be three times the diameter of the liṅga;
or, once the liṅga's diameter has been made into a square [by squaring it], [the pedestal should be three times that].
The width of the pedestals, specifically, should be twice the length of that [base], or even one and a half times,
or three times.
The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is declared to be one-third or one-fourth of the inner sanctum (garbhageha), and its height is equal to one part of Viṣṇu.
These pedestals (piṇḍikā) are common to all lingas, such as the nāgara and others;
however, for all of them, the specific measurement is the external width of the base (upāna). || 16 ||
Then, its front width should be reduced by one-eighth, one-ninth, or one-tenth;
its height should be equal to the portion of Viṣṇu, being either one and a quarter or one and a half [times that]. (17)
For ordinary pedestals, however, the height of the *nāgara* style and others is standard;
this is the general characteristic of the pedestal for all *sakala* liṅgas.

In the case of a full rising (sakalodaya), the ninth part is the smallest rising (kanyasodaya), while the tenth part is the best measure; between these two, when divided by eight, [the intermediate values are obtained].
The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be ninefold, and its width is declared to be equal to that height;
such a pedestal is called the inferior one.
The width of the best [type] is double [the length]; when these two are divided by eight in the middle, it is known as being ninefold in extent, especially for the Sakalas.
The pedestal for the liṅgas is prescribed as being provided with a cow’s mouth (gomukha);
however, for the sakala-liṅgas, the pedestal is specifically one devoid of the cow’s mouth.
For the lingas, however, a square, an equilateral shape, or an elongated shape is prescribed; likewise for the image or the pedestal, it may be circular.

The lotus-seat (padmapīṭha), the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), the altar (vedikā), and the circular seat (parimaṇḍala)—these, O best of the twice-born, are known as the fourfold types of seats for decoration. || 24 ||
One should divide the height of the *tuṅga* (the upper part) into six parts; with two parts, the height of the *upāna* (base moulding) is formed.
Below that, the lotus and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) have a height of five parts, resembling a sandal (*pāduka*).
The upper lotus, however, shall consist of four parts; the height of the fillet (paṭṭikā) shall be two parts;
the height of the ghee-water (ghṛtavāri) shall be one part of Śiva (one-sixteenth); and it shall be endowed with sixteen petals.

O observer of noble vows! Between those two, there should be a small petal, or else eight great petals; the height of the tip of each petal should be half a finger-breadth according to the measurement-finger (mānāṅgula).
The height of the tip of the petal should be half an aṅgula, or equal to the width of the liṅga;
one-third of the width of the pedestal is said to be the length of the gomukha and other features.
The width at its base is said to be similar to its length;
the width at its tip shall be one-third of the thickness at its base. (29)
From the base to the top, that solid mass gradually diminishes, becoming similar in width [to the base];
its summit (nīvr̥) may be three-quarters, half, or one-third of a part.
The width of the water channel should be one-third of the vyāsa;
it should be as deep as the height of the fillet (paṭṭikā), or slightly less, or extended from that.
One should practice beauty through the attire of the limbs, such as sandals and so forth, or one may fashion a lower garment (nīvra) like the attire of the foundational limbs. || 32 ||
The lotus-seat (padmapīṭha) has been fully described; now the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) is being explained. Having made the height sixteen parts, the step (upāna) is said to be one part.
In the Jagatī style, however, the height of the base (vedī) is one-fourth [of the total height],
the height of the moulding (guṇa) is one-sixth, the height of the kumuda is one-eighth, the measurement of the fillet (paṭṭikā) is one-fourth, and the measurement of the neck (kaṇṭha) is one-sixth.
The portion above that, measuring one part, should be the *kaṃpa*; the *paṭṭikā* should consist of two parts;
and the *ghṛtavāri* should be one-sixteenth of a part—this is called the *bhadra*.
In the case of a high pedestal (pīṭhocca), the height of the plinth (pāduka) shall be two parts out of nine;
the measurement of the molding (jagatī) shall be three parts, and the height of the kumuda shall be equal to that.
The portion of the sky (vyomāṃśa), measuring one part, is to be made vibrating; its height is two parts.
Its upper vibration is one part, and the fillet (paṭṭikā) should consist of three parts.
One part should consist of ghee and water; this is called Bhadraka.
Likewise, what is known as Bhadra is placed upon the altar and pedestal.

In the thirteenth part, the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is two parts; the height of the plinth (pāduka) is likewise two parts. Above that, one should fashion the lotus-base (padmatas) equal to that [plinth], and the fillet (kaṃpa) with one part.
The measurement of the neck is two parts; the upper portion is one part of Śiva.
Above that is a lotus of one part, and the fillet (paṭṭikā) is equal to that.
One should determine the rise [of the shadow] by means of a portion of the sky, using ghee as the liquid;
or else, the rise is in an eighth part, while the height of the upāna is a ninth part.

One part shall be the ghee-water (ghṛtavāri), and the remainder the altar (vedī) with four corners. That which is called the pedestal (pīṭha) is the same as the plank (paṭṭikā) consisting of six parts.
Indeed, the single [altar] should be prepared in three ways; it is called a *vedikā* or a pedestal (*pīṭha*).
It may be a lotus, an auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*), circular, or oval. || 43 ||
Alternatively, one should conceive of the seat (pīṭha) as having limbs like those of the foundational deities;
or else, it may be conceived like the limbs of the secondary seats (upapīṭha), being celebrated by their respective names.
A square shape bestows victory; one should fashion a shape like a womb (yoni); a bow-shaped mandala brings peace; and a triangle destroys enemies. (45)
For increasing [prosperity], it should be circular; for bestowing nourishment, it should be five-cornered;
and for destroying disease, it is known to be eight-cornered—thus they understand the sequence.

O best of the twice-born! In these forms, construct the limbs of the *pīṭha* according to the previously stated rule, using excellent materials or even new ones, or in the case of a restoration of an old one. (47)
O Brahmin, one should repeatedly perform the work exactly as it was previously fashioned; afterwards, another form may arise, whether it be virtuous or deformed.
Straightness or a beautiful face is auspicious if it is symmetrical and auspicious;
one must never make the pedestal longer than the lingas.
Whether it be square, circular, oblong, or otherwise, all [these forms] should be made as the locus of all perfections for those who possess them. (50)
The characteristics of the pedestal have been declared; now hear concerning the foot-stones, the mountain-base, and so forth.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, the Piṇḍikā-lakṣaṇa-paṭala, in the Aṃśumat-kāśyapa [treatise].
Now I shall specifically describe the characteristics of the foot-mountain and so forth;
its width is three liṅgas, and its height is three-quarters of that.
The height is classified as superior, middling, or inferior; between those two [extremes], it is divided by eight.
The width, however, is divided into nine parts, and its height is stated to be three-quarters of that.
Half of that is the minimum height; between those two, the height is divided into eight parts.
Thus, the height is said to be ninefold; the wise know this as the stone-base (pādāśman) in the Nāgara style.
The best Vyāsa is declared to have eyes as wide as the interior of the sanctum;
half of that is said to be the smallest, and between these two, there are eight intermediate sizes.
The extent of the stone slab is ninefold; the best height is three-quarters of that, while the lowest is known to be half of that. Between these two, it is divided into eight parts.
Its height is ninefold; thus indeed is the Drāviḍa style described. One-third of the nālīgṛha constitutes its excellent width.
Half of that is known as the lowest; between those two, when divided by eight, the width (vyāsa) is ninefold, while the height (tuṅga) is one-third of that for the best type.
Half of that is the lowest height; between those two, when divided by eight, the height is said to be ninefold, provided with a stone base and a vestibule.

The width of the cavity (avaṭa) is one-eighth greater than half the width of the liṅga; when that [total] width is divided by eight, one part constitutes the depth of the cavity, which has a shape like the base of the liṅga.
One should fashion a cavity nine cubits in extent and devoid of living beings;
elsewhere one should ensure levelness—this is known as the stone called the Ādhāra (Foundation).
Then, from the edge of the stone pedestal up to the *nandyāvarta* stone,
or from the *liṅga* down to the end of the pedestal, the measurement should be increased by one, two, or three finger-breadths.
In the Nāgara style,
the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is prescribed as being equal to the width of the temple, or one, two, or three yavas, or extending up to the limit of the Drāviḍa style and so forth.

In the case of the Liṅga-vyāsa-navāṃśa (nine-part measurement), by increasing the width by one unit at each stage from the pedestal, the width of the Nandyāvarta stone is established; that indeed is the Vesara style, which is ninefold.
One should fashion four squares around the liṅga;
their length is declared to be appropriate for the square.

One should place the northern end toward the east in the eastern section, and the eastern end toward the south in the southern section; one should place the northern end toward the west in the western section, and the eastern end toward the north in the northern section. (15)

The tip of the first [line] is in the direction of Śaṅkara (the North-East); the tip of the second is in the direction of Anala (the South-East); the root of the third is in the direction of Nirṛti (the South-West); and the root of the fourth is in the direction of Vāyu (the North-West). || 16 ||
Having thus smeared the Nandyāvarta stone with a paste of flour and water,
the wise should fix the pedestal (piṇḍikā) by applying an upward-binding mortar.
One should employ a pedestal (pīṭha) coated with either lime or diamond-bond (vajrabandha);
a pedestal made of a single stone is the best, while one made of two stones is indeed a mediocre seat.
The lowest pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be three, four, or five [units] high;
for the pedestals above the neck, one should construct them with one [unit] at the horse's [position].
Place many objects beneath the throat; let the *pīṭhadhara* rest upon the throat.
If there are two stones beneath the throat, one should place them first and then the other.
Three [lines] to the north, one to the left, and two further to the left;
if there are four, one should fashion a square with four corners. || 21 ||
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be made with two sides and endowed with the proper characteristics;
alternatively, it should be made very firm and without gaps by means of eight bands.
If it is made of bricks, it should be constructed by many people and plastered with lime;
likewise, it may be made of metal, jewels, or wood.
The binding of all [these parts] is designated as the "eight-fold bond" (aṣṭabandha).
One should raise the pedestal (piṇḍikā) above the boundary that marks half the portion of Viṣṇu.
One should not make [the base] uneven; for if it is made so, the agent is destroyed.
One should lead the stone beneath the pedestal using neuter stones. (25)
Thus, the [characteristics of] the Brahma-stone and so forth have been explained without distinction.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Foundation Stone and Other Elements," in the *Aṃśumat* section of the *Kāśyapa-śilpa*. || 53 ||
Now I shall explain specifically the characteristics of the extraction of proportions;
the fashioning of the face of the *liṅga* is intended as the extraction of its characteristics.
Either in front of the temple, or to the south of the temple of Śaṅkara,
one should construct a square pavilion measuring nine, eight, or seven cubits.
Provided with sixteen pillars and adorned with all ornaments,
construct an altar in the center of one-third of the pavilion.
Having smeared it with cow-dung, one should decorate it with flour-powders— a surface one cubit in height and resembling the belly of a mirror.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice, especially upon an altar (vedikā), adorned with various archways (toraṇa) and decorated with various flowers.
One should construct the pavilion (maṇḍapa) for the three lower classes of liṅgas in this manner, adorned with rice, sesame seeds, darbha grass, parched grain, and flowers.
For the remaining [deities], the width of the altar (vedikā) shall be equal to the length of the liṅga; the expansive width of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) shall be three times that [length].
One should perform all other rites of adornment exactly as before.
One should place the liṅga upon the altar with its head facing east and its face turned upward. (8)
Having placed eight jars all around— equipped with blades of kusha grass, provided with lids, accompanied by threads, enriched with new cloths, and filled with scented water.
The preceptor should worship the world-protectors, who are rich in gold and covered with garments,
with perfumes, flowers, and incense, each by their own name.
One should place the pedestal to the left of the base of the liṅga;
having wrapped both the liṅga and the pedestal with red rice, one should worship them.

Then, on the eastern side of the altar, the preceptor should perform all the rites beginning with the establishment of the fire (agnyādhāna), as prescribed for the fire-ritual, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with fuel-sticks of the Brahma-tree while remaining self-restrained,
[one should do so] with the mantra "ā vo rājā" and the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu".
One should perform the worship and the fire-oblation (homa) with the mantra "brahmajajñānam.
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru), one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times for each [deity] with the "aghora" mantra.

O best of the twice-born! Having tied the protective cord (pratisara) around the linga and the pedestal at night with threads of gold, silver, or cotton, while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). || 15 ||
Having worshipped the fire as before, one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Thus, having kept a vigil at night, [one should perform the rites] at an auspicious moment in the morning.
And the preceptor, having become pure and having consecrated his body with ritual protections (sakalīkṛta),
shall be adorned with a white upper garment and white garlands and unguents.

Adorned with a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), born of a family of auspicious Brahmins, the master architect, having become pure, shall wear the sacrificial thread and the purifying grass-belt (*pavitra*). (18)
At dawn, during an auspicious moment, one should perform the removal of the marks;
one should offer an oblation of milk-rice mixed with ghee at the location of the head.
Having set aside the red rice, one should worship with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the heart-mantra;
one should draw that linga with a gem and cast the central thread in the middle.

In the middle of the facial portion, however, the wise one should fashion a stalk endowed with its proper characteristics; the width of the cord is said to be according to the measurement of the liṅga.
One should take the portion arising for Rudra, provided with the measurement of the head;
having divided it into two hundred and twenty-four parts, one part is established as one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
A portion of that is to be divided by the earth; it is released as one barley-corn.
For the most excellent of the excellent liṅgas, the thread is five barley-corns long.
For the remaining types of lingas as well, one should increase [the measurement] but not decrease it;
for the three lower types of lingas, the thickness of the thread should be one barley grain (yava).
The width of the trench should be thus, and its depth should be equal to that;
a mark on the head indicates disease, while one on the forehead portends death. (25)
If [the mark] is on the line of the eyes, there is epilepsy; on the mouth, the destruction of food;
on the chin, the loss of kinsmen; and on the ear, the destruction of the shoulder.
It kills the child at the region of the breasts; therefore, one should avoid that region.
When divided by the parts of the qualities (guṇas), the head consists of eleven parts along with Rudra's portion.
O Brahmin, one should perform the extraction of the characteristic marks at one part above the [central] position, at that same part above [the head], and at the part below that. (28)
Having the shape of a lotus bud, according to the proper method and form, it serves for the increase of the twice-born and brings victory to kings. (29)
The two swords possess a form endowed with counter-signs, having a shape like that of an elephant’s eye;
and the conch shell, through its distinction from the two goads, leads to the prosperity of kings. (30)
The shape of the Vaiśyas' [mark] is like that of hollowed palms joined together, or circular like a cow's ear; likewise, it is triangular, or shaped like a trident, or elongated and circular.
For a Śūdra, it increases prosperity; for Vaiśyas, there are three [units]; such is its characteristic.
The portion specified for the extraction of the characteristic is divided into eleven parts (the Rudra-portion). // 32 //
One part is for the emergence of the bud, and its width is also equal to that;
the length of the stalk at its base is declared to be nine parts.
Therefore, it should not consist of a single thread, nor even two or three threads joined together;
if it consists of two or three threads, there must be an interval of three barley-corns between them.
Or else, O best of the twice-born, one should mark the boundary-line at a distance of two barley-grains from the stalk, or at the base and the tip of that stalk. (35)
If that stalk is a single thread, especially in the middle of the *liṅga*,
one should fashion the width and the excavation as prescribed by the Sūtras at the length of the stalk.
Below the stalk, however, leaving a space for the sky (the central void), one should then fashion a jeweled band above the head of Viṣṇu, extending from the bud down to the end of the hips.
The space between the jeweled lines at the base of the lotus should be equal to the lotus itself;
it may be one-third, one-fourth, or one-fifth of the lotus diameter.

Whether it be one-fifth or one-fourth [of the total], or even half the distance between the lotus petals, such is the interval at the base of the bud; now hear about the interval at the base of the stalk.
The dome (vārḍha) should be equal to the height of the neck (nālā), or three-quarters, or four-fifths;
then, in the upper part, it should be one-third or one-fifth of that height.
At the base of the *nāla*, at the level of the two lines of the jewel, there is an interval;
from the base to the tip, it gradually tapers off, and from there, fashion the line of the jewel.
At the base of the neck, one should join two [lines] horizontally; at the back, however, one should bind them together.
The excavation for the width of the jewel-line should follow the appropriate measurement of the linga.
It should be as long as the stalk supporting the jewel-line, or equal to its height;
therefore, from its base to its top, it should be divided into eight parts.
O Brahmin, the support of the jewel-line (maṇirekhā) is proclaimed to be ninefold;
indeed, it is thus in all the extractions of characteristics within the jewel-line.
The first characteristic has been declared; now hear the second characteristic.
As for the portion for the extraction of the characteristic, it is divided into ten parts. (45)
One part should be for the emergence of the bud, eight parts for the length of the stalk, and one part for the space below the stalk; having thus determined these, the remainder is as before.
The second characteristic has been declared; now hear the third characteristic:
it is the portion for extracting the characteristics, divided according to the portions of the *dharmas*. (47)
One part [of the height] should be as high as a bud, and nine parts should be the length of the stalk;
the remainder is specified as before—now hear the fourth characteristic. (48)
Having divided the portion for the characteristic marks into nine parts, one part is for the bud;
the length of the stalk is seven parts, while the remainder is exactly as before.
The fourth characteristic has been declared; now hear the fifth. Having divided the portion of the characteristics by eight, the portion of space is the emergence of the bud. (50)
The length of the stalk should be six parts, while the portion below the stalk is one part of Śiva;
that same [portion] is declared to be seven parts in length for the stalk.
The remainder should be performed as before.
Regarding the proportions, however, in the sevenfold division, one part is for the bud's emergence,
five parts are for the length of the stalk, and the rest is exactly as previously described.
One-sixth [of the total height] shall be the length of the stalk, while the remainder is as previously specified by number;
thus, O best of the twice-born, the eightfold measurement of the stalk's length is proclaimed.
O twice-born one, from the lotus bud at the tip of the stalk, which measures twelve [units],
a stalk of excellent quality should be fashioned according to one's desire, measuring eight units for me.
A firm thread should be drawn at the front edge according to the measurements prescribed for the lingas;
then one should install the linga, facing east or north, upon the eight-petaled lotus.
One should examine the face of the pedestal and place it toward the north of the liṅga;
then, having bathed both the liṅga and the pedestal with the consecrated jars, the Guru should do so while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.

Having bathed [the image] with cow-derived scented waters, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth—[the image] being provided with a hanging beard (*lambakūrca*) and adorned with all ornaments. (58)
Having circumambulated the village while mounted on a chariot or a palanquin,
one should honor the preceptor and the artisan with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
Then, having reached a reservoir of water, perform the ritual consecration in the water;
the extraction of characteristics has been explained—now hear the characteristics of the image.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the *Aṃśumat*, titled "The Chapter on the Procedure for Extracting the Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇoddhāravidhipaṭala*).
I shall describe the characteristics of the images; listen with a one-pointed mind.
They are of three kinds: immovable, movable, and both movable and immovable.
That which is made of clay, of gravel, or of stucco is known as movable;
likewise, that which is made of stone, wood, minerals, or jewels [is considered immovable]. || 2 ||
That which is known as "moving and unmoving" is indeed moving when made of metal;
it is of three kinds: half-painted, painted, and appearing like a painting. (3)
An image in which only half the body is shown is known as *ardhacitra* (half-painting);
that in which all the limbs are seen is indeed designated as *citra* (full painting).
The conception of a cloth, a wall, and so forth, is devoid of high and low [reliefs];
whereas "half-painting" (ardhacitra) consists of half [the work] done with lime and the other half like a painting.
One should produce the appearance [of the deity] by means of the elements according to the rules for the practice of painting.
A complete painting, a half-painting, and a mere appearance yield results that are respectively superior, intermediate, and inferior. (6)
The cloth image is superior to the brick image; the illuminated image is better than the cloth image;
the painted image is half as good as the illuminated one; and the earthen image is indeed superior to that [painted] one.
An image made of wood is superior to one made of clay; an image made of stone is better than one made of wood;
and an image made of metal is superior to one made of stone. Such is the fruit for the makers as well.
Gold is the best among those made of metal, silver is middling, and copper is known as the lowest; likewise, the fruit obtained from each of them is according to its quality.
The measurement of the image and the substance may be superior, intermediate, or inferior;
however, among all substances, the divinity is known to be exactly the same.
If the fruit were the same for the Lord of Gods and the divine beings, how could there be such a distinction between the result in saline soil, fertile ground, and soft earth? (11)
However, for the installation of a single tree of a distinct species, one should specifically follow the availability of fruit-bearing branches according to the requirements of the site. || 12 ||

Just as there is no difference in the tree itself despite the difference in its location, so too is the substance and its fruit equal; it bestows the fruit even when there is a difference in the substance.
Therefore, perform the entire rite for them with whatever materials are available;
that man who has performed it on earth shall be united with sons, friends, and wife.
O Brahmin! Endowed with objects of one's desire, the happiness found in the realms of Śakra and others, as well as that residing in places such as Sāla-udyāna, does not perish.
The person who, through mind, action, or speech, acts with these as concurrent causes, experiences the fruit obtained by the agent in accordance with his wealth. (16)
Therefore, another person should perform that rite which has Śiva as its essence;
first, a comfortable seat [should be prepared], and second, Umā and Skanda.
The third is Candramauli, the fourth is Vṛṣavāhana,
the fifth is Nṛttamūrti, and after that is Gaṅgādhara.
The seventh is Tripurāri, the eighth is likewise Vaivāhya,
the ninth is Ardhanārī, and the tenth is Gajahārin.
Then one should know the Pāśupata; Kaṅkāla is remembered as the twelfth;
the thirteenth is Harerardha, and Bhikṣāṭana is the fourteenth.
The fifteenth is declared to be Caṇḍeśvaraprasāda;
the sixteenth is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, after which Kālāri is mentioned.
From that, indeed, the Liṅga arose; there are eighteen forms.
Now, I shall first state the measurement for all these images.
For all types of lingas, excluding the measurement of the head, the measurement taken includes the head along with the other existing parts. (23)
In that same broad area, one should take twice the portion used for worship as the circumference and width; this should then be divided evenly into thirty-two parts.
Among those, it should indeed be twenty-seven parts, or twenty-five parts,
or twenty-one parts increased by one-third, or simply twenty-one.
Either nineteen parts, or sixteen, or thirteen;
or eleven parts, or nine, or seven, or five. (26)
Alternatively, when divided into nine parts, starting from one part out of those and increasing by one part at a time, [the height] is elevated by the portion of Rudra. (27)
Indeed, for as long as it is a twenty-seventh part, so long is it twenty-sevenfold;
when the exaltation of the Rudra-part is high, the exaltation of the image has thirty-eight divisions.
In the same manner, one should determine the proportions for the *liṅga-tāra* and the *liṅga-nāha*;
however, the difference in height between the *liṅga* and the *bimba* shall be one hundred and twelve units.
The inner sanctum (garbhageha) should first be nine units high in its portion;
alternatively, the inner sanctum may be divided into three parts.
There should be twenty-seven measures by increasing one part at a time;
or alternatively, the inner sanctum (garbhageha) may be divided into eighteen parts.
The height of the pure door, divided into four parts, consists of eighteen units by means of a single part and a single increment for the bimba.
The measurement of the door is of three kinds: the best is five parts of the height, the middling is four parts, and the lowest shall be three parts. (33)
Between the lowest and the highest [dimensions], divided into eight parts,
the height of the neck (galottuṅga) is prescribed as ninefold according to the measurement of the door.
Alternatively, when the height of the door is divided by twenty-seven, the height of the image is twenty-seven [parts] less one part for each [unit]. (35)

Thus, by the measurement of the door, there is the emergence of thirty-six *kautukas*; likewise, by the measurement of the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is divided according to the measurement of the pillar (*stambha*). (36)
One should determine the measurement in cubits for the width of the exterior of the temple;
the measurement in cubits is ninefold, ranging from one cubit up to nine cubits.
From one *tāla* up to nine *tālas*, it may likewise be of nine kinds;
[the proportions] may extend to the heart of the maker, or to the breasts, or having the arms as their limit. (38)
Its jaw-line and the boundary ending at the eye-threads should be made equal to the height of the artisan,
or according to the preference of the patron.
Alternatively, when the height of the builder (the temple) is divided into nine parts,
the total rise of the *sakala* [pedestal] is ninefold, with each part being reduced by one.
When the portion for worship is divided into one hundred and twenty-four parts,
one part is known as an *aṅgula*, which is commensurate with the *aṅgula* of the root-liṅga.

The "measure of the hand" (mānāṅgula) was previously described for the measurement of the nine types of temples; it is defined as the middle phalanx of the middle finger on the right hand of the architect.
The rule for the measurement of the fingers (mātrāṅgula) is traditionally taught as being either long like a joint or long like a star;
beginning from seven fingers, it increases by two fingers at each step.

The measurement of the image should be made up to twenty-three units, or up to one hundred with an increase of three finger-breadths; however, for the sake of others, it may be made according to two measurements.
In a domestic setting, however, the measurement for images intended for one's own use must be made using the *mātrā-aṅgula*;
otherwise, if it is done differently, the destruction of the maker will occur.
An auspicious image fashioned from all kinds of precious gems, measuring one finger-breadth (aṅgula), possesses slightly beautiful eyes according to the measurement of finger-breadths. (46)
One should not plant a seed of noble quality in [spots] measuring three finger-breadths;
for any measurement other than one finger-breadth, one should divide it by eighty-four.
Therefore, one should plant one part from that [total], which is the portion belonging to the birth-sign and the signs of the twice-born and so forth;
having divided it by sixty increased by two parts, it is endowed with one part.
Thus, the portion belonging to the royal caste is indeed the cause of prosperity for kings;
having divided it into twenty-four parts, it is endowed with one part. (49)
It is known as the Vaiśya-jātyaṃśaka, which brings prosperity to the Vaiśyas;
by adding a sixteenth part of its measure, it becomes the Śūdra-ṛddhikara (the one that brings prosperity to the Śūdras).

In this manner, having added the portion for the birth [sign] and multiplied that portion by eight, when divided by twenty-seven, the remainder shall be the first [sign], starting from Aśvinī. || 51 ||

If that day, the lunar mansion (jāti), and the asterism (ṛkṣa) coincide with the day of the king’s birth or his residence, and are further joined by an auspicious [lagna], it is favorable for the builder’s residence, the king, and so forth.

When the height of the image has been divided into parts starting from thirty and ending at one hundred, one should plant the lunar portion (the first part) as far as the occurrence of the auspicious [signs] and so forth. 53.
That measurement, from the base up to the uṣṇīṣa (the crown protrusion), should be the height of the pinnacle;
this is known as the length-measure, and one should arrange it starting from one part.
O twice-born one, one should increase the portion by eight and decrease it by twelve;
that which remains is known as the *āya*, which is the portion multiplied by eight. (55)
When diminished by twenty-seven, the remainder shall be the asterism beginning with Aśvinī.
Then, having multiplied that by nine, one should subtract the resulting degrees from the *nāḍīs*. || 56 ||
The remainder is known as the expenditure (vyaya);
one should indeed increase that portion by eight (vasu) if it is deficient, and the remainder shall be the Dhvaja and the other [planets]. (57)
One should increase the portion by nine and decrease the day of waning by seven;
one should increase it by the number four (four) and decrease it by the number nine.
The remainder is said to be the "portion" (aṃśaka); in this way, there are six [factors] beginning with income (āya).
An excess of income and diminished expenditure is highly auspicious, characterized by abundant income. || 59 ||
The banner, smoke, lion, dog, bull, donkey, elephant, and crow—these are the eight wombs; among them, Ketu is a monkey and Rāhu is a bull.
An elephant is to be known as a giver of auspiciousness, while those born from other origins are censured;
likewise, one should avoid the *pratyara* and the *vaināśika* [positions]. || 61 ||
The sixth, eighth, and twelfth ascendants are to be avoided; the remaining ones bring auspicious results.
Likewise, one should consider the day of the village’s birth-star (grāmanakṣatra) as well as the day of the king’s construction (vāstu). || 62 ||
One should count up to the asterism of the image and accept one that is auspicious;
as for the day of the week starting from Sunday, however, one should avoid Tuesday.
The Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are known as the "middle" [planets]. Starting from Sunday, they are associated with four asterisms each, beginning with Viśākhā. (64)
Yoga, death, destruction, and immortality respectively; the thief, the power of enjoyment, the fortunate one, the king, and the eunuch. (65)
One should send forth the chariot named Abhaya and the one called Navāṃśaka;
among those, however, one should avoid the thief, the eunuch, and the debtor. (66)
Among the various groups, one should avoid even the slightest contact with those who are divine or human;
having thus examined them, one should properly arrange the measurement that is rich in beauty.
For the sake of the prosperity of the four castes, one should employ the portion of the caste;
therefore, even a mixed portion is praised as a source for the household and the lineage.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, on the characteristics of images, in the Āṃśumatī [Tantra] of Kaśyapa. 55.
Now the supreme characteristics, beginning with the ten *tālas*, shall be described. If the image (*bimba*) is indeed made of clay, one should perform its installation upon the ritual stake (*śūla*).
If the image is made of stone, the mention of "stone" applies just as it does to the linga;
if it is made of metal, it is fashioned entirely from beeswax.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains in a pavilion in front of the temple;
having prepared a seat of kuśa grass, one should spread it over with darbha grass and flowers.
Having placed a wooden plank above that, with its tip pointing toward the eastern direction,
the preceptor and the artisan shall take hold of the pure measurement.
Then, one should not cause the limbs to be massaged with that measure;
rather, one should place [the body] upon a plank with the head toward the east and the face turned upward.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps,
the preceptor should then establish the Śiva-fire on its right side.
One should offer eight hundred oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
at the end of each substance, having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation, one should then offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra.
Having meditated on the form [of the deity] within the midst of the fire, one should utter the root mantra;
reciting the heart-mantra, one should manifest that very form of the deity as oneself.
The distance from the tip of the big toe to the heel is seventeen finger-breadths.
Below the *hikkāsūtra*, the arm should be long by one *ṛkṣāṅgula*;
the height of the elbow (*korpara*) should be two *mātras*, and the forearm (*prakoṣṭha*) twenty-one [units].
Therefore, from that point, the limit should be at the tip of the middle finger, measuring thirteen and a half [units];
then the width of the mouth should indeed be seven and a half units.
The width of the opening of the mouth is thirteen and a half finger-breadths;
the top of the neck is one and a half *nanda* parts, and the base of the neck is ten finger-breadths.
From the base of the throat to the limit of the arms, it is forty-one cubits;
the distance between the two armpits is twenty-two and a half parts.
The width at the base of the arms shall be nine parts plus four barleycorns;
the breadth at the region of the breasts shall be twenty-one parts.
The width from the heart to the navel is nineteen aṃśulas;
the middle diameter is declared to be one-sixteenth part [of that] plus four yavas.
The width of the hips is declared to be nineteen parts; the width at the front of the waist is said to be twenty-seven finger-breadths.
Below that, extending to the ends of the waist and sides, there are twenty parts, each half the width;
the breadth at the base of the thighs is one part less than a full measure.
The width at the middle of the thighs is one and a quarter parts;
the width of the knees is declared to be three-quarters of a part. || 18 ||
The width at the base of the shank is one and three-quarters parts;
the width at the middle of the shank is six and three-quarters parts. || 19 ||
That which is spread between those two is declared to be the portion of the *vīrabhāga*; the width of the *nalaka* shall be three-quarters of that *pakṣa* portion. || 20 ||
The width of the ankle is declared to be five parts plus three yavas;
the height from the axle to the top [of the wheel] shall be four and a half finger-breadths.
The width of the heel (pārṣṇi) is equal to the [width of the] toe; the height of the heels is indeed the same.
The middle of the sole (tala) should be one-sixth [of the foot's length], increased by two barley-corns (yava).
The width at the tip of the petal is said to be seven parts;
it should be two barley-corns more than four parts [in height], and the length of the big toe [of the foot] should be one part.
Its width is said to be two parts plus one-quarter of a yava;
its thickness is half that of the star, and it is circular with a diameter reduced by one-quarter.
The portion of the Veda provided with three folds is said to be the length of the index finger;
however, the portion of the Veda that is one-quarter less should be the length of the middle finger. || 25 ||
The portion for the fire, provided with barley-measures, is prescribed for the ring finger;
the length of the little finger is to be one and a half pakṣa-āṃśas. (26)
The wise know that, in order starting from the *prādeśinī* [finger], the measures are nine, seven, seven, six, half of its own *tārā*, and a *nakha*, as previously stated. (27)
The wise one should divide the width of each respective finger into four parts;
three parts shall be the height of the tip of the finger, and the remainder shall be the projection of the nail.
The width at the middle of the upper arm is eight parts plus three yavas;
the width of the elbow is said to be seven parts plus one quarter.
The width of the middle section of the inner chamber (prokōṣṭha) is said to be three-quarters of a rasa-part;
the width of the wrist-band (maṇibandha) is four parts less one-quarter.
The length of the little finger (tala) is seven parts, while the middle finger is six and a half digits;
that which consists of four parts plus one-quarter is said to be the length of the ring finger (anāmikā).
The length of the index finger is said to be five parts plus one barley-corn;
