the lengths of the thumb and the little finger are each four parts plus one-quarter.
The width at the base of the thumb is declared to be eight *yavas*;
that of the index finger is known as eight *yavas*, and that of the middle finger is known as nine *yavas*.
The ring finger is said to be eight barley-corns in width, and the little finger seven;
this measurement from the thumb to the end of the fingers refers specifically to the width at the base.
Its base, however, is one-sixteenth part of a kalā, diminished at the top and broad at the apex;
its tip is one-sixth part [in height], while its width is five parts of a nail (finger-breadth).
The remaining [portion] on both sides is fleshy, having the shape of rounded and long nails; that [measurement] is declared to be the length of the toe-nail, equal to the width of the nail. (36)
The length of the nails, measured by the tip of the first joint, is praised;
the thumb is seventeen barley-corns long at its base joint. (37)
The root joint of the index finger is two finger-breadths long,
while the length of the root joint of the middle finger is eighteen barleycorns.
The thirteenth barleycorns are prescribed for the root-joint of the little finger;
[this measurement applies] to the joints situated in the middle of the length between the root and tip joints.
The thumb should have two joints, while the remaining fingers are joined with three;
the tip of the palm of a Brahmin should measure four and a half finger-breadths, which constitutes the "Brahmin-measure" (vipralambha).
The width at the middle of the fleshy part of the palm is that of the hand itself;
however, the breadth at the base of the palm is said to be six and a half parts.
Beginning from the base of the thumb and ending at the base of the index finger;
beginning from the base of the thumb and ending at the wrist. || 42 ||
The length is said to be twelve finger-breadths (vedāṅgula), and its thickness should be half of that;
the width at the heel is one-third of a cubit, while the tip decreases like the thumb.
Below the fingers, the fleshy part extends for one and a half parts;
the heel of the hand is two parts wide, as broad as the belly of a parrot.
The remaining middle surface should be depressed by four, four, and three [units] respectively;
one should draw a fine line upon it, or [the symbols of] a conch, a wheel, or a trident.
O best of the twice-born! One should fashion the palm as having the luster of a lotus, with lines [drawn] such that each line is depressed by one barley-corn (*yava*) for each season. (46)
Having divided the circumference of the desired limbs into five parts,
one should take one part for the width, which is twice as long as it is wide.
That which is known as "I" here is not imagined by that very [self];
above the ears and the head, it is not "I," and it would be thirty finger-breadths in extent.
Above the ear, on the other side, there should be twelve finger-breadths;
above the ear, on the front side, it should be twenty-two finger-breadths.
The width at the back of the two ears is declared to be twelve finger-breadths (bhānu);
the portion situated between them is the distance between the two ears.
From the center of the head to the crown, the circle is four finger-breadths;
from the tip of the forehead to the end of the hair, it is declared to be nine and a half finger-breadths.
From that same mandala to the end of the hair on the neck is nine finger-breadths;
from the mandala to the end of the hair on the back, it shall be one and a half dharma-finger-breadths.
The forehead of animals is declared to be nine finger-breadths;
the hairline is the cord for the right side, and the position of the eyebrows is between the two.
Make the tips of the eyebrows raised like the shape of a bow;
O Brahmin, the distance between the two eyebrows should be one and a half *yavas* of a Veda.
The length of the eyebrows is five finger-breadths, their width at the center is two barley-corns, and they taper like the edge of a crescent moon; the tips of those eyebrows are equal to the middle.
The width of the pupil is said to be the measure of one barley grain;
the width of the black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) and its elevation shall be six barley grains. (56)
Its width is equal to its white edge, on both sides of the black circle;
it may be shaped like a Śabara or indeed like a bow.
Alternatively, O twice-born one, one should fashion the shape of a half-moon or the form of an eye; its height should be proportionate to that shape, and it should be white for both mandalas.
At the corner of the eye, there is a red circle measuring half a barley-corn (yava) with a white portion;
one-eighth part of that constitutes the circle of the pupil in its center,
which measures one and a half barley-corns and is extended upward by an eyelid.
The lower armor is equal to that; it is eighteen barley-corns in length.
O Brahmin, the distance between the two eyes should be two and a quarter finger-breadths.
O Brahmin! A downward gaze is prescribed for the eye;
an upward gaze causes the destruction of the maker, while a sidelong gaze brings about misfortune.
If there is a glance from the side by the village-dwellers, there will be the loss of kinsmen;
therefore, with every effort, one should look straight ahead.
Thus the eye has been fully described; now, furthermore, the characteristics of the nose:
the external nostril [measurement] is eighteen barley-corns (ayava) in width.
Its width at the top should be half of that [width at the base], and its width at the base should be half of that [width at the top].
From the root of the *goji* (the neck-base), the height of the nose-tip should be two finger-breadths.
Between the two nostril cavities, there is a wall which is also known as the *puṣkara*;
it is situated at a distance of one and a half barleycorns from the tip of the nose along the line of the nostrils. (66)
The upper lip, known by the name *goji*, is praised as being one and a half *yavas* in height and half that measure in width, with its depression situated above it.
O twice-born one, having made the nose-bridge (*goji*) extended by the measure of a barleycorn (*yava*),
they know the length from the mouth to be four parts less than that, measured transversely.
The upper lip should be long and its width is declared to be equal [to the lower];
in the middle of the upper lip, however, the *tāra* (central point) should be three and a half *yava*s.
Having made a depression for sprinkling water at its edge and reaching its boundary,
the wife should place a thick barley-grain upon the upper lip.
The upper lip is curved at three points;
its length is said to be eighteen barley-corns, equal to that of the lower lip. (71)
O best of the twice-born! Its width is one finger-breadth plus a barley-corn;
now the lower part, the *pālikā*, is said to be the measure of one and a half barley-corns.
The height of the lower lip from the chin is said to be six and a half barley-corns;
one should fashion the face with a slightly smiling expression. (73)
The distance from the chin to the lower lip should be one and a half finger-breadths (pakṣāṅgula);
from the chin to the jaw, the neck (vaṃśa) is said to be eight and a half barley-corns (yava).
Its width at the jaw-joint should be two and a half finger-breadths, with a circular opening for the passage of the tongue;
the distance from that joint to the end of the ear-attachment is twelve finger-breadths.
Starting from the exterior of the *haroḥ*, at a distance of three-quarters of a *yugamātra*, it is known as the *karṇaveśa*; after that, I shall describe the *karṇa*. (76)
The distance from the outer corner of the eye to the end of the ear is seven units;
the width of the ear is recorded as eighteen barley-corns.
From the top of the eye-line, the height of the ear is eighteen barley-corns;
its upper band is half of that, and the remainder above is circular.
Seventeen barley-corns below the eye-line is the ear-binding;
from there, one should let its stalk hang down for four and a half finger-breadths.
The diameter of the two tubes is declared to be one and a half parts for the front section and one part for the rear;
their thickness is half a digit.
The interval between the stalks is three parts, the height of the pedestal is four parts, and the length of the creeper is eight parts;
the entire height from the ear to the top is eight fingers minus one barley-corn (yava).
The *pippalī* should be half as thick as the *ghana*, twice as long, and its height should be one and a half measures; from the base to the tip, it should gradually taper away. (82)
Drinking [the liquid] for two parts, it should be long and have a width of two and a half yava-parts;
the axle-beads and so forth, as well as the ear-opening, should be half a finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The ear-opening is deep, perfectly circular, and even;
the lobe of the ear is thick, measuring one and a half yavas in width and four yavas in length.
The width of the back-ear is declared to be one and a half finger-breadths;
from the hairline to the back-ear, however, it is two and a half units.
At the end of the hair on the back, there is a depression measuring half a part;
below that, the height and length of the back is four parts plus three *yavas*. (86)
The nape of the neck and so forth measure nine finger-breadths;
the width at the base of the back of the neck is ten and a half finger-breadths.
The neck is said to be circular in form, gradually tapering from the base to the tip;
above the line of the throat-veins, the junction of the shoulders is four finger-breadths high.
The ear-attachment and other parts extend for six and a half mātrās up to the boundary of the shoulder;
the shoulder is seven aṅgulas thick and diminishes gradually down to the level of the heart.
Below the neck and the back, however, the *kakud* (hump) measures ten finger-breadths;
from there down to the junction of the hips, it extends for a length of nine *ṛkṣa*-parts (twenty-seven finger-breadths).
Its width, inclining toward that [measurement], is sixteen and a half barley-corns;
from the base of the beam downward, the root of the beam is three finger-breadths.
Others, however, say that the height should be thus; O twice-born one, I shall tell you the width in that case: the distance between the two armpits is said to be one and a half ṛkṣa-angulas.
The space below the armpit, from the shoulder-blade to the end of the arm, should be seven finger-breadths high;
the space above the armpit, up to the limit of the upper arm, is likewise declared to be seven finger-breadths.
The middle width is declared to be sixteen and a half mātrās;
however, at the line of the navel, the width should be twenty and a half aṅgulas.
The width at the hip joint is declared to be three-sixths [of the total];
the width of each buttock mass is one-quarter less than the portion of dharma.
These two are declared to be equal; between them, there are four *yavas*.
Others have stated that it is indeed the *tāra*; now the lateral width is being described. (96)
The width at the top of the armpit is said to be seven *mātras*;
it should be sixteen and one-quarter *mātras* wide along the line of the breasts.
The thickness of the middle and the sides shall be one-twelfth of the circumference;
the thickness at the hips and the sides shall be seventeen finger-breadths.
Thereafter, O Brahmin, the emergence of the hips is described as being seven [units] in measure;
it is four units below and three units above the line of the navel. (99)
Below the hips and above the waist, the height should be one and a half finger-breadths;
the thickness of that waist, O wise one, should be seven and a half finger-breadths.
The buttock-mass (sphik-piṇḍa) is from the base of the thighs; the waistband (nīvra) is one and a half yugas [twelve aṅgulas] from that.
The support for that mass is half [of its width], and the thread-mark (sūtra) extends downward by one aṅgula.
Below the hips, on the buttocks, it is one and a half finger-breadths below the yoke-line;
at the base of the armpits, it should be two and a half finger-breadths deep.
The neck should have a good circumference and be encircled by two lines;
its root at the base of the ears should be broad, elevated, and four barley-corns in measure.
The *jartṛsūtra* is said to be equal in measure to the *svākṣa*;
from the middle of the *hikkā* to the end of the armpit, it is one-quarter less than the *bhānu-aṃśa*.
The line from the root of the neck to the end of the breasts should be equal to the distance between the breasts;
between the heart and the base of the breasts, there should be a depression measuring one and a half mātrās.
One should fashion a mark in the middle of the ear, measuring three barley grains, or half that size, made of sesame seeds, circular in shape, and resembling the *tripuṇḍra*. (106)
One should fashion the *nata* at the root of the ear, below the *hikkāsūtra*;
however, one should fashion the *nīlakarṇa* above the *hikkāsūtra*.
The height of the heart and the breasts is declared to be two finger-breadths;
the width of the breast-circle is said to be seventeen barley-corns.

In the middle of that, the height of the nipple is two barley-corns, and its width is likewise two barley-corns; the depth and breadth of the navel is one part of the void (vyoma) plus two barley-corns.

O best of the twice-born! That center of the navel is clockwise-rotating, with its root-star measuring two barley-corns, situated in the middle of the hollow of the navel, and it is the thread of the navel.
From the navel to the hip, measured by the foot, it is five *mātrās* high;
below that, the waist and hips should be three and a half *aṅgulas*.
Therefore, from the root of the penis to its tip is the penis-base (meḍhrapīṭha), measuring four finger-breadths;
the length of the linga is declared to be five parts of that. || 112 ||
The base of the liṅga should be broad, measuring seventeen barley-corns in width;
one-third of the length of the liṅga should be the top, and the maṇḍī should be one barley-corn.
The base of the front knot (or ghaṇṭī), however, is the size of a barley grain and quite large;
the tip of the front ghaṇṭī is said to have the luster of a red lotus bud.
The scrotum should be non-expansive, measuring four and a half finger-breadths;
its thickness should be three and a half parts, while its base, upper part, and front-fastening should be proportionate to that. 115.
The width of the base of the penis, including its root, is seven and a half *mātrās*;
from the end of the base of the penis to the root of the thigh, it is fleshy. (116)
The width of the kneecap is four finger-breadths,
while the space between the foot and the kneecap is said to be three and a half finger-breadths.
It is said that the height from the back to the knee should be two and a half finger-breadths;
in the middle and on the sides, one should act according to the remaining requirements for beauty.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter [of the *Aṃśumat*], the section on the procedure for the ten-fold supreme proportions within the *Kāśyapa*.
The measurement for women will now be described using ten *tāla*s as the intermediate standard:
Umā, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Uṣā, Bhūti, and the Mothers (Mātṛs). || 1 ||
Perform the rites for Lakṣmī and Jyeṣṭhā according to this procedure;
she is designated as the power (śakti) of Īśa, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu. || 2 ||
The measurement corresponding to those [deities] is the measurement for their respective powers;
however, the height of Śambhu’s power, reaching to the limit of the tip of his nose, is indeed the most excellent of the excellent.
The area up to the limit of Śambhu’s breast is called the lowest of the low;
in the middle of those two, at the eighth division, is the ninefold seat of power (śaktimānaka).
The region above the navel of Śambhu is excellent, while the region between the breasts is the lowest of the low;
between these two, at the eighth part, is the ninefold seat of power (śaktimānaka).
p. 282) Thus, with a height of eighteen [units] from the feet up to the limit of the uṣṇīṣa, one should apply a portion of one jāti and a portion of one māyā for those who desire the sequence.
For images in the tribhaṅga posture, for those with other names,
and for the goddess Ucca, the standing position should be with feet even, according to the proper rule.
Durgā, Jyeṣṭhā, Lakṣmī, and especially the Mothers—
having thus conceived the measurements for the liṅgas according to the Mānakalpa, the preceptor [proceeds].
One should fashion Gaurī for the primary liṅga according to the measurement of the liṅga; when the female measurement is divided into one hundred and twenty parts, [the following applies].
One part is known as an *aṅgula*; its eighth part becomes a *yava*. The measurement of the limbs is determined by these *yavas* and *aṅgulas*.
For the goddesses beginning with Umā, the height of the crown is one part, which is a yava;
the rise of the turban is one part, while the hairline is three parts.
From the hairline to the end of the eye-line, it should measure three and three-quarter *yuga* (twelve) finger-breadths;
from the eye-line to the edge of the eyelid, it should be four and a half finger-breadths.
From the nostril to the jaw, it measures three and three-quarter finger-breadths;
below that, the measurement of the throat is declared to be four parts.
From the *hikka* to the end of the heart, from the heart to the boundary of the navel,
and from the navel to the end of the vulva, each is exactly thirteen finger-breadths.
The length of the thigh is twenty-six [units], while the measurement of the knee is four finger-breadths (yuga);
the shank is equal in length to the thigh, and the length of the sole of the foot is two finger-breadths (yuga). || 15 ||
The length of the sole of the foot is one-sixteenth part [of the total height], extending from the heel to the tip of the big toe;
the length of the index finger is declared to be four parts. (16)
The middle finger is three and a half parts; the ring finger is three parts;
and the length of the little finger is two and a half parts. (17)
The width of the toes of the feet, from the thumb (big toe) to the little toe, is two times eight [sixteen] plus seven and a half parts, measured in barleycorns. || 18 ||
The width of the nail should be three or two parts; it should be circular and its length one-quarter less than that.
The height of the tip of the fingers should be equal to the width of the nail. || 19 ||
The width of the forepart of the foot is six mātras;
the middle part is five aṅgulas, and the heel is four aṅgulas in width.
The width from the eye to the ankle is prescribed as five parts;
the middle of the shank, measured from the bone [the knee], is six finger-breadths.
The knee-span is seven parts, while the root of the thigh is twelve parts;
the width of the two hip-joints is twice the number of sun-parts (twenty-four).
The width of the vulva-base (yonipīṭha) is declared to be seven finger-breadths;
the thickness of the vulva is one-fourth of that, and its lower part is like the leaf of an Aśvattha tree.
One should fashion the womb (yoni) with a height equal to its width and well-fleshed;
at the location of the hips, however, the width should be twenty finger-breadths plus one barley-corn (yava).
The depth and width of the navel is proclaimed to be six barleycorns;
the breadth of its center is declared to be eleven finger-breadths (rudrāṅgula).
Below the breasts, the width should be thirteen and a half finger-breadths;
the diameter of the breast should be nine parts, and the nipple three parts.
The breasts should be elevated by one and a half units (vedāṃśa), with the space between them raised by the middle finger's breadth;
having made both breasts round and exceedingly beautiful, the space between them and the breasts themselves should likewise be well-formed.
The space between the breasts is one-eighth of a yava; there, indeed, is the channavīra.
O Brahmin, the distance between the armpits is recorded as seventeen finger-breadths.
The width up to the end of the arms should be thirty-one finger-breadths;
from the line of the *hikkā* downwards, the length of the arm is twenty-six finger-breadths.
The upper arm (korpara) should be two parts high; the forearm (prakoṣṭha) should be eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgula).
The length of the palm (tala) from the wrist (maṇibandha) is declared to be seven finger-breadths.
Therefore, the middle finger shall be six [units] long; the index finger shall be five-fifths [of that];
the ring finger is equal to the index finger; and the portions for the thumb and the little finger are [as follows]. (31)
The length of both hands and the fingers should be nine, seven, eight, or seven [units]; the width of the thumb and the other fingers should be one yava each.
One-fourth of that sixth part is said here to be the width of the nail (tāra);
the length of the nail, however, should be sharp and two barley-corns greater than its width.
The width of the palm of the hand is prescribed as five finger-breadths (aṅgulas); the width of the wrist is three parts, and that of the elbow is five parts.
The forearm is six parts long, while the upper arm at its base is seven parts;
from there down to the wrist, it is slender like a bamboo shoot.
The width of the neck should likewise be one-seventh of the span of the hand;
at the front and at the base, however, its width should be six parts plus one barley-corn.
The width of the face is one-eleventh part [of the total height], having the shape of a hen’s egg;
the distance between the end of the eyebrows and the hairline shall be two and a half finger-breadths.
At the end of the space between the eyebrows, that [measurement] should be two finger-breadths;
at the end of the mouth and nostrils, it should be one barley-corn and one finger-breadth. || 38 ||
Half of that is the length of the goji; half of that is its width.
The lower lip is one finger-breadth thick, and the remainder is the measurement for the end of the jaw.
From the chin, the earlobe should measure three and a half finger-breadths;
the width of the ear should be two parts, and its thickness one-fourth of that.
Therefore, one should cause the stalk known as the *karṇadīrgha* to hang down;
its width at the ear (*karṇa*) should be two parts, and it should be four parts including a quarter-part.
Therefore, one should cause the stalk known as the *karṇadīrgha* to hang down;
the hanging stalk should consist of five parts and be joined with the ear-fastening.
The foot should be made like an elephant's trunk and the hand like a cow's tail; the rest should be performed according to the method described for the *uttamatāla*.
This indeed is common to all women; now hear the specific [description]:
Gaurī has two arms, is peaceful, and her lotus-face is serene. (44)
Alternatively, they may have a basket-shaped crown or be endowed with a tiara-crown;
fashion upon them a beautiful crown or a hair-binding ornament. (45)
From the hairline to the top of the crown, the lowest measurement is eighteen finger-breadths; the middling is twenty-one finger-breadths; and the best is twenty-two finger-breadths. (46)
There should be an abundance of headbands and the like; the crown is broad at its base.
Having divided the base into seven or eight parts, the width at the top is reduced by one part.
One should likewise fashion the crown and tiara, as well as the arrangement of the hair;
for the karaṇḍa and the tiara, however, it should gradually diminish from the base to the tip.
One should fashion the top of the crown in the shape of a lotus bud,
adorned with three, five, seven, or nine caskets.
It is joined with four tiers, beautified on both sides by various flowers,
provided with a forehead-plate, and shaped like a pearl or an āmalaka fruit.
On the ear, there should be an earring joined with a *kuṇḍala*, four *mātrās* in height and length;
it may be a shark-shaped (*makara*) earring or simply a circular (*vṛtta*) earring.
Adorned with bracelets and waist-bands, joined with necklaces and throat-ornaments, provided with armlets and accompanied by hidden heroes. || 52 ||
Or she may be depicted wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), beautifully adorned with armlets,
clothed in fine silk (dukūla), and possessing limbs as beautiful as a dark-complexioned goddess.
The right foot should be well-placed and the left foot bent;
in the case of a side-bend (ābhaṅga), it should be three parts, while in a symmetrical bend (samabhaṅga), it should be four parts.
I shall describe in due order the sūtra known as *natamāna*:
[it is drawn] from the middle of the forehead to the left eye-corner and to the edge of the eyelid. (55)
Having grasped the left knee and likewise the space between the two [knees], the right thigh should touch the right side of the navel. (56)
One should let the heel of the right foot hang down against the left side [of the body],
and the distance between the two big toes should be sixteen finger-breadths.
One-third of that [measurement] is declared to be the distance between the heels (pārṣṇi).
Thus has the "bent" (ābhaṅga) style been described; now hear about the "even-bent" (samabhaṅga) style.
Having extended the Brahma-sūtra from the middle of the forehead, through the tip of the nose, and to the middle of the heels of the feet, I shall now describe the distance of two cubits.
Between the two threads, on the left side, there should be three finger-breadths;
from that thread, on the right side at the navel, the *nīvra* should be two finger-breadths.
From that line, three finger-breadths to the south is the middle of the base of the yoni;
from that line, to the left, the knee and the waistband should be four and three finger-breadths respectively.
The distance between the two big toes is eighteen finger-breadths;
the distance between the two heels is desired to be one-third of that.
The distance from the navel to the wrist should be equal to the span of a hand with the thumb extended upward;
it shall measure thirteen and a half finger-breadths.
The distance between the middle and the outer sides is seven units;
the hip-joints are four [units], and the forearm of one whose hand is hanging down is [the same].
The distance from the thighs to the wrists is two spans (dvantara), which is said to be the measure of Manu.
From the tips of the thighs to the tips of the hands, it is declared to be ten finger-breadths (daśāṅgula). || 65 ||
One should visualize Gaurī in this manner; furthermore, this shall be stated:
the left foot should be well-placed, while the right one should be bent.
Having extended the Brahma-thread from the center of the forehead and the tip of the nose to the middle of the heels of both feet, it is measured to be two cubits in length.
From that line, two *guṇa*-fingers to the right of the center of the breasts [is the mark];
from that same line, two fingers to the left is the navel, and the *nīvra* (the lower garment's border) should be two fingers [below].
From that thread, three finger-breadths to the left is the center of the base of the *yoni*;
from that same thread, to the right, the knee and the *nīvra* shall be three finger-breadths.
The remainder is indeed indicated as before, namely the characteristics of Gaurī;
or else, the characteristics of Sarasvatī and the other Śaktis are stated previously.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, concerning the measurement of women as one hundred and fifty *tālas*, within the section on Āditya in the *Kāśyapa* [Śilpaśāstra].
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall describe the smallest [image] measuring ten tālas;
therein reside the Moon, the Sun, the Aśvins, the sages, and likewise the planets.
The wise [architect] should have the preceptor (Ācārya), Śatamakha, and Caṇḍeśa made at ten tālas, while the Kṣetrapālaka should be made at nine tālas. || 2 ||
The crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) is said to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula), and the length of the hair is four finger-breadths;
from the end of the hair to the base of the neck, it should be five and a half finger-breadths.
O best of the twice-born, the measurement of the ear is said to be four finger-breadths (yuga);
from the *hikkā* line to the end of the breast-line, it should be five and a half finger-breadths (*sārdhabhānu-aṅgula*).
The area from below the breasts down to the navel is proclaimed to be equal to that;
and from the left [breast] to the base of the penis is twelve and a half *mātrās*.
From the base of the penis to the tip of the urvā grass [the height] should be twenty-five measures;
the knee should be four finger-breadths [in thickness], and the shank and thigh should be equal in proportion.
The height of the feet is prescribed as one-fourth of the [total] height;
thus, from the top of the crown (uṣṇīṣa) to the end of the hair at the back, it shall be six and a half aṅgulas.
From the crown of the head to the end of the hair on the side is recorded as eight finger-breadths;
from the crown of the head to the end of the hair in front is declared to be five finger-breadths.
The measurement from the hairline to the end of the bow, when divided by the [nine] qualities, is known as the space-portion (vyomāṃśa) from the hairline to the eye-line. (9)
O twice-born one, from the eye-socket thread to the edge of the eyelid, and likewise from the edge of the eyelid to the temple,
the distance between the two eyes is two finger-breadths plus one barley-corn.
The length of the eyebrows is equal to that [of the eyes], being the measure of one *bhūta*;
from the midpoint of the eyebrows to the end of the hair above is seventeen barley-corns (*yava*).
The width of the eyebrows at the midpoint is one *yava*, and they become gradually thinner toward the tips;
the width of the eyes is one-sixth [of the face], and the upper eyelid is half a *yava*.
The lower eyelid is equal to that; there should be a *karavīra* and a *yava*.
Having divided the length of the eye into three parts, one part is the black circle (*kṛṣṇamaṇḍala*).
In the center of the black circle, there is a circle of light the size of a barley grain; the gaze should be fixed upon the center of that circle of light, at the measure of a louse. (14)
One should specifically place the eye-thread situated below the armor;
between the two hairlines of that [face], the eyebrows are positioned like a half-moon. 15.
The location of the ear and its measurement is considered excellent when it is like ten *tāla*s;
the width of the root of the nose is declared to be one *yava*.
The width of the tip of the nose is declared to be one *aṅgula* of space;
the length of the lower lip is declared to be two *aṅgulas*.
Half of that is its width; the chin, however, is two barley-corns [in height].
One should know its width to be equal to that, and it should be depressed by half a barley-corn.
Therefore, from the base up to the end of the lower part, it is a single *yava* in height and consists of mere space;
however, its width at the root of the neck is declared to be eight *aṅgulas*.
The width of the top of the neck should be seven and a half finger-breadths,
while the width of the chest region should be thirty-seven units.
The length of the arm is declared to be twenty-five units; from that [point] down to the edge of the lower lip, there is a space of one *yava*. || 21 ||
The width at the base of the neck is declared to be eight aṅgulas,
while the length of the forearm is nineteen aṅgulas.
Therefore, that [measurement] from the middle finger to the tip [of the little finger] is twelve and a half mātrās;
half of that is the length of the palm, and the remainder is the measure of the middle finger.
The length of the thumb is recorded as eighteen barley-corns;
the length of the ring finger is said to be four and a half digits (aṅgulas). (24)
In the same manner, the length of the index finger is one yuga-part [four units] less than that of the little finger;
its width from the thumb onwards is six, eight, six, and five yavas respectively.
At its base, the remaining width is reduced by one-eighth;
at the tip, however, it is not expanded beyond one-fifth or one-fourth of the base width.
The length of the nails is declared to be one-quarter greater than their width;
the thumb shall have two joints, while the other fingers have three joints each. (27)
In the middle of the palm, it should have the appearance of a trident by means of three lines, or like the petals of a lotus;
at the base of the palm, there should be a thick [mark] in the center of the *kolaka*.
That which is reduced by one-eighth part is designated as "solid" (ghana).
It should be equal in length to the base (tala) and likewise equal to the width of that same base. || 29 ||
The width of the wrist (maṇibandha) is said to be three mātrās plus two yavas;
the width at the base of the forearm (prakoṣṭha-mūla) is declared to be four and a half aṃśas.
The width at the tip of the forearm is said to be six and a half [aṅgulas], while the breadth at the middle of the forearm is declared to be seven aṅgulas. (31)
The width of the base of the arm is declared to be eight *aṅgulas*; from the sūtra of the *hikkā* to the end of the armpit, it is declared to be eight measures (*mātras*).
The distance between the armpits is declared to be twenty-two finger-breadths;
the width up to the heart should be eighteen finger-breadths.
The width of the abdomen should be seventeen finger-breadths, and the width of the hip region should be eighteen finger-breadths. (34)
The width of the navel should be six barleycorns, and its depth should be two;
the width of the circle of the breasts is declared to be half a finger-breadth. || 35 ||
The nipple is said to be two barley-corns [in width], and its elevation should be equal to that;
the space between both breasts should be twelve and a half mātrās.
The length of the scrotum should be four parts, and its width should be equal to that;
the penis should be five finger-breadths in length, resembling a closed lotus bud.
The width of the hip region is eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) consisting of six barley-corns;
the breadth at the base of the thighs, however, is twelve and a half mātrās.
The width at the middle of the knees should be one and a half finger-breadths,
while the width at the base of the shanks is said to be six and a half finger-breadths.
The width of the shank should be four and a half finger-breadths;
the width of the forepart of the sole of the foot is said to be one Kauśika finger-breadth.
The width at the middle of the base is declared to be one *bhūta-aṅgula*,
while the length equal to the big toe is declared to be four *mātras*.
From its tip to the middle of the ankle, it measures twelve and a half finger-breadths (mātrās);
the length of the ring finger, however, should be thirty-three barley-corns (yavas).
The middle finger should be equal to that [the index], and the ring finger should be one-fourth of it;
the length of the little finger, however, should be three and a half fingers.
The width of the fingers, beginning with the little finger, is prescribed in sequence as seven, eight, nine, and thirteen *yavas*. (44)

The width is said to be equal to the height from the top to the base; when that is divided by three, two parts constitute the width of the nail (nakhavistāra), which is circular and as long as that [width].
From the tip of the palm to the base of the thumb, it should be one and a half finger-breadths;
at the base of the little finger, its thickness should be three barley-corns.
The distance from the axle to the heel is one part, and the height of the heel is equal to that;
the width of the rear circle is nine units less a quarter.
On the chest, O Vyāsa, it is twenty-five mātrās;
the distance between the armpits and on the back is twenty-four mātrās.
Whatever else has not been mentioned here is all of the highest quality, like the ten-span [measure].
Thus has their characteristic been described, with their forms as previously stated. (49)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Ten-Finger Span Measurement of the Lower Grade," in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*.
I shall describe the supreme nine-tāla measurement; listen with a one-pointed mind.
[Therein dwell] the Vasus, the eight-formed [Lord Śiva], the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas).
And other deities as well [should be made] according to the excellent nine-tāla measurement;
however, the body (bera) is divided into twelve hundred parts when measured by the human scale.

The *uṣṇīṣa* [should be] one part; the hairline (*keśānta*) is three finger-breadths (*guṇāṅgula*). From the hairline to the end of the eye-line is prescribed as four finger-breadths (*vedamātra*). (3)
Therefore, it is declared that from the eye to the corner of the eyelid, the measure is one Veda (four units);
from the corner of the eyelid to the bridge of the nose, a quarter of a Veda (one unit) is prescribed.
The measurement from the ear is one-fourth of a *veda* (one-eighth), extending to the heart;
from the heart to the limit of the navel is likewise twelve *mātrās*.
From the navel down to the base of the penis, it is prescribed to be one *bhānu* (twelve) units;
the length of the thighs is twenty-four units, and the knees are ten units with four parts (*aṃśaka*).
The length of the shanks and thighs should be equal, and the rise of the feet should be one-fourth [of that].
The length of the arms below the *hikkā* [should be] twenty-four parts.
The chamber (koṣṭha) should have eighteen parts, while its width at the base (tala) should consist of eleven parts;
the length of its middle finger-breadth is declared to be six parts.
The smallest [size] is declared to be ten tālas; one should perform the remaining [procedures] according to that path.
Therefore, one should indeed apply this to each limb, increasing it by half a barleycorn (yava).
Thus has measurement been fully explained; the defining characteristics were declared previously.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, concerning the procedure for the nine-fold supreme [mandala], in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*.
(p. 295) I shall now describe, in brief and in due order, the medium proportion of nine tālas for the hosts of yakṣas and apsarases, as well as for the weapon-forms and the groups of Maruts. || 1 ||
O best of the twice-born! The middle [image] should be made with nine tālas;
when the height of the Lord is divided into one hundred and eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas), it should be so fashioned.
The uṣṇīṣa is one part of the sky (the forehead); the hair is three parts minus a quarter;
from the end of the hair to the end of the eye-line is four parts less one barleycorn.
The end of the *puṭa* should be equal to that, and likewise it should extend to the jaw;
the measurement of the neck is declared to be three-quarters of a fourth part.

The portion from the navel to the heart is twelve finger-breadths (yavonas) long; that from the heart to the anus is equal to that, and likewise, that from the root of the penis to the end is equal to those.
Endowed with a quarter more than the [standard] proportions, the thigh should be one-twentieth longer;
its height should be equal to the knee and the neck, and the shank should be equal to the thigh.
The height of the sole should be equal to the knee, and it should be the same as the arms and thighs;
the length of the forearm is said to be seventeen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).

The length of the palm [of the hand] should be reduced by one-sixth and by the measure of a fire-grain (yava); the length of the middle finger should be equal to that, and the remainder should be executed with due skill.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, the section on the procedure for the intermediate *navatāla* [measurement], in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kāśyapa.
Now the characteristics of the lowest *navatāla* will be described;
it is for the hosts of Vidyādharas as well as for the Asuras. (1)

The Pitṛs, Siddhas, and Gandharvas [occupy the space] by the lowest of the nine proportions (navatāla); however, that hundredth part of the Veda is divided according to the height of the *kautuka*. || 2 ||
The uṣṇīṣa should be one-third higher [than the head], and the hair should be three and a half parts;
[this measurement] extends to the heart.
Therefore, it should not end at the navel; likewise, it should end at the base of the penis.
Its length is prescribed as twenty-three finger-breadths less one barley-corn.
The neck is equal in length to the soles of the feet; the shanks are similar to the thighs;
the forearms are as long as the thighs, and the wrists are sixteen finger-breadths in length.

The length of the base should be one part of the elements (five parts), and the middle finger should be equal to that; the remaining parts should be fashioned with due proportion, for thus all the limbs are prescribed.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, the section on the procedure for the binding of the Adhama-nava-tāla, in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*.

Now I shall specifically describe the supreme procedure for the eight-fold measurement (aṣṭatāla). Having made the height of the image one hundred parts, the uṣṇīṣa (the crown protrusion) is one part of Śiva.

The hairline (keśānta) shall be two and a half parts; from the hairline to the boundary of the bow (dhanus-sīmaka) shall be one-quarter less than eleven parts (pādonarudrabhāga); this [latter portion] shall be divided into three equal parts.
The portion of Śiva extends to the end of the thread of the [central] face and likewise to the end of the cavity; it is equal to that.
From the end of the cavity to the end of the *dhanvantara* is the remainder, which is one and a half fire-parts (three and a half units), the height of the neck.
From the throat down to the heart, it consists of two minus one parts of Rudra;
from there down to the navel it is equal to that, and likewise from there down to the base of the penis.
The length of the thigh is declared to be three hundred and fifty parts;
the knee should be as high as the ear, and the shank should be equal in length to the thigh. || 5 ||

The height of the surface of the knees should be equal to the length of the arms and thighs; the forearm (prakoṣṭha) should be one-sixteenth part [of the total height], and the palm (tala) should be five and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The middle finger should be equal to that; the rest is prescribed as before. It is said to be three or five finger-breadths in length, with the sole of the foot being as long as that.
Whatever has not been mentioned here is all of the smallest [category], like ten *tāla*s.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter on the procedure for the eight *tāla*s in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*. 62.
Now I shall specifically describe the supreme procedure for the seven-fold proportions (saptatāla).
The height of a Piśāca image should consist of eighty-eight parts.
The uṣṇīṣa is one half-part; the hairline is one part of the moon (one-sixteenth);
the end of the eyes is two and a half parts; and the corner of the eye-socket is three and a half parts.
Up to the chin it is equal to that; the portion for the neck's emergence is four parts (vedāṃśa);
up to the breasts it is seven parts (saptabhāga), and the limit of the navel is eleven parts (rudrāṃśa).
p. 298) Likewise, from the base of the womb to the end [of the thighs], it is twenty parts long;
the knee measures two parts, and the shank should be equal in length to the thigh. || 4 ||
The height of the feet is two parts; the length of the soles is sixteen parts (manu-aṃśa);
the length of the thighs is equal [to the height]; and the length of the forearms and wrists is fifteen parts (tri-pañcaka).
The length of the base should be one-fourth [of the total], and its width one-fifth;
the middle finger should be as long as the length of that base.
The remainder should be expanded according to what was previously stated;
this is declared to be the seven-fold *tāla*, while the rest is as described before.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, the section on the ritual for the seven palm trees, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of the *Kāśyapa*.

Now I shall explain in detail the supreme method for the comfortable posture (sukhāsana), which is characterized by rectitude and the quality of passion (rājasa); this is the comfortable posture on an auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha).
One should place the left foot upon the pedestal and let the right foot hang down;
above the upper body, it should extend by one and a half times four (six) finger-breadths.
This measurement up to the buttocks is specifically for the area above the seat;
from the seat upward to the hairline, and from the knees upward to the outer limit.
The outer [measurement] is from the knees to the hairline at the forehead, and from the knees to the tips of the forearms;
the inner [measurement] occurs between the two hands of another person. || 4 ||
(299) There is a new thread on the seat; now hear about the previous thread:
[it is located] in the middle of the crown, at the tip of the nose, at the end of the breasts, and in the middle of the navel.
One should hang the Brahma-sūtra from the middle of the left ankle;
from that sūtra to the right knee, it should measure thirty-one finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
Alternatively, the distance from the end of the thread to the ankle of the foot is twelve finger-breadths, whether it be thirty finger-breadths or twenty-nine.
The height from the pedestal to the heels of the feet should be thirteen finger-breadths or even fourteen finger-breadths; the fillet (nīvra) above them should be two or three finger-breadths.
O best of the twice-born! From that sūtra, ending at the middle line on the hand of Abhaya, the interval is said to be fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
In the *abhaya* [mudrā], the tips of the middle fingers should reach as far as the chin, remaining level above it;
from that line, the wrist joint should be at the center of the hand.
O best of the twice-born, the distance from the waist to the end of the hip-joint (maṇibandha) is said to be fifteen finger-breadths,
or it may be one, two, or three finger-breadths.
A bracelet or a *siṃhakarṇa* ornament is fashioned upon that hand;
[the fingers] from the forefinger (*tarjanī*) to the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) are made with their respective bases excluded.
The thumb should be slightly bent, thus forming the shape of a bracelet;
from the middle [of the hand] to the center of the palm, the ring finger should extend halfway to its tip.
The remaining fingers are curved as before; this is the supreme Siṃhakarṇa [mudrā].
One should make the two other hands equal to the line of the *hikkā* at the tip of the scissors.
In the *vakra* [mudrā], the ring finger and the thumb are curved, with their palms ending halfway;
the little finger is slightly bent, while the remaining two fingers are straight in the performance. (15)
In this manner, the carving with the chisel shall be executed, and the characteristic mark shall be exceedingly beautiful;
the elbow [should extend] from the hip and side by five, six, or seven mātrās.
One should touch the previous sūtra at the middle of the abdomen and at the tip of the nose;
from the base of the penis, the middle of the left ankle is six finger-breadths away.
Alternatively, it may be seven units or even five units;
from the center of the navel to the middle of the left foot, the distance is fourteen units.
Alternatively, it may be thirteen finger-breadths or even twelve finger-breadths;
the distance from the middle thread to the tip of the base is two finger-breadths, according to the measure of Manu.
The Lord, seated comfortably, straight-armed, reaching to the end of the thirteen [fingers] or exactly thirteen finger-breadths, is like a young coral sprout.
Three-eyed and with a serene countenance, he was endowed with the quality of passion (rajas);
he wore a tiger-skin garment and was likewise clothed in fine silk.
He holds two scissor-like weapons (kartarī) with his two outer hands, their faces turned inward; he places an axe in his right hand and a black [object] in his left, resting upon both hands.
On the right [hand] there is the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and on the left a bracelet like a lion’s ear;
specifically, one should place a conch-leaf ornament on the left ear.

It should be three, four, or five *maṇḍalas* in thickness, with six or seven *maṇḍalas* at the base; the thickness of the tube-like stem (*karṇanāla*) is likewise [three], while the width of the petals is triple that. (24)
Barley-corn-sized [gems] are said to be dense with leaves, white in luster, and extremely soft;
on the right side, there should be an earring shaped like a crocodile or indeed a lion. (25)
Having fashioned an earring that is three, four, or five finger-breadths in height and elevated at its center,
and having fixed the earring, one should place it upon the shoulder.
Alternatively, O Brahmin, one should place circular earrings upon the ears;
the width of these circular earrings should be eighteen yavas.
Its height should be four finger-breadths; one should fashion it as a water-pot, a lotus bud, or a blue lotus, or otherwise as something beautiful, provided with circular earrings.
O Brahmin, it should be joined with a crown of matted locks, possessing an even number of such locks;
the height of the crown should be twenty-four finger-breadths.
The height of the crown from the hairline should be either twenty-one finger-breadths or eighteen finger-breadths,
and it should be provided with a forehead-band.
O Brahmin, the crown should be similar in width to the face at its base and broad at the root;
its width at the tip should be less by one, seven, eight, nine, or ten parts.
The waist-belt, joined with four layers of skin and adorned with a face [of metal],
consists of three strands of thread, each as thick as a barley grain.
Above the junction of the hips, one should fasten a waistband made of animal skin,
five, six, or seven finger-breadths in width.
One should fashion [the pedestal] above the penis as high as its width;
the measurement from the waist-belt to the thighs should end at the middle third.

Within the great necklace of pearls, that which is joined with jewels in its interior is declared to be the waist-string (*kaṭisūtra*). Now hear about the bracelets and bangles (*kaṭaka* and *valaya*). (35)
O best of the twice-born!
A bracelet (valaya) is that which is worn on the wrist together with a bangle (kaṭaka), while a ring (valaya) is indeed that which has the circumference of the little finger. || 36 ||
Alternatively, one should place upon the forearm a thick bracelet, measuring two or three barley-corns in width, fashioned with segments of gems.
O twice-born one, having fashioned a bracelet of soft material or set with jewels, and having placed an armlet upon the upper arm that is thickly adorned with bracelets; (38)
The armlet, however, should be of a single form, joined with eight lotuses measuring one mātrā each,
adorned with various gems, or else having the appearance of aquatic moss.
O best of the twice-born! That which is joined with a leaf-filling [mark] on the middle of the arm, and whose leaf-filling stalk is thick like an armlet (keyūra), is so described. || 40 ||
That city is exceedingly lofty and adorned externally with three or two enclosures,
or it may extend for three, four, or five measures, filled with foliage.
That arm-band (bāhuvalaya) should have a height equal to one and a half times its width, or one and three-quarters times its width, or even twice its width. || 42 ||
Excluding the middle finger, the remaining fingers are provided with rings;
the ring is situated on the root joint, circular, and as thick as a barley grain.
The width of the waistband should be one, two, or three finger-breadths;
the thickness of the waistband should be one barley-corn or two barley-corns.
Adorned with various ornaments and variegated with diverse jewels, one should bind it above the navel, leaving out the portion corresponding to the belly. (45)
Other than the middle of the feet, [the fingers] are provided with their own finger-rings;
all [the fingers] are two barley-corns [in width], while the middles of the three-finger-widths [are one].
O best of the twice-born! His two feet are joined with webs below the ankles;
the webbing-band of the feet is as thick as two barley grains.
From that thread, the support for the lattice should be five and three *yavas* in measure;
the stalk from the lattice should be three *yavas*, and the remainder is indeed the height of the lattice.
That [portion] which is elevated and level has a width of one barley-corn (yava), while its thickness is the remainder;
or it may have the depth of that [width], or its thickness may be less than that depth.
The *vṛtta* (circular) type is firmly joined and provided with stone teeth;
that which is devoid of solid stone and measures half the height is called *nīvraka*.
The axe is said to be as long as a deer [in height] and twelve finger-breadths wide;
one should fashion the beauty of both the axe and the deer with skillful artistry.
It should be joined with the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), provided with eight parts thickened by barley,
consisting of three triple-strands, and equipped with a belly-string.
In this very way, the urusūtra (waist-thread) should be made of a single thick cord, even;
it is placed over the left shoulder at a distance of one finger-breadth below the navel.
The sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) should extend from the navel down to the right side; one should cause it to be placed resting against the back of the waistband.
Taking the chest-thread as a reference, it should be eight finger-breadths away from the breast;
thus the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be made. Now listen to the description of the channavīra.
Like the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), as before, having placed it upon both shoulders,
on both sides, and above the hips, one should hold it as a single strand between the breasts.

One should know the necklace (hāra) at the neck; six finger-breadths below the *hikkā* [the upper limit of the chest], having suspended it four finger-breadths [downward], the width (*tāra*) is three barley-corns and its thickness (*ghana*) is likewise.
Having fashioned an exceedingly beautiful necklace from various gems and gold,
one should fasten it around the neck, positioned above the line of the hiccup.
Whether it be a rudrākṣa, or a gem, or a golden circular jewel—this is known as the "upagrīva" (necklace). Now, the "hṛnmālā" (heart-garland) is being described.
One should fasten the rosary from the ear to the end of the waistband;
this is the heart-garland (hṛdayamālā), and it is likewise called the shoulder-garland (skandhamālā).
Upon the shoulder, however, there should be a garland of the aggregates (skandha-mālā) adorned with various flowers;
one should fashion the god, beautiful in all his limbs, and perform the remaining rites according to the prescribed method.
Thus has the comfortable posture been described, as well as that accompanied by Umā and Skanda.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Form of the Comfortable Posture" within the section on Aṃśumat in the Kāśyapa [Tantra].
Now, O twice-born one, I shall describe in detail the Lord Somāskandeśvara;
the deity is to be fashioned according to the prescribed method of the comfortable posture (sukhāsana).
On the left side of the God, however, one should place Pārvatī on a comfortable seat;
she should rest her right foot and let her left foot hang down. (2)
Above the seat, one should arrange a cushion measuring four finger-breadths in thickness,
aligned with the upper body.

The face is slightly tilted toward the deity, with a drooping expression characterized by a gentle smile; the left hand is in the boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā), while the right hand holds a blue lotus (utpala).
All [the fingers] are slightly curved and positioned above the palm of the left hand;
it is renowned as the Varada mudrā, resembling a lion’s ear when holding a flower.
The goddess has the luster of green grain, adorned with all ornaments;
the goddess wears red garments and is accompanied by the Channavīras.
Alternatively, O lady of beautiful thighs, I shall describe to you another method for the dissolution of the Goddess:
one should place [the syllables] from the outer seat (pīṭha) onto the palm of the left hand.
The right hand is said to be joined with the lotus as before;
the right knee is slightly raised from the seat.
The distance from the pedestal to the knees should be three, four, or five units;
or alternatively, the distance from the pedestal to the knees should be six, seven, or eight finger-breadths.
Thus, in these two ways, the measurement of the goddess is prescribed; however, the measurement of the goddess should be taken according to the path taught for the measurement of women. (10)
For the goddesses of the *sthānaka* positions, the goddess should be in the *sthānaka* position;
on the seat (*āsana*), it is known as the *āsana* position; otherwise, it brings about misfortune. (11)
(p. 306) The characteristics of the Goddess have already been stated; now the characteristics of Skanda are described.
One should install the image of Skanda between the Goddess and the Lord of Gods (Deveśa).
For the Goddess, the highest [measurement] ends at the conclusion of the hiccup;
the middlemost ends at the breasts; and the smallest would be between those two when divided by eight.

The measure of the *skanda* is ninefold; one should calculate the three triads beginning with the "excellent" (*uttama*) as either joined with the birth-portion (*jātyaṃśaka*) or even without it. (14)
When that measure is divided into six parts according to the Vedas, one part is known as an *aṅgula*; an eighth part of that shall be a *yava*.
The measurement of the head is one finger-breadth, and the hairline is equal to that;
the end of the eye-line is two parts, and the corner of the eye is equal to that. || 16 ||
The portion of the neck from the chin-limit is three finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula), while the height of the neck is also three finger-breadths;
the distance from the line of the hiccough to the end of the breasts is declared to be nine parts.
The distance from the end of the breasts to the boundary of the navel is declared to be eight *aṅgulas*;
from the left [breast] to the base of the penis, it is traditionally remembered as seven parts (*saptabhāga*).
The length of the thighs should be equal to that of the sun’s lineage (twelve *aṅgulas*); the knees should be two *aṅgulas* long;
the shanks should be equal in length to the thighs; and the middle part [of the body] should be joined with the soles of the feet.
The length of the sole of the foot is ten units, and the length of the forearm is fourteen;
the length of the torso is ten parts, while the sole is four finger-breadths in width.
The middle finger should be one-fourth of a yuga (four fingers) minus half a finger;
the ring finger is equal to that; the index finger should be as long as that; and the little finger should be three fingers in height.
The portion for the fire-altar (agni-aṃśa) should be the length of a thumb; the width of the palm should be four parts (yuga-aṃśa);
the tip of the forearm should be three parts (guṇa-aṃśa), while its base is four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula).
O best of the twice-born! The width of the base of the arm is five parts;
the width of the face is eight and a half parts; and the width of the ear is seven parts.
The internal width between the armpits should be thirteen finger-breadths; the width of the heart is twelve parts (dvādaśāṃśa), and the width at the middle is eleven parts (rudrāṃśa).
At the location of the hips, however, there is a solar (twelve) portion; at the location of the waist, thirteen;
and the width of the root of the thighs is declared to be eight finger-breadths.
The width of the knee is six parts; the base of the shank is four finger-breadths; the distance between the two shanks is three parts;
and the width of the sole is six parts.
The width of the heels should be one-eighth of the yoke; the remainder should be determined by skillful calculation.
At the hairline, it should be provided with a base and adorned with a crown-case and a diadem.
In both hands there should be a flower, or the left hand alone may display the *varada* (boon-granting) gesture;
or else, there should be a bracelet on that hand, or even a *siṃhakarṇa* (lion-ear) ornament.
His right hand holds a flower, or else a wood-apple or a mango fruit;
he is naked, yet possesses a waist-string and is endowed with the secret heroism.
Adorned with finger-rings, necklaces, and other ornaments for the young,
he may perform the dance while either sitting, standing, or moving about like Skanda.
When seated, one should place both feet upon the seat;
when standing, the two soles of the feet should remain as if evenly bent.
Both feet are slightly bent, as if in the act of walking;
if it is a dance, the left foot is well-positioned and joined with a curve.
Having lifted the other foot from the pedestal to a distance of seven finger-breadths,
one should raise it for six measures or up to five measures.
The left hand, resting upon a fruit, should be well-adorned with ornaments;
or else, having placed a fruit in the left hand, one should extend it outward.
Having drawn out the hikkā-sūtra as the upper limit from the maṇibandha,
one should perform the two-antar space and the hanging sūtra like the form of a dancing figure.
Listen to the description of Hara, who bears the moon and is accompanied by Umā and Skanda.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, concerning the characteristics of [the image of] Umāskandasahita, in the *Aṃśumat* of Kāśyapa.
Now, I shall describe in detail the characteristics of Candraśekhara.
The embrace with Gaurī alone may be of three kinds. || 1 ||
The God and the Goddess, who are innate and joined with Gaurī, embrace one another with a single hand. || 2 ||
This is known as the Umā-liṅga; thus it is said to be of three kinds:
either standing with feet together (kevala) or with feet apart (sahita). || 3 ||

The Liṅga of Candraśekhara is known to grant liberation when it is perfectly symmetrical (samabhaṅga), and it grants both [merit and liberation] when it is naturally formed (sahaja), whether slightly asymmetrical or even very asymmetrical (atibhaṅga). || 4 ||
(309) That [form] is the Linga, the embodiment of the Moon-bearer (Śiva), which bestows the fruits of all desires.
O observer of noble vows! First, hear about the standing posture (*sthānaka*) with feet even among those [postures]. || 5 ||
One should first of all determine the measurements of the image's height;
now, the measurement by suspension will be explained in due order.
The length of the broad face [of the stone] is forty-five digits;
its width is eighteen digits, or one and a half, or two digits thick.
Equipped with four legs, with the feet elevated and each joint raised,
and measuring twelve aṅgulas, one should place it upon level ground.
Having fixed the boundary-line upon the hanging plank,
one should stretch the measuring-line toward the east, the west, and both sides.
At its end, one should fashion a hollow space and then suspend threads;
O best of the twice-born, one should have the image made in accordance with those threads.
One should suspend [the lines] on the two eastern sides, at the back, and in the middle of the body;
these five lines are declared to be the Brahma-line.
One should hang two [lines] at the armpits and two at the corners of the mouth;
thus, the standing posture is endowed with nine lines on all sides.
In the center of the crown, from the middle of the forehead,
in the middle of the tip of the nose, and likewise in the middle of the jaw.
From the middle of the throat and the heart, from the very center of the navel, from the middle of the lingam and the thighs, and from within the soles of the feet; 14.
Having thus relied upon the previous sūtra, the subsequent one is now stated:
from the center of the crown and from the center of the back of the neck (kṛkaṭīkā). (15)

From the middle of the nape of the neck to the middle of the spine, likewise between the two buttocks, from the thighs to the knees, down to the ends of the calves, and likewise between the two heels. || 16 ||
In this way, one should fix the thread, for it must indeed be independent of anything else;
[it should extend] from the ends of the ear-lobes on both sides, as well as from the middle of the neck. (17)
Supporting the middle of the two arms, one should let [the cord] hang down to the middle of the ankles;
when it has reached the middle of the body, one should not let the five cords hang further.
One should suspend the thread from the interior of the ears, passing it through the center of the nipples,
and then let it hang down between the middle toes of the feet.
One should likewise suspend [the body] from the thighs, the knees, the ends of the shanks, between the two heels, the middle of the axle, the sides of the hips, and the middle of the hips.
From the first sūtra, the base, the tip, and the middle are said to be twelve mātras each;
from the second sūtra, however, the base, the tip, and the middle are said to be six mātras each.
From the previous sūtra, the distance to the forehead is two mātrās;
from the subsequent sūtra, the back of the head is three and a quarter finger-breadths.
From the previous sūtra, however, that [line] ending at the jaw is said to be two *yavas* and two parts;
whereas the subsequent sūtra from the nape of the neck is at an interval of three *aṅgulas* less one *yava*.
From the previous sūtra, however, the line ending at the hikkā is one finger-breadth inward;
from the sūtra below the kakudha, it is sixteen barley-corns apart.
From the center of the chest, the distance to the previous sūtra is two units, which is two mātrās;
from the middle of the shoulder, the distance to the subsequent sūtra is four and a half units. (25)
One should touch the previous line at the center of the belly; the other two lines should be equal to that.
The next line, following the slope of the beam, should be at an interval of one and three-quarter parts.
From the previous sūtra to the middle of the navel, the interval is one and a half mātrās;
at the back, level with the navel-sūtra, it shall be one and a half pakṣāṅgulas.
Prior to the thread, the distance ending at the base of the penis is declared to be nine finger-breadths;
on the other side, however, the interval from the thread is one and a half mātrās.
In the middle of the thighs, likewise in the middle of the knees, in the middle of the shanks, and in the middle of the lower legs, [the deity] is situated in front. || 29 ||
Having first determined the horizontal line, the internal distance is measured;
one should likewise lay down the horizontal lines at each of those respective positions and in the space beyond.
From the sūtra situated at the middle of the thighs, two finger-breadths (aṅgula) to the east [is the first mark];
right there, the end of the other sūtra is four finger-breadths minus one barley-corn (yava). || 31 ||
From the sūtra situated at the middle of the knees, six aṅgulas from the eastern sūtra,
and likewise from the end of the opposite sūtra, the foot is one-quarter [of the measure], not five mātrās.
The middle of the shank, measured from the previous line, is said to be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
from that same point to the end of the subsequent line, it shall be twenty-six barley-corns (yavas).
From the previous sūtra to the middle of the *nalaka* it shall be five and a half finger-breadths; from the *nalaka* to the end of the subsequent sūtra it shall be four and three-quarter measures.
The tip of the two thumbs [is measured] as one and a half [units] specifically from the previous line;
from that line to the edge of the heels, it is desired to be one and a half *manvaṃśas*.
From the previous sūtra, the sūtra situated in the middle of the body should be eighteen finger-breadths [long].
From that sūtra in the middle of the body, the back of the head is four finger-breadths [from the center]. (36)
From the middle of that body, however, the hump is two and a half finger-breadths;
at the region of the middle of the chest, it is six and a half finger-breadths on the back.
From the sūtra, the middle of the belly should be four and a half aṅgulas on the back;
at the region of the navel, however, it should be five and a half aṅgulas on the back.
The waistband (nīvra) at the hip should be six and a half [parts], and the edge of the buttocks should be eight and a half parts;
the middle of the thigh and the other [measurement] should be four [parts], as should the knee and the back.
The middle of the shank should be one-third of the [total] length, while the bone (nalaka) should be two finger-breadths;
both side-lines and the central line are situated along a straight line. || 40 ||
From the side-line forward to the end of the arm is four finger-breadths;
from that line to the end of the other arm is eight finger-breadths.
The forearms and middle sections [of the arms] should be joined up to the elbows;
the external width of those hands is desired to be four finger-breadths.
The tips of the hands of the other [person] should meet at the scissors;
the tips of the middle fingers of both should be level with the line of the breasts. || 43 ||

The right hand is said to be the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) mudrā, and the left the *varada* (boon-granting) mudrā. From the eastern sūtra, the middle of the *abhaya* hand is fifteen finger-breadths [from the center].
One should fashion the left hand as the Varada mudrā, facing downwards; its palm-base should touch the hip, and the hand should extend as far as the genitals. (45)
Grasping the tips of the middle fingers, the waistband of the thighs should be four finger-breadths [apart];
with the faces turned upward, the hands bestowing boons should be aligned so that the backs of the hands are level with the navel and the private parts.
From the middle of the palm of the hand granting boons (varada), one-sixteenth of an angula from all the sutras [is the mark];
the scissors (kartarī) should be at the wrist, and the arm should face outward.
Alternatively, the portion for Rudra is ten fingers, or even seven;
from the elbow to the end of the eastern line is sixteen or seventeen fingers.
It should be eighteen or nineteen finger-breadths [in width];
the distance between the two inner sides of the roots of the thighs is declared to be one finger-breadth.
The distance between the middle of the thighs is declared to be twenty barley-corns;
the distance between the knees is four mātrās, and that of the shanks is five mātrās.
The distance between the ankles is six parts; the distance between the two heels is one part of the elements (five parts);
the distance between the two heels is four mātrās; and the distance between the soles of the feet is six parts.
O best of the twice-born! One should thus fashion the straight posture known as Rājasambhava, wherein the distance between the tips of the two big toes is eight finger-breadths.

[He should meditate on] the Lord who holds two scissor-like hands, is endowed with a crown of matted hair, or has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel; he resembles coral, possesses three eyes, has a gentle countenance, and is adorned with all ornaments. (54)
The god wears yellow garments; on both sides, at the ends of the cloth, are Nala and Kāntaka. Thus, the garment reaches as far as the middle of the thighs. (55)
For it has been declared that [the deity] alone is thus described as being accompanied by Gaurī on the left;
that is known as being together with Gaurī, or else as a single distinct seat (pīṭha).
In that very same [posture], joined with the *bhaṅga* (bend), the Goddess and the God face each other;
the God, with his hand granting boons, embraces the Goddess who leans upon him from the outside.
Make the left side embrace the space between the breast and the navel;
or alternatively, let the left arm embrace from beyond the line of the side.
The Goddess, with her right hand,
touched the flower held in her left hand above the waist-cord on the right side of Śambhu.
Alternatively, as before, the Lord of Gods holds a red lotus in his right hand while the left hand is allowed to hang down beside the Goddess.
In this manner, one should conceive the form of the embrace in three ways according to the path,
endowed with all ornaments and accompanied by a halo of light.
Now hear the description of the form known as Candraśekhara, who is mounted upon a bull.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, the section on the characteristics of the Candraśekhara form, in the Aṃśumat-kāśyapa [treatise].
Now, the characteristics of the form whose vehicle is the bull shall be described.
The best of those skilled in ritual procedures should fashion it with either a slight bend or an even bend.
The right foot is well-placed, while the left foot is drawn up;
likewise, [the hands] are at the center of the crown on the left and at the forehead on the left.
At the end of the left eye, at the interior of the left nostril,
on the right side of the breast-base, and in the middle of the left navel.
One should hang a thread from the middle of the left thigh to the middle of the two heels;
in this way, there will be an equal bend, and that measurement is not four finger-breadths.
In the mouth it is as previously indicated; likewise, [it is] on the right breast;
on the left side of the navel in the portion of the qualities (guṇāṃśa), and likewise in the middle of the left thigh.
When the feet are well-placed, one should let the Brahma-sūtra hang down from the ankle;
this is known as the "excessive bend" (atibhaṅga), and it should not be five finger-breadths [from the ground].
O Brahmin, one should place the left upper arm above the head of the bull,
at a distance of nine times two (eighteen) finger-breadths below the line of the *hikkā*.
Hanging from the left elbow, it reaches as far as the boundary of the seat;
this is known as the rising of the bull, and the bull should be fashioned according to its characteristics.
On the head of the bull, one should make a mark with the hands at the limit of the tips of the middle fingers,
level with the line of the navel, or otherwise, one finger-breadth above or below that.
From the center of that palm, two lines for Yama should be drawn facing downward; one should then extend that hand forward.
On the right, at the front hand, the wise one [should fashion] a bend from the heel down to below the navel,
measuring sixteen *mātrās*, shaped like a lion’s ear.
One should fashion a curved staff-weapon upon that [body], moving and unsteady;
it should extend from the standing foot and knee upward to the limit of the boundary, elevated as far as the end of the *hikkā*-sūtra.
The circumference at the base of the handle should be equal to that of the little finger, and it should be curved at the tip;
one should have it made either of metal or wood with a curved shaft.
The distance from the wrist of that hand to the root of the thigh should be five,
six, or seven *mātrās*, or eight or nine fingers (*aṅgulas*).
He should hold a chisel and a black antelope in his two hands;
the chisel is in the right hand, while the antelope is in the left hand.
The tips of both hands should be level with the line of the *hikkā*;
they may be bent by one, two, three, four, or five *mātrās*.
He may be depicted with a crown of matted hair, or with a charming mass of matted locks;
or he may be shown wearing a bound coil of matted hair, according to the desire of the artist.
Adorned with all ornaments, having a reddish luster, and wearing red garments;
on his left side is the goddess Umā, and especially on the right.
The right foot is firmly planted while the left foot is drawn up;
the right hand holds a lotus, and the left hand is extended. (19)
One should have the goddess Umā fashioned according to the procedure prescribed for a woman;
her vehicle is said to be a bull, and her dancing form is now described.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter in the *Aṃśumat*, titled "The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Bull-riding Form of Kāśyapa."
Now I shall specifically describe the characteristics of the Dancing Form (Nṛttamūrti);
for the purpose of subduing [the demon] Ruru, she became Carmamuṇḍinī.
Having made the killing of the ruru deer their sustenance, they were then considered to be of the same rank as themselves;
for then the gods, eager for non-violence, acted for the sake of the cessation of that suffering.
Then indeed I shall perform a dance for the welfare of all the worlds,
for the destruction of the afflictions of the gods, and for the increase of the king and his kingdom.

O best of the twice-born! First, the ninefold division of the dance consisting of eight hundred types is declared; the measurement of the image should be taken according to the previously stated rule.

One should fashion the entire body according to the ten-tāla measurement for the highest [class]; the height, including the bowing during dance, should be one-tenth of the [total] parts of the sun (twelve) and Rudra (eleven).
From the center of the crown, lead [the breath] to the left forehead, then to the middle of the right;
having reached the auspicious finger-breadth on the left, it reaches the edge of the eye and the corner of the eyelid.
She resides on the left side of the heart, in the region of the hiccups, in the center of the navel,
within the interior of the left thigh, and in the middle of the ankle.
From the center of the circle of light, one should hang the eastern thread;
from the forehead, the thread-measure should be four parts minus half.
p. 318) And in the same manner, the interval of the thread from the ankle is prescribed;
from the middle of the *hikkā*, however, the end of the thread is seven and a half [or] eight finger-breadths.
The crown [should extend] from the tip of the wing by eight and a half parts;
likewise, the upper belly should touch the eastern line—one should arrange it in this manner.
From that sūtra, the end of the swinging arm (ḍolabāhu) is one and a half kalās and aṅgulas;
from that, the end of the other arm is declared to be four aṅgulas.
Therefore, [the measurement] from the fire [altar] to the tip of the hand should be thirty-eight fingers, or forty fingers; from that, the first [section] should be three fingers wide.
Having extracted it from the Hikkā-sūtra, one should place it at the tip of the middle finger of that hand,
or in the middle of the palm of that hand, or on the joint at the tip of the middle finger.
Having placed the fire, either in the middle of a joint or within a vessel, or even without a vessel,
the fire should be five parts in extent and provided with a width.
One should fashion the height of the tongue as seven, eight, nine, or even five, three, or seven finger-breadths, according to what is appropriate.
One should apply the measurements in sequence on the left side: either twenty-eight units, or thirty finger-breadths, or forty units. (16)
In that [hand], above the wrist, it should be level with the line of the hiccups;
in the ḍamaruka [drum], it is raised from the middle pedestal up to the tip of the needle-ear.
The tip of the index finger should be pure, and the index finger should remain straight;
alternatively, a leather strap may be pressed upon the middle finger.
Above the ring finger, one should imagine a hand-drum (ḍamaruka);
its length and width should likewise be eight and five finger-breadths respectively. (19)
