One should fashion the middle part in the shape of a lotus, with a width of one guṇāṅgula,
joined by two rings and bound with a thread of armor.
One should fashion the image with the same material as that used for the original object.
From the tip of the needle to the boundary of the ear, it measures forty units.
Fifty-five, twenty-eight, and likewise three;
the needle should be equal to the side-line, and your middle finger shall be the measure for the fire-altar.
On the right, one should fashion the first hand in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*);
from the eastern line, the middle of the *abhaya* hand is two finger-breadths [from] the sun.
The tip of the middle finger from that [point] is raised along the line of the *hikkā*;
from the end of that line to the elbow (*korpara*) is the *nīvra*, measuring exactly forty [aṅgulas].
In the *abhaya* [mudrā], the preceptor should place a serpent-bracelet in the middle of the forearm; he should then apply one-quarter of the circumference of that middle of the forearm. (25)
This very [object] described above should have a hood five fingers long;
it should be seven fingers in width and one finger in thickness.
The best of those who know the ritual procedures should fashion a serpent-bracelet, complete with a tongue and provided with a hood, positioned in front.
From the string, the space between the armpits on the left side is twelve finger-breadths;
from the string, the middle of the belly on the left is declared to be nine finger-breadths.
On the left side, the distance from the suture line to the fleshy part of the hip is eighteen finger-breadths;
the distance from the suture line to the bent knee is ten finger-breadths. (29)
One should fashion the measurement of the knee-bend (natabhāga) according to the sequence of nine, eight,
and ten finger-breadths, using the measurement of the bow.
One should arrange the left foot so that its heel rests upon the knees of the standing feet;
the distance between the two ankles should be three, five, or eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in three ways.
The wise one should measure from the middle of the ankle-bone of the standing foot to the inner side of the left heel;
that is prescribed as forty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
It should be forty-six, forty-five, or forty-four finger-breadths;
when standing with knees raised, it should measure twenty-four units from the heels.
The distance between the heels is thirty-three finger-breadths;
the distance from the raised sole of the foot to the top of the standing knee is likewise the same.
When the feet are raised above the knees, they should be level with the line of the navel;
for one whose hands are extended in the *aḍḍola* posture from the elbows, [the hands] are ten finger-breadths from the line of the navel.
Alternatively, one may fashion it to extend eleven finger-breadths to the end of the elbow;
that hand [should reach] from the wrist to the space between the left knee and the [other] knee.
It should be made ten finger-breadths long, or even nine finger-breadths;
however, in the case of a swing-hand, it should specifically end at the tip of the middle finger.

On the left foot, up to the end of the calf, the space between [the feet] should be merely a *dharma* (one finger-breadth), or nine finger-breadths, or even eleven finger-breadths (*rudrāṅgula*). || 38 ||
With a hand-held swing (*ḍola*), one should end in fear; the interval between the two [hands] should be ten finger-breadths (*daśāṅgula*).
Other methods have been taught for the *nīvrās*; one should perform them according to their beauty. (39)
From the hairline to the edge of the Bakapakṣa [mark], it should be eighteen aṅgulas high, or seventeen aṅgulas, or even sixteen aṅgulas. || 40 ||
Its width should indeed be half or three-quarters of that;
it has a mass of matted hair well-spread out, and five or seven *nandaka* [units] in length.
Or, O Brahmin, there may be eleven Rudras on both sides;
beginning from thirty-two finger-breadths, it extends up to sixty-one finger-breadths.
The length of the matted hair is said to increase by one finger-breadth at a time;
thus, the length of the matted hair below is likewise [measured], and from there it extends higher and higher toward the top of the head.
The circumference of the matted locks is said to be equal to that of the little finger;
one should especially adorn the spaces between the locks with flower garlands.
Nāga, arkapuṣpa, and likewise dhurdhūraka flower; hasita, śīrṣaka, karoṭī, and ratnabandhana. || 45 ||
Having adorned the southern [side] with Marut, he should worship the one who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
whose Skanda is decorated with vermilion, and who is adorned with rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.
His divine limbs were smeared with ashes, his face was slightly smiling,
he was endowed with a sacred thread and possessed a large waist-string.
O twice-born one, [the line] on the left side, extending halfway out from the middle of the belly or the chest,
rests upon the halo and reaches the front of the waistband.
O best of the twice-born! Having fastened the tiger skin above the swinging arms, it reaches down to the end of the three parts of the thighs, being covered by the tiger-skin garment. (49)
O best of the twice-born! The support should be at the base of the arm, extending one cubit or a span, or half of that, or three-quarters of that in width.
The feet were joined with anklets and adorned with all ornaments;
all the fingers of the hands and feet were graced with rings of jewels and gold.
Excluding the middle finger, the remaining fingers are indeed held in the form of a ring;
the right foot is bent and placed upon the other.
Having placed the sole of the foot obliquely, one should perform the dance of Maheśvara;
having lifted the left sole of the foot, the right arm follows obliquely.
Then, having raised the hand with the *ḍola* [gesture], *apasmāra* (the seizure demon) is described;
the length of *apasmāra* consists of three, four, or five faces. (54)
Or, let the arising of the epilepsy [portion] be forty-eight parts;
the uṣṇīṣa shall be one part, and the hairline (keśānta) shall likewise be so.

The length of the face should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas), the neck half a finger-breadth, and the width of the ears one and a half finger-breadths; the remainder [is for the other parts]. || 56 ||
From the *hikkā* (the glottis) down to the heart, it is declared to be one *rasāṅgula* (six finger-breadths);
from the heart down to the navel, it is likewise proclaimed to be of that same measure.
The measurement from the navel to the base of the genitals is said to be six units;
the length of the thigh is seven parts, and the length of the knee is two finger-breadths.

The shank should be equal to the long thigh; the emergence of the foot consists of two parts. The forearm consists of fourteen parts, extending from the navel to the limit of the tip of the middle finger. (59)

The remainder should be performed according to the prescribed method; one should lie down facing downwards, placing the head toward the left [north] of Śambhu and the feet extended toward the right [south].
Apasmāra, Udara, and Ucca, however, consist of eight *dharmanandās*;
having raised their faces, they are filled with joy and the playful grace of serpents. (61)
O best of the twice-born! He held a serpent in his left hand, while on his right was a ring; he had the appearance of a dark-green grain, and he was possessed by epilepsy.
The height of the lotus pedestal (padmapīṭha) shall be one-sixteenth part [of the total], and its width shall be four times that;
its length shall be one and a quarter, one and a half, or double that [width].
The upper lotus and the lower lotus with its pedestal are as described in the characteristics;
it is fashioned according to this procedure, complete with a circle of light.
Starting from one *guṇāṅgula* up to a limit of one hundred *aṅgulas*,
the rise of the sun [of breath] occurs at an increase of half an *aṅgula* for each [stage], up to eight *nadīs*.
Starting from one finger-breadth and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time,
the cube of the number as previously described is known for the first staff.
Each successive [measurement] above is diminished by one-eighth;
[the lengths are] one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten [units]. 67.
Again and again, one should likewise arrange the numbers in ascending order;
and among those, you must certainly determine the number of staves by means of the scissors.
Adorned with various creeping plants and beautified by diverse flowers, above that [tree] is Anala, whose form is like fire in his hand. (69)
O Brahmin, one should perform [the visualization] all around, equal to that, extending to the intermediate directions;
the wise one [should visualize him] as being within a circle of light, fixed within a solar orb.
On his left, perform the worship of Goddess Umā according to the previously mentioned procedure;
this shall be the first dance, which brings welfare to all the worlds.
That very [stream] becomes the Jāhnavī at the tip of the matted locks on the right side;
it is sixteen finger-breadths high, measured by the finger-breadth of Śambhu’s own body.
Endowed with the limbs described for women and with palms joined at the heart,
she likewise performed the second dance accompanied by the Jāhnavī.
That same left foot is placed upon the one suffering from epilepsy;
the right foot is raised, and the left hand is extended. (74)
From the middle of the forehead to the left nostril, one should extend the Brahma-thread, which reaches down to the ankle of the foot. (75)
The remainder should be performed as before, and likewise the third dance;
[the deity] has a mass of matted hair well-spread, joined with a crown of matted locks.
Endowed with a circle of matted locks, the remainder is as in the first dance;
for this fourth dance brings benefit to all living beings. (77)
One should raise the right foot up to the height of the sun above the uṣṇīṣa;
the left foot, however, should be placed upon the person suffering from epilepsy, pointing toward one's own mouth.
Endowed with eight arms, this is called the pentad: [he holds] the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a trident, and a noose in his right hands; [and] a *ḍamaru* drum [in the left]. (79)
The skull is the vessel for the fire, and the bell is like an elephant’s trunk;
one should extend the right hand, which resembles an elephant’s trunk. (80)
Just as one would extend the initial cord for the first dance, so too is it known that the mark for the fifth dance is established in exactly the same way. (81)
He is endowed with sixteen arms and accompanied by Gaurī on his left;
holding [the child] upon his shoulder, he has his hands joined in *añjali* in his left hand.
Then Skanda, with his hands joined in reverence at the waist until the end of the hiccup, respectfully held his chin and breast with two terrifying hands.

Thus, having beheld the Lord, Gaurī spoke with these words, her two hands displaying the gestures of fearlessness, the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), the thunderbolt (vajra), and likewise the trident (śūla). (84)
Likewise, he holds a noose and a staff in his right hands, as well as a serpent;
and with the secondary left hands, he holds a basket, a vetāla, and a rosary for recitation.
The sword, the mirror, the bracelet,
and the banner, as well as the bell and the skull, are held in the eight left hands.
The fifth [type] of dance is performed with the foot; the sixth is likewise described in this manner. Listen to the seventh, O observer of good vows! (87)
He has three eyes and eight arms, with well-spread matted locks;
his left foot is drawn up as he stands upon an epileptic. 88.
On his left side is his head, and on the right, his foot is well-spread;
the right foot is raised, with the big toe reaching as far as the limit of the top of the calf. (89)
According to the previous sūtra, however, the nīvrāṅga should be twelve finger-breadths;
[he holds] the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a trident, a noose, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in his right hands.
In the left [hands], he holds a skull-cup, a fire-vessel, and likewise a hand in a gesture of wonder; the fourth is indeed just like an elephant's trunk. 91.
With a hand resembling an elephant’s trunk, following either the right or the left,
[one should move] from the middle of the forehead to the middle of the breast on the left.
One should let the Brahma-sūtra hang down to the middle of the ankle of the left foot;
from that sūtra, the nīvi (the lower edge of the garment) should be nine aṅgulas above the left knee.
The tenth part shall be the *natamāna*; on the left, it is joined with Gaurī.
This is declared to be the seventh dance, which destroys the afflictions of the world.
That very [deity], endowed with six arms, likewise holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and a hand-drum (ḍamaru);
on the right side, however, he holds a trident (śūla), a skull-cup (kapāla), and likewise a gesture of wonder (vismaya). || 95 ||
The thread on the left, resembling an elephant's trunk, consists of the eight [beads] previously mentioned;
now hear, O observer of good vows, about the sixth [thread] of the fifth dance.
Two [of these] are renowned as having two eyes, while the remaining three have one eye each;
they are four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with a crown of matted hair. (97)
In the right [hands] he holds the *abhaya* mudrā and the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), while in the left [hands] he holds [the trident] like the trunk of a fire-elephant;
with the exception of the epilepsy (Apasmāra), his left foot remains bent upon the seat.
(327) With the little toe of the right foot placed upon the seat directly in front of each [mark], one should skillfully bend that foot and, using a thread, skillfully suspend it. 99.
The ninth dance has been described; after this follows the opinion of Gaṅgādhara.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*, concerning the characteristics of the forms of dance.
O you of noble vows, listen as I shall briefly describe Gaṅgādharasana:
the right foot is firmly planted and the left foot is drawn up.
Having led [the breath] from the center of the forehead to the left for the distance of nine barley grains, and likewise to the limit of the right eye and to the end of the left nostril; || 2 ||
Having focused evenly between the eyebrows, two finger-breadths to the right of the navel, and at the end of two finger-breadths from the middle of the base of the penis on the right; || 3 ||
One should hang the Brahma-sūtra from the middle of the two heels;
its bending measure is four parts, while it rises to the level of both big toes.
It is said to be eighteen finger-breadths long, with the two heels elevated by one-third [of that length];
it should have a loose joint and a braided topknot, while the face on the left side is slightly inclined downward.
On the right, let your first hand rest upon the face of the Goddess Varadā;
on the left, embrace the Goddess with your first hand.
On the right, he raises his hand up to the top of his turban, joined with matted locks and the Ganges; on the left, he holds a black antelope.
On the left side of the God is Gaurī, with a beautiful face;
her left foot is well-placed while the right one is bent. (8)
The one most skilled in ritual procedures should fashion the bent thread with a curved break;
having extended the right hand, the left hand should hold a flower.
Alternatively, the right forearm may extend horizontally below the hip,
its form appearing like a piece of cloth being held up.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with every kind of jewelry,
the Lord, whose desires are fulfilled by sages, appeared profound on his right side.
[One should worship] the god Gaṅgādhara Hara, and then indeed Tripurāntaka.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*, concerning the characteristics of the form of Gaṅgādhara.
Now, the characteristics of the form of Tripurāntaka shall be described.
The measure of the bow should be three, four, and five units respectively. || 1 ||

One should determine the measurement of the break (bhaṅga) as threefold: slightly broken (ābhaṅga), evenly broken (samabhaṅga), and excessively broken (atibhaṅga); indeed, one should fashion the break so that it is bent at each joint and elevated.
The distance between the two big toes should be sixteen finger-breadths;
one should know that when there is a bend it is eighteen finger-breadths, while when straight it is equal [to sixteen]. || 3 ||
It is declared that there are three types of excessive bending (atibhaṅga), each measuring twenty finger-breadths;
the distance between the two heels should be one-third of that measure.

(329) Having grasped [the breath] on the left side of the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), at the corner of the eye, at the edge of its lid, on the left side of the jaw, and on the left side of the right breast. (5)
On the right side of the navel is Vāmoru, on the left side is Savyapārśvaka;
on the heel of the right foot, one should cause Lambaya to be situated on the left side.
The sūtra for uneven curvature has been explained; now hear that for even curvature:
[the line from] the forehead, through the tip of the middle of the nose, to the middle of the heels of the feet. (7)
One should hang the eastern thread; now I shall describe the interval:
on the left side of that thread, the center of the *hikkā* is one *śivāṅgula*.
Half a finger-breadth to the left of that line is the center of the heart;
two finger-breadths to the right of that line is the center of the navel.
From that same line, to the south, the tip [of the mark] is likewise at a distance of four finger-breadths (yuga-aṅgula);
from that line, the distance to the left knee is twelve barley-corns (yava).
This is known as the "equal break"; now hear about the "excessive break":
from the crown of the head, on the left side, at the edge of the eye, and within its fold. (11)
From the middle of the right breast, that thread extends for three finger-breadths;
from the middle of the navel, on the left side, the end of the thread is two finger-breadths away.
From that same thread, the middle line is established reaching to the left knee;
one should then hang the side-thread from the heel of the left foot to the right side.
One should not cause the touching, the entering, the thatch, or the standing with feet together to be mixed in this way within the lines of the three-fold bends (tribhaṅga). || 14 ||
For the form of Tripurāntaka, the one with excessive bending is considered superior, that with even bending is middling, and that without bending is known as inferior. (15)
The right foot is well-placed and the left foot is bent;
the right hand is raised above, reaching down to the level of the navel-sūtra.
The lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa) should be at that [same] distance from the hand, with the middle of the palm pressed;
the span of the arrow (bāṇāyāma) is prescribed as twenty-seven finger-breadths.
The circumference of the hand of the Lord of Gods should be equal to the span of the little finger;
the mouth should have a width of five fingers, be one mātrā in height, and its height should correspond to its width.
The tail is equal in height to the mouth and extends one finger-breadth beyond it;
holding a bow in the left hand, the tip of that hand reaches up to the armpit. (19)
Its eye-socket should be one, two, three, or even four finger-breadths;
it should be twenty finger-breadths in height, and three, five, seven, or nine finger-breadths [in width].
The weapon of the bow is of nine types, either inferior or superior;
however, it should not have a full grip, being gradually thinner from the middle toward the tip.
Its width at the top and middle should be one finger-breadth, circular, and variegated with colors;
its thickness should be one-third of that of an arrow, while the thickness of the cord should be that of a thread.
In the case of a bow, however, the length of the cord is one-seventh of its single long dimension;
that which conforms to the length of the bow is declared to be its curvature. (23)
Alternatively, it may be provided with three bends and resemble the crescent moon;
it may also be shaped like a bow, and it may be made either of metal or of wood. (24)
The Kartarī [form] has two hands in the position of another; it is endowed with a chisel and a black deer.
A chisel is held in the right hand, while a deer is held in the left hand. (25)
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and decorated with all ornaments, he has a complexion like coral and is accompanied by Gaurī on his left side. (26)
Now, this is first of all the defining characteristic of the form of Tripurāntaka:
that very left foot is positioned upon an epileptic seizure (apasmāra).
The remainder should be performed as before; this shall be the second characteristic. The left foot should be well-placed, while the right should be bent. || 28 ||
The remainder is to be performed as before; the sūtra for the side of the funeral pyre is thus described.
This is declared to be the third characteristic; now hear the fourth characteristic.
That same left foot, however, is positioned upon Apasmāra;
the fourth characteristic is indeed the specific distinction as previously described.
On the wrist, at the base of the hand that holds the arrow, the middle line should be one-sixteenth of a finger,
or one-fifteenth, or one-fourteenth, or even thirteen fingers [in length].
Alternatively, the distance may be twelve or eleven fingers; thus the interval becomes sixfold.
In that hand, the elbow, the shoulder, and likewise the side of the hip should be positioned.
From the armpit to the wrist in the hand of one holding a bow, and likewise from that hand to the elbow, [the measurement] up to the heart is declared. (33)
Whether it be one, two, three, four, or five measures, or even less than that;
I have thus described the common interval for all [the notes]. || 34 ||
(332) Those same two forearms are placed as bracelets at the boundary of the heart;
the left and right hands are positioned respectively facing upward and downward. (35)
The left hand holds the base of an arrow, while the right hand raises a bow;
in the other right hand there is a chisel, and likewise a bow in the left.
In his hand, however, he holds a deer, or else on the left side, accompanied by Gaurī;
with the exception of Apasmāra, the foot is bent and the cord is as before. (37)
Thus, the embodied form may be fivefold, endowed with four arms;
or it may be provided with eight hands, characterized by extreme flexibility.
In his right hands, he holds an arrow, an axe, a sword, and the gesture of granting fearlessness;
likewise, in his left hands, he holds a bow, a hand of wonder, a shield, and a bracelet.
It is declared that [the measurement] from the previous sūtra to the end of the hand is to be placed in the left hand;
one should fashion it so that it is beautiful and prominent, or joined with Gaurī.
Thus the sixth [form] has been fully described; the seventh is endowed with ten arms, holding an arrow, a discus, a trident, an axe, and a thunderbolt in the right hands.
Likewise, the bow, the conch, the needle, the marvel, and the shield are declared to be in the five left hands; and above them is the Atibhaṅga mudrā.
One should cause that very right knee to be placed beneath the chariot; then, having placed the sole of the left foot upon the chariot as before, [one should proceed]. || 43 ||
The chariot, however, was provided with a *mukula* (a protective covering), and that *mukula* was enclosed by a cord;
within the *mukula* was Brahmā, four-faced and four-armed.
In his two right hands he holds a bamboo staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*),
and in his two left hands he holds a small vessel (*kuṇḍikā*) and a lotus-noose.
The one most skilled in ritual procedures should fashion a white-colored bull beneath the front of the chariot, as the chariot enters its path.
O best of the twice-born! That which is called Tripurāntaka is said to have eight divisions;
its color is like coral, and it is characterized by the qualities of rajas and sattva.
Adorned with all ornaments, having one face and three eyes,
fashion the goddess Umā to his left according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the form of the Destroyer of Tripura, in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*.
Now, the characteristics of the auspicious form (kalyāṇamūrti) shall be described:
from the middle of the forehead to the end of the left eye.
One should suspend it at the end of the left nostril and in the middle of the hiccup;
or, from the center of the navel, one *aṅgula* to the right of the deity-fire.
Having led [the cord] from the ankle to the middle of the heel, one should hang the thread; the inner measurement-thread should be such that it forms an even bend.
The left foot should be firmly planted while the right is bent;
the right hand should hold the hand of Gaurī.
The left hand is in the boon-granting gesture (*varada*), while the two other hands are extended;
in the right [of these] is held an axe, and in the other left hand is held a black antelope.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and decorated with all ornaments,
the god has the luster of excellent coral, especially as the Lord of the Gods.
The goddess, resembling the dark-green hue of a grain crop, is endowed with the same proportions and other attributes as before;
she holds a blue lotus in her left hand, while her right hand [is extended].
Taking hold of Śambhu’s hand while leaning for support on the water,
Śrī-Bhūmi, adorned with all her ornaments, followed after Pārvatī.
O twice-born one, Prajāpati should touch these two with his hands at Gaurī’s waist;
he should then perform the rite of Homa in a sacrificial pit before the deity.
The wise one should [visualize] the rising of Brahmā at the boundary of Śambhu’s breast—
four-armed, four-faced, and adorned with all ornaments.
In his left hands, he holds a water-pot and a rosary;
in his right hands, he holds a *sruk* and a *sruva* ladle respectively.
Sitting upon a lotus throne facing north, Prajāpati [is seated];
O Goddess, the two lords of gods have their heads directed eastward, and the Goddess is to the right of the God.
Viṣṇu faces south, while the northern direction is assigned to the oblation (homa).
For Śambhu, the area up to the edge of the mouth is excellent, whereas that ending at the nipples is inferior.
Between those two, with an eighth part [of the space], the manifestation of Keśava is ninefold;
he is dark-complexioned, with a symmetrical posture, and holds a conch and a discus in his other hands.
Having taken water with a golden vessel, one should offer it, preceded by water, into the two hands of the donor, which are positioned as palms facing upward. (15)
I give this Gaurī, who has arisen from the primordial lineage, to that Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who has arisen from the beginningless lineage. || 16 ||
Having spoken thus, Hari devotedly offered water into the hand of the Granter of Boons;
[so too did] the lords of the eight worlds, the lords of knowledge, and the hosts of Siddhas, Yakṣas, and others.
The sages, the Gandharvas, the Mothers, and other deities, endowed with their respective powers, joined their palms at their hearts. || 18 ||
Filled with bewildered minds, they stood looking all around at the auspicious form [of Śiva] as Ardhanārīśvara.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*, titled "The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Auspicious and Beautiful Form."
Now, O observer of noble vows, listen as I describe the form of Ardhanārīśvara;
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds: four-armed and two-armed. (1)
In the posture called *samabhaṅga*, according to the very path already described,
the right foot is well-placed and extended, while the left foot is bent.
The left half is joined with Pārvatī and the right half is Maheśvara;
holding the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and an axe in the right hand, that is a portion of Śiva.
With the forearm resting upon the head of the bull, the left hand [is placed there];
on the other left hand, however, is a bracelet adorned with flowers. (4)
She has two arms; the right hand displays the gesture of granting boons, while the left hand holds a flower.
She wears the ornaments of Śiva on her right side, and is adorned with feminine jewelry on her left.
For a man, the breast is on the right side; for a woman, it is the breast on the left.
Alternatively, the left foot may be drawn up while the right foot remains well-placed.
The right hand should hold a trident and the left hand should hold a flower;
the right hand should be in the boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā), while the other [left] hand rests upon the head and shoulder of a bull.
A skull [should be held] in the right hand, while the left hand is extended;
there should be a fierce gaze on the right side, but a cool [gentle] one on the left side.
The *dukūla* garment reaches to the middle of the thighs; one [leg] extends to the left ankle and the other likewise.
Thus has the form of Hara as Ardhanārīśvara been described in brief. (9)
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter in the *Aṃśumat*, titled "The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Form of Ardhanārīśvara" within the lineage of Kaśyapa.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the form of the enemy of the elephant (Viṣṇu):
[the measurement] from the middle of the forehead to the tip of the nose, or from the tip of the nose to the middle of the chest.
From the middle of the left buttock, one should extend a cord to the east;
from that cord to the south, O twice-born one, is the distance between the left heel and [the eastern point].
O twice-born one, it should be either thirty-eight finger-breadths or thirty-six finger-breadths from that thread to the tip of the big toe of the left foot.
Either twenty-one fingers or nineteen fingers [in height], adorned with all ornaments, and having either four or eight arms. (4)
If he has four arms, there is a noose and an elephant hide in the right [hands],
and an elephant tusk and a shield in the pair of left hands.
Thus has the four-armed form been described; now the eight-armed form is being stated:
[he holds] a trident, a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), a noose, and an elephant hide in his right hands.
An elephant tusk, a skull, an elephant hide,
and a water-pot— thus the four hands on the left side are proclaimed.
One should place the head of an elephant beneath the left foot of Śambhu,
and the elephant's tail above the crown.
One should fashion the elephant’s feet on both sides according to the proper method;
the remainder should be fashioned as an elephant hide, like a halo of light.
Clad in a tiger-skin garment and also endowed with fine silk raiment,
he was adorned with all ornaments and possessed a luster equal to the most excellent jewels.
In this manner, the form of Gajahā is first prescribed; a trident, a sword, a shield, and an elephant tusk are held in the right hands. (11)
In the left [hands], he holds a skull-cup, a shield, a bell, and an elephant hide;
[the mantras are recited] from the middle of the forehead, the tip of the nose, and the middle of the right breast.
O Teacher! One should let the Brahma-sūtra hang from the middle of the left buttock, while keeping the left foot well-placed upon the head of an elephant.
The right foot should be raised and extended obliquely;
the distance from the heel of that foot to the buttock is four finger-breadths. (14)
One should draw a level boundary-line from that knee to the left eye;
thus it is declared to be of two kinds, and it is also called the "elephant-stealer. (15)
The goddess Dyumā, extracted from the *Skanda-purāṇa*, stands on the left side of Śambhu, filled with fear;
indeed, an image fashioned in this manner bestows prosperity upon the king and his kingdom. (16)
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*, titled "The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Elephant-Harmer Form."
Now I shall describe the characteristics of the Pāśupata form;
its standing posture with feet even is like that of the Candraśekhara form.
Three-eyed, four-armed, and gentle, with hair standing upright and a massive body;
his two right hands display the gestures of fearlessness and hold a trident. (2)
His two hands on the left side display the gesture of granting boons and a rosary;
he has the luster of coral, with gentle eyes that are exceedingly cool.
Adorned with all ornaments and with a slightly smiling face,
that image— whether in a standing posture or seated— is for the sake of eternal festivity.
That very [form] had ears equal to fire, red eyes, and crooked eyebrows;
it was endowed with a mouth of sharp fangs and a serpent as its sacred thread.
Wearing a garment of intense red, having the form of a crest of garlands of flames, he holds a trident with its point facing downward and a skull while displaying the gesture of granting boons. (6)

Alternatively, having placed the base of the trident in his hand without the [gesture of] fear (abhaya), the tip of the trident is held with the very same [hand] that displays the boon-granting gesture (varada); thus it is held with three fingers.
In the right hand there is a ṭaṅka, and in the left a sword;
this form of Raudra-Pāśupata is worshipped in both the image and the liṅga. || 8 ||
I shall now describe that form for the purpose of meditative worship;
one should contemplate this form even once, which destroys all enemies. (9)
However, one should not have this fierce form made as an image.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the Pāśupata form, in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*.
Now, the characteristics of Kaṅkālamūrti shall be described.
His feet are provided with sandals, and the left foot is firmly placed.
Behold him with his left foot slightly raised,
possessing a complexion like pure white, and adorned with all ornaments.
His body is encased in a cloak of jewels, adorned with a crown of matted locks;
he holds a nāga with flowers dripping with fragrance in his left hand, while the moon serves as his crest-ornament on the right.
Maintaining a smiling face attended by hosts of celestial singers,
he displayed a most graceful vision with a slight internal radiance revealed.
(340) The face is thus proclaimed as being endowed with song and erotic sentiment;
the ears are adorned with earrings, and on the left there is a sprig of a branch.
In the two front hands, the left holds a ḍhakkā drum and the right a striking instrument;
on the right side of the face is a deer-face, and it is extended like a lion’s ear.
In the left hand, however, one should hold a peacock feather and a bone from a skeleton;
thereafter, one should fashion its form as possessing two feet and two hands.
The wise one should bind with a cord the two feet of the skeleton-staff, which has the dark-blue appearance of Kṛṣṇa, at the anus, in the manner of a staff.
Or, having brought forth the beautiful [deity] Ketukiṅkiṇinetrāḍhya,
one should place it by the name Kaṅkāla upon the left shoulder.
He was attended with reverence by many female spirits (bhūtas) who were his consorts;
he was a being holding a vessel for offerings, moving forward with his left side foremost.
Having placed the ladle upon that vessel, the wife of Kṛti, naked and with her vulva slightly revealed, joined together [with him]. || 11 ||
All his wives, their minds filled with agitation,
[beheld it] many times on the left side of the forehead, at the corner of the eye, and within the eyelid.
On the left side of Hanvantu, likewise in the middle of the hiccup, in the heart,
two finger-breadths to the right of the navel, and on the ankle of the left foot.

One should hang the Brahma-thread in the middle, ensuring it is neither too short nor too long; then, according to the prescribed method for avoiding distortion, one should determine the degree of curvature.
Clad in a tiger-skin garment and endowed with silken raiment, one should fasten a small dagger to the right side of the waist. (15)
A razor-edged sword, golden in appearance and provided with a hilt,
adorned on both sides of the handle with various serpents.
By the ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others, who joined their palms at their hearts with minds filled with agitation. (17)
The Wind-god shall sweep the streets of that city which is ever-joyful, well-honored, frequented by them, and highly revered; and the Rain-god shall sprinkle it with water.
The gods showered a rain of flowers and blew conch shells;
and in every city, one should offer praise with the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas.
[One should play] the carmabandha, the kaṃsa, the kadamba, or indeed the suṣira [instruments]. (20)
Accompanied by the sound of conchs and the fivefold music of great charioteers,
Tumburu, Nārada, and all others performed the art of song according to its proper characteristics.
Holding a sun-bright parasol and divine fly-whisks,
celestial women [attended] Indra in his palace and other dwellings for the sake of benefiting all the worlds.
"O Brahmin, I shall perform a protection rite that grants liberation to Kaṅkāla.
Kāśyapa said:
How indeed did the origin of this skeleton, which was supported by you, come to be?
Now, O Brahmin, when Janārdana stands before one at the time of death,
he [withdraws] that body, the worlds, and his own powers from that fear.
Then, when the entire cosmic egg has trembled, those who dwell within that egg and pray to me with devotion for the removal of their fear—[for them I shall act]. (25)

O great twice-born one! For the sake of the stability of the cosmic eggs, for the benefit of all the worlds, and for the purpose of liberating Kaṅkāla, that [sacred site] was indeed maintained by him.
At the end of the alms-round, one should release this skeleton; it occurs in the month of Mādhava.
Thus the skeleton has been described; now hear about Haryardha. || 27 ||
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter [in the Āṃśumat-kāśyapa], titled "The Characteristics of the Kaṅkālamūrti."
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme form of Hara as half of Hari;
the god stands upright and well-poised in a standing posture with feet together.
In his right [hand] is the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and in his left is a bracelet resting upon his thigh;
in his right hand is an axe, and in his left is the supreme weapon, the conch.
On both the right and left crowns, one should fashion a crest of matted hair,
coral-colored and dark-hued, adorned with appropriate ornaments.
The right gaze should be fierce, while the left gaze is exceedingly cool;
the gaze directed toward the forehead is slightly upward-looking and luminous.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with suitable garments,
with a head joined by a discus— this is said to be its characteristic.
O Brahmin, it should be eleven fingers wide, with a thickness equal to its diameter;
it may be perfectly circular like a wheel or even in the shape of a lotus.
The head-wheel, however, is seven times as large as the stalk;
O best of the twice-born, the width of the stalk of the head-wheel is one-seventh [of that]. (7)
One-third of the wheel's diameter should extend upward from the wheel to the top of the head;
the stalk of the head-wheel should be positioned at the front of the forehead-plate.
Above the two nape-joints (kṛkāṭī), the placement of the wheel-shaft (cakranāla) occurs at a distance of nine finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula).
Measuring nine finger-breadths downward from the center of the wheel, the flower-garland (puṣpamālā) is situated.
One should indeed act in this manner toward all the gods and goddesses as well.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Half-Form of Hari," in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kāśyapa. || 76 ||
Now I shall describe in detail the Great Lord’s wandering for alms:
the feet are joined with sandals, while the left foot is firmly planted.
Having slightly raised his left [hand], the Blessed One, eager for departure,
[placed it] eight or nine barley-grains' distance from the middle of his forehead toward the left.
From the tip of the nose to the left lip, from the middle of the hiccough to the left [side],
in the center of the heart, and on the right side of the navel— at an interval of sixteen barley-corns [is the location].
One should hang the eastern thread from the middle of the standing ankle and the ankle-bone;
it is known as either "with a bend" (ābhaṅgavat) or "evenly bent" (samabhaṅga).
His feet may be joined with sandals or even devoid of sandals;
his mass of matted hair may be beautifully disheveled, or it may be arranged in a circular coil. || 5 ||
Then, with his matted locks loosened from their bonds, he appeared naked in form with a bowed face;
his forehead was broad and marked, and the crescent moon rested upon the peak of his head.
Adorned with all ornaments except the waist-string,
it is described as resembling pure white and decorated with various *nāgas*.
The first right hand should be in the form of a deer's head,
while the first left hand should be in the boon-granting gesture (varada) and holding a skull-cup.
O twice-born one, he should hold a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in his right hand,
and a peacock feather fan (śikhipiñcha), held coolly, should be placed in his left.
He wears a white cloth as an upper garment, his waist is encircled by a serpent,
he has a white sacred thread, a blue throat, and bears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Above the lotus seat, however, the remainder [of the body] is like the form of a skeleton.
Kāśyapa said:
You alone are capable of speaking; you ought to tell me the very cause of that.
The Lord said:
In the great battle between the gods and the asuras, the head of Brahmā was carried away;
that side shall always be called Dāva, and one should speak of it as being without a lord (anīśa).
By him those Asuras were conquered, and the gods took refuge in their own splendor;
O twice-born one, all the deities, seeking my welfare, would entreat me.
For the sake of the victory of the gods, for the benefit of all the worlds, and for the destruction of the Dānavas, I shall slay the embodiment of Brahmā. (14)
All the egg-shells of the universes trembled at that blow,
and all the lords of those universes were seized with great fear.
The great gods should enter and speak from the mouth of a child for the sake of the firm establishment of others and for the purpose of granting fearlessness to the gods. (16)
O twice-born one, for the sake of benefiting the entire world and bringing welfare to all living beings,
and for the sake of the liberation of that skull, I am a mendicant.
When this has been done at the end of the alms-round, one should declare liberation through the skull.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Form for Alms-Rounding," in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*.
Now I shall describe in detail how the grace of Caṇḍeśa occurs:
he is accompanied by Umā, and everything [is situated] to his left, with his face slightly bowed.
On the right, however, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) is to be avoided; that hand should instead be in the boon-granting (varada) mudrā.
On the left, the bracelet is to be avoided, having been placed upon the head of Caṇḍeśa.
With his heart and palms joined in reverence, Caṇḍeśa was filled with devotion;
seated comfortably, Caṇḍeśa shone like gold.
O twice-born one, between the Goddess and the Lord of Gods, excluding the form of Skanda,
there is the renowned Caṇḍeśānugraha, and beyond that is Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter [of the *Aṃśumānakāśyapa*], titled "The Characteristics of the Form of Caṇḍeśa’s Grace."
Now I shall describe in detail the characteristics of Dakṣiṇāmūrti:
the right foot is suspended, with the tip of the big toe of the left foot [touching it].
The left foot should be placed upon the top of the right thigh, while the right foot should be laid down;
[the gaze] should be directed toward the forehead, the right [eye], the corner of the left eye, and the edge of its eyelid.
To the left of the center of the *hikkā*, the heart is located at the middle-left;
having moved a distance of three *yava*s, it is suspended on the middle of the left side.
From the middle of the base of the penis, one should hang a front thread;
it should be bent by one and a half mātrās and provided with four arms.
One should form the *jñānamudrā* with the right hand on the right side,
while the other right hand is provided with a rosary (*akṣamālā*).
The left hand should be in the boon-granting gesture (varada), or alternatively, holding a staff;
when in the boon-granting gesture, the back of the palm should rest upon the left knee.
If one places the staff upon the left knee with the elbow resting on it, while holding either fire or a serpent in the other left hand; || 7 ||
With an exceedingly straight face and all limbs of softness, like a crystal casket,
with the top of his head beautifully adorned, or else [wearing] a mass of matted locks (jaṭāmaṇḍala).
On the left is the Dhūr-dhūra nāga, and on the right is the crescent moon upon his crest;
he is endowed with a smiling face and adorned with all ornaments.
He has a white garment as an upper cloth and a white sacred thread;
he has three eyes, a conch-shell leaf [on his ear], and all his ornaments are earrings on the left side.
The two ears are adorned with conch-shell ornaments, leaf-shaped earrings, or earrings;
and the neck is decorated with a garland of rudrākṣa beads and smeared with sacred ash. (11)
Clad in a tiger-skin garment and free from all afflictions, Nārada, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Dakṣa are on the right. 12.
Bhāradvāja and Śaunaka were on the right side, while Agastya was on the left;
with Nandin, Kinnaras, and others, they supported the temple of the banyan tree.

Above the *apasmāra* line, one should place the *lambapādatala* (the hanging soles of the feet). From the [central] thread to the end of the heels, measuring three times the width of a finger-breadth (*anumātra*), are the feet and calves.
The distance from the feet to the knees of the Sūtrātman is the measure of a man;
he is dark-complexioned, possesses epilepsy, and is endowed with the grace of a serpent. (15)
The best of those who know the ritual procedures should thus fashion the form of the expounder of the Dharma;
that very same [form] is joined with the left foot placed upon a small stool.
O best of the twice-born! Holding a lute (vīṇā) with both hands in front, the rest should be performed as before; this is the Vīṇākara [mudrā]. || 17 ||
That same [form], however, is without the lute and is endowed with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā);
the left hand is extended upward above the left knee.
In the right [hand] there is a rosary, and in the left a lotus with an utpala;
his complexion is like pure white; the rest should be performed as before.
O Brahmin, one should place the soles of the feet against each other below the buttocks; this is known as Jñānamūrti, the cause of all causes.
The Jñānamudrā: one should place the hand with the palm facing inward at the location of the heart;
the left hand, however, should be placed in the boon-granting gesture (varada) upon the seat of the penis.
Others [should have] a lotus garland in the right hand and an eye in the left hand;
looking at the tip of the nose, the eyes, the straightness, and the thread upon the body.
Others, however, should be matted-haired (jaṭāla), the excellent one served by the sages.
It is renowned as Yogamūrti, the supreme destroyer of all sins.
Thus, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is described through many such varieties.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, in the Aṃśumat of Kāśyapa. 79.
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall specifically describe the characteristics of Kāladāha; its extent is one-eighth, one-ninth, or one-tenth of a *nata*.
Alternatively, the measurement of the nose is said to be eleven or twelve fingers;
likewise, [the distance] from the right side of the forehead to the middle of the left eye is the same.
At the midpoint of the *hikkā*, one and a half [units] to the left is the eye of the left breast;
to the right, from the center of the navel, the interval of the thread to the left is eight barley-corns.
From the middle of the base of the penis, one should lead [the line] six finger-breadths to the left;
then, having positioned it at the middle of the ankle of the foot, one should extend the eastern thread.
The right foot of the Lord, situated upon a lotus pedestal,
is like the right-positioned foot of the primary dancing form.
Having raised his left foot with its sole turned upward and its toes extended,
he should place it upon the heart of Kāla.
He has fangs and a mouth, three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair;
he is endowed with four arms, or even eight.
The right fore-hand holds a trident raised to the level of the ear;
the right hind-hand holds an axe, or alternatively, the left [hind-hand] may hold it.
On the left, the first hand [should be placed] facing downwards like a needle, reaching as far as the boundary of the navel;
from the tip of the needle to the end of the previous thread, it should measure one *kalā* or one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
One should place the trident at the ear or in the hand, or alternatively between the wrists;
on the left, however, one should form the gesture of astonishment with the other hand.
The chisel is equal to the *hikkā*-sūtra, and the handle is twice that distance;
having raised it up to the end of the *uṣṇīṣa*, the tip of the ring finger is used for the expression of wonder.
The space from the tip of the ear to the base of the wrist, equal to the length of a trident held in the hand, is declared to be four cubits;
now hear about the eight-cubit [measurement].
In his right hands he holds a trident, an axe, a thunderbolt, and a sword;
in his left hands he holds a shield, a noose, a needle, and a hand. (13)
Having an appearance resembling coral and adorned with all ornaments, she is called Kālahāmūrti; because she stands below, she is called Kāla.
Seeing me with my hands joined at the heart in the noose that is fraught with great fear, and with my feet sprawled out, he shall lay me down with my face turned upwards.

p. 350) The form known as Kālahā is declared; after this follows the Liṅgodbhava. Thus ends the seventieth chapter [in the Aṃśumat-kāśyapa] concerning the characteristics of the Kālahārimūrti. || 80 ||
Salutation to the Lord of the Tandava dance performed with inverted feet.
Now, hereafter, I shall describe in detail the origin of the Liṅga;
in the center of the form of the Liṅga, it is like the form of Candraśekhara.
O Brahmin! The Nalakas and the soles of the feet are endowed with the Liṅgārūḍha;
while Brahmā, in the form of a swan, is situated above on the left side.
Viṣṇu, in the form of a boar, is situated below in the southern portion;
Viṣṇu is on the right side, while Pitāmaha is on the left side.
With their hands joined in the *añjali* gesture at their hearts, they stood gazing upon the Liṅga—
the Lord, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha— who possessed red, dark, and golden splendors respectively.
Thus, the origin of the liṅga and likewise the collection of trees has been declared.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Form of the Liṅga Origin," in the *Aṃśumat* section of the *Kāśyapa*. 81.
Now I shall explain in detail the supreme collection of trees;
the tree for the sake of the trident of the gods and goddesses is now described.
Females, males, and neuters—thus the classification of trees is threefold. [A tree] that grows on moist or dry ground, which is straight, very firm, and dense, [is to be selected]. (2)
The fruit is joined with small clusters, possesses five petals, and is firm; it is a mixture of cool and warm qualities, endowed with little oiliness and flavor.
That which is called the "male sign" (puṃliṅga) among the gods is described here:
it is found on smooth ground or moist soil, and is characterized by straightness and extreme softness.
From the root to the tip, the flowers, fruits, and petals gradually diminish;
they are endowed with extreme softness and extreme coolness.
And the juice should likewise be endowed with excessive oiliness;
this is declared to be the "Woman-tree," suitable for the goddesses' trident-rites.
A leaf, flower, or fruit that is joined with diminished roots and characterized by extreme weakness is declared to be *ṣaṇḍa*.
Sandalwood, campaka, and red sandalwood; sāl, khadira, somaśīrṣaka, and tinduka. || 8 ||
Arjuna, Śiṃśupa, Rājādana, Madhūka, Āmraka, Kusuma, Saptaparṇa, and Dhanvana. (9)
The trees suitable for the trident (śūla) are well known; one should construct that very firm [structure] from them.
Those that are decayed, crooked, with gaps between the joints, or lacking a head, as well as those resembling grain-stalks (śālikā), should be avoided.
The trees had fallen of their own accord and were withered by themselves;
they were full of crooked hollows and inhabited by serpents and birds.
(352) Pierced by the feet of wind-storms and covered with species of creepers, they take refuge in thickets and anthills, or are inhabited by outcasts. || 12 ||
Trees growing near temples, assembly halls, shrines, cemeteries, roads, royal palaces, and workshops [are forbidden]. (13)
Resorting to the temple of Rudra and taking refuge in the dwellings of leather-workers, they became blind like trees, employed in other menial tasks. || 14 ||
One should avoid [such a site] with great effort, for when it is taken, it causes the destruction of the builder;
therefore, one should avoid that which is full of defects with every possible effort. (15)
On auspicious lunar days, one should select an excellent tree;
here, the preceptor and the artisan should gather it at the site of the tree. (16)
Having inspected many trees, one should select the tree previously described;
then, having removed the roots and other defects from beneath the tree, the preceptor should perform the sowing.
Having recited this mantra, one should cast the bali offering in the eight directions:
"The gods, dānavas, and piśācas who dwell in these trees [accept this]. (18)
O Nāgas, Garuḍas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas: you may go from the tree for the sake of the image as you please. (19)
Having spoken thus, one should offer the bali-oblation consisting of curd, clarified butter, and rice, together with flowers, mixed with red sandalwood and accompanied by scented water. (20)
Then, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the north-eastern direction of the tree;
one should prepare an altar (sthaṇḍila) out of sand, measuring one cubit in size.

(353) The preceptor should perform all the rites beginning with the installation of the fire as prescribed for the *agnikārya*; having performed the oblation (*homa*) with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), he should proceed. || 22 ||
One should offer the fuel-sticks with the Heart mantra and the clarified butter with the Root mantra;
having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, one should perform eight hundred oblations for each.
One should perform oblations with the *jayā* and other *ābhyātāna* mantras, as well as the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* mantras.
Then, having formally dismissed the fire and sprinkled the tree with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), [one should proceed].
Having recited the mantra "śivātmaka," the wise one should touch the tree;
the front of the tree is in the east, while the back is in the west.
The right side shall be the western flank, and likewise the left side the northern;
having meditated thus and marked it out, one should thereafter begin the cutting.
One should mutter the weapon-mantra at the foot of a tree and observe it for three cuts;
milk, water, and ghee are excellent, as are the sacrificial ladles made from forest wood.
In the event of blood flowing, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) with the Astra-mantra;
meanwhile, the master carpenter should cut down the entire tree at its root in due order.
The falling of a tree toward the east or the north is auspicious;
however, one should carefully avoid a tree that has fallen in any other direction. || 29 ||
Then one should perform the cutting of the trunk; make that tree straight.
Having bathed it with cow-products and scented water, it should be adorned with perfumes and garlands.
Having covered it with a new cloth, or with *darbha* grass, or with a fine rope,
the wise man should place it upon a chariot, in a palanquin, or carry it on his shoulder.
Having taken [the materials] and proceeding very slowly, one should perform the ritual in the Karma-maṇḍapa;
having swept the maṇḍapa, apply a coating of cow-dung.
Having adorned it with flour-dust, the wise man should prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) in its center using coarse sand, shaped like a trident and equal in length.
Its half should be provided with a width and raised four finger-breadths;
upon it, one should lay the trident-tree with its tip pointing eastward and facing downward.
The wise man should preserve it while still moist for a month or even for a fortnight;
afterwards, however, the piercing should be performed, but one should not do so hastily.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter in the *Aṃśumat*, titled "The Compendium on Trees" within the *Kāśyapa*. 82.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme characteristics of the *śūla* (trident):
the bamboo staff is said to be as long as the upper body [of the deity]. || 1 ||
For one whose belly is broad in the middle, the width at the base should be one-fourth [of the circumference],
while its tip should be extended such that it is reduced by one-eighth part.
Up to the navel it is square, up to the heart it is eight-cornered;
above that it is said to be circular, or the remainder may also be simply round.
The breast-pillar (vakṣodaṇḍa) should be thirty-two aṅgulas in length;
its width should be six and a half mātrās, or alternatively, seven and a half aṅgulas.
The chest is known to have a thickness equal to half its width; that is called the *daṇḍa*.
Its width at the tip is four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), becoming gradually thinner from the middle toward the tip. (5)
In the middle of the breast-pillar (vakṣodaṇḍa), however, there is a cavity measuring one and a half times the width of a finger;
it extends from below the line of the heart (hikkāsūtra) down to a distance of two fingers.
The upper part of the chest-staff (vakṣodaṇḍa) should have the same proportion; one should apply two parts to the staff.
O Teacher, the length of the hip-staff (kaṭidaṇḍa) should be sixteen aṅgulas.
That silver [ring] should be eight finger-breadths in circumference and four finger-breadths in thickness;
its central aperture should be four finger-breadths wide, located five finger-breadths below the navel.
O Brahmin, one should join [the cord] to the backbone in the middle above the hip-bone,
and likewise to the tips of the two breast-bones and the tips of the two hip-bones.
Then the wise one should perform the face and crest (mudrās) according to this procedure,
using one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight fingers.
That which is suitable for the image has a number [of measures] accompanied by curved tips;
the length of the crest is two finger-breadths, and the number of hands is likewise measured from that.
The width of the chest-pillar (vakṣodaṇḍa) is divided by the number of cubits;
one part of that shall be the width of the crest (śikhā), which becomes gradually slender from the base to the tip.
The length of the curved tip at the ends of the waist-staffs shall be three finger-breadths;
its width shall be one and a half finger-breadths, perfectly circular, and its thickness uniform.
O twice-born one! If the entire *sthānaka* is above the long thigh, having added eight finger-breadths, it becomes the length of the *ūruśūla*.
On the seat, one should not place the entire [foot] above the thigh;
rather, the wise man, having made a hollow at the base of the thigh, should place it between the tips of the two shanks. (10)
Having joined the tip at the crest-lock, as far as the strength allows,
one should divide it into two parts reaching the knees, for both the thighs and the shanks.
Therefore, the wise man should determine the measurement of the crest;
the measurement of the crest is three finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula), joined with both the lengths of the shanks and so forth.
It should be provided with a central hole, have its upper part facing upward, and be endowed with two prongs;
one-third of the base of the shank is declared to be the width of the prong.
Or else, perform the entire [posture] while standing without the knee-joint;
thus is the "Pain-in-the-Leg" (aṅghriśūla) posture, devoid of the joint, prescribed. || 19 ||
One should erect the part above the shanks to a height of one *tāla*;
the width of the thigh-shaft (*ūrudaṇḍa*) shall be one-third of the middle of the thigh.
Its tip should be three-quarters [of its base], while the base of the shank is equal to that;
the width at the top of the shank is reduced by one-third of the width at the base of the shank.
Having divided the length from the soles of the feet into three parts, it should be provided with two parts;
its width at the tip of the hall should be endowed with two, three, or two parts respectively.
This [pedestal] should be a square with its base equal to the sole; beyond that, it should be elongated.
A cavity should be made therein, extending further than the end of the shank. 23.
Having joined [the parts] and made the base of the arm smooth and firm, it is then described:
the width of the base of the arm is declared to be one *guṇa-aṅgula*.
The tip [of the arm] should be two *aṅgulas* in width, broad at the end of the forearm;
and the elbow of both the upper arm and the forearm should be shaped like a knee. || 25 ||
One should join the crest-piece (śikhā) of two finger-breadths in such a way that it is firmly fixed;
one should then join it to the side-pieces of the bamboo staff at the sides of the staff.
The inner chamber (kakṣāntara) should be as long as that [central hall], and its width should be three finger-breadths;
the roof (nīvr̥) should be level with the bamboo beam (vaṃśadaṇḍa), and it should be provided with a pinnacle (śikhā) at the top and bottom.
One should join the two tips firmly to the chest, the two bases to the pelvic staff (kaṭidaṇḍaka), and the portion of the string within the hole to the intermediate space.
The two tips and the two roots should be restrained, as well as the two sides of the spine;
one should join the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and the ears with the copper plate.
In the case of a straight image and likewise for a curved one, fashion the trident in that same manner;
such shall be the trident of the gods, and now the [trident] of the goddesses will be described.
Dividing the middle of the belly into three parts, one part shall be the width of the beam;
the width at the front, reduced by one-eighth, shall be perfectly circular.
The length of the chest-pillar (vakṣodaṇḍa) is equal to the width up to the arms; the remainder, diminished by half the length of the arms, should extend to its end.
The measurement of the back should be one-sixteenth of the yuga; the remainder is for the cavity.
A wise man should fix the shank at six mātras from the staff within the pedestal.
Halfway through the entry into the womb-chamber, it should extend below the floor;
thus is the *śūla* described, and it is called the *upadhāśūla*.
Starting from the middle of the wall, extending to the chest and ending at the tip of the staff,
it is said that the *upaśūla* should be eight finger-breadths wide and long.
The wise man should make that pedestal four finger-breadths high, using wood suitable for the trident;
its middle hole should be equal in width to the trident and provided with a spike.
Having firmly secured the base of the trident from the middle of the wall by the wise,
and having held the breast-staff and waist-staff, [one should fix] the trident known as the "bamboo."
In the opening, one should establish a very firm fire, preceded by the binding of a ritual stake (kīla);
and from the tip of the secondary trident (upathāśūlaśikhā) to the city of the chest-staff (vakṣodaṇḍapura), it should be made equal.
At the tip of the flame of the secondary fire, one should make a hollow at the end of the bamboo;
then, one should firmly join a peg made either of metal or of wood.
The *bimba* is declared to be the trident; therefore, one should act as previously described.
The characteristics of the trident have been explained; now the installation of the trident is being stated. (40)
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, the Section on the Characteristics of the Tridents, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of Kaśyapa. 83.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme installation of the sacrificial post (śūla),
to be performed during the month prescribed for the plowing ceremony, under an auspicious constellation, day, and moment.
Having determined [the site] and performed the preliminary rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa),
one should construct a square pavilion (maṇḍapa) in front of the temple on an auspicious day.
It may be five cubits in length, or even nine cubits;
it is provided with three rows and endowed with sixteen pillars.
It should be eight finger-breadths in height, with a width and depth equal to one *paṅkti*, its circumference as large as can be obtained, free from blemishes, made of wood, and firm.

One should cover the sacrificial pit, which is enriched with bamboo and its derivatives, with a canopy made of coconut leaves and the like, adorned with garlands of pearls and wreaths of darbha grass.
It was provided with wave-like enclosures, equipped with gate-arches,
endowed with four gates, and furnished with pillar-surroundings.
Except for four doors, the pavilion should otherwise be without gaps or lattices;
in its center, occupying one-third of the area, is a spacious altar.
One-third of that [height] is desired for the elevation of the altar (vedikā);
its width and height should be three finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula), and below that is the secondary altar (upavedikā).
Having fashioned [the image] out of red clay so that it resembles the surface of a mirror,
and having prepared the fire-pits elsewhere, perform [the rites] according to this procedure.
One should fashion a square, a bow-shaped, a circular, and a lotus-shaped fire-pit in the directions starting from the east;
and between the regions of Indra and Śaṅkara (the northeast), one should prepare a circular pit.
Thus has the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) been described specifically for those [deities] alone;
however, if it is an image accompanied by Gaurī, it should have [protrusions] at the corners like the leaves of the Aśvattha tree.
One should fashion the remaining sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) just as previously described;
having constructed each pit according to its defining characteristics, the preceptor (deśika) should prepare all the pits.
Having smeared it with cow dung and adorned it with flour-powder, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there and then cause them to pronounce the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha). || 13 ||
On the Mahendra site, having performed the Vāstu-homa according to the prescribed rule,
prepare the altars, the fire-pits, and perform the rite of circumambulation with fire.
On the night preceding that day, during the first watch,
one should consecrate the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) upon the altar with eight droṇas of śāli rice.
There, a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp should be fashioned,
adorned with rice, sesame seeds, darbha grass, parched grain, and flowers.
One should fashion the seat using a garment that is indeed beneficial;
then one should worship it with incense, lamps, flowers, and water offerings.
One should construct a bathing pit on the northern side of the pavilion;
having placed a wooden seat in its center, one should set [the vessel] upon it.
One should place the trident facing east and sprinkle it with cow-products,
having purified it with the *śucirvo havyam* mantra and with scented water using the *hṛdaya* mantra.
One should install the God and the Goddess and worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
O God, one should tie the protective thread (kautuka) on the right hands of the two.
One should bind it with flowers, cotton threads, or indeed with armor;
it should be provided with a hanging tuft of hair and wrapped in a new cloth.
Accompanied by dance and song, and accompanied by the sound of the Vedas,
one should place the trident upon the bed with its head toward the east and its face turned upward.
To his left is indeed the goddess Umā, and likewise a trident to his right;
one should place those two jars in the region near the heads of those two. (23)
That which is provided with its thread and lid, well-wrapped with an excellent tuft of grass,
and completely filled with a droṇa of fragrant water is called a Śiva-kumbha.
Half-filled with water and equipped with the thread and other items as before,
this excellent Gaurī-pitcher is joined with the Gaurī-śūla.
Having placed the root mantra upon the auspicious pitcher, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings;
likewise, having specially worshipped the pitcher of Gaurī with their respective mantras.

Having placed eight jars all around, provided with threads, cloths, and other requisites, and having established them with the root mantras of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings.
Having consecrated the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Vāstuhoma fire,
the preceptor should perform all the rites beginning with the placement of the fire (agnyādhāna), as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
O twice-born one, one should place an *aśvattha* tree in the eastern pit, a firewood [tree] in the south-eastern direction,
a *saundara* tree in the south, and a *khadira* tree in the south-west.
One should place a *bilva* tree in the western quarter, a *māyūra* tree in the region of the wind (the northwest),
a *vaṭa* tree in the northern pond, and an *arka* tree in the region of Īśa (the northeast).

O best of the twice-born! At the principal [site] of the Brahma-tree, it is provided with fuel-sticks and Gaurī; however, there are no sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the corners, nor is Gaurī present there.

One should offer the fuel-sticks with the *hṛdaya* mantra, the oblation of clarified butter with the *puruṣa* mantra, the *caru* with the *aghora* mantra, and one should offer parched grain (*lāja*) with the *vāma* mantra. || 32 ||
One should offer groats with the Īśāna mantra, sesame seeds with the Śiras [mantra], mustard seeds with the Kavaca [mantra], and indeed mudga beans with the Śikhā [mantra]. (33)
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations for each [ingredient] with the *gulamastra* mantra;
at the end of the substances, having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, [one offers] equally to the Goddess and the Lord of Gods.
One should perform oblations with the Jaya and other hymns, the Abhyātānas, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛts;
one should study the Vedas in the cardinal directions and recite hymns in the intermediate directions.
Having recited the study [of the texts] there, one should perform the silent (upāṃśu) oblation;
[this consists of] eight hundred oblations of the root mantra of the Goddess and the Lord of Gods.
Then, having offered oblations with ghee and touched each other's tridents,
they passed the remainder of the night with dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
At the clear dawn, the wise preceptor, together with the image-keepers (mūrtipās),
should perform a bath in water, followed immediately by a bath in sacred ash.
He should wear a white upper garment and a white sacred thread (yajñopavīta),
and be adorned with white garlands, unguents, and the fivefold ornaments.

The preceptor, born of a family of Śiva-devoted brahmins, with a pure soul and a highly serene mind, should approach with the sacred grass (pavitra) in hand and his body consecrated by the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
Having entered the pavilion, one should thereafter worship the trident, the pitcher, and the fire with perfumes and other offerings, performing especially elaborate worship.
One should perform oblations with the Jaya and other mantras, as well as the Abhyātānas and the Rāṣṭrabhṛts; then, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne."
Having entered the inner sanctum, however, one should establish eighty-one squares;
or else, on the square known as Maṇḍūka, or with seven-sevenths [of a square]. (43)
The inner sanctum (garbhageha) should be constructed, knowing it to be the station of Brahmā and the other [deities];
the standing place (sthānaka) is in the portion belonging to the goddesses, while the seat (āsana) is in the human portion.
The best of instructors should place the seat upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) in the rear part of the inner sanctum, while the standing image is placed upon the altar (vedikā).

According to the previously mentioned procedure, one should calculate the square of the breadth and length of the pedestal; upon that, one should fashion a beautiful base and install the stone known as the *ādhāra*.

One should place the stone called the *ādhāra* (foundation), which is one-third the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*); it may be either square or rectangular, and its thickness should be half of that [width]. || 47 ||
O best of the twice-born! If the entire site is to be established, one should fashion a gem-encrusted pit upon the stone known as Ādhāra, situated beneath the feet.
The depth of the pit is known to be six finger-breadths, and its width is three finger-breadths;
one should place either the nine gems or gold therein at the base.
The wise one, endowed with strength, should first prepare a space six mātrās in length beneath the soles of his feet for the purpose of establishing [the deity].
Having placed a four-measure length upon the bamboo staff on the seat,
he should announce it to the Guru when the auspicious moment (muhūrta) has arrived.
But the preceptor, having lifted [the image] and circumambulated it clockwise,
accompanied by all musical instruments and provided with every kind of music, || 52 ||
One should enter the inner sanctum while reciting the root mantra;
one should then firmly install [the object] in the pit beneath the base of the trident. (53)
Having made it firm with the eightfold binding, or especially with lime,
one should specifically place the trident of Gaurī to its left.
On the stone known as the *ādhāra*, one should prepare the cavity for the womb-vessel (*garbhabhājana*),
measuring five, six, seven, or nine finger-breadths in the width of the pit.

Having installed the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) right there, together with the vessel for the embryo, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should establish the trident as before, and the root [pedestal] which is indeed the womb-vessel;
furthermore, whatever remaining work there may be should be performed especially by artisans.
The master architect (sthapati) is said to be a craftsman endowed with the [proper] characteristics;
the master architect who knows the art of painting should employ others, but not have them do it himself.
"O Brahmin, if it has been done otherwise, another will become the performer;
in that case, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings. (59)
There, one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of five niṣkas of gold to be given.
The procedure for the installation on the stake has been declared; now hear about the binding with ropes.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the *Aṃśumat*, the section on the ritual procedure for the installation of the sacrificial stake (*śūla*) within the *Kāśyapa* tradition.
Now I shall explain in detail the binding with cords; listen, O twice-born one!
At all the joints of the trident, one should wrap them with copper plates.
Having smeared [the victim] with eight bindings on the stake, they then know it as the "rope-binding" (rajjubandha).
Likewise, there is the Śrīveṣṭaka, the Kunduruṣka, the Guggula, and the Gula. || 2 ||
Sarjarasa and gairika [are mixed] with ghee and oil for the eightfold binding;
śrīveṣṭana is four parts, and kunduruṣka is one-third part.
Guggulu should consist of five parts, and gum-resin (gula) is said to be one part;
resin (sarjarasa) should be eight parts, and red ochre (gairika) three parts.
Having made these six into a fine powder and mixed it with ghee and oil,
one should place it in an earthen vessel and cook it until it takes on the appearance of honey.
Then, having smeared the trident, perform the cord-binding;
the cord-binding from the navel to the center should extend upward in three ways.
The Suṣumnā is in the middle, while the Piṅgalā is on its right;
the Iḍā indeed resides on its left—these are the principal channels.
Their circumference is two finger-breadths, and they are indeed said to be joined together; the union of those three channels occurs at the midpoint between the eyebrows.
Below that, the two parts of the staff, which are well-proportioned and open at the bottom, rest upon the previous [elements];
from the middle of the eyebrows to the top of the head, the three channels (nāḍīs) become one.
Above its head, however, are the channels that branch into seven:
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī; || 10 ||
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī are their designations; Gāndhārī extends to the corner of the left eye, while Hastijihvā and Itarākṣikā [extend to] the eyes. (11)
Puṣā extends from the right ear to the end; Yaśasvinī is at the left ear; Alambuṣā extends to the base of the penis; Vakradantā and Kuhū are located there as well.
The support of the Śaṅkhinī extends down to the center of the navel;
at its beginning, there are four channels (nāḍīs) endowed with a thickness of three barleycorns.
The remaining three channels, however, have a thickness of four barleycorns;
all of them are proclaimed to be two vitastis in length and coiled to the right. || 14 ||
There exist ten channels, beginning with Suṣumṇā and ending with Saṃkhyā;
however, the root of these three principal channels extends from the base to the penis. (15)
Among them, eighteen channels (nāḍīs) are recorded as being pierced by the [principal] channels:
Vimalā, Śoṣiṇī, Pṛthvī, Mahasī, and likewise Tejasī. || 16 ||
Vāyavī, Gaganī, Mardanī, Rodanī, Rasavādī, Mṛdaṅgī, and Saṅginī... || 17 ||
Thus, having completely enveloped the base of the thighs and the beautiful shanks on all sides.
They are declared to be long and indeed yellowish-brown;
these six, beginning with Śabda and Aṅga, arise at the root of the Iḍā.
This indeed is the tongue-canal; on the left foot it is like the right, having encircled the tip of the ankle once and coiled six times.
The remaining [channels] originate from the base of the *suṣumnā* and extend along the sides of the spinal column;
these, however, run obliquely from above the chest-bone toward the arms. (21)
Gaganī, Mardanī, and Rodanī are on the right hand;
Rasavādī, Mṛdaṅgī, and Saṅginī are on the left arm.
Covering one [shoulder] at the base of the arm, the tip [of the cloth] should be single across the three [parts];
