from its tip, there should be eight branches on the right and likewise on the left.
From the base to the tip of the upper arm, eight channels extend; O Brahmin, their tips are joined as one, and they are enclosed by the single wrist-joint.
One should perform [the rite] for each hand, whether there is one or many hands;
thus, for images, there are twenty-eight primary channels (nāḍīs). || 25 ||
The knower of the cosmic cycles (kalpa) should thus conceive of the primary channels;
furthermore, O Brahmin, their branches consist of sixty-four channels.
Therefore, the channels (nāḍīs), which completely pervade all the limbs, are manifold;
indeed, seventy-two thousand channels have been proclaimed.
One's own excrement, like the leaves of the *śūla*, *jīrṇa*, or *aśvattha* trees, or coconut fruit-skin, mixed with very little water; (28)
Having extracted the essence from the leather and having removed any other non-essential parts,
they fashioned those tubes, and afterwards, the tubes were covered.
One should prepare a strong cord six yavas in circumference;
thereafter, one should bind it tightly with two cords, turning it toward the south.
The wise one should cause an eight-petaled heart-lotus to be made with a cord; its stalk, reaching down to the navel, is bound together with the *suṣumnā*. (31)
Indeed, I have told you that this lotus is the abode of the individual soul (jīva);
having recollected the root mantra, perform this binding with a cord.
This is known as the "Rope-binding" (rajjubandha); hereafter follows the "Preparation of Clay" (mṛtsaṃskāra).
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter on the procedure for rope-binding in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*.
I shall describe the preparation of clay; listen briefly, O observer of noble vows!
Clay is of three kinds: from arid lands (jāṅgala), from marshy lands (anūrūpa), and even (sama). || 1 ||
Due to a lack of strength, digging until the end may result in a very firm mass of earth; when mixed with fine sand, it becomes impossible to dig out due to the resulting hardship. || 2 ||
In the *Garta* [mudrā], one sees a beautiful form that is consistent with its name;
because their appearance is as if blended together, it is called *Miśrabhū*. || 3 ||
On those delightful, pure grounds free from impurities and moisture,
or by a river or a large pond, [one should draw] a white, yellow, or black line.
Having collected the mud in vessels, one should strain it through a new cloth;
one should dry the mud in the vessel until it is saturated with the liquid extract.
One should first protect it with necklaces made from the wood of the four milky trees,
and then, after consuming water from the Arjuna tree, one should grind the cooked substance in a vessel.
One should dry it until it is capable of being formed into a pill;
then, having pierced it, one should dry it again and again with water infused with the three myrobalans (triphalā).
Having fashioned a lump from that clay mixed with the desired liquid, one should then see a line upon the lump in the hand; thereafter, fashion the lump.
In the case of the eightfold [mandala], it should not be measured with the standard finger-measure (mānāṅgula);
rather, a circumference of eleven fingers (rudrāṅgula) is declared to be most excellent and soft.
One should mix sand, śikhā, and cūrṇi, along with a portion of similar material that has been cut out, together with clay.

Having added one part of earth to the waters of the three myrobalans (triphalā), along with eight parts of water from the directions, seven parts of black pepper, and also wheat, [one should mix them] with the water from coconut fruits.
Then, after ten days have passed, one should thoroughly rub [the ingredients] in a vessel:
śrīveṣṭa, guggulu, and likewise kunduruṣka.
Likewise, the wise one should add powdered resin (sarjarasa) to a portion of clay equal to a sixteenth part,
mix the clay into a vessel, and knead it with curd.
Ginger, long pepper, black pepper,
and turmeric— these should be made into an equal powder and combined with one-tenth part of clay.
One should rub the clay in a vessel with honey, milk, and ghee;
then, take equal parts of the powders of *kapittha* and *bilva* resin. (15)
One should thoroughly rub the clay, mixed with its fifteenth part of powder and oil,
along with kuṣṭha and haritālaka, in the proper sequence.

p. 370) Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, yellow pigment (rocanā), and so forth, equal in measure to those [other ingredients], should be collected and ground into a powder, combined with ten parts of clay. || 17 ||
The best of preceptors should grind gold and silver powder together with linseed oil in an anthill hole where crabs dwell.
One should especially take earth from a long river, from fields where crops have grown, from the shore of the ocean, from the tusk of an elephant, and from the horn of a bull. (19)
Having gathered whatever is available, combined with various fragrances,
the wise man should grind it with the juice of wood-apple sap or with honey.
Then, after five nights have passed, one should take the inner bark from a coconut fruit,
measuring one and a half finger-breadths in length.
The wise one should cut [the wood] to a measurement of two finger-breadths thick;
then, combined with clay on the fourth day, he should begin the application of the middle layer.
Above that, having smeared it with clay, one should then wrap it with a rope;
O Brahmin, the space between those ropes should be one, two, or three finger-breadths.
O twice-born one, after applying clay over that as well, one should observe it until it is dry;
meanwhile, the application of clay should be performed very gradually.
On the exterior of the trident, having divided the width into four parts,
it is described as being smeared up to one part, according to the proportions.
The mixed [type of land] should have two parts at the end; however, the *jāṅgala* type is free from fire.
One should smear the portion of the altar there with the very soil of that respective region.
Having filled the remainder of the paste with one-sixteenth part of the total,
one should apply that remaining paste, mixed with cotton-seed oil.
This is known as the preparation of clay; now the preparation of the paste is described.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the preparation of clay, the eighty-sixth [chapter] in the *Aṃśumat* of the *Kāśyapa*. 86.
Now, I shall describe the procedure for preparing the medicinal paste (kalka) in brief and in due order:
[it may be done] at a river, or a pond, or even at a large oblong pool.

Likewise, O Brahmin, in a field of grain, or in auspicious water containing three kinds of minerals, where the tips of the stalks are well-formed and uniform, and which rests upon coarse sand; || 2 ||
Having gathered the sugar of these [ingredients], grind it and perform the washing;
having dried the sugar, make it into a fine powder.
Having cleansed it with water from the three myrobalans (triphalā) and formed it into a ball, one should dry it;
the water of the exudation of the *kapittha* tree is said to be of three kinds.
One should take five parts of resin, or five and a half, or sixfold; likewise, one part of clear boiled water—these are the proportions stated in sequence.
One should grind the mass with the clear water of the sprinkling until it becomes like fresh butter;
thereafter, having mixed it with cotton-wool, one should thoroughly knead it.
But that which is distinct from the paste is like the fibers within the trunk of a plantain tree;
having first smeared this very paste, one should indeed apply the paste itself. (7)
From the resin, [the quantity] is threefold, or three and a half times, or fourfold;
for the *marīci* and the three fruits (*triphalā*) are likewise recited as being of these three kinds. (8)
Having moistened them with water, one should rub them repeatedly;
then, one should gradually apply the paste, making it thick by two or three barley-corns [in thickness].
Having gradually and sequentially plastered it so that it is free from cracks and holes,
one should then allow it to dry for two months, or a month and a half, or even just one month.
Then, O Brahmin, having placed the brush, one should grind the remaining ingredients in sequence;
thereafter, one should fill the vessel to its proper measure with clear water.
Having established the measurement many times over, one should bring it to completion;
then one should fashion the limbs, the minor limbs, and the sub-limbs, endowed with their characteristic marks.
The hands, feet, belly, and so forth are designated as the "limbs" (aṅga);
the ornaments are known as the "subsidiary limbs" (upāṅga); and the emblems and vehicles are the "minor limbs" (pratyaṅga). || 13 ||
From the resin of the *kapittha* tree itself, one should prepare a paste with water three and a half times its quantity;
then, having ground it, one should apply that paste as an ointment.
Then, having added a paste of that [substance] equal to one-eighth part of the barley, one should let it sit for ten days;
thereafter, one should sprinkle the resinous liquid with a brush and cause it to dry.
One should decorate it with ornaments above that, adorning it with auspicious marks; afterwards, having smeared it with a glossy substance, one should then apply white color.

Thus ends the description of the preparation of the *kalka* for the entire [mantra], according to Aṃśumat in the lineage of Kaśyapa. This is the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Preparation of the *Kalka*."
Now I shall explain in detail the characteristics of the refinement of the castes (varṇas),
as well as the true state that is beyond Śiva, which arises from the Unmanifest as peace.
From Śānti, Nāda together with Bindu is produced;
from that, Vyoman is produced; and from that, Anila arises. || 2 ||
From wind, fire is produced; from that, indeed, water is produced;
from that, the world was born; and within the world, the birth of the castes occurred.
It is of four kinds: white, red, yellow, and black.
That which arises in water has the appearance of white, while that which arises in fire has the appearance of red.
In the world [of fire], yellow is produced; in wind, black is produced.
Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Dhātṛ, and Rudra are, respectively, the lords of these colors.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as those of white complexion and so forth, exist;
O Brahmin, [the colors] are fourfold: white, red, yellow, and black.
Śveta, śukla, dhavala, avadātaka,
muktābha, induvarṇābha, and śvetavarṇa are recorded as synonyms for white.
That which has a color like a conch shell is declared by me to be "white-colored" (śuklavarṇa);
it should be as bright as silver and as pure white as cow's milk.
O Brahmin, it is described as being like a star and pure white;
furthermore, it is of four kinds: ruddy, red, crimson, and pale pink.
Aruṇa is like the blood of a rabbit; rakta is like the color of the Japā flower;
śoṇa has the luster of the Kiṃśuka flower; and pāṭala is like the essence of lac.
Realgar is of four kinds: golden-yellow, tawny-yellow, and greenish-yellow.
That which is equal in color to gold is called *svarṇa*; the tawny variety is like the essence of turmeric. (11)
Haritāla may be yellow, or green like the eye of a cat;
it is also of four kinds: blue, dark, black, and deep black.
It is dark blue like the color of a cloud, or dark-green like a wild crow; it is as black as a peacock's neck, or black like the wing of a house-crow.
Thus, the syllable is sixteenfold and independent;
it is red, born from the earth, the moon, the [letter] *cha*, and the feet of the swan (*haṃsa*). (14)

Alternatively, the mineral known as haritāla, which is born from the Godāvarī, is traditionally considered to be of two types according to its genus and characteristics, both of which have a reddish luster.
That which resembles the flower of the linseed plant is called *rājāvarta* stone;
that which has the essence of a dark stone is designated as *śyāma*. (16)
Furthermore, the powder produced from the lamp is declared to be black in color; such are the various colors of the *kalā* (fragrant paste), which therefore appear in that [lamp] in many ways.
Mṛccheda, lākṣāsāra, and likewise the dust arising from a lamp, as well as padma, aviri, and nīla—this is designated as the mineral (dhātu). || 18 ||
Thus, those who are independent and predominant [attain] the status of being worthy of the colored image in due order.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, the "Chapter on the Origin of Colors," in the *Aṃśumat* of the *Kāśyapa*. 88.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the color worthy of gold:
it should be yellow like yellow stone (pītāśman), or made like the powder of that stone. || 1 ||
When mixed with coconut water, it becomes like red curd;
that sudhā-karma would be red, while the conch-shell handle would be white.
The two stones, rājāvarta and śyāma, are both honored;
O observer of noble vows, others that possess a similar luster may also be used in rites involving sudhā.
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the color of the boar: it is declared to be a mixture of white and red, which is called "fair" (gaura). || 4 ||
That which is an equal mixture of white and yellow becomes variegated (karburaka). An equal mixture of white and black is declared to be smoke-colored (dhūmra). || 5 ||
White, black, and yellow, when mixed in equal proportions, this is known as *sāraśavi*, which is prescribed for the application of colors in ritual acts.
White and red mixed together are declared to be *karbūraka*;
red and yellow mixed in equal parts have the shape of the *bakula* fruit.
This supreme [color] is called Jvalanacchavi (Flame-skin) and is the color of fire;
when yellow is mixed with twice as much red, it becomes Atiraktaka (Exceedingly Red).
This color, which is like the rising sun, is called "varṇa. Gulavarṇaka is red doubled and mixed with yellow.
Half of that yellow, when mixed [with white], becomes tawny (kapila).
Yellow enriched with a fourth part of red becomes like the color of a śaphara fish. || 10 ||
When black is mixed with twice as much red, it becomes *kaṣāyaka*;
when white is mixed with twice as much yellow, it becomes *piṅgala*. (11)
For the white [pigment], yellow mixed with three parts of it is like the color of the *kalhāra* lotus;
for the black [pigment], yellow mixed with two parts of it is like the color of the *cubuka*.
That very complexion of men may be black or like yellow; it may be like yellow orpiment, like dark grey, mixed, or like the wing of a parrot.
That same substance, with an excess of yellow orpiment (haritāla), is declared to be *dhānyāṅkura*.
When it is dark-colored (*śyāma*) and rich in green orpiment, it contains half as much realgar (*manaḥśilā*) as yellow orpiment.
Mixed with grain it would be dark-green; black when combined with lac; and when accompanied by the fruit of the *jambū* tree, that is called "color" by me. (15)
That which is as red as lac or the essence of red sandalwood is called "equal in species and mark" (jātiliṅgasama);
that which is like black or blue is declared to be the mixed "hair-colored" (keśavarṇa). || 16 ||
Green like grain, red, and their mixture in eight colors;
black, equal to red, and mixed—these are declared to be the honey-colored [gems]. (17)
That very same [complexion], when there is an excess of rajas, is called the human color;
the human color has an excess of rajas and is dry, like a yellow myrobalan fruit.

Therefore, the color of the *nātra* has been described as being endowed with the luster of sapphire; among those [colors], that substance which is small yet possesses great measure [is the best]. (19)
That which has much substance but little value is known as "bahusāra"; the wise know that which has little substance but is highly valued as "alpasāra. (20)
"Thus, the suitability of the castes is based upon this very [principle].
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, the Section on Mixed Castes, in the *Aṃśumat* of the *Kāśyapa*. 89.
Now I shall describe in detail the excellent application of color; indeed, the application of color consists of three types: stone-based, clay-based, and that with *ṣaṣṭika* rice as its core. (1)
In the case of an image made of stone, the primary and secondary limbs are indeed composed of stone;
having covered it from above with a cloth, one should apply plaster over that.

Having smeared that area above with a smooth paste, and then having applied colors such as white and so forth until it resembles the intended form of the image, one should properly perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Alternatively, in the case of an image made of stone, having covered it with cloth from above,
one should apply a smooth coating of sugar paste the size of a barley grain.
One should apply white and the color of a mirror (bimba) in due order as appropriate;
this is known as "the stone-womb" (śilāgarbha), or one may use that very same [stone] with its colors distinguished.
The ritual for installing the sacrificial post (śūla) and so forth, including the wooden interior, is as before;
it may be painted in full or half-painted, and constructed with baked bricks and plastered with lime.
Having completed all the limbs, one should then cover the cloth; however, in the case of an image made of stone, all the materials such as sugar and the rest should be applied accordingly.
It should be constructed either with bricks, or mixed with wood and bricks;
thus, in these three ways, it is described as having a core of colored materials.
First, having smeared [the surface] with something resembling white, one should apply the color by means of very clear water,
smearing it in sequence with three types of water.
Above that, O best of the twice-born, one should apply a pale-colored plaster;
it should resemble a white orb and be well-mixed so as to be pale-white.
The bimbas should be white in color and possessed of a pale hue;
one should fashion them with a pale color that resembles the appearance of a blood-red glow.
The binding, the clear [inner part], and the middle—thus the belly becomes threefold;
one should fashion the triple-binding with the exudations of the wood-apple (*kapittha*). || 12 ||
That which is clear like oil is known as middling; that which resembles honey is superior; and that which has the appearance of clarified butter from curd is smooth and most excellent. (13)
One should perform the preparation of the mixed paste with thick water;
however, the task of kneading the paste should be carried out with medium water.
One should perform the grinding with water that is clear of dregs;
likewise, the work of whitewashing with water, and [the tanning] of cow and buffalo hides. (15)
The binding should consist of the essence of Pācya, and there should be a cloth for catching the water;
O twice-born one, where there is no water-catcher, there should be a Kapittha fruit.
He should not cause any other binding to be made with resinous water;
rather, having divided the paste into sixteen parts, he should use six, five, or four.
O best of the twice-born! He should apply a smooth, glossy ointment using the resin of the kapittha tree mixed with pure water. 18.
It would be a smooth, essence-like paste; such a thing would be smooth.
Upon the falling of water, it would be like a stream of plaster; upon the falling [of it], it would be like moist sugar. (19)
One should thus fashion the two types of *cikkaṇa* as appropriate;
however, for the *cikkaṇārhaka* type of *bandha*, it should be divided into ten parts.
A bond that lacks a single part is suitable for application with lime;
or a bond with a smooth surface is used for the work of white plastering.
Alternatively, it may be equal to the white-binding [measure], or even less than that;
for one of pale complexion, the binding should be performed with a pale-colored application applied three times.
Then, having inscribed the six syllables in their proper sequence,
the preceptor should likewise inscribe the syllable that is the very nature of the image six times.
The *pāṇḍubandha* occurs at the twentieth part; that water which is diminished by one part is called *bandha* for the first of the six groups of letters, according to Umā’s long discourse.
Then, the arrangement of syllables starting from that [first] should be reduced by one-twentieth;
such would be the arrangement of the second syllable, and the binding likewise.
In this manner, one should gradually increase the binding for all six types of bonds;
starting from the first, one should apply the appropriate bindings and inscribe the six syllables in sequence.
They know that these six—[the offering of] leaves, a drop, soup, ointment, a roll, and color—are the application of unguents. || 27 ||
That which is known as the "long leaf" (dīrghapatra) is indeed devoid of horizontal extension; that which is like a bed of mustard seeds is described as the "dot" (bindu). || 28 ||

The subtle drop (sūkṣmabindu), however, is the incense; therefore, it is indeed the subtle drop. That which is above its mouth is called the "named" (namākhya); that is high and divided by that. || 29 ||
One should apply a color-paste mixed with fine powder that brings about the desired hue;
indeed, one should thus apply the sequence of the six colors to one another.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter in the *Aṃśumat*, titled "The Chapter on the Sequence for Applying Color" within the *Kāśyapa*. 90.
Now I shall specifically describe the supreme characteristics of devotees;
for all devotees, there are indeed four types of stations. || 1 ||
Sālokya, Sāmīpya, Sāyujya, and likewise Sārūpya— O Brahmins, these fourfold distinctions have been declared.
Whether it be a man or a woman, the wise person should have an image fashioned according to the specific feet upon which that individual stands,
endowed with the marks of their own caste and established in the state of *sālokya*.
Likewise, there is proximity to the gods, or else my own characteristic form.
Those endowed with my characteristic form are indeed the remaining ones who rely upon the three steps;
they are proclaimed to be of three states: childhood, youth, and old age.
Starting from three years until the completion of sixteen years,
those devotees who have passed away within that interval of age are known as "children" (bāla).
Therefore, those endowed with youth until the end of the seventieth year are [considered young]; the wise know that those possessed of an age beyond that are "the aged. (7)
But the child, by means of five tālas and the remainder of his lifespan, [performs] standing posture, sitting posture, as well as riding and dancing. (8)
O wise one, my human devotees should be fashioned in four ways:
as having no division, having equal divisions, or indeed having excessive divisions—thus in three manners. (9)
Either the left foot or the right foot is contracted and placed upon the other;
both hands bear the specific marks of their respective classes, or they are joined in the *añjali* gesture at the heart. (10)
Holding a *ṭaṅka* in the right hand and displaying the boon-granting gesture (*varada*) with the left hand, one should adopt this standing posture with the hand characterized by its roughness. (11)
Or, like a lotus, one should rest the left foot upon a comfortable seat, while letting the right foot hang down; the hand should indeed be positioned as previously described.
Indeed, this is declared to be the posture; one should employ the Kuṭilāsana, holding a ṭaṅka in the right hand and a noose in the left hand.
Or, O Brahmin, one may fashion another vehicle-form according to reason or as it has been maintained.
Dance is declared to be of three kinds: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.
And that which is known as tāmasa—extending respectively to the external, the internal, and the innermost—I have declared to be suitable for devotees endowed with [appropriate] age. (15)
O observer of noble vows, listen! First, I shall describe the sattvic dance;
the manifestation and honor of the devotees shall occur as described in the Kalpas.
Alternatively, the measure of the bend is prescribed as six or seven finger-breadths;
he should place his left leg, which is bent, upon the lotus-seat. (17)
The right foot should be raised from the seat by the measure of four finger-breadths (mātrās),
or by five, six, or seven mātrās, according to the measurement for raising it from the seat.
The Brahma-sūtra is aligned with that [central line], reaching as far as the nail of His big toe.
From the wrist of His hand, the distance is thirteen finger-breadths;
they know the elbow on His hand to be the first point from the back-sūtra.
The wrist-joint shall be the boundary of the path; one should cause the hanging [cord] to hang down. || 21 ||
One should suspend the Brahma-sūtra from the middle of the forehead and the tip of the nose down to the midpoint of the navel, and from there to the middle of the soles of the feet.
To the left of that line, the center of the navel should be one and a half finger-breadths;
to the right of that line, [the distance] for the left hand is merely [one finger-breadth].
According to the Sūtra, [the image] should have the feet and knees aligned; it may measure six, seven, or eight units (mātras).
From the forehead to the end of the ankle, the measurement should be one eye-unit (akṣāṅgula).
The Brahmasūtra should touch the nose and the middle of the lips;
then one should touch the sūtra at the sides of the abdomen and also touch the tip of the nose. || 25 ||
Alternatively, with the right foot placed on a seat and the left foot raised, the rest [of the body] is aligned accordingly. (26)
The best of those skilled in ritual procedures should fashion [the image] as a child, either adorned with all ornaments, or entirely naked, or clothed, or wearing only a loincloth. (27)
Those who are young and those who are advanced in age, adorned with various garments—this is declared to be Sāttvika dance; now listen to the Rājasa, O observer of noble vows! || 28 ||
Alternatively, its needle or staff may be curved, or it may have joined hands (at the top);
or it may measure ten, nine, or eight units, with its feet raised from the pedestal.
The remainder should be performed as before; indeed, it is the same for the Rājasa [rite].
However, without the right hand holding the staff, one should touch the left hand or the crown.
Holding the staff in his right hand with his face slightly bowed,
he should lift one or two or three steps from his seat.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes and adorned with rosaries, he is indeed described as being of the nature of *tamas*; such is the characteristic of a devotee.
The mantra for devotees is said to consist of their own name, preceded by the syllable Om and ending with the word "namaḥ"; one should perform worship using that very mantra.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Devotees," in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*. 91.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of Caṇḍeśa;
indeed, the one who is a portion of Rudra’s star is designated as Caṇḍeśa. (1)
When the Lord is worshipped within the enclosure of Gaṇeśa, he becomes likewise [gracious].
[He holds] a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, and even a goad. (2)
The dagger, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and the staff—these shall be the eight weapons in the right hands;
likewise, the shield, the javelin, the noose, and the bell [are in the left]. (3)
Holding the gesture of granting boons (varada) and a tiger-skin in his right hands, and a needle and a serpent in his left hands;
he is endowed with a crown of matted hair and possesses a fierce gaze. || 4 ||
In the Tretā age, however, he has eight arms and a complexion like that of deep red;
he is known by the name Vikrāntacaṇḍa and possesses well-disheveled matted locks.
One should know his vehicle to be a horse with a slightly smiling face;
in his right hands, he holds the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, an axe, and a sword.
In the Dvāpara age, however, he has four arms, is golden-hued, rides upon a lion, and holds in his left hands the boon-granting gesture, a shield, a noose, and a bell.
Adorned with a circle of matted locks and a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
he holds a chisel and a trident in his right hands,
while in his left hands he holds a noose and a goad; he stands upon a noble throne.
In the Dvāpara age, he is proclaimed by the name Caṇḍeśa with two arms;
but in the Kali age, he has two arms, is peaceful, and is adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Either endowed with a circle of matted locks or else with bound hair, appearing black or even red, and possessed of a gentle face and eyes. (11)
(385) It may be with a bend, or evenly bent, or in a standing posture with feet even;
if there is a bend, the right foot is contracted while the other remains standing.
Alternatively, with the right foot standing and the other drawn up,
this position or posture is known by the name Vīracaṇḍeśa.
If he is seated, one should cause his left foot to rest [on the ground] while the other is suspended;
or likewise, his right foot may be resting while the left is suspended.
He holds a ṭaṅka in his right hand and the gesture of granting boons (varada) in his left;
or else both hands are joined at the heart in añjali, with the ṭaṅka held appropriately within.
Or if the flower is lacking its stalk, it should be held in the hollowed palms as a garland;
or else, with the face slightly inclined toward the right side.
The bull is known as his vehicle, and he wears excellent white garments;
thus, Ādicaṇḍeśa is described as being of four kinds.
Regarding the retinue of the images, the stated measurement is prescribed:
one should fashion the entire body of the smallest [image] at ten tālas. || 18 ||
The characteristics of Caṇḍeśa have been declared; now his proportions are being stated.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of Caṇḍeśa, in the Āśumān of Kāśyapa. 92.
Now I shall describe the specific dimensions in detail; listen, O observer of noble vows!
It may be equal in its base and its apex, or likewise unequal at the top.
The shape of the womb, the half-moon, the triangle, the circle, the pentagon, the hexagon, the heptagon, and the octagon. (2)
The form has been described by Rudradhā; now I shall state the method of measurement.
One should measure the entire site from east to west and from south to north.
*Bhuja*, *hasta*, and *kara* are synonyms for the arm; likewise, *pārśva* is a synonym for the side. Furthermore, the upper part of the leg or the thick portion of the foot is called *bhuja*. (4)
Thus has the equal-sided [altar] been described, as well as the elongated one;
now listen to the specific distinction regarding the irregular-sided one. || 5 ||
By joining the two hands, right and left, together, there shall be half an arm;
by doubling that measure, one obtains the length of a full arm. (6)
The half-moon has been fully described; now hear about the triangle.
One should measure the hand-span within the triangles using a measuring rod.
Half of that, with fewer cubits, would be the most excellent of the excellent (uttamottama) for its side; those with great arms should measure it starting from a barley-corn down to a pebble.
Thus the triangle has been described; now hear about the circular form.
I shall not divide it into parts of *kalā*; its width is five parts.
Having divided that radius into fifteen parts, one should discard two parts;
the remainder, which is thirteen parts, shall be the side of the circle.
That same [shape] is known as *alpabhujā*, and it becomes *mahāhasta*;
thus the circle has been fully described, and now the five stages (*pañcāśrama*) are being explained.
This is declared to be equal for pentagons, hexagons, and heptagons, starting from the center of the safe [sector] up to the center of the side. (12)
When divided by that measurement, the wise one should measure the circumference;
and for those [lines] situated outside the circumference, he should measure them as in the case of a triangle.
Thus has the five-fold hermitage been described; now the eight-fold hermitage is being explained.
At the ends of the arms, within the great quarters, [lines] directed eastward and northward [should be drawn].
The wise one should lay down two threads each; there are five [threads] for the four-cornered [figure], and four for the triangle and the quadrangle, arising from that. 15.
The wise man should measure that four-cornered [figure] and the triangle as before;
thus has the eight-cornered [figure] been described, and the remainder should be performed with logical application.
A square [plot] measured by five daṇḍas is known as the *kāka* according to the rule;
one-quarter of that is five māṣas, and four such quarters constitute a *pāṭikā*.
One should join together a square consisting of fifteen *krośas*, two of which are half-*karṇas* (ear-lengths), while the third is said to be a full *karṇa*. || 18 ||
Thus has the nature of the ground been explained; now the village and so forth will be discussed.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, the "Section on the Ritual for the Earth," in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] by Kāśyapa. 93.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of villages and other settlements,
beginning with a length of fifteen *daṇḍas* and increasing by two *daṇḍas* at each step.
The extent of villages and other settlements is declared to be nineteen *daṇḍas*, forty-three *bhedas*, and four *atyābhāsas*. (2)
The first class, however, consists of one hundred punishments and so forth, increasing by ten-fold increments up to a maximum of eight thousand; thus there are thirty such classes.
The beans, having been gathered together, shall become fivefold through illusion;
for the sake of the perfection of the elements beginning with earth, the punishment is ordained without the cutting of the staff.
Whether inferior or superior, it may be grasped as vital energy (ojas);
O twice-born one, the increase is double that of the sun, amounting to three hundred [units] for the Brahmins.
One hundred and sixteen, and likewise two hundred and fifty;
these are declared to be the threefold divisions of the site (vāstu) presided over by Brahmins.
And there are twenty-four thousand varieties, which are of three kinds;
[furthermore], the divisions of meters (chandas) are of three kinds, numbering seven thousand, six thousand, and five thousand.
The number twelve thousand, ten thousand, and likewise eight thousand; thus, according to the distinction of their origin, there are three types.
O best of the twice-born! There is another ninefold division of manifestation, beginning with one and ending with nine, which consists of the power of manifestation and its absolute non-existence.
The wise know that the length of the arms and the flood of the [forearm] are derived from the same;
the intelligent man should increase it by eight and divide the product by eight. (10)
The remainder [indicates] the flag and so forth as the birth sign (yoni), and likewise the affliction-tree;
furthermore, from the remainder of half of thirty, the Nandā and other treasures arise.
The Sun, the maker of day, is devoid of his host of rays during the eclipse;
he has an excess of income but diminished expenditure, yet he remains the very seat of all prosperity.
The *yoni*, the *dhūma*, the *dhāna*, and likewise the *kharakāka*—these would mutually increase one another's diseases, afflictions, fears, and sufferings. (13)
The banner, lion, bull, and elephant bring happiness;
on the days of Venus and the Moon there is growth, and on Thursday it bestows prosperity. (14)
Avoiding other days of the week and so forth, which would be a source of distress if undertaken, the lunar days Bhadrā, Jayā, and Pūrṇā are indeed auspicious. (15)
If the Nandā tithi is empty (riktā), it is inauspicious for the installation of Śrī-Śrikāma;
however, the path [of the ritual] should be determined by the birth star of the performer and so forth, bounded by that specific day.
One should count the birth asterism, the Veda, as well as the season;
the eighth and ninth days are excellent, as are the birth-day and so forth, again and again. (17)

The others are to be honored, but one should avoid those that lead to destruction; having fixed upon the twelfth lunar mansion as the auspicious moment, one should avoid the Asura lagna with deliberate intent.

One should apply the lunar days, weekdays, and so forth, while avoiding what is unsuitable; likewise, one should avoid the day of birth, the day of death, the house-day (dvāstu), and names that are in conflict with the asterism (nakṣatra). || 19 ||
Having thus examined it in many ways, hear now concerning the arrangement [of the signs]:
Aries, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Libra, and Scorpio.
When the Sun has entered Aquarius or Capricorn, and the lunar fortnight and asterism are auspicious,
the commencement of a village and the like is excellent, as is the commencement of a house.
When the sun is situated in Sagittarius, Pisces, or Virgo,
one should not undertake the founding of a village, nor should one cause such contrary works to be performed.
O twice-born one, how is it that disease and grief are said to exist for those dwelling there? For that place is presided over by Brahmins and is possessed of impurity and misfortune. (23)
That which was formerly known as Nṛpavāsa shall become Vaiśyānāṃ Nāgara; the villages shall be Anyavāsa, and it is celebrated as Kuṭikā.
It is renowned as Kheṭaka and celebrated as Viṭapa;
it is endowed with all castes and engaged in the activities of buying and selling.
It was filled with goods from other continents, such as fine cloth, jewels, and wealth;
and by the side of the oceans, it extended as far as the ocean itself.
The conduct of each [of these] has been declared; the remainder is to be understood through reasoning and verbal description:
[the killing of a mountain-like elephant] in water, or in a forest, or in a mountain battle. (27)
Whether by gods, bhūtas, or piśācas, it serves as a harmful instrument for mortals;
it is endowed with all types of beings and possessed of all substances. (28)
O Brahmin, that which is joined with a royal palace is known as Vartadurga;
perform the demarcation of the directions according to the previously mentioned rule.
Having made the ground level, one should perform the placement of the steps;
thus, the entire foot [measure] shall be formed, while the *pecaka* consists of four feet.
The seat (pīṭha) is said to consist of nine parts, and the great seat (mahāpīṭha) consists of sixteen parts;
there should be twenty-five secondary seats (upapīṭha) and twenty-six secondary seats.
The sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) shall consist of seven parts each of seven [units], and the Maṇḍūka [portion] shall be eight parts;
together with ninety-six [additional units], this constitutes the hundred-fold auspicious great seat (śatabhadra-mahāsana).
The lotus-womb (*padmagarbha*) is declared to be two hundred and twenty-five;
with six additional parts and five more, it becomes three hundred and thirty-one. (33)
The enjoyment consisting of two hundred and eighty-nine seats is proclaimed;
and that which consists of three, six, and four is proclaimed as the Karṇoṣaka. || 34 ||
And it consists of well-composed words, totaling forty-four feet. || 35 ||
It is eighty-four cubits long, four hundred cubits wide,
five parts of which are fifty-five cubits, and its breadth is fifteen large units.
Seven hundred and sixty-five are known as the "womb of the Brahmin" (vipragarbha);
it consists of five hundred and twenty-six [units] together with the compartments (*koṣṭha*).
The sixty-seven and the sixty-six are for the enjoyment of Brahmins; the seventy-nine and the seven hundred are for the rejection by Brahmins. (38)
The Viśālākṣa-pada consists of eight hundred and eighty-seven parts;
for the Brahmins, it consists of eight hundred and fifty-one parts.
This is declared to be the essence of Viśveśa, consisting of nine hundred parts;
when increased by one hundred and eight, it constitutes the thousand-fold manifestation of the Lord.
It is joined with twenty-four thousand heart-pleasing [units];
half of the village-layouts shall consist of thirty paces. || 41 ||
Among those, first there is a fivefold division: the "excessive appearance" (atyābhāsa) and the "non-appearance" (abhāsa);
at the end of that is the "appearance equal to that" (tatsamābhāsa), which concludes with the "conceptual" (savikalpa).
At the end of the fivefold alternatives, the division of the meters (chandas) is prescribed;
there shall be a division of the remaining classes, which constitutes the sequence for the half-arrangement.
In all architectural sites (vāstu), the site-plan follows the will of the builder.
In the even portion, it is at the center of the thread; in the odd portion, it is at the middle of the square.
One should construct all the various [elements] and not cause anything else to be made;
the width of the pathway (vīthi) should be one, two, three, four, or five daṇḍas.
The path situated in the center of the site, facing either east or north,
is known as the Brahmavīthī and is also called the Nābhivīthī.
That which is surrounded on the outside is called the auspicious path (vīthi-maṅgala);
that very path is the "hip" (jaghana), and here it is called the chariot-path (ratha-vīthi).
The royal road is said to be connected with the gate-quarters; that which is connected with the side-gates is designated as the *nārā*. 48.
The road facing north is known as Kṣudrārgalā;
it is praised by the name of the path for the Vīthīnārācaka and other [military formations]. (49)

Especially in villages and the like, as well as in other places designated by names, and among the people on the streets, the Vaṣṭhā [constellation] brings about happiness through domestic activities. (50)
The desired [proportion] is not determined by the fourfold sūtra-junctions and so forth;
therefore, construct the house according to your desire upon the prescribed measurements.
Outside the main thread, however, there is the obstruction of the subsidiary threads and so forth;
at the front of the first path, the house rises outside the ritual area.
The *daṇḍaka*, the *svastika*, and the *prastāra* are proclaimed; as well as the *nandyāvarta*, the *parāga*, the *padmaka*, and the *śrīpratiṣṭhita*. (52)
The classification of the site (*vāstu*) should be known as eightfold, each being established in many ways.
There may be a single street in the shape of a staff, facing either the east or the north. (54)
That which is joined with two wings, possesses a backbone like a staff,
and terminates at each opening, is called a *daṇḍaka*.
There should be one path facing east and one facing north in the middle;
thus, with the *karkarī* and the staff-like structure, there is an exit from the house toward the four directions.
That very [area] is the surrounding path (vīthī), which is provided with outer wings;
likewise, it extends to the portion of Parjanya, the portion of Pūṣan, and similarly to that of Dauvārika.

O best of the twice-born! When the portion of the Nāgas has been traversed, it shall be half the way to the house; at that point, O best of the twice-born, the street shall end where the path of the people terminates.
In the intervals between the streets there should be a lattice, or it may be a vaulted roof within the range of the wind;
this indeed is the "Glory-Bringing Staff" (Śrīkara-daṇḍaka), which provides the excellence of a staff for all.
That same [configuration], excluding the two [lines] at the navel and the svastika, is called the *guṇavīthī*; it has its tips pointing eastward and likewise northward. (60)
O best of the twice-born! A mandala (prastara) constructed with four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine squares is known as the "all-pervading" (sarvabheda). || 61 ||
The *nīva* and the *śrīkara-daṇḍaka* should be formed by the portion of the path;
the Vedic path (*vedavīthī*) should have its front facing east and likewise facing north.
It may consist of five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, or even thirteen lines; thus, the *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous) type is of nine kinds.
O Lord, one should likewise arrange the entry of Mahendra, Grahakṣata, and Puṣpadanta into the body of Bhallāṭa. (64)
The path of fire (vahnivīthī) should face east and have thirteen lines running northward;
it may consist of fourteen, six, or seventeen squares.
This *nandyāvarta* [maṇḍala] is prescribed here with five varieties;
its entry into the sectors beginning with Mahendra is to be performed as in the *prakīrṇaka*.
The chariot-path should face east, while the sixteen [paths] face north;
there are twenty-three paths for a single [type of] chariot, and the supreme tradition is eightfold.
The "parā" [measure] is to be performed as before; now the secondary doors (upadvārāṇi) are described:
in the portion of Parjanya, in the portion of Antarikṣa, and in the portion of Puṣya... || 68 ||
If there is Parāga associated with the eight secondary doors, located in the Dauvārika, the Pāpāṃśa, and the Codikāṃśaka divisions; || 69 ||
Facing east, there should be seven rows; facing north, twenty-one.
Up to twenty-eight, they increase by one each time.
Thus, the eightfold characteristic of the glorious Pratiṣṭhita [temple] is known;
it is endowed with eight main gates and accompanied by eight secondary gates.
Alternatively, one may likewise [employ] Vedeśa or Upaveśa as before;
furthermore, there is the distinction of the eight garments beginning with Daṇḍaka, as well as Hinaka.
One should divide the extent of the village and other areas into fifteen parts according to the sun and dharma,
and then take a seventeenth part of those parts consisting of mountains.
(395) Now hear the rule for the division of parts according to the sequence of the elements (bhūta), the Vedas, and the fires:
O Brahmin, outside the measuring-line (mānasūtra), there shall be an inner space consisting of six types.
It may be one, two, three, four, or five cubits in width;
or it may be three, five, seven, nine, or eleven cubits [in length]. || 75 ||
Alternatively, it is declared that [the height] may be thirteen cubits, or specifically eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, sixteen, or seventeen cubits. (76)
Having made the base [of the structure] from that [material], one should fashion it with stones, bricks, or clay, having its width at the top equal to one part.
Having a variegated luster or appearing like a bubble, with a form resembling a chameleon,
one should perform the rite at the secondary gate of the rampart, near the summit of the embankment.
One who performs the work with a paste of *karāla*, *mudga*, *gulma*, and *uṣa* should smear a hundred thousand [units] above; for those two as well, one desiring prosperity should do so with bricks.
One should cover it with earthenware, wooden vessels, or grass and the like; both on its exterior and interior, it should be encircled by a frame of mats.
For the sake of providing shelter, one must especially protect the bees and other such creatures;
outside of that [structure], it should be enclosed by a pathway made of bricks.
O Brahmin, one should construct a moat outside with the desired measurement; within the embankment, the installation of the deities should take place.
O best of the twice-born, the temple of Śiva and the hall of the Mothers may be located outside, or even on the near side of the moat, without any fixed rule.
In the portion of Āditya, there shall be Bhānu; in the south-east (Āgneyī), the temple of Kālikā;
in the portion of Bhūta, the house of Viṣṇu; and in Sugrīva, the abode of the Sugata.
One should place the temple of Jina in the northeast (padoṃkāra) or in the west (payakṣa), Vināyaka in the northwest,
and the stable for horses in the north, along with the subjugation of Virgo (Kanyā).
The abode of the mantras should be in the north, the northwest, or the northeast;
likewise, the temple of Śiva may be situated within these directions or even in the intermediate space between them.
O Brahmin, whether the deity is Jaya in the portion of Parjanya, or Mahendra in the portion of Indra, or even Varuṇa in his own portion, a temple of Śiva should be constructed. 87.
The chamber of the Mothers should be made facing outward from the temple of Śiva;
Viṣṇu faces inward, while Vivasvat faces westward.
All the remaining [deities] should be made facing east according to the prescribed ritual,
whether at the intersection of the threads, at the quadruple junction, or even at the eight points of the Śiva-diagram.
One should not construct a temple at the front of a street within a group of six [houses];
however, one may arrange for ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth everywhere.
The assembly hall is in the portion of Brahmā; the temple of Hari is in that of Varuṇa;
outside is the area for potters in the portion of Śakra, and for barbers in that of Śaṅkara.
To the south, indeed, is the residence of the Romadaṇḍins and the Karuṇas;
it is said that the Matsyopajīvanas dwell to the west.
And in the Śāṅkara [courtyard], the purchase of goods and their ornamentation should take place near it;
whether outside or inside the rampart, artisans and others should be stationed in a windless spot.
Outside of that, not very far away, there should be the house of the washermen; it should be located in the south-eastern direction from Mahendra, where food, both hard and soft, is sold. (94)
The sale of garments, rice, grains such as coriander and the like, salt in the north, as well as oil, sandalwood, and flowers [is forbidden]. 95.
Outside of that, at a distance of one krośa, the dwelling of the Caṇḍālas is said to be located;
and further outside, at a distance of one hundred daṇḍas, is the cremation ground belonging to Śaṅkara.
Or, in the northwestern direction, there should be a cremation ground, especially when [the site] is being consecrated;
the measurement line for the boundary should extend outside, reaching the interval between the walls.
Gold, gems, and so forth should be placed outside in every case.
The characteristics of villages and the like have been declared; now hear concerning the layout of houses. 98.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter in the *Aṃśumat-kāśyapa*, concerning the characteristics of villages and other settlements. 94.
Now, the image (bera) is prescribed as being made of copper, stone, or wood.
An earthen image is superior to one made of wood, and a stone image is the most excellent of all, even better than the earthen one.

If the fixed image (dhruvārcā) is made of stone, that which is made of copper is primary; otherwise, one may make it of stone or copper. The height of the mobile image (bera) should be half the height of the fixed image, which is the best measure. || 2 ||
From the portion of the qualities (*guṇāṃśa*), take two parts from the middle; from that middle part, take one-fifth part.
Having divided the half extending from its abode into two, take the latter half and divide it into twenty-six parts; from that, take one part of the former half.

One should join them together one by one; thus its height becomes twenty-seven [units]. Of the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra), it should be four-fourths, three-fourths, two-fourths, or half of five parts, or half of the womb [of the sanctum].
Its other half should be made as before. This applies to either the height of the pedestal (pāda) or the height of the door (dvāra).

The base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be one-quarter less than that, or half, or three-quarters less, or reduced by one-eighth; it may be equal to one-quarter, one-half, three-quarters, one-and-a-quarter, or double the height of the pillar. According to that measurement, using the *guṇāṃśa* hand-measure (*hasta*) where one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) is twenty-five [units], starting from twenty-five fingers...
The measurement up to forty fingers increases by two fingers at each stage; it does not remain otherwise.

Having divided that measurement into eight parts on all sides, there are nine varieties [of face] according to whether one, two, three, or four parts are added to the eyes, the nose, the arms, and the breasts. Having determined the desired measurement among these, [one proceeds].

From the feet up to the uṣṇīṣa, one should cause the *dhruva* (the fixed image) to be made. That [image] is of three kinds: *citra* (painted), *citrārgha* (half-painted), and *citrābhāsa* (reflected). The best is the *citra*; the middling is the *citrārgha*.
The *citrābhāsa* consists of six measures (*māna*) together with the half-measure of the width of the *citra*; it is the *ardhacitra* (quarter-image) by virtue of its height and breadth.

The inferior [image] appears as if effortless; it may be made entirely of metal or entirely of clay. One should not have it made variegated, nor half-variegated, nor half-variegated at all. If one were to do so, it would become malevolent (*ābhicārika*). One should have it made of metal, wood, or variegated, or even half-[variegated]. The *ābhāsa* [image] refers to what is to be painted on cloth, walls, and so forth, or on a physical form (*bera*).

Worship with a painted image (*citrārca*) bestows fruits both in this world and the next; worship with a half-painted image (*ardhavicitrārca*) bestows fruits only in the next world; and worship with a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*) bestows fruits only in this world. Furthermore, that semblance is of two kinds: "immovable" (*acala*), which is what is painted on an immovable wall, and what is painted on a cloth (*laṃpaṭa*).

Therefore, one should have [the image] made as immovable. Having performed the purification of the fixed icon (*dhruvabera*) by drawing its reflection upon a wall so as to captivate the eyes, the measurement of the Goddess is as follows: the measurement of the two goddesses is up to the end of the arms and breasts, or up to the end of the neck. For others, it is the remainder of twenty parts of the *manu*.

The attendants should be made equal to those respective [deities], or one-quarter less, or half, or according to the capacity of their respective shrines. One should have Brahmā and Śaṅkara made equal to the *dhruvabera* (the permanent image), or nine-tenths, or eight-tenths of its size. With whatever material the deity was fashioned, with that...
One should have the image, from the Goddess down to the retinue, fashioned according to the sequence of their respective shrines using the prescribed materials.
Thus ends the chapter on the rules for the proportions of the height of the images, as proclaimed by Marīci in the Śrī Vaikhānasa.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of images;
the syllable *pra* is known to destroy sins, while the syllable *ti* is understood as pacifying (*śāntika*). (1)
The letter *ma* brings about an increase in sons, and the letter *na* shall bestow merit; the measurement of the primary image (*mūlabera*) should be made according to the proportions of the temple.
One should cause images to be made by dividing them into two parts: the portion consisting of the base (ālaya) and the portion consisting of the figure (janman). || 3 ||
One should know that the best [height] for the principal image is one and a half, two-thirds, or two parts; the middle [height] is three-quarters of a part.
A fourth part is proclaimed as the lowest portion; likewise, there are the highest, the middle, the low, and the smallest.
One should determine the measurement for the images;
having then deliberated upon what is appropriate and inappropriate, one should have the images fashioned.
The procedure for the selection of stones (p. 401): The procedure for taking the stone;
those [stones] that possess internal cores are to be recognized by their external characteristics.
Having marked them, one should smear [them with ointment]...
Brahmā, Vajrapāṇi, Śūlapāṇi, and Vaiṣṇava. || 1 ||
Then, having mixed it with goat’s milk, one should smear the stone;
whatever part becomes moistened by that application after being left for one night, [that shall be extracted]. || 2 ||
One should recognize [the signs] within the womb: a white cow, a snake, or a scorpion;
and when black [substances] have decayed, one should soak ferrous sulfate (*kāsīsa*) and yellow *lodhra* in cow’s milk. (3)
When the stone smeared with that [substance] takes on the appearance of blood,
then for three days it should be left with barley-meal, having likewise remained overnight.
That state is to be understood there as being like a tortoise; of this there is no doubt.
Here, the Earth is Śūlinī, while the Brahma-world, the Earth, and the milk are what remains.
When smeared with the end of a stone, it bestows fearlessness from blood;
there, a black snake or even a lizard may appear.
Having ground together a small amount of karavīra, kuṣṭha, and the three myrobalans (triphalā),
one should nourish [the mixture] with breast milk alone.
If there were a stone capable [of removing it], one might apply it;
however, one should not touch the kālakūṭa poison with the hand. || 8 ||
Having thus ascertained the characteristics of the planets, one should begin the selection of the stone;
then, having established the stone, one should subsequently prepare the ground nearby.
Then the Guru:
Having sprinkled [it] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Pavamāna hymns,
[he should offer] fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings as well.
Having offered the *sadya* and other mantras with the left hand, one should perform the full worship upon the stone;
then, on its eastern side, one should commence the rite of fire-offering (*homa*).
Having made that linga-width fivefold and rendered it square,
one should take two parts of its diagonal, or twice that, or even half of that.
That which is known as the "extent of the pedestal" (pīṭhavyāsa) is three or four times that;
the width of the inner sanctum (garbhageha) should be equal to that, or the wall may be equal to the inner sanctum.
One-third [of the width] or half of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) is known as the width of the fire-altar (agnivyāsa);
it is measured from the śaktika as before.
A portion of Rudra (eleven parts) is declared to be the width of the pedestal-tower (*pīṭhatāra*);
by that [unit], the width of the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*) is two, three, or fourfold.
Having contracted the *nālīgṛha* by one part or even three-quarters, it is called the *bhittikā* as before; its width (*nāha*) is that of a portion of Rudra.
Once the area has been made square, the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is declared to be equal to its diagonal; or it may be twice, three times, or four times that [diagonal].
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be large; its wall-extension should be half of that, or one-fifth, or one-ninth, or even one-twelfth [of the width of the sanctum]. (7)
One should fashion the height as one-fourth or one-eighth [of the base], as previously described;
it should be a quadrangle at the height of the portion for worship, or a double quadrangle.
The width of the *karṇa* (corner) should be broad, and the width of the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) is declared to be two, three, four, or five times that.
O best of the twice-born, the width of the wall is known to be one part out of three, four, five, or six [parts of the whole], as previously described for rites of pacification and prosperity.
When the distance between the Rudra-lines is doubled and made into a square, it is known as the "extended ear-base" (karṇapīṭha); twice that [square] is the width of the inner sanctum (garbha).
Alternatively, its width is said to be three, four, or even five times that [thickness],
or it is stated to be a portion of the wall's thickness divided into three, four, or five parts.
When the circumference of the portion for the pedestal (pūjāṃśa) is divided into sixteen parts,
the platform (mañca) should be square in appearance and as wide as the ear-base (karṇapīṭha).
The spacious *nāligeha* should be twice, thrice, or even four times that size; the thickness of its walls should be half of that.
The inner wall of the sanctum (garbhakuḍya) should be one-fourth, one-eighth, one-sixteenth, or even one-thirtieth part [of the total width],
as previously described.
A wise man, having made the diameter of the liṅga and its width into a square,
states that the diameter of the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is one-tenth of that diagonal.
p. 404) The width of the tube-house (nālīgṛha) should be two, three, four, or five times that; the thickness of its wall should be half of that. || 17 ||
One should cause the width of the floor to be divided into three, four, five, six, or seven parts, and its height to be one such part, just as previously described. (18)
The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is declared to be three times the diameter of the liṅga;
or it may be two or three times that, which constitutes the width of the hollow chamber (nālīgeha).
The width of the wall should be half, a third, a fourth, or one part [of the total];
for rites of pacification and prosperity, it should specifically be performed as previously described.
In the case of a square *viṣkaṃbha*, the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) should then be one and a half times the diagonal,
or twice, or one and a half times twice, or three times [the side length].
Therefore, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be two, three, four, or five times [the width of the door],
equal to the breadth of the pedestal (pīṭha), one and a half times that, or twice that.
The width of the wall is known as *vyāsa*, and its height is indeed the same as that;
the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is declared to be double that of the portion for worship.
The width of the wall is declared to be two, three, four, or five times that [unit], or half of it, or three-quarters, or one-third. (24)
The best of instructors should arrange for the rites of pacification and prosperity as before;
in inferior cases or those of inferior dimensions, [the measurement] is divided by two, eight, or ten.
O twice-born one, each of these— the extent of the pedestal (pīṭha), the extent of the wall (kuḍya), and likewise the extent of the house with its towers (harmya)— should be made in nine ways.

Whether it has one or many stories, or is provided with towers, inner chambers, and so forth—whether supported by a foundation or free-standing—construct it according to the previously mentioned rule. (27)

In this way, for the self-manifested (svāyaṃbhūva) liṅgas, those known as Bāṇa-liṅgas, and for liṅgas made of jewels or metal, the length of the pedestal, the neck, and the chamber [is specified]. 28.
One should indeed have it made especially for the welfare of all the world;
its base should be thick, its head thick, and its middle part thick according to the tradition of the sages.
In a large area, one should not collect even a supporting pillar;
one should collect stones and the height [of the structure], excluding the measurement of the head (the pinnacle). || 30 ||
I do not worship those of other genders, such as the human form and so forth, even three times sevenfold;
rather, from among those lingas, I worship that which is situated to the right within the center.
Having set aside the central line of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should likewise establish the central line of the temple (prāsāda) and the center of the door. || 32 ||
One should construct the temple by fashioning the sūtra according to the *nema*-yukti; for whatever measurement was established for the linga, that same measurement shall apply to the residence.
Whether it be a pair or an even number of hands, one should complete the cutting of the hand-measures;
[the dimensions] may be less or more by a range from a *yava* up to a *rasa* (twelve).
The interior of the temple (*garbhagṛha*) should be square, with its length equal to its width.
That [measurement] may be one-fourth, one-half, one-and-a-quarter, double, or triple [the standard]. || 35 ||
The wall is known to be as long as the interior of the sanctum (garbhagṛha) and half as wide;
alternatively, it may be three-quarters or one-third [of that length], while the remainder is exactly as previously described.
In the Nāgara style, there are peaceful forms; in the Drāviḍa, those of the *rājasa* temperament;
and in the Vesara, dancing forms as well as fierce and processional forms. (37)
The temple should be constructed sequentially according to its specific principles;
those who desire the fruit of all prosperity must not act in a contrary manner. || 38 ||
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, the section on Liṅgas and Temples, in the *Aṃśumat* [treatise] of the *Kāśyapa* school. || 95 ||
Now I shall explain in detail the supreme procedure for the restoration of the decayed;
just as an embodied being abandons a worn-out body, so too is another [body] prescribed [to take its place]. (1)
Then, when that body has decayed, the asuras and others who depend upon its qualities [will take possession];
therefore, one should swiftly and with effort perform the restoration of the decayed [body]. || 2 ||
Whether it be a liṅga, a temple image, a palace, a pavilion, a gateway, a rampart, or a retinue— if these have become dilapidated, that indeed possesses the characteristics [of decay].
With that material, one should construct, as previously described, a cage, a peaked-roofed chamber, or a large or small nose-ornament (mahānāsya).
The ground, the pedestal, the materials, the altar, the lattice-work, and the archway—
whichever of these parts has become damaged, that part should be restored as it was before.
If the sandals and so forth, or the dwelling, are broken or torn, or if a transgression occurs,
one should discard those items and proceed with the first bricks and other materials as in the initial commencement.

p. 407) In the case of pride and the other [afflictions], that which is superior should be rendered inferior by means of their corresponding characteristics. However, through delusion, if one performs the reverse—making the inferior superior—it results in the depletion of the practitioner's wealth and lifespan. || 7 ||
These [planets] may always cause disturbances in the kingdom or even bring about the death of the king;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the propitiatory rites for the house as previously described.
But when they have reached a state of decay and have resorted to that pride by an improper path,
they become further endowed with excessive pride and the like according to the path described in the scriptures.
One should perform rites that bring victory and longevity, which always benefit the king;
however, one should not cause him to perform again any rite that has previously been exhausted by past actions and the like.
One should not perform [these] out of excessive delusion, for it would become a locus of all faults:
the retinue, the temple, the pedestal, the enclosure wall, and likewise the gateway. (11)
The image-shrines, pavilions, and assembly halls,
though already highly venerable from of old, were once again made even more auspicious through further ritual work.
Whether it has gone to the previously mentioned place or has again gone outside,
one should once more make it very firm as before and then perform the consecration with sprinkling.
If a limb of the images made of metal should become deficient,
one should fashion that limb as before and perform the installation correctly.
But when [the connection] above the throat is severed, one recites another [mantra], whether the severance occurs at the neck and so forth, or at the feet or the hands. (15)
With that very same worn-out iron, one should fashion an image as before;
however, that iron should specifically be buried in the ground for three years.
p. 408) Having subsequently melted [the image] in the fire, one should fashion the image again;
however, if it was made of clay and lacks color, one should fashion it again as before. || 17 ||
If the clay for the *kalka* cord, or even the clay itself, should become cracked, broken, or otherwise damaged,
that respective limb must be fashioned again, and the trident (*śūla*) likewise.
Whether it be made of wood or brick, the wise man should accept that which is free from defects such as cracks, and avoid that which is full of flaws.
If the linga or the pedestal is deficient, or if it is devoid of the [prescribed] lines,
the wise man should remove the linga and the pedestal and install them again as before.
One should place a worn-out liṅga, its pedestal, or the image itself into the ocean—
whether it be of Ṛṣi-origin or human-origin, or even one for which no temple was previously constructed.
One should construct a Śiva temple that surpasses previous structures in its materials and is nine stories high;
it may be designed with five halls, either externally, internally, or both.
One should not construct a foundation, a level ground, or especially a superior dwelling within the interior of a large enclosure wall that possesses a rampart. (23)
One should construct the *ālaya* (the central sanctuary) with its foundations diminished, or else outside the three triple-lines;
having gone to the exterior of the great boundary-line (*mahāmaryādā*), one should fashion the *ālaya*.
Thus, the supreme inner space has been described as it is thus conceived; likewise, the intermediate space is [located] either outside the great enclosure or as previously stated. 25.

Having brought about destruction, it specifically causes the ruin of the progeny of the performer, a great disease, and the destruction of the *kalahaṃsa*; it is accomplished here, of this there is no doubt. || 26 ||
On all sides, in the portions belonging to the remaining deities, a temple of Śiva should be constructed;
it brings victory and long life, and increases one's sons, grandsons, and progeny. (27)
In that very place where the mansion is to be constructed, facing either east or west, the best of architects, having first examined the fundamental site, should thus perform the planning.
O Brahmin, that which is provided with a retinue is situated between the medium and the superior;
however, that which is devoid of a retinue is designated as being between the inferior and the medium.
In this very way, O Brahmin, one may conceive of another deity in the abode [of that deity];
or one may worship another deity there, who has been worshipped in the primary temple. || 30 ||
The Ārṣaka is superior to the Pauṣa; the Vaigāṇava is better than the Ārṣa;
the Devika is superior to the Gāṇava; and the Svāyaṃbhuvam is better than that.
This is declared to be the "Field-Palace" (Kṣetra-harmya), which yields a fruit exceeding ten millionfold;
O best of the twice-born, that ritual should be performed by those seeking such fruit.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, the "Restoration of the Worn-out," in the *Aṃśumat* [section] of the *Kāśyapa*.
The external characteristics have been indicated; now hear that which is internal.
A wise person should properly cut the stone into a square shape. (1)
And where a stake is seen at the place where Takṣaka was cut down, one should know that to be the end of the fetus, provided it is examined with care. (2)
On a [ground] the color of madder, one should draw a frog; on yellow orpiment, a crab;
and on a yellowish-black ground, a snake with the colors of fireflies and honey. (3)
One should know that in a reddish-brown stone there is a mouse; in one with the luster of crystal, muttering [of mantras] is prescribed;
in a red circular stone, there is a scorpion of variegated color.
The *śaphara* [is used] on a black-and-variegated [surface], while the *indragopaka* resembles the *kiṃśuka* flower;
these [are applied] at the height of the *śaṅku*, which is divided into ninety-six and eight parts.

The wise one should [measure] each part as two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula) according to the proper method; the measurement of the height of the gnomon and its shadows [should be taken] to the south and further south.
Gain of wealth and loss of home, as well as the death of one's wife;
suffering, gain of wealth, death, happiness, and even sovereignty. (6)
One should know the sequence beginning with the circles; one should eliminate the pit in the center.
Likewise, one should avoid the central corner and the cord on both sides of the door.
Regarding fields, groves,
and houses, the procedure for the installation of wells is specifically prescribed for the southeast corner of a temple.
Alternatively, the site may be prepared in the field in accordance with the builder's desire;
it should be specially inspected from below and worshipped.
One should avoid those with faces turned sideways or facing downwards, and prefer one facing upwards;
one should also avoid those with gaps in their wings, the Riktā lunar days, and the Kṛṣṇa constellation.
One should avoid the *vyatīpāta*, *parigha*, and *vaidhṛti* yogas;
one should have [the image] carved on Wednesdays, Fridays, Thursdays, or Mondays. (11)
If a well is completed within ten days of a birth-impurity, one should perform the *puṇyāha* rite afterwards;
in this very manner, according to the prescribed rule, one should follow the sequence for the ritual installation of the well.
Indeed, these eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśvaras) have three eyes and four arms;
they are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and are equipped with an axe and a trident.
Red, white, blue, yellow, black, saffron, and resembling the glow of dawn or collyrium— these are the colors according to their sequence and measure.
One should worship [the deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin on the eastern petals and so forth;
moreover, the wise one should make the mouth of the weapons long.
The measurement from one finger-breadth up to the desired limit is prescribed for the "I-am-not" (nāham) mark;
however, the wise practitioner should ensure that it does not become a full fist. 16.
The natural movement of weapons is thus prescribed.
I shall describe the great worship of Śiva; listen, O you who were born from the Śara reeds!
One should worship Śiva in a liṅga, an image (bera), or likewise in another pedestal (pīṭha).
The partless (niṣkala) should be known as partless, and the whole (sakala) as having a whole form;
the best of those who know the ritual rules should fashion their pedestal (pīṭha) accordingly.
O Guha, one should especially construct the door in the east, the west, the south, or the north; however, the western door is the bestower of liberation.
The northern [direction] should be known as bestowing peace; the southern-facing one is victory.
That which is divine and human is between the south and north for men.
The self-born (Svāyambhū) is divine, while Bāṇa is the refuge of all the directions of the gods.
O Six-faced One! In this manner, one should indeed fashion the linga as the primary element, as well as the image (bera), whether it be of divine origin (daivika) or of sage origin (ārṣaka). || 6 ||
One should have it made either of stone, of metal, or indeed of brick;
for the sake of accomplishment, one made of brick is used, while that made of stone is supreme for bestowing liberation.

The iron-made [image] should be known as bestowing happiness, as well as the stone-made, whether mobile or immobile; likewise, there are those in standing posture, seated posture, on a vehicle, or in a dancing form. (8)

The standing posture (sthānaka) is for the sake of accomplishing all things, while the sitting posture (āsana) is known to bestow happiness; O Guha, the standing and sitting postures are [preferred], whereas the reclining posture (śayana) is considered tamasic.
For the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation, dancing in beautiful forms brings happiness;
listen now to the specific rules regarding standing and sitting postures during worship at the *liṅga*.
The Linga is known to be increasing, stationary, seated, or superior to Śiva;
whatever its activity may be, it is to be understood as Śiva—thus is its classification described.
While being consecrated, one should fashion either a *liṅga* or an image (*bera*);
or, by virtue of the *liṅga* and the image, one may cause a temple (*dhāma*) to be constructed. || 12 ||
(p. 413) The form consisting of conceptual construction has thus been described; now hear the form of meditative concentration (dhyāna):
it may have three eyes and four arms, or two eyes and two arms. || 13 ||
He may have one face, two faces, three faces, or four faces;
he may even be endowed with five faces, or indeed a hundred thousand.
In this very manner, [the number] from two hundred up to one thousand is prescribed;
it may be one quarter, two quarters, three quarters, or even the full thousand.
White in color, red, and likewise dark-complexioned;
blue in color and black—thus the colors are prescribed.
Or he may have matted locks with hair standing upright, or his matted locks may be tawny;
he may be armed with a serpent and a sword, or even armed with a trident and a noose.
Whether holding a hammer and a spear as weapons, or even having all types of weapons in hand,
or even being without any weapon at all— one should cause [the image] to be made in this very manner.
Whether bearing all weapons or even with hands weaponless,
he saw the Ganges at the tip of his matted locks, appearing indeed in a threefold form.
Alternatively, one may adorn the crown with the full moon;
or one should fashion Mahāśiva as half-Hari and half-Girijā.
On the right side is the half-form of Hari, and on the left side is the half-woman (Ardhanārī);
on the left is the half-form of Girijā, and on the right is the form of Rudra.
One should worship Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, Dhanada, or Vijaya, who subdues hostile kings and bestows all dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Gaurī, Skanda, or even the Bull may also be placed on the right and left of the central seat;
or one may install them as before. Thus, it is considered to be of two kinds. (23)
Furthermore, one should have either a *sakala-liṅga* or a *kevala-liṅga* fashioned;
if their installation is through union (*yoga-pratiṣṭhā*), the *sakala* type should be supported by a wall.
O child! One should install either a Bāṇa-linga or a human-made linga in the center of the temple, or one should worship a mobile linga (cala-liṅga) in the presence of Śiva.
The *bāṇa* [liṅga], the jewel-liṅga, or the crystal one, as well as the mobile [liṅga],
may extend to the edge of a cloth-band, to the neck, to the end of the sacrificial fire-pit, or to the tip of the *kumuda* [pedestal].
One should place the water-outlet at the boundary of that [tank], or the pipe itself; I shall now describe the location for the pipe, whether in the east or in the north. (27)
One should likewise cause the *pratibandha*, *padmabandha*, or even the *pādabandha* to be performed through the path of power (*śaktimārga*) alone. || 28 ||
One should construct [the temple] according to one's preference for caste, desire, or conceptual design, whether it be Nāgara, Drāviḍa, or Vesara, with four times the length [of its width]. (29)
Whether circular, oval, or even in the shape of an assembly hall (sabhā),
a structure that is twice its width in height is called a *harmya*.
Whether joined with a single trunk, or even joined with two divine trunks;
or even devoid of a trunk, or even devoid of a vehicle. || 31 ||
He may be mounted upon a lion, or mounted upon a bull, or even mounted upon a spirit;
he may be devoid of directional forms, or likewise possess these very forms.
The gods, the dānavas, the yakṣas, the apsarases, and likewise the ṛṣis [were there],
