joined with various weapons and crowded with beings of various origins.
O Six-faced One! In this very manner, one should fashion the abode; the teacher [should prepare] the seat according to the measurement that is half the height of the image.
The pedestal for worship should be made with a measurement of seven units;
it should be provided with three girdles and endowed with eight petals. || 35 ||
One should likewise fashion what is known as the pedestal for the image (arcāpīṭha);
this is declared to be the form of the image (arcārūpa), yet it does not possess a portion for worship. || 36 ||
The invocation and dismissal are not mentioned, nor is there any distinction in the worship;
one should perform the invocation and dismissal at every juncture of the worship.
O child, one should perform worship especially on every day, every fortnight, every month, and every year, as well as during each of the Yugas.
One should worship the God, the Lord of Gods, with Vedic and Tantric mantras according to the path taught in this Tantra; one should not perform it by means of other tantras.
One should draw a wheel in the shape of a chariot, endowed with nine parts:
four sets of chariot-wheels and two pins therein.

At the front, there are two; likewise, on the pedestal, the constellation of the Lord and the Sun; the chariot-wheel and three others are in the east; and likewise, three constellations are on the stake.
Two cords, two wheel-rims, and a pin; then a rear wheel-rim and a pedestal—one should arrange these as the sense-organs in due order. (3)
In these locations of the constellations, one should place three [stanzas] each;
in the location of Tvak, the Śāsti and Mandārā are situated there, bestowing destruction.
If the chariot wheel is situated in the directions of Kadhara, Sūnu, Śani, or Āhvaya,
then that part of the chariot wheel will be broken upon the earth.

If the Sun and the others are in the *kīlaka* yoga, whether there be two planets or even three, and they have their rays eclipsed by the Sun and are in their signs of debilitation (*nīca*), one should predict his defeat.
If the cord is in a state of destruction, there is the ruin of the cord; if it is on a seat (pīṭha), there is the destruction of the deity.
When [the cord] is diminished, the results are certain in conjunction with the Moon, depending on whether it is situated in a debilitated, inimical, or ignorant sign.
If Venus or Mercury is situated in a succedent (paṇaphara) sign, or even in a mutable (āpoklima) sign, one should know that a chariot wheel will be found, splitting wood; of this there is no doubt.
When the center of the wheel is in a *paṇaphara* house and is aspected by Saturn and Mars, it destroys a man with a chariot wheel broken by ropes; of this there is no doubt.

During festivals, at the commencement of a journey, and likewise during the installation of a fixed image; at the mounting of a chariot and the hoisting of a banner, one should act when the moon is in a movable sign or in both types of signs (movable and fixed). || 10 ||

If there is a retrograde planet in the fourth, eighth, or twelfth house, or if its own division (varga) is also the ascendant, it causes the destruction of wealth even for one who remains diligent at the gateway. || 11 ||
In that [chart], the signs of Cancer, Capricorn, and Libra are the heads of the movable signs; however, when Saturn is situated in Sagittarius or Pisces, all malefic planets become benefics. || 12 ||
If the Moon is in an even sign (Apoklima), and Jupiter and Venus are likewise in a quadrant, there shall be journeys by chariot; provided that Mercury is in the eighth or the fifth house. (12)
If the eighth house from the ascendant of the journey (yātrālagna) is a malefic trine (naidhana), that is, the fifth or ninth house,
and if the Moon, Sun, Mars, Saturn, or others are situated there, or if Jupiter is pierced by Rāhu’s tail (rāhudaṇḍa) or Ketu, the doer suffers loss of sons, wife, and wealth.
When malefic planets are situated in the three, sixth, and eleventh houses from the ascendant and other such positions, and are joined by benefics,
one quickly mounts that chariot like the sun in the autumn season.
If the lord of the ascendant is devoid of strength, situated in the eighth house, and aspected by or conjoined with malefics;

if the Sun is in the eighth house from the ascendant, the banners fall. If Saturn is conjoined with the Vipratichakra yoga-killing weapon (the *kīla*), and Rāhu is likewise conjoined [with it], [the same occurs].
If there is a planet situated in the ninth house (Chidya), there will likewise be a residence on the ground of a chariot-lord.
If the lord of the ninth house (rathaprayāṇalagneśa) is the lord of the tenth house (cakreśa) and is conjoined with a malefic planet,
the wheel falls upon the ground and is shattered along with its axle-pin.
When Jupiter is strong in a trine and endowed with strength in a quadrant,
the chariot arrives swiftly, like the sun in the autumn season.
At the centers of the chariot's movement, Ravi, Āhva,
and Bhānuja strike with ropes, stakes, and other means, and that wheel shall fall to the earth.
When the Sun rises during the march and its son [Saturn] is at the setting point,
it quickly destroys that army with stakes and ropes.
Just as a chariot wheel does not sink into the earth like a palace, so too, when the Sun is strong and situated in a quadrant (*kendram*), whom would the Lord not reach? (20)
When Mercury is weak and situated in a quadrant, or when the lord is in a trine, and the malefic planets are located in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses, the chariot proceeds perfectly. (21)
When a malefic planet is in a trine or an angle and there is an *udaya* (emergence) of a chariot procession,
the performer meets with death and he destroys the kingdom.
And that wheel, together with the chariot and the rope, was destroyed. || 23 ||

A chariot procession is desired when [the Moon] is in dual signs; it is middling when it is in fixed signs, provided that malefic planets are situated in angles or trines and benefic planets are in the sixth or twelfth houses.
If [the Moon] is aspected by malefics but freed from the aspects of benefics, there will be travel by chariot after a long time;
provided that Saturn is situated in a quadrant or a trine, yet occupies the twelfth or eighth house.
Within three days, and so forth, one should predict the breaking of the chariot;
listen, O gentle one, when the Moon is in a quadrant (kendram) and Jupiter is in a trine (koṇa), being aspected by Mercury. || 26 ||
When the journey is undertaken at the Caralagna, it lasts for thirteen ghaṭikās;
if malefic planets are in the twelfth and ninth houses, and the Lagna is occupied by a malefic aspected by a benefic. (27)
If a benefic planet occupies the second house at midday, there is travel by chariot; if Rāhu is joined with the Ascendant and Saturn is in the seventh house, it is the same. || 28 ||
If the *kīlaka* yoga is conjoined with a malefic planet, a breakdown of the chariot occurs here; likewise when the Sun is on the *pīṭha*, or when Mars is on the *rathāṅga*. (29)
If the cord is on a gentle pin, the journey by chariot will take a long time;
however, if the Moon is worshipped on a pedestal, the journey by chariot will be immediate.
If the left wheel is the Moon and the right wheel is the Sun, and they are aspected by benefics;
I shall now describe the *bali-pīṭha*; there are four external seats (*pīṭhas*).
When the seat is established in the east, it is celebrated as *Śrīkara*. (1)
When the seat is placed in the south, it is known as Śrīviśāla;
when the seat is placed in the west, it is celebrated as Śrībhadra. || 2 ||
The pedestal established in the north is known as Śrīnivāsa;
it was for the prosperity of the Brāhmaṇas during the installation of Śrīkara in the east.
For the prosperity of the Kṣatriyas during the installation of Śrī Viśāla,
and for the great increase of the Vaiśyas during the installation of Śrī Bhadra.
For the installation of Śrīnivāsa and for the prosperity of the Śūdras,
in this very manner, [the rite should be performed] especially at the four gates.
Śrī, Sarasvatī, Brāhmī, and Sāvitrī are likewise [the deities] of the presiding lords of the seats (pīṭha), starting from the east and so forth, in due order. || 6 ||
In the *Suprabheda*, [this is] the definition of the sacrificial pedestal (*bali-pīṭha*).
420) In five parts of the inner sanctum (garbhageha), the height of the fourfold structure (catuṣka) is said to be excellent when it occupies four parts,
middling when it occupies three parts, and inferior when it is remembered as occupying two parts.
The best [height] is equal to the height of the door; the middling is one-third of that;
and the lowest should be known as half the height of the door. Its width should be equal to its height.
Then, having well divided the height into nineteen parts, the height of the plinth (upānaka) shall be one part,
and the base-moulding (jagatī) shall consist of four parts.
The *kumuda* should occupy three parts; above that, a fillet (*paṭṭikā*) should be one part.
One should make the corner (*karṇa*) with three parts, and the upper fillet with just one part.
The great fillet (mahāpaṭṭikā) is two parts; the height of the petals is three parts, consisting of eight petals;
and the pericarp (karṇikā) is one part—this is declared to be the excellent height.

I shall describe the entrance and exit, along with the proportions for their width and height: the entire portion (upāna) shall consist of twenty-four parts, and likewise the jagatī of fourteen parts.
One should know that the *kumuda* is twelve parts, the *paṭṭikā* likewise ten parts,
the width of the neck eight parts, and the upper *paṭṭikā* ten parts.
One should make the great band twelve parts wide, the extent of the eight petals ten parts,
and the square pedestal as desired, excluding the lotus petals; then,
at the conclusion of the installation, one should worship these especially.
The supreme guide should perform [the rite] according to the procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*);
the offering to the retinue (*parivārabali*) is performed in the *kāraṇa* [vessel].
The height of the door from the base (mūladhāman) should be equal to the width of the pedestal for the best [type of temple];
one-third of that is declared the medium, and half the height of the door is the smallest.
The width of the pure entrance (śuddhadvāra) is called the inferior pedestal (pīṭha);
twice that is declared the middling, and thrice that is called the superior. || 2 ||
Alternatively, the lowest [pedestal] is said to have a width of one cubit;
the middle is declared to be two cubits, and the best is said to be three cubits.
Having made it as high as its width, [the height] should be twenty-eight [parts];
the height of the base (upāna) should be two parts, and the plinth (jagatī) should be six parts.

The height of the *kumuda* (pedestal) is one part of the *bhūta* (twenty-five parts); the *kaṃpa* (projection) is said to be one part; the measurement of the *karṇa* (ear/ornament) is four parts, and the upper *kaṃpa* is one part of Śiva (eleven parts).
The portion for the two great bands (mahāpaṭṭī) should be two parts, or specifically two parts;
the height of the lotus (padmatuṅga) should be four parts, and the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be two parts.
Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be one-third [of the lotus],
the height of the lotus (padma) should be five parts, and the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) should be two parts.
The height of the pedestal (upāna) should be one part according to the Śiva-proportion; the remainder is exactly as before.
This is the characteristic of the small pedestal (kṣudrapīṭha).
Within the inner circle, however, it may be supported by a wall or otherwise.
The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) should be constructed with a height equal to the width of a kuśa finger;
the lowest is twice that, the middle is three times that, and the highest is the most elevated.
One should fashion the entire pedestal as either four-cornered or circular;
its height should be equal to its width, or it may be three-quarters or even half [of that]. (10)
One should fashion it with three girdles, or even two;
it may be provided with a single girdle, topped with a lotus.
One should construct a lotus-seat (padmapīṭha) that is lotus-shaped and possesses a pericarp;
there should be a nine-seat arrangement for the Mothers, with three seats dedicated to Jyeṣṭhā.
For others, it may be thus for just one; and for Caṇḍeśa likewise, there is a sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭhaka) for Indra and the other [deities] within the area of the inner maṇḍala.
One should establish them in due order outside the base of the pavilion,
equal to or double the radius of the inner mandala.
The knower of ritual procedures should arrange the outer enclosure outside the inner star;
in its central portion, he should place the eight attendants.
One should install [the deities] beginning with Vṛṣa and ending with Caṇḍa in the eight directions;
for each, a width and length of five cubits is prescribed.
It may be increased by one-fourth, or by one-fifth, or indeed by one-third; it may also be doubled, or increased by half of five (i.e., two and a half times). || 17 ||
For the gate-towers (gopuras), the length is prescribed as being equal to [the width], double that, double plus a quarter, or half of double.
The width of the palace is here called the *daṇḍa*;
starting from the base structure, it is measured in units of six or eight *daṇḍas*.
One should fashion the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) with ten or twelve staffs, ending with the staff of Manu, or even with sixteen or eighteen. (20)
Alternatively, the location for the pedestal (pīṭha) is prescribed in another manner:
in a temple with three halls, or in one with four or five halls, specifically in the middle hall.
The great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) should be constructed; its characteristic is now stated:
the width of the excellent pedestal should be equal to the height of the door of the primary sanctuary (mūladhāma). || 22 ||

The middle [measurement] is said to be three-quarters of the height of the door, while the smallest is half the height of the door; the width of the base (pīṭha) for a plain door is the smallest [of these].
A height of two cubits is declared to be middling, while three cubits is said to be the best;
having made the height equal to its width, it should be twenty-eight [units].
The height of the upāna should be two parts, and the jagati should be six parts;
the height of the kumuda should be five parts, and the kampam is said to be one part.
The ear-measure should be one-fourth [of the width], while the upper projection (ūrdhvakaṃpa) is one-eighth;
the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) is three parts, or specifically two parts.

The portion of the Vedas (four parts) shall be the lotus-tuft (padmatunga), while the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) shall be two parts. The height of the upāna (base-molding) shall be one part of Śiva (one part), and the elevation of the pericarp (karṇikā) shall be two parts.
Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be one-third [of the lotus];
the height of the lotus itself should be five parts, and the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) should be two parts.
The height of the pedestal (upāna) should be one part of Śiva; the remainder is exactly as before.
Or else, O Brahmin, make the elevation of the pedestal (pīṭhodaya) equal to the surface of the earth (dharātala).

(424) Above that, the measurement of the lotus is said to be one-ninth of the height of the pedestal (pīṭha). One should perform the entry and exit according to the method prescribed for the base (adhiṣṭhāna). || 30 ||
In the case of Padmatārā, the width of the pericarp should be one-fourth or one-fifth of the [total] extent;
the temple of the pedestal (pīṭha) may be quadrangular, circular, or even octagonal.
Alternatively, it should be made of eight petals; from that [mandala] comes the lotus of the mandala.
It may be made of metal, stone, or even of brick.
Its interior was lined with plaster and adorned with various colorful paintings;
it was further embellished with figures of spirits, sea-monsters, serpents, and bulls. || 33 ||
One should adorn it with various colors and with gold and silver ornaments; this should be done upon the extent of the pedestal, divided into six, seven, eight, or nine parts.
One should make the height of its subsidiary pedestal (upapīṭha) as previously described for the pedestal;
above that, however, is the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha), endowed with the emergence as previously stated.
O best of the twice-born! A pedestal may be constructed even without a secondary pedestal (upapīṭha).
Āmoda should be placed on the eastern petal, and Pramoda on the petal in the southern direction.
He faces forward toward the west and likewise has his back turned toward the north;
he is free from obstacles in the direction of the Lord (the northeast), while the creator of obstacles resides in the southeast.
The Sāttvika [form] is in the south-western quarter, the Rājasa in the north-west corner,
and the Tāmasa, having the form of Nīlarudra, is in the center of the pericarp.

O best of the twice-born! That great seat (mahāpīṭha), which consists of the earth, the atmosphere, and heaven, and which is composed of the qualities of all beings, is said to be the soul of all things.
(425) Regarding a palace facing west, I shall state a slight variation:
one should place Kumāra in the position of Vṛṣa, and Vṛṣabha in the position of Kaumāra. || 40 ||
In the Vāruṇa [direction], however, there is a great seat (mahāpīṭha); one should perform the remainder as previously described.
The procedure for the retinue has been declared; hereafter follows the characteristics of the liṅga.
Betel nut, a bamboo staff, sandalwood, or even khadira wood;
campaka, devadāru, clusters of jasmine, and bilva. (42)
It should be straight, free from blemishes, and devoid of holes caused by worms;
it should be level with the temple or even aligned with the neck of the temple.
The height of the *daṇḍa* is said to be equal to the *vṛṣasthala*, or equal to the height of the *gopura*, or extending up to two or three stories.
Betel nut, nālika, and palmyra; campaka, bilva, and sandalwood; aśvattha, khadira, nyagrodha, sāra, and tṛṇiṇī. || 45 ||
The Palāśa, the Nṛpasāra, likewise the Bilvasāra,
and the Madhūka-sāra tree— these are said here to be suitable for the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa).

The measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) is said to extend from the end of the bull-base (vṛṣasthala) to the neck (grīvā) and ending at the gate-tower (gopura); this is here called the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa).
The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) should have that same measurement, with its height equal to that of the pericarp (karṇikā);
one should install the sacrificial pedestal between the temple and the gateway (gopura). || 48 ||
One should install the vehicle, the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), and the flagstaff pedestal (dhvajapīṭha).
The flagstaff is considered to be of two kinds: large and small, and it should be erected high. (49)
The small temple, its height, and the flagstaff are thus remembered;
[the measurements extend] to the end of the stūpa, the end of the spire, the end of the nose (nasikā), and the end of the neck (gala). || 50 ||
The height at the end of the prastara should be two cubits with an additional daṇḍa;
it may then be reduced by half a cubit and a quarter, ending at one cubit. || 51 ||
Thus the procedure for the long [temple] has been declared; beyond that, however, is the lotus-shaped [temple], whose width is equal to the width of the main temple or three-quarters of it. (52)

The raising of the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) is declared; its measurement is desired according to the path [of the site], extending from the eastern to the western end of the gateway (gopura), or equal to the palace (prāsāda). 53.
The Paiśāca-pīṭha is placed below, occupying half the temple's height and one-third of its width;
it may measure three, five, seven, or up to nine cubits.
The height [of the base] is ten parts; the gajāsara is three-sevenths;
the height of the padma is one part; the kampa is one part; and the ambuja is one part.

The *kumuda* (fillet) is thus three parts; the upper *padma* (lotus) is one part of Śiva; the *madhya-kampa-padma* (middle-recessed lotus) is said to be one part; and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is declared to be four parts. || 56 ||
The portion for the *kampa* (projection) should be made, and the lotus-portion (*padmāṃśa*) should be a triple band (*paṭṭikā*).
The central part is a single-petaled lotus, with the *kampa* portion being the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
The fifth lotus, however, is prescribed as having three parts;
it may be a wheel, or a trident, or even half of a temple.
The height of the weapon should be one-eighth less than three-quarters of the [main] height;
the determination of measurement is desired to range from one cubit up to nine cubits. (59)
Thus, O master who has reached the further shore of the scriptures, the retinues have been described:
eight for Nandā, eight for Paṅkti, nine for Aṣṭā, and twenty for Kumbha; and [the measurements] from the top of the head to the neck-base are as follows.

The Nārāyaṇya style, which consists of a single story (ekabhūma) extending from the base of the pillars to the top of the stūpa, is the primary [type], with its proportions reduced by one-quarter at the beginning and so forth.
There are four types: the vehicle, the standing posture, the reclining posture, and the sitting posture;
namely, the standing posture of the Sages (ārṣaka) and the sitting posture of the Self-born (svāyaṃbhuva).
The human [bed] is made of arrows, the Rākṣasa of Gāṇava wood, and the Devika is said to be made of Yānaka wood; such is the description of their characteristics.
The standing posture is said to be square, while the sitting posture is perfectly circular; the vehicle posture is said to be triangular, and the reclining posture should be octagonal.
The nature of the pedestal (pīṭha) is likewise described by these characteristics:
Gaurī is seated upon a circular pedestal, while Bhadrā has a square pedestal as her seat. (64)
The bed, the lotus-seat, and the seat of offerings are here called the powers (śaktis) of the Lord;
likewise, Āmoda, Pramoda, Pramukha, and Vimukha [are the attendants]. (65)
May those deities presiding over the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), who create obstacles, be free from obstruction.
[The structure] is elevated from its base to the pinnacle (stūpī), extending outward from the width of the pillar.
Alternatively, the height of the vimānas may extend up to the pinnacle;
[this applies to] the offering deities (balidevatās).
But that of Bhava and others is divine, while that of Indra and others is human. || 67 ||

For the Bhūtas and others, it is self-manifested (svayambhūta); for the Ṛṣis, it is the Ārṣaka; for the Vasus, it is the Parivāraka; but in the case of Bāṇaliṅga, it belongs to the Vidyeśvaras and is Daivika.
The Yakṣas and others, as well as the Rākṣasas, are proclaimed to be the deities of the bali offerings.
Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, and Nīlalohita [are the forms of Śiva]. (69)
Likewise, there are eight forms, namely Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva;
and [the colors] yellow, saffron, black, reddish-brown, and the luster of crushed collyrium.
Blue, white, and likewise red are the colors of the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti);
all have four arms, granting the gestures of fearlessness and boons, and holding a noose and a goad.
They have three eyes, one face, and two feet, and they wear anklets;
endowed with matted hair and crowns, they are proclaimed to be the very forms of the deity.
Between one pillar and another, a place for the flagstaff (dhvaja) is prescribed; or else, one should begin the main temple according to the measurement of the staff.
By increasing the number of staffs by two, three, or more, one reaches five, seven, nine, up to eleven, thirteen Rudras, or fifteen, seventeen, or twenty-one. (74)
The measurement of the staff (daṇḍa) is proclaimed to be nineteen [units];
it is two-fifths when divided into five parts, and three-sevenths when divided into seven parts.
In a ninefold division, the walls are prescribed as four parts; if the front [entrance] is of greater width, it should be made according to beauty and according to one's preference. (76)

Thus it has been taught in many ways; one should, however, arrange it according to one's preference, starting from the middle of the inner mandala, the hall, and so forth, up to the central gateway (gopura). || 77 ||
Even though there are nine, five, or one staffs in the four cardinal directions,
the principal ones are considered to be the banners located in their respective positions, equal in number to those [staffs].
May there be auspiciousness.

In the cavity of the pedestal, one should fashion a vulva-shaped [receptacle] in the center of the womb, complete with its characteristic features and with its tip pointing upward; alternatively, it is called a cavity.
The form of the vulva (bhaga) is described as being in the center of the womb (yoni), arranged sequentially from below to above;
likewise, the arrow, the jewel, and so forth, constitute the characteristics of the Goddess’s seat (pīṭha).
In the middle of the aperture, one should draw the seat of Lakṣmī in the shape of a vulva with its tip pointing upward;
at the base of that very aperture, one should draw a bee using two parts.
One should bind the portion for the emergence of the pedestal (pīṭha), one part consisting of gems,
and ten parts joined with sand, in five portions respectively.
One-sixteenth part of the pūjāṃśa is prescribed as the height;
that same measure is the width of the pedestal (pada), and it is likewise called the eight-fold bond (aṣṭabandha).
Just as when a jar is broken, the space within it dissolves into the [great] space, so too [the deity] is absorbed;
however, an aged image should not be discarded, for one that has been worshipped would otherwise become fruitless. (84)
There is no seeing, no service, no worship, and no salutation;
one who performs worship out of delusion shall go to his death. (85)

When the god has grown old and is created again by the Eastern Goddess as her husband, he should be united with those same goddesses once more; thus one should create him again, inseparable from them.
One should not perform a marriage ceremony, but should worship the existing deity;
when the linga has become worn out and is fashioned anew, the Lord remains established in the yoga of the original [site].
Likewise, one should join Bhogavīra with the eastern [direction], and then create another;
furthermore, no marriage should be performed while worshipping these deities.
If the *liṅga* has become decayed, one should discard only the *liṅga*;
if the pedestal (*pīṭha*) has become decayed, one should discard only the pedestal. || 89 ||
One should abandon the pedestal of the liṅga when it has become worn out to the same extent as the liṅga-piṇḍikā;
likewise, having joined a Bhogavīra [liṅga] from the east, one should create another that is not different.
Having understood that the *liṅga* is of four kinds as prescribed by the scriptures— namely, the stationary (*sthāvaram*),
the divine (*daivikam*), the ṛṣi-related (*ārṣakam*), and likewise the collective (*gāṇavam*) and the human (*mānuṣam*)— [one should worship it].
Among the four types of divisions, hear the characteristic of the divine; this is the divine liṅga.
The liṅga shall be long in shape and endowed with depressions and elevations. || 92 ||
The liṅga is joined with lines and hollows, elevated at the mouth by the extent of the star (tārā),
shaped like a mountain peak, with a broad top and a crest-point in front.
With both hands joined in the shape of a casket (saṃpuṭākāra), devoid of the sacred thread (brahmasūtra)—a liṅga endowed with these characteristics is called divine (daivika). || 94 ||
This is the characteristic mark of the Ṛṣis.
The base of the liṅga should be thick, and likewise its tip;
however, among the liṅgas, that which is thick in the middle has the shape of a coconut fruit.
Having the shape of a plantain fruit or the shape of a bilva fruit,
the liṅga known as ārṣaka is declared to be devoid of the brahmasūtra.
The Gaṇa-liṅga.
It has the shape of a *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit, the form of a *mātuluṅga* fruit, the shape of an *urvāruka* fruit, and the form of a *kapittha* fruit. || 97 ||
The Gāṇava-liṅga is said to have the appearance of a palm fruit;
it is the Mānuṣa-liṅga.
Or the measurement of the door, or the measurement of the womb, or even the measurement of the cubit. || 98 ||
Or it may have its height shaped like an umbrella according to the measurements prescribed in the treatises on architecture;
it should be of a single color, very smooth, and provided with the Brahma-thread (the central vertical line).
An image endowed with these characteristics is said to be human;
now I shall specifically describe how one should worship Śivarātri. 100.
In the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages— having worshipped [the deity] in each respective age— one should perform the sacrifice to Guha when the Kṛta age has arrived.
In the Tretā age one should worship with Vighnarāja, and in the Dvāpara age with Acyuta;
in the Kali age, Hara is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and the sages. (102)
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, on the second day of Phālguna, on the thirteenth day of Caitra, and on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha; 103.
One should worship on the third day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, on the eighth day of Āṣāḍha,
on the twelfth day of Śrāvaṇa, and on the fifth day of Pūrvāṣāḍha.

On the seventh day of the month of Tulā, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight when the moon is in Kṛttikā, on the twelfth day of the month of Bhādrapada, and on the seventh day of the month of Puṣya. (105)
Thus, for one who observes the fast on Śivarātri for a year,
the fruit of that Śivarātri is obtained on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha.
In a single month, however, there may be two fortnights; in such a case, the night is considered superior to the lunar day.
By worshipping Śiva during that night, a man obtains its full fruit. || 107 ||
In this way, the side-eye should be level; one should worship Śiva during the first watch of the night.
Therefore, with every effort, one should especially do so throughout the entire night.
If the night is the longer part [of the lunar day], the worship of Śiva is prescribed;
on that night it shall be Śivarātri, and there is indeed the presence of the God. (109)
But the night is devoid of its [proper] half and likewise abounds in defects;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform it throughout every month in due order. || 110 ||
But at the conclusion of the constant practice, one should observe Śivarātri;
specifically, during each watch of the night, one should perform the worship of Śiva with particular distinction.
Neither on the seventh day, nor on the fifth day, nor even on the third day should the offering of sprouts be performed;
rather, one should offer the sprouts afterwards, in accordance with the previously mentioned procedure. (112)
On the day prior to that, one should then purify the pavilion;
having worshipped it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then tie the protective thread (kautuka).
Having worshipped the bilva leaf together with all types of fragrances, the wise man should wrap it in a cloth; this is the consecration (adhivāsana) of the bilva leaf.
At the clear dawn, the wise preceptor should perform his bath;
he should perform the libation in the forenoon and the circumambulation at midday. (115)
Having performed worship in the evening, one should likewise observe the vow;
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras should do so while observing a fast. (116)
For all twice-born ones who are devotees of Śiva, for all living beings as well, and likewise for all women, fasting is prescribed in the same manner. (117)
One should accomplish all tasks with diligent effort while not sleeping;
likewise, one shall obtain whatever fruit, every accomplishment, and even that which is desired.
It bestows long life, spiritual success, and likewise complete liberation;
though one may have fasted on inauspicious days, one becomes most auspicious in a future birth. (119)
Whether one who observes the fast is without a wife or is again accompanied by a wife,
the desired fruit of one's cherished wishes is attained through fasting on Śivarātri.
If one sleeps during the fast, the fruit is diminished; if one is devoid of sleep [during the day], that fruit is lost.
Therefore, with every effort, one should observe the fast without sleeping.
The preceptor should perform the worship together with Brahmins and sages who are experts in the four Vedas—Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan—as well as in the Pratiyāmaka. || 12 ||
One should first worship Vighneśa, and after that, the worship of the Sun;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains, one should then cause the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
In the first [stage] there should be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); in the second, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta);
in the third, bathing with water; and in the fourth, the essence of sugarcane.
The supreme guide should perform worship with particular distinction during each watch;
however, for the first watch, it is prescribed that there be one hundred and eight ablutions.
In the second [rite], the ceremonial bath is prescribed with fifty jars;
in the third, the ceremonial bath likewise consists of twenty-five in number.
In the fourth [watch], one should perform the ceremonial bath and worship with a new water-pot;
the wise person should especially cause the bathing to be performed during every watch.
Having established [the deity] during the first watch of the night, one should worship with bilva leaves;
in the second [watch], with lotus flowers; and in the third, with jasmine flowers.
Having worshipped with *nandyāvarta* designs, one should worship the four watches;
one should perform the worship at the four junctions of the day, accompanied by *bilva* leaves.
On the first day, there should be food made of mung beans; on the second, milk-rice;
on the third, kṛsara rice; and on the fourth, pure rice.
One should worship the Guardian of the Field with particular distinction during each watch;
one should perform the bali-offering and oblation with particular distinction during each watch. || 131 ||
One should worship the guide there with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule, one is glorified in the world of Śiva on a radiant and blazing pedestal composed of the sun, moon, and fire.

I perpetually bow in my mind to her whose fame is ever-praiseworthy, who holds in her own hand the goad, the noose, the arrow, and the sugarcane bow, who wears the crescent moon as a crest-ornament, and who possesses three eyes. 133.
The earth is the house; the lotus with divine petals has eight leaves; the worlds are the hexagon, the decagon, and the octagon;
within is the triangle; this is the primordial central seat.
O Mother, I remember all of that as your very form.
I worship Śivā, who possesses the luster of the orb of the rising sun, who has four arms and three eyes,
and who holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows.
May there be auspiciousness.
